## silent failure

*2016-08-02 to 2016-08-15 · 31 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/silent.20failure/with/10441)*

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 13:43 UTC

One of my users just reported that every time they have sent messages since the 29th the messages have not gone through and there has been no indication in the desktop app of the failure. Could this be something to do with web socket for sending messages?

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 13:44 UTC

The user was using the Old (non-electron) desktop app on a Mac running ElCap

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 18:01 UTC

I'm curious to hear more about this situation, since it seems somewhat surprising

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 18:02 UTC

I assume by "no indication", they mean that the timestamps correctly didn't appear (which is how Zulip indicates whether a message has actually been delivered), but that the attempt to send didn't explicitly fail (which causes Zulip to display a red failure notice with a retry button)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 18:03 UTC

If that's the case, then it sounds like indeed there was a problem with the websockets system failing but not producing a visible error

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 23:53 UTC

the data that I have is that the user was using the Desktop app and logged in on the 29th and had been sending messages from mid day on the 29th until today around 10 am

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 23:54 UTC

hmm

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 23:54 UTC

they been receiving messages and attempting to send messages but they appeared in the UI without the red unsent message

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 23:55 UTC

my best guess at this point is something to do with not processing websocket 302s properly

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 23:55 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 23:56 UTC

Ahh, interesting.  So probably their client was just completely offline from the perspective of the serve

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 23:56 UTC

That last data point is interesting, is that we don't use websockets at all for the code paths that handler your not being authenticated

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 23:57 UTC

Was he by any chance using a narrow window?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 23:57 UTC

One annoying problem we have right now is that network errors only show up in the right ("users") sidebar, which is hidden if your window is narrow

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 23:57 UTC

by narrow window you mean px width rather than narrowing the view of the content with the search box?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 23:58 UTC

yes

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 23:58 UTC

i dont know, i will drop them a note to check

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 23:58 UTC

So it could be that the dominant problem here is that those errors really should be put somewhere smarter

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-02 23:58 UTC

I'll open an issue about that regardless, it's kinda unacceptable whether or not it was the problem in this case :)

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 23:59 UTC

a similar issue occured using Safari on an ElCap Mac when the user's vpn dropped resulting in 2 messages being lost

**Tim April** · 2016-08-02 23:59 UTC

I think that is a similar loss just in a shorter time window

## css media settings

*2016-08-03 to 2016-08-05 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/css.20media.20settings/with/10983)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-03 19:18 UTC

Does anybody have experience from other projects on how best to organize `@media` settings in your CSS?  I'm thinking about this in terms of ease-of-development, responsive web design (particularly mobile), and accessibility.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 13:59 UTC

yes

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 13:59 UTC

We have some in Zulip, but we weren't necessarily methodical about organizing where we put them, so they're mostly at the bottom of `zulip.css`.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 14:01 UTC

We've talked about splitting out `@media.css` as kind of a first step toward getting more organized, but we don't really have a finalized roadmap of how our CSS should be organized across different components, media types, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 14:41 UTC

**Akash** · 2016-08-05 14:43 UTC

Cool. Let's go with it for now.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 14:43 UTC

## css

*2016-08-05 to 2017-06-14 · 50 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/css/with/11502)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 20:47 UTC

So I have been digging into CSS reorganization a bit, and I have some thoughts.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 20:49 UTC

I'll start with some fairly non-controversial stuff.  We had pretty good consensus to extract media.css, so that's now on master.  There are also parts of the CSS that are so obviously related to a particular component, that I think they should be pulled out.  A good example is `message_failed`, which is basically a heavily animated spinner for when your messages don't hit the server.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 20:50 UTC

But we're still left with about 1500 declarations in zulip.css, and as I started to figure out how to divvy those up, I'm starting to think we really want to divide our css up by function, not by component.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 20:52 UTC

Somewhere close to 50% of our CSS is related specifically to alignment, which is kind of a huge deal for our app, since we're very oriented to a single-page workflow, and real estate is scarce.  So we have a lot of fiddly margin/padding code, and the CSS reflects the fact that our component's geometries are couple together.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 20:53 UTC

So I'm thinking a major broad stroke that we take to break down our CSS is to divide it into two concerns:
- alignment/positioning
- formatting/color/font style, etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 20:55 UTC

Just to make sure I understand, for alignment/positioning, how does that break down between e.g. "the arrangement for the left sidebar" vs. "how the panes of the app are configured"?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 20:57 UTC

I am using alignment and positioning as vague synonyms.  Basically, we have a bunch of CSS code that determines where things are (float, etc.) and how big they are (height/width/margin/padding), and there are often dependencies between siblings.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:01 UTC

For whatever reason we have lots of duplication between declarations:

```
$ grep height static/styles/zulip.css | grep px | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -7
   8     height: 40px;
   6     line-height: 18px;
   5     line-height: 17px;
   4    height: 0px;
   4     height: 25px;
   4     height: 20px;
   4     height: 0px;
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:02 UTC

I see

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:02 UTC

It seems like a lot of the alignment/positioning stuff we have can be divided into the 3 major panes of the app (left, center, right)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:02 UTC

Do you think trying to refactor the main zulip.css into those pieces would make sense?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:02 UTC

Imagine we had two volunteers.  Alice is really good at alignment, and Carlos is really good at colors.  If we set them both on `zulip.css` to try to clean up duplication, they'd be butting heads.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:03 UTC

One thing I worry about with that kind of architecture is Barry who is good at both being annoyed that the CSS for a particular element is spread in different places

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:04 UTC

Well, what I'm proposing to do first is split `zulip.css` into two mostly orthogonal files:
- geometry.css
- non-geometry.css

And, yes, I'm concerned about Barry, and thanks for keeping the names alliterative, haha!

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:05 UTC

I guess a good prototype might be trying to create e.g. `left-sidebar-geometry.css`

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:05 UTC

I'm always willing to impose minor tedium on Barry to remove complexity from Alice, but, yeah, that's a valid concern.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:05 UTC

Since that would be a lot less work to produce, and we could get a feel for how the divided CSS feels

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:06 UTC

(or maybe that's too small an experiment, idunno)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:06 UTC

I imagine like 80% of the geometry complexity is all in the center pane

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:08 UTC

So splitting up the two components into geometry/non-geometry can be a total mechanical process.  Extracting just the bits that are related to left sidebar geometry is more analytical, and part of what it makes the analysis hard is that zulip.css has a lot of noise to wade through if you're Alice or Barry wearing his alignment hat.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:08 UTC

I see, you're imagining using your fancy new parser capability to make `geometry.css`

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:09 UTC

Stepping back, my overall process would be something like this:
* Peter Python, i.e. an automated process, splits the files
* Alice/Carlos establish better patterns for both

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:09 UTC

yes

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:11 UTC

I also think it's healthy for color and alignment css files to diverge a bit in how they look at the HTML.  For doing alignment stuff, you want to think about how components are related geometrically, whereas for color, you are thinking more about how colors relate semantically.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:12 UTC

To put it more concretely, it's natural for an HTML node to inherit the color scheme of its HTML parents, but it's non-sensical to inherit the padding or the margin.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:17 UTC

One thing I want to do first is get a count of how many declaration blocks are...
- purely color/font-related
- purely geometry
- muddled

If we don't have many muddled blocks, then I think it's kind of a no-brainer to split the files, as we'll essentially be taking two disjoint things and unraveling them from an overly big file.

If we have many muddled blocks and go with the split, then we're making more work for Barry, but hopefully we're empowering Alice and Carlos.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:17 UTC

yeah, that seems like a good test!

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:22 UTC

I do think that such a split could be pretty promising (and would make it simpler to describe what one needs to do in order to e.g. "add a theme for Zulip") if that's every something we want to do

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:22 UTC

Since presumably themes would not impact geometry at all

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:23 UTC

yeah, for sure, and we sort of conversely want to lock alignment down

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:23 UTC

right

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:24 UTC

alright, I'm getting back to another thing for now, but I'll probably have some broad stats in a few hours

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:24 UTC

cool!

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:25 UTC

If we find there's a lot of stuff that's muddled, we may be able to characterize those and make them their own third file (or whatever), so even if there is, I think the cause is not lost.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:35 UTC

One thing that I think causes a lot of muddling is borders, because they have size info and color.  I think border sizes are internal, so they don't necessarily have as much sibling coupling as things like height and float.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-05 21:36 UTC

So we could either just treat borders as non-geometric entities or put them in a third file, so that somebody who links rounded corners can go to town or whatever.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-05 21:40 UTC

yeah, keeping them as non-geometric isn't crazy

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-06 00:23 UTC

So actually about 2/3 of our declarations are size-related.   (Right now I ignore display: none declarations, which are kind of murky, and probably belong in their own css, since they are more about the initial state of the app than anything permanent.)  580 size-related declarations live in pure blocks; 490 are muddled with non-size declarations.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-19 22:27 UTC

One coding standard I'd like to suggest, which we can retrofit in a fairly automated way, is to split out border-color settings from the geometry settings.  So, instead of...

```
border-bottom: 1px solid #e2e2e2;
border-top: 1px solid #e2e2e2;
```

...use...

```
border-bottom: 1px solid;
border-top: 1px solid;
border-color: #e2e2e2
```

Thoughts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-19 22:30 UTC

Don't have strong feelings.  I sorta feel like both are sorta "how the border looks visually", so that doesn't seem that exciting to me.  What do you think @Brock Whittaker?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-19 22:49 UTC

Some of it's a consistency thing.  If you want to find all the styles with 1px borders, it's easy if styles are just broken out for specific attributes.  I don't feel strongly; any tooling we write can be improved to handle this, it's just a little more work.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-19 22:50 UTC

I'd also be happy if we only used "border" with the long syntax; it's the mixing of the two different styles that bugs me mildly.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2016-08-20 00:04 UTC

I don't really see it as a style preference as much as a way to define a border-color global for a class.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2016-08-20 00:04 UTC

It doesn't bother me either way.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2016-08-20 00:05 UTC

But I definitely understand your perspective. Usually even when defining several borders they have the same color. It just doesn't lend itself well to cases where you'll have something like:

```css
border-color: #e2e2e2;
border-top: 1px solid;
border-bottom: 1px solid #444;
```

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-20 00:11 UTC

In strange cases where you want your bottom border to be different than the rest of the border, you can always say `border-bottom-color`, I guess.  I can understand how a little bit of flexibility is probably a good thing, but if there are places where we just arbitrarily have different coding styles for expressing how we style the borders, that's where I'd like to move for some consistency.  (I'm using "style" in two different contexts here--coding style and HTML style.)

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-20 00:13 UTC

Also, @Brock Whittaker, to give you a little context of where I'm coming from, I'm trying to write some automated tools to clean up our CSS so that it's not all one gigantic `zulip.css` file.  My main goal is to make it easy for tools to track down things like obsolete CSS classes, or break out color styles to a file that people re-skin.  All of my concerns are trumped by whatever designers think makes it easier to iterate on the Zulip CSS.

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-06-14 04:25 UTC

Why are we using webpack as a passthrough to render css as opposed to just using less or sass directly?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-14 16:41 UTC

@Paul Weaver currently we're using django-pipeline, and the reason is mostly that we did all our CSS tooling in 2012/2013 and haven't changed it since.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-14 16:41 UTC

I guess the reason to have webpack involved would be for its hot-reloading feature, I think?

};

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-01 20:56 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-01 20:56 UTC

I wonder to what extent remapping hotkeys should be thought of as a feature with long-term value vs. it being a workaround for poor hotkey mapping choices in the product that should be fixed more directly.

**Greg Price** · 2021-07-01 22:59 UTC

Yeah. I think that mostly comes down to a question of what are the use cases for remapping hotkeys.

One that comes to mind is that people have different keyboard layouts, and some of our hotkey choices are (quite reasonably) made partly on the basis of what keys are next to each other. I think there's probably fundamentally always going to be a difference between the best choice of hotkey mappings for a QWERTY user and for a Dvorak user.

## jquery upgrade

*2016-08-25 to 2017-03-20 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/jquery.20upgrade/with/19225)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-25 22:20 UTC

So we are about to push some changes to master that upgrade jQuery.  Our node tests mostly test non-jQuery aspects of our JS code, but we do use jQuery for some of the tests.  The node version of jQuery is called "jquery", and I think there are only very minor packaging differences between the browser version and the node version in the jQuery code itself, although I'm not completely sure about that.  But, of course, under the hood, on the node side, you're dealing with a headless browser and another module called jsdom...

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-25 22:21 UTC

they will be exactly the same when the upgrade lands

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-25 22:24 UTC

When we upgraded the jquery version for the node tests, we didn't have to make too many changes, but one little change caught my eye.  We used to use the jQuery method .css() in one of our tests to inspect the style attribute of some HTML we generated in our tests.  Before the upgrade, this worked fine.  After the upgrade, it stopped working, because the css() method was looking into strange things like the bounding rectangle of the div, which seems reasonable enough, but it never did that before.  After the upgrade, I had to change the test to use attr('style') and see if it said 'background: green'.  The test code probably should have done that originally, since we weren't interested in any externally-applied styles, so I just simply fixed the test.  But I'm minorly concerned we may have production code that could be subtly influenced by these changes.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-25 22:25 UTC

And just to put a huge caveat on what I observed, this was all in the middle of some pretty hellish environment problems I was facing, so it's possible this was a red herring.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-25 22:31 UTC

Yeah, I did read through the entire deprecation changelog carefully and I believe we got everything, but it seems totally possible we missed something

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-25 22:33 UTC

I was able to repro it just now, and the incriminating jquery code is to support IE6-8, bug #4512.  That does not give me warm fuzzies!

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-25 22:35 UTC

Well I suppose that's one reason we might want to move to jquery 2/3

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-25 22:35 UTC

I still think it's mostly an artifact of the test using a headless browser, it's just kinda scary when you read the comment in the jQuery code.  We use the getter style of css() in our resize code, but I think that code has always probably had to do some rectangle calculations.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-25 22:37 UTC

I assume the newer jquery versions de-support some of the older browsers, so fewer scary hacks?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-25 22:44 UTC

Yeah.  https://blog.jquery.com/2013/04/18/jquery-2-0-released/ and https://blog.jquery.com/2016/06/09/jquery-3-0-final-released/ are good reading

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-25 22:44 UTC

Basically by removing those hacks they can support some more features and also shrink the size of the library

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-25 23:29 UTC

so we'd probably jump to 2.2 or 2.3 next, after a little baking in of 1.12

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-25 23:32 UTC

yeah

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-20 19:23 UTC

How do folks feel about upgrading jquery? #4094 is a two-line fix :)

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-03-20 19:28 UTC

Did the api stay the exact same v1 to 2 O.o

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-20 19:50 UTC

yep, same api, just less ancient browser support

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-26 18:06 UTC

It's intended behavior for now, but it's definitely up for discussion on whether we change it.  The idea is that if people click out, they're often trying to abandon composing a message to respond to another stream, so we clear out the compose box to make it easier to start over.  You can "restore draft," but it's admittedly awkward.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-26 18:09 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-26 20:09 UTC

Highlighting the individual messages is part of Zulip's "unread message" UI.  We use the highlighted message to know that's how far you've read.  This way, if you switch to another stream and come back, we don't assume that you've read the whole page before.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-26 20:10 UTC

It also allows you to hit "i" to get a popup menu that applies to the specific message without having to use the mouse.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-02 02:04 UTC

* What should `[](url)` for an image file do?  I think showing the link as the text, as described, makes sense.

For `![](url)`, I think there are two reasonable options:
* Make `![](url)` to do the same thing as `[](url)` (But eating the `!`).  The only thing that's sorta wrong with this approach is that the `![]()` Markdown syntax is supposed to place the image inline at the place in the message, which is different behavior from what will happen (the image appearing at the end of the message).  But it is simpler implementation-wise, since we don't need to restructure our existing link processors to support the different placement.  And the big benefit here is that if you use any sort of HTML to markdown converter when pasting an image, it will generate `![](url)`, and our current setup does something that feels pretty broken, whereas this would be basically OK.
* Make `![]()` actually place the image there in the image.  I think this is long-term what we'll want to do, but I'd settle for doing the other option and then planning to migrate to this later if it looks like it'd be a complicated refactor.

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-10-13 08:03 UTC

I typically have 500+ unread messages on the RC realm each day, and deal with this by scrolling a bit, diving into a thread if it sounds interesting, reading all the way to the end, and heading back to the home stream to scout out other interesting threads.

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-10-13 08:08 UTC

**Alicja Raszkowska** · 2016-10-13 08:26 UTC

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-10-13 08:27 UTC

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-10-13 08:37 UTC

Exploring a bit more, when going back to the home stream after reading a thread, the read messages no longer have the green line on the left - even if they are after the "current" message on the home stream. So I'm guessing hiding them should be doable.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-13 13:41 UTC

For high-volume sites like RC (and even this site, lately), I definitely think this is a good conversation to have: figuring out muting, collapsing, pointer advancement, explicit mark-as-read, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-13 13:44 UTC

I find muting to be a really effective tool when you're already "caught up" and you're online during normal working hours.  If some thread that is only vaguely interesting to you starts getting a lot of traffic, I just mute it for later reading, and then stay on top of all the other traffic.  The UI for muting is not perfect, but I've found that I can mostly use it effectively once I'm caught up.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-13 13:49 UTC

We have tried collapsing in the past, and the experiments were deemed as failures, so we didn't pursue them further, but I think it's worth a re-visit.  The basic idea behind collapsing is pretty uncontroversial--you want to hide messages that have already been read but are still in your stream.  (Or another variation is you want users to be able to collapse sections explicitly.)   The previous experiments failed mostly, I believe, due to the UI being hard to pull off in a non-clunky way.  Zulip's message stream is already kind of visually busy, especially in interleaved mode, and adding collapsible sections makes it even more busy.  I don't think this is an impossible problem, though; we abandoned the experiment due to lack of resources and other priorities, but that can be fixed.  Also, at the time, we were dealing with smaller realms, and collapsing is more of a win for large realms.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-13 13:51 UTC

For advancing the "read" pointer, part of the issue here is simply a known bug, where we don't advance the pointer after you come out of "narrowed" views.  (You could call it either a bug or a not-yet-implemented feature.)   We intend to fix this fairly soon.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-13 13:55 UTC

Last but not least, I think there's a place for explicitly marking messages as read and unread.  It's a really uneasy feeling when you're trying to catch up on 500 messages, and you get to a clump of messages where you know you need to take some action (replying to messages or whatever), but you can't do it right away, and you're also just trying to get caught up on the "big picture" first.  We either need a mechanism for you to mark messages/topics/streams as unread, or we need an effective way to mark the messages for later consumption (probably beyond simply "starring" the message).

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2016-10-13 15:11 UTC

@Tim Abbott is this the kind of conversation we could pull designer Tim (Van Damme) into?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-13 15:36 UTC

We want UI designers to be part of this conversation, but I think we're still in the phase of collecting input from users on what the pain points are for big sites like RC, and, increasingly, even this site, as traffic has picked up noticeably here in the last month or so.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-13 15:46 UTC

Yeah, I've been thinking about to what extent we should make something starring that shows more like an unread message until you dismiss it, precisely for the purpose of "I need to come back to this"

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-18 16:07 UTC

OK, I think this is a reasonable path forward:
* We plan to use KaTeX pending some testing
* We do a test of sending 1000 messages containing a line or two of simple LaTeX into the Zulip development environment with Reid's branch, and see how slow it is.
* We do a test of having KaTeX be rendered on the backend using the KaTeX server-side thing, and see how slow viewing a page using that is (basically to see to what extent the perf cost is for parsing vs. actually drawing)
* Based on those, we decide whether we need a backend or frontend implementation.
* If we go for a backend implementation, we read KaTeX's parsing code to see whether we'll need to sandbox KaTeX.  Conveniently, it doesn't have a lot of dependencies, and we'd be using a subprocess to call into it anyway, so sandboxing it probably wouldn't be that annoying.

## topic lists

*2016-10-29 to 2016-10-29 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/topic.20lists/with/47375)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-29 14:27 UTC

@Tim Abbott Currently the way topic lists work is that we only ever build one topic list per stream, and for a stream that has, say 25 topics, we build a list of 25 topics before you ever hit "(more topics)", and we use a combination of markup and CSS to hide the last 20 topics.  The HTML class is called "zoom-out-hide", and here is the relevant CSS:

```
.zoom-out .zoom-out-hide {
    display: none;
}

.zoom-in .zoom-in-hide {
    display: none;
}
```

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-29 14:32 UTC

There advantage of the current approach is pretty obvious--when you zoom in or zoom out, you don't need to rebuild the DOM in code, and you simply allow the browser to re-render based on the changing between `class=".zoom-out"` and `class=".zoom_out"` on the `#stream_list` element.  I believe this was originally motivated by performance concerns, but perhaps it was merely done to simplify the code.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-29 14:39 UTC

So I'm not sure this approach still makes sense in a world where we go back further in topic history then we do now.  There are two reasons:
* I'm concerned about having all the DOM elements lying around, even if they're mostly hidden.
* When we start hitting the back end to get deeper topic history, we are going to end up having to re-render the DOM anyway, so we lose the basic advantage of the current approach.

For the second point this would perhaps be mitigated by some intelligence in knowing when we really need to fetch more stuff from the back end, but it's pretty much unavoidable to pay the penalty at least once for any user that has deeper history than we send on page load.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-29 14:41 UTC

So I'd like to consider an approach where we have two lists per stream:
* We have a truncated list of <= 5 topics that is always attached to the DOM (but hidden when we zoom in).
* We have an ephemeral list of up to, say, 100 topics, that we build when we zoom in and subsequently destroy when we zoom out.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-29 14:45 UTC

That sounds reasonable; the only thing I'd worry about is whether part of the purpose of the current mechanism of having >5 is to help with maintaining them when topics get renamed; I kinda doubt that story though.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-29 14:48 UTC

Yeah, me too.  I think some of the original code simplicity concerns were valid to a degree--if I keep the short lists in memory, then I need to be updating them even when I'm zoomed in to the big lists, as new messages arrive, so there's a bit of extra bookkeeping.  But I would weigh that factor differently now than when we weighed it in Cambridge.  Back then it was an experimental feature and we were trying to iterate quickly.  Now that we have validated the feature and are in more a polishing paradigm, I think we can be more patient.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-29 14:50 UTC

Cool.  -> GSoC Mentor Summit for me! :)

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-29 14:50 UTC

I also think from a performance standpoint, most users spend 98% of their day zoomed out, so we will generally be incurring the cost of updating one list.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-29 14:50 UTC

Ah!  Ok, I'll proceed with this and see how it goes.  Thanks!  Have fun!

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-29 14:50 UTC

yeah

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-29 22:31 UTC

One thing I noticed today is that we often re-render the topic list twice on narrows--once for the narrow, and then again for the subsequent history updates.  I think this is actually semi-intentional, so that we're both responsive and accurate.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-29 22:52 UTC

yep!

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-08 17:08 UTC

Right now we lazy-load the innards of all our settings pages.  But then when we exit the overlay and re-enter settings, we call `reset_sections`, which forces us to rebuild sections.  The good part of that is it covers up some flaws related to live updates (as long as the data piece was updated, we'll re-draw the GUI correctly the next time you  enter settings).  The bad parts are this:

* more work to do
* obscures live-update bugs
* can lead to duplicate handlers

I **think** doing the `reset_sections` logic is kind of a necessary evil, since live-updating the settings UI can be quite tricky, and it's fairly pragmatic to just wait until the next time somebody goes into settings and lazy-load off the latest and greatest data.

So assuming we continue to have `reset_sections`, the thing to tackle is duplicating handlers.  @Tim Abbott do you agree?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-10 06:48 UTC

I'm not sure.  I think it's possible we shouldn't be doing `reset_sections` as much as we do, given that we've already done the work to make live-update in most of ours settings pages work great.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-10 15:27 UTC

@Tim Abbott You wouldn't have to twist my arm too hard to get rid of `reset_sections`.  It would eliminate a whole class of bugs, make things zippier the 2nd/3rd/4th time you  go into settings, and simplify the code.  Plus, failures to do live-updates always  have the workaround of just hard-reloading the page.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-10 19:04 UTC

I don't know if this comment is relevant, but for a lot of settings pages just having "This page has been updated, please reload" is probably fine. (I think we already do that for the open invitations page, so the wording can be copied from there).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-10 19:05 UTC

Yeah, we already do that for super complicated things like updating language (e.g. English -> Spanish) where writing robust live-update code would be impractical.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-10 19:06 UTC

Although that's maybe a bad example, since it's something where only one person is involved.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-10 19:07 UTC

The more subtle scenario is something like you have two admins.  Bob makes some change, and Alice's page doesn't update, and then Alice goes to do something and it fails on the server due to obsolete data.  No real harm is done, other than wasting a bit of Alice's time.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-10 19:08 UTC

Also, the bar is a bit lower for admins than normal users.  For normal users, we want robust live updates, since normal users are super prone to confusion, and it can impact all N people who are currently online.  For admin stuff, way fewer people are affected (typically 1 or 2) and  they are more likely to be able to understand what's happening and work around it as needed.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-10 19:10 UTC

(For org updates, of course all N users have stale data, but if they can't edit from the panels, the stale data is harmless in terms of race conditions, etc.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-10 19:13 UTC

Also, many user settings only affect the one user (albeit possibly multiple clients for that user).  The big things are things like name changes that Normal User A can modify, but which are visible to all other users, and we're generally pretty good on those.  Whereas nobody besides Fred cares whether Fred is using light mode or dark mode.

Right now we only have a few settings options where we make people reload after changes on other clients, and I think we should aim to have none.  With our standard communication design, it's usually about the same amount of work to make it live-update for just you (which is pretty essential) or for everyone.

## unicode emoji

*2016-11-03 to 2016-11-03 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/unicode.20emoji/with/49046)*

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-03 21:13 UTC

is the expected behavior of inserting \ud83d\udca7 (unicode-emoji) in message is to displaythe equivalent emoji?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:14 UTC

yes

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-03 21:15 UTC

So is this broken?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:15 UTC

hmm, good question.  Let's look at the tests to see how this usually works

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:16 UTC

It may be that it only works for the emoji in our emoji set, for example

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-03 21:17 UTC

I got this from node tests

```json
 {input: "\ud83d\udca9",
     expected: '<p><img alt="\ud83d\udca9" class="emoji" src="/static/third/gemoji/images/emoji/unicode/1f4a9.png" title="\ud83d\udca9"></p>'}
```

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-03 21:18 UTC

echo.apply_markdown is producing the correct output.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:18 UTC

Oh, yeah, but it's expecting the actual emoji symbol

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:18 UTC

☃

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:18 UTC

Like what I just sent, but for something we have

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-03 21:23 UTC

@Tim Abbott So the output of entering \ud83d\udca9 is \ud83d\udca9 right?

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-03 21:23 UTC

I mean the expected output.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:24 UTC

yes, that's right

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-03 21:25 UTC

Okay. Thanks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:25 UTC

The key thing is that programming languages interpret `\u` as meaning what follows is an encoding for the unicode character

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 21:25 UTC

But what we render as emoji is the actual character, not the written-out encoding

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-03 21:33 UTC

I think I understood it now. Thanks for clearing.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-06 04:49 UTC

I'll summarize my thoughts on minification:
* **Does it compress the payload?**  Yes, but there are other tools there.
* **Does it protect your proprietary source code?** No, we're an open source project.  There is no code to protect here.
* **Is it a huge pain for troubleshooting?** Yes, it's always been.
* **Does it complicate our asset pipeline?** Of course it does.
* **Does it make prod behavior differ from dev behavior and expose us to prod-only issues?** Of course it does.
* **Does it have inertia**?  Yes, it's like a government program.

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-12-06 04:54 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-06 04:55 UTC

I was thinking minimal in terms of effort, but what you propose is minimal in terms of impact, I think, which is an interesting way to look at it.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-06 05:00 UTC

If you look the `'app'` section of `JS_SPECS` in `zproject/settings.py`, you'll see that it's mostly Zulip source code, which is pretty small already (and therefore benefits marginally from minification), and some third party jquery stuff.  So we could just remove the Zulip app stuff from the minify pipeline as an incremental step for minimal impact.

But I'm still mostly interested in minimal effort, to state my biases clearly.  Just rip out the whole minify pipeline and gzip it or similarly compress it.

* **JS minification** - minification is like Unix *gzip*, except that it's no better than gzip and creates a bunch of problems

`zoom-out` does not mean `display: none` ? I'm not CSS expert - just asking.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:38 UTC

sorry, had it completely backward, just edited

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:39 UTC

```
434 .zoom-out .zoom-out-hide {
435     display: none;
436 }           
437         
438 .zoom-in .zoom-in-hide {
439     display: none;
440 }  
```

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:40 UTC

If we set `zoom-out` on the UL, then the LI elements with `zoom-out-hide` get hidden via `display: none`.

**Tomasz Kolek** · 2016-12-13 17:40 UTC

ahh right.

**Tomasz Kolek** · 2016-12-13 17:40 UTC

So yeah, your idea is clear for me now.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:41 UTC

Cool.  I'm not a huge fan of this CSS hack, because it's kind of confusing and "magical."  But the alternative solution also has issues.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:42 UTC

If we were to eliminate the CSS hack, then we'd eliminate some CSS (yay!) and some sort of cryptic jQuery code (yay!), but then we'd be responsible for manually hiding and showing the Fay/Greta/Hank rows.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:43 UTC

And when we originally render the template, it's one big list, so you have to be a little bit careful about hiding the elements without a brief flicker between rendering the list and hiding Fay/Greta/Hank.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:44 UTC

And then you could say that we only build the first five rows, but then that has some pitfalls related to unread counts getting updated.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:45 UTC

Long story short, I think we should stick with the CSS hack for now.  But I wanted to let you know there is an alternative approach here, if you want to think it through more.

**Tomasz Kolek** · 2016-12-13 17:46 UTC

OK, Thanks!

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:47 UTC

And if we're comfortable with the CSS hack, I think we can eliminate a few redundant lines of code as part of your commit.  Let me find them...

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-13 17:48 UTC

## realm emojis in picker

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-12-19 11:28 UTC

It looks like the emoji map is generated by adding divs with classes that look like `emoji-<emoji_name>`. The actual images are then loaded from the sprite.css in `static/third/gemoji` which uses sprite.png generated by `tools/setup/emoji_dump/build_emoji`. 
Realm emoji don't have a stylesheet/sprite image, so they aren't rendered in the emoji picker (even though there is a a div with class `emoji-zulip`)

@Arpith Siromoney thanks for investigating; it sounds like we should just load them by URL directly in the code that generates the spritesheet

there are unlikely to be hundreds of them

~~~ .js
function update_draft(draft_id, new_text) {
  with_persistence(function (drafts) {
    drafts[draft_id] = new_text;
  });
}

function with_persistence(f) {
  var drafts = local_storage.get(KEY) || create();
   f(drafts);
   local_storage.put(drafts)
}
~~~

@Steve Howell For the localStorage tests, I created these stubs:

```js
var ls_container = {};
set_global('localStorage', {
    getItem: function (key) {
        return ls_container[key];
    },
    setItem: function (key, val) {
        ls_container[key] = val;
    },
    removeItem: function (key) {
        delete ls_container[key];
    },
    clear: function () {
        ls_container = {};
    }
});

function stub_timestamp (timestamp, func) {
    var original_func = Date.prototype.getTime;
    Date.prototype.getTime = function () {
        return timestamp;
    };
    func();
    Date.prototype.getTime = original_func;
}
```

## narrowing links

*2017-01-06 to 2017-01-06 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/narrowing.20links/with/117036)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-06 01:20 UTC

@Tim Abbott We seem to have inconsistent approaches to links for narrowing.   Sometimes the links are true links that presumably go through our hashchange mechanism; other times we have click handlers, but when you hover over the links, the URL doesn't match what will show up in the browser when you click.  What's the best approach here?  I am noticing this with PMs.   If you try the upper left corner, the message menu, the buddy list link, etc., they all narrow correctly, but they have different behaviors w/r/t to what the browser shows.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 01:28 UTC

Both code paths need the work

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 01:29 UTC

We use the click handler usually when we have a specific center message that we want to go into the narrow

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 01:29 UTC

(e.g. if you click in the left sidebar, we always take you to the first unread, but if you click on a message header, we center the narrow around that specific message)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 01:35 UTC

So, the inconsistency is somewhat intentional, in that we only bother to build a click handler in the event that we have a specific message to center arround

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-06 01:35 UTC

So it seems to me for PMs, the upper left corner and the buddy lists should all just work on hrefs, since they don't have any context, and they should be consistent, but I probably need the click handler for the message menu, and I should clean up the URL for cosmetic reasons, even though the click handler essentially ignores it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 01:35 UTC

However, even in those places, we still set the href properly in case the user copies the link

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 01:35 UTC

We also use the click handler somewhat for tracking where the narrow was initiated from in some logging

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 01:36 UTC

Yeah, because of copy-link it's a bit more than cosmetic, but that's right

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-06 01:38 UTC

Cool.  So I started slugging all the pm-with narrows on my branch, but I think I want to clean up some of the stuff we're talking about here before pushing it, although it's mostly backward compatible.

We seem to use the`attr` style often.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2017-01-09 20:05 UTC

We use `data('foo')` everywhere right?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-09 20:07 UTC

no, we use the other style in 56 places

**Sampriti Panda** · 2017-01-09 20:15 UTC

There are some functional differences too.

`.attr` actually updates the DOM and adds the data- attribute which you can see in the DOM (Inspect Element).
`.data` stores the data values in some place inside jquery and the DOM isn't updated

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-09 20:21 UTC

We only use the read version.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-09 20:21 UTC

And we want the DOM to be explicitly updated.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-09 20:22 UTC

I should say we mostly use the read version, as we mostly write these with templates.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2017-01-09 20:22 UTC

By "read version" you mean?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-09 20:23 UTC

jQuery has two different versions of the function

**Sampriti Panda** · 2017-01-09 20:24 UTC

Ok yeah, so for `attr` we only use the read version?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-09 20:24 UTC

.attr(foo) returns the attribute (read)
.attr(foo, bar) sets the attribute (write)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-09 20:24 UTC

generally more read than write

## subs.js bug

*2017-01-20 to 2017-01-20 · 2 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/subs.2Ejs.20bug/with/134088)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-20 21:57 UTC

I found a pretty obscure bug in subs.js where if we subscribe ourselves to a stream using the subscriber list (rather than the easier check mark), it correctly turns sub.subscribed to true, but it doesn't add us to the set sub.subscribers.  You can reproduce it as follows:
* open inspector
* open stream settings, pick a stream
* unsubscribe with checkmark
* open right tab
* add yourself to the list of subscribers (and the checkmark will go back on)
* unsubscribe with checkmark

You'll see a console error.  I am fixing this in my branch now.  I thought I'd mention it here in case it has shown up in blueslip errors or if anybody remembers an issue for this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-20 22:54 UTC

good find


## avatar updates

*2017-01-21 to 2017-01-22 · 24 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/avatar.20updates/with/134352)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 18:28 UTC

I am starting to dig into avatar updates some more.  A couple observations:
* server events seem to be fine
* there's a small id/user_id change that will make live updates work again for avatars already in your message stream
* we use message  as the authoritative source for avatars (rather than try to get them from people.js)
* image caching in the browser is a problem, because we don't have a concept of "generation" for avatar urls that remain the same url but point to different images

@Tim Abbott We should discuss this when you get a chance.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:47 UTC

Cool, now works

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:48 UTC

I guess one option is we could do something on the backend to change the URL when you change avatars.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:48 UTC

E.g. make the avatar URL contain the hash of the avatar file

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:49 UTC

I think it'd be reasonable to have the webapp use people.js as the source for avatar URLs, but still include avatar URLs in the messages (for use by third-party API tools that don't pay attention to the user events)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 19:51 UTC

Regarding attaching the avatar url to messages, I'm totally on board with that.  (Even in the browser, we apparently don't send down avatar urls in page_params, but once we see it in a message, we can easily cache it in people.js.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 19:53 UTC

For live updates, you can defeat the cache with `&y=<timestamp`, so we may be able to live with the current backend behavior, although there's still the scenario that when the user reloads, they may regress back to the cached version with the `&y=` hack.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:54 UTC

Oh, probably it's a good idea to add them to page_params; we'll likely want that some day to support showing avatars in the right sidebar user popovers

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:55 UTC

Yeah, the problem with the `&y=` thing is that it's not clearing the cache of the wrong version of the file

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 19:55 UTC

Yep, and you do want the cache to work for users who haven't made changes.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 19:56 UTC

I think we would need to change UserProfile to support generation-aware avatar urls.  They are computed dynamically.  We'd either need to just store the whole url on the model (problematic due to different storage mechanisms) or add an integer avatar_generation field.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:58 UTC

hmm, yeah

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 19:59 UTC

We'd also need to think about migrating the files themselves, although I think that's easy enough--just make sure the hash with generation=null is equal to the old hash.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:59 UTC

avatar_generation isn't crazy, though it might be in some sense be simpler to store at least an `avatar_path_id` if not a full URL.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:59 UTC

UserProfile database migrations aren't too expensive to do

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 19:59 UTC

Actually, if we had generation, we wouldn't need to bother with the hash--we'd just stick it in the url

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 20:01 UTC

(We wouldn't need to modify the hash, I mean.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 20:04 UTC

`avatar_path_id` would bloat our memcached a bit, although that doesn't concern me too much.

I'm more -1 on `avatar_path_id` to the extent that it doesn't really relieve us from computing the url dynamically, so in some sense it's an extra moving part.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 20:06 UTC

yeah, I kinda agree

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 20:10 UTC

On my branch, I basically have a working version for live updates; it just doesn't clear the cache for the non-timestamped images.  My browser (Firefox) seems to clear the images on reload, so I only needed to combat per-page-load caching, so it's working for me.  But I like having the back end having a "generation" field, and I can implement that if we can bikeshed a name for it.

I'm not too worried about sending avatar_url in `page_params`, as I want to keep the logic to use it from `message` as a fallback, anyway, and we can always do it later once we upgrade the buddy list.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 20:12 UTC

(I haven't pushed my changes yet.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 20:52 UTC

Haha, we need to be careful about testing with the tutorial--the tutorial has fake messages with legit avatar urls but bogus senders with no sender_id.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 21:45 UTC

@Tim Abbott How about `avatar_version` for the new field name?  see #3408 for fixes related to avatars

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-22 00:39 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-09 00:53 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-09 00:54 UTC

I think it would be probably reasonable to just call a does-not-exist-yet `blueslip.disable()`that would block reporting of exceptions while the browser is in the process of reloading

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-09 00:54 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-09 00:54 UTC

thoughts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-09 00:54 UTC

The alternative argument is that maybe Zulip shouldn't throw JS exceptions even when trying to reload itself

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 00:57 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 00:57 UTC

Another thought here is to just tune the blueslip reporting so that it's super easy to spam-filter the during-reload errors, but still report them.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 00:58 UTC

What area of code is the TB happening in?

in `cleanup_before_reload`

* just start knocking out some of the things that probably are things we should fix, such as scrolling

scrolling is unfixable; the whole point is that earlier in the reload process we deleted everything in that part of the DOM

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-27 17:38 UTC

I got curious about this, and the reason we don't handle spaces is just a quirk of our autocomplete code.  We do this:

~~~ js
215     var strings = q.split(/[\s*(){}\[\]]/);
216     if (strings.length < 1) {
217         return false;
218     }
219     var current_token = strings[strings.length-1];

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-27 17:42 UTC

we want to do something more like...

~~~
prefix, current_token = q.match('(.*)([#:@].*)')
if (! (prefix == '' or prefix[-1].test(/[\s*(){}/) )
   return false;

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-27 17:57 UTC

I think to do this right, you really need to allow typing spaces while in autocomplete, and it's just a matter of translating my pseudocode rubbish to something that's reasonably fast--perhaps iterating backward through the string instead of a regex.  Without space support, you end up typing stuff like @steve inadvertently thinking the autocomplete worked.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-27 18:29 UTC

working on this now

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-27 18:29 UTC

So just to confirm is your model to have space escape autocomplete only if there's no matching continuation?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-27 18:30 UTC

that approach certainly makes sense to me

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-27 18:31 UTC

correct

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-27 18:36 UTC

awesome!

#3487 if anybody wants to look at it (I saw Tim did already)

Deployed!  Manual testing appreciated :)

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-01-27 19:17 UTC

it's 20 characters

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-27 19:26 UTC

There's a minor performance tradeoff where you don't want to go too far back before the cursor to find tokens to autocomplete, since in the unlikely event they had a match, the user would have already easily autocompleted them earlier (or probably was trying to type something different and is sick of the popup).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-27 19:31 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-27 19:34 UTC

## typing notifications

*2017-02-08 to 2017-02-08 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/typing.20notifications/with/147007)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 18:27 UTC

H folks, @Divyanshu Agarwal was asking me over PMs about what I think is "typing notifications," although he may be asking about something slightly different.  What is our current status for that effort?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-08 18:28 UTC

the backend is merged, and there's a frontend PR that I need to spend some time on

**Divyanshu Agarwal** · 2017-02-08 19:24 UTC

I know that typing notifications include whether someone is typing or not but does it also include that our message has been sent to the server or not and whether other person have seen our message or not that is there in apps like facebook .

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:31 UTC

Our approach for the first problem--making sure messages get sent to the server--is that we optimistically assume the server will see your message.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:33 UTC

So we have a system called "local echo" that puts your message in your message stream before the server has really looked at it.  But, then, of course if the message does not get delivered, we notify you.  This happens so rarely to me that I don't even really know what that looks like off the top of my head.  I also think we have a PR pending to handle timeout failures more robustly.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:35 UTC

Regarding your second question, the email terminology for that feature is something like "read receipts."  We could conceptually do that, but there's a bit of a privacy issue, where folks might not want to indicate that they read a Zulip and ignored it or failed to act on it.  I remember "read receipts" had a lot of pushback in email days.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:39 UTC

I have occasionally wanted an "ack" feature.  Let's say you send me a message, but I'm busy working on something, and the pot's boiling, and the dog's barking, so I can't fully address your message right away. I want a really simple way for me to tell you that I got your message but just don't have time for a fully reply.  Of course, I could type "ack" as a reply, but that requires social conventions and it spams the stream.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:49 UTC

One of the goals of Zulip is to facilitate communication in a non-disruptive way, so that people don't feel like they should have to respond to every message instantly (and conversely, people should understand that they won't always get an immediate reply).

**Divyanshu Agarwal** · 2017-02-08 19:54 UTC

I think we can have read receipts feature in zulip and for those who don't want to have this feature active we can put something in privacy settings to inactive it, as organizations may want this feature for their own way of interactions with their employees, as i thought .

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:57 UTC

Ok, I wonder if we've ever created an issue for this.  It's probably worth doing a quick search of PRs for "read receipt" to see if we have a ticket for this already.  If we do, you should add to it; otherwise, create a new ticket.

**Divyanshu Agarwal** · 2017-02-08 20:07 UTC

Sure:)

**Divyanshu Agarwal** · 2017-02-08 22:11 UTC

I have created this issue#3618 for read receipt feature, Can anyone suggest any source where we can find workflow of this feature.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-08 22:25 UTC

AFAIK there's no preexisting issue for that

**Gittenburg** · 2020-06-26 12:34 UTC

The layout of our frontend is currently very inflexible (for example the layout completely breaks when you change the widths of the sidebars). Our CSS is full of `calc(100% - some px)`, which makes it harder to maintain and very cumbersome to customize. The heights of some components are even calculated with JavaScript on window resize.

Fortunately **CSS Flexbox** [is supported by all modern browsers](https://caniuse.com/#feat=flexbox). So I would like for us to switch to using Flexbox (instead of manually calculating dimensions). Yesterday I already successfully recreated the Zulip layout with Flexbox ... so it's totally possible.

The first obstacle for us switching to Flexbox is that the package that we currently use for our fancy scroll bars, SimpleBar does not support Flexbox. Since I couldn't find a good alternative, I implemented FlexBox support in SimpleBar and submitted it as an upstream pull request: https://github.com/Grsmto/simplebar/pull/488

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-06-26 12:36 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-26 18:03 UTC

Awesome!

**Wyatt Hoodes** · 2020-07-06 02:32 UTC

This is a great initiative!

**Gittenburg** · 2020-07-06 07:35 UTC

The Simplebar maintainer replied to [my Simplebar PR to fix a bug with flexbox](https://github.com/Grsmto/simplebar/pull/488), as it turns out you just need to add one line of CSS, so this is no longer blocking. Before I start working on converting our layout to flexbox, I want us to start using CSS color variables (my PR  #15547), which is currently blocked by my other PR #15666 to unify the sidebar hover effects.

## live update quirks

*2017-02-22 to 2017-02-23 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/live.20update.20quirks/with/155508)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-22 15:54 UTC

For email/avatar updates, I think there is still some quirky behavior in these scenarios:
* User A sends to stream
* User A changes personal data
* User B sees live updates
* User B replies to message
* Immediately prior message from B reverts to old info

I think this is due to fancy incremental re-draw logic where we're going through a different codepath and getting old message_store data.  I haven't investigated fully, just something to watch for.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-23 01:13 UTC

I have a PR to fix the avatar thing by just doing a more blunt full update of messages for avatar changes.  It turns out the issue with emails is different, but also easy to address.  We need to make util.same_recipient and util.same_major_recipient use ids from the messages.  I believe stream_id is already on the message object, and we have a helper for converting reply_to to user_ids, so this should be an easy fix.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-23 01:17 UTC

#3767 is the avatar fix

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-23 02:47 UTC

cool

if (cap = this.rules.escape.exec(src)) {
      src = src.substring(cap[0].length);
```

Where `cap[0].length` is basically the length of the matched string.

`String.substring()` in JavaScript, when only provided 1 argument, takes a substring from the provided position to the end.

They set up the regexes with parens around the whole thing so that cap[0] captures the whole string, even if you only care about cap[1] or cap[2] or whatever.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-04 20:00 UTC

(speaking from memory, so grain of salt)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-04 20:03 UTC

BTW this is a pretty common technique in parsers--you sort of "eat" the input as you go.  Depending on how the implementation of your language works, it's often better to advance an index through the original string, but for small strings it usually does not matter.

## viewport

*2017-03-09 to 2017-03-11 · 27 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/viewport/with/164743)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:44 UTC

So, Brock and I made a fascinating discovery today!

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:44 UTC

As many of you know, the Zulip webapp has had serious problems with not working at all on Chrome on iOS

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:44 UTC

It turns out that the reason is that we have a JS module called `viewport`

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:45 UTC

Apparently, Chrome on iOS masks that module, so that accessing `viewport.scrollTop` accesses undefined

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:45 UTC

I can't find any documentation of this

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:45 UTC

However, renaming the module to `newport` "fixes" the problem :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:46 UTC

So we need a new name for that module

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:48 UTC

Options include:
* `message_pane.js` 
* `message_scrolling.js`
* `message_viewport.js`

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:48 UTC

Probably others

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:49 UTC

The main functions that one accesses are things like:
* `.scrollTop`, `.height`, `.set_message_offset`, `.visible_groups`, `.recenter_view`, etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 04:50 UTC

`message_view.js` feels a bit not great given that we have `message_list_view.js` already

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 05:06 UTC

`message_scrolling.height()`  kinda sucks, but we could make it `message_scroll.viewport_height`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 05:07 UTC

Opinions welcome :)

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-03-09 05:08 UTC

`message_pane` seems good to me

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-09 05:09 UTC

One thing which isn't great about `message_pane` is that apparently there's currently a `viewport.message_pane`, but I guess we could rename that

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-10 22:50 UTC

I think I'm going to go with `message_viewport`; the name `viewport` has been fine so far except for this stupid Chrome-on-iOS bug :).

## search operators

*2017-03-11 to 2022-05-23 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/search.20operators/with/166210)*

**Cat-Thu Nguyen-Huu** · 2017-03-11 21:07 UTC

Hi @Steve Howell ! What are your thoughts so far on the search operators?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 21:08 UTC

Hi, I think we want to have a more generic approaching to dealing with multiple operators.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 21:09 UTC

The existing code is structured to generally only deal with one operator for search suggestions, with maybe a few minor exceptions.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 21:10 UTC

I think we want to build a more general mechanism that does something like this:
* Use all-but-the-last tokens (if any) to limit what search suggestions make sense.
* Do a generic search suggestion algorithm on the last token to find possible expansions (with the limits from the earlier tokens).
* Produce search suggestions with the all-but-last tokens part of the descriptions.

**Cat-Thu Nguyen-Huu** · 2017-03-11 21:27 UTC

Would that look something like:
`frontend search steve`
to return messages from steve on the frontend stream and topics that include "search"?

**Cat-Thu Nguyen-Huu** · 2017-03-11 21:31 UTC

Or:
`stream: frontend topic:search sender:steve` to
- limit to the frontend stream and topics that include search
- look for messages from steve in there
- produce search suggestions with descriptions like "narrow to the stream front end and topic search"

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 21:31 UTC

For the case of `frontend search steve`, where there are no operators, you would treat it basically as if I had typed `search:frontend search:search steve`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 21:32 UTC

So your suggestions would be something like:
* search for token frontend and token search in messages sent by Steve Adams
* search for token frontend and token search in messages sent by Steve Smith

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 21:34 UTC

For the case of `stream:frontend steve`, you would consider "sent-by" suggestions for all Steves, but not "pm-with" suggestions.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 21:35 UTC

You can imagine how complex this will get, and we're going to be looking at either of the following:
* not a ton of code, but fairly mind-bending recursion
* lots and lots of code to handle all the different cases

(It will actually be somewhat in between.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 21:36 UTC

So the big-picture question is whether you want to dive into this as your first ticket. :)

## #3978 auto-collapsing long message bug

*2017-03-15 to 2017-03-17 · 27 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/.233978.20auto-collapsing.20long.20message.20bug/with/170683)*

**James Wang** · 2017-03-15 09:01 UTC

i have some questions 
1) is this bug a recent regression? or has this always been problems with autocollapsing large messages sent one right after the other?
2) does our repository have a record of the pull request that implemented this auto-collapsing in the first place? i can't find it.

thanks!

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-15 13:50 UTC

We've had this feature almost since the beginning of the project, so the original code was written before we were even on GitHub, so you won't find the original PR (pull request).  You should be able to find some commit history by doing `git blame` on `static/js/condense.js` and other files.

I suspect this bug is **not** a recent regression, but I'm kind of guessing.  I would try to do something like this:
* Find a consistent way to reproduce the bug.
* See if you can still reproduce the bug on master~1000 and master~2000.
* If evidence suggests it's a recent regression, you can use `git bisect` to try to find a suspicious recent commit (or maybe just search the logs a bit).
* In the more likely event that this piece of code has just always had quirks, I would just try to fix it going forward.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-15 17:53 UTC

I'm pretty confident it's been like this for years

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-15 17:53 UTC

So not worth trying to find where it was introduced

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-15 20:02 UTC

Yeah, probably the most important step is to get a consistent way to reproduce the bug.  Once you have a consistent repro, you can probably figure out what's happening (or not happening) to cause the bug.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-15 20:04 UTC

I think it's reasonably likely the bug has to do with likely-buggy logic that tries to not collapse it if the entire message would fit in the viewport

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-15 20:04 UTC

Since I seem to recall we thought about doing that

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-15 20:08 UTC

Yeah, I'd personally be fine if we collapse even in cases where the message would technically fit in the viewport.

**James Wang** · 2017-03-16 00:47 UTC

so the most consistent way to get this bug is simply if you're sending a long message and it gets added to a message group. every way i've tested it, it will break the moment you send a long message that gets appended to the message group. if you send a long message that gets its own message-group created, then it will collapse correctly most of the time, but i just found out that there are certain kinds of text that you post that breaks it regardless if its being appended to a group or getting its own message group. 

also another thing to note is that if you log out and log back in, all of the messages are correctly collapsed.

**James Wang** · 2017-03-16 00:50 UTC

oh so then maybe the logic isn't looking at the actual message or message row but its actually testing it off the message group for violation of the viewport when it comes to collapse or condense?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-16 00:50 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-16 00:51 UTC

gtg shortly but that explanataion makes a lot of sense to me, since we use a different codepath for the two cases

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-16 00:51 UTC

So it might just be a missing if statement in the `message_list.js` or `message_list_view.js` code for appending to an existing message group

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-16 00:51 UTC

Nice find, hope you can figure out more.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-16 01:08 UTC

I agree with Tim here.  It's very plausible that this requires something like a 3-line fix to just invoke the correct logic in the append-to-group code path.  It's also possible that something more subtle is going on here, too, of course, and the fact that certain types of messages appear to break this regardless of whether you're adding to a message group suggests we might have two problems at play here.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-16 01:09 UTC

If there are two separate, semi-related issues here, we should strive to fix them in separate commits.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-16 01:12 UTC

Also, @James Wang, your observation that things seem to work on reload resonates with what I've seen in the app, so that's more evidence that we're just doing the collapse logic in the wrong place of our code or in not enough places in our code.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-16 01:16 UTC

One tricky thing to watch out for is that we have both a "condense' and a "collapse" concept.  I believe condensing means we show part of a long message, whereas collapsing means we basically show none of the message (other than the sender/timestamp).  Condensing is mostly controlled by an algorithm (is the message just too big?), whereas collapsing is controlled by the user ("this animated gif is really annoying").

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-16 01:17 UTC

correct.

append never actually calls a rerender; so I just said to rerender the entire thing after appending and it properly condensed the message

this is probably not what we want because the rerender takes a really long time

```
 // Insert new messages in to the last message group

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-17 20:41 UTC

~~~ py 
 ~/zulip (showell-dot) $ cat tools/lib/graph.py 
from collections import defaultdict

def make_dot_file(graph):
    buffer = 'digraph G {\n'
    for node in graph.nodes:
        buffer += node + ';\n';
        for child in graph.children[node]:
            buffer += '{} -> {};\n'.format(node, child)
    buffer += '}'
    return buffer

class Graph(object):
    def __init__(self, *tuples):
        self.children = defaultdict(list)
        self.parents = defaultdict(list)
        self.nodes = set()

        for parent, child in tuples:
            self.parents[child].append(parent)
            self.children[parent].append(child)
            self.nodes.add(parent)
            self.nodes.add(child)

    def remove_exterior_nodes(self):
        still_work_to_do = True
        while still_work_to_do:
            still_work_to_do = False # for now
            for node in self.nodes:
                if self.parents[node] and self.children[node]:
                    # we are an interior node still
                    continue
                self.remove(node)
                still_work_to_do = True
                break

    def remove(self, node):
        for parent in self.parents[node]:
            self.children[parent].remove(node)
        for child in self.children[node]:
            self.parents[child].remove(node)
        self.nodes.remove(node)

def test():
    graph = Graph(
        ('x', 'a'),
        ('a', 'b'),
        ('b', 'c'),
        ('c', 'a'),
        ('c', 'd'),
        ('d', 'e'),
        ('e', 'f'),
        ('e', 'g'),
    )
    graph.remove_exterior_nodes()

    s = make_dot_file(graph)
    open('zulip-deps.dot', 'w').write(s)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    test()

So, if there are no problems in doing this I can proceed further on this line.

I am pasting a copy of `build_stream_list` for reference:
```
exports.build_stream_list = function () {
    // This function assumes we have already created the individual
    // sidebar rows.  Our job here is to build the bigger widget,
    // which largely is a matter of arranging the individual rows in
    // the right order.
    var streams = stream_data.subscribed_streams();
    if (streams.length === 0) {
        return;
    }

    streams = filter_streams_by_search(streams);

    var sort_recent = (streams.length > 40);
    var pinned_streams = [];
    var unpinned_streams = [];
    var parent = $('#stream_filters');
    var elems = [];

    function add_sidebar_li(stream) {
        var sub = stream_data.get_sub(stream);
        var sidebar_row = exports.stream_sidebar.get_row(sub.stream_id);
        if (sort_recent) {
            sidebar_row.update_whether_active();
        }
        elems.push(sidebar_row.get_li().get(0));
    }

    _.each(streams, function (stream) {
        var pinned = stream_data.get_sub(stream).pin_to_top;
        if (pinned) {
            pinned_streams.push(stream);
        } else {
            unpinned_streams.push(stream);
        }
    });

    pinned_streams.sort(util.strcmp);

    unpinned_streams.sort(function (a, b) {
        if (sort_recent) {
            if (stream_data.is_active(b) && ! stream_data.is_active(a)) {
                return 1;
            } else if (! stream_data.is_active(b) && stream_data.is_active(a)) {
                return -1;
            }
        }
        return util.strcmp(a, b);
    });

    streams = pinned_streams.concat(unpinned_streams);

    if (previous_sort_order !== undefined &&
        util.array_compare(previous_sort_order, streams) &&
        util.array_compare(previous_unpinned_order, unpinned_streams)) {
        return;
    }
    previous_sort_order = streams;
    previous_unpinned_order = unpinned_streams;
    parent.empty();

    if (pinned_streams.length > 0) {
        _.each(pinned_streams, add_sidebar_li);
        elems.push($('<hr class="pinned-stream-split">').get(0));
    }
    if (unpinned_streams.length > 0) {
        _.each(unpinned_streams, add_sidebar_li);
    }

    $(elems).appendTo(parent);
};

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-25 21:22 UTC

We should definitely figure out a way to break up this function so that there's a testable part and then some simple UI code.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-24 13:38 UTC

Yep, that's correct, @James Wang.  The model that I want to move us to is something like this:
* back ends send # of unread counts
* front end computes unread count from its local messages
* as long as the back end count > front end count, we trust the back end count and increment/decrement it as new messages either come in or get read
* if the front end count and back end count are the same (or become the same as you fetch old messages), then start to ignore the back end count and just use our current methodology

This sounds pretty complex, but I think we could mostly encapsulate it so that the rest of the JS code doesn't really care about the counting mechanism.  (We're already pretty much there, so all the surgery here is going to be in `unread.js`.)

## double-click bugs

*2017-03-24 to 2017-03-24 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/double-click.20bugs/with/178574)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-24 19:45 UTC

We have a class of bugs, or maybe a class of glitches, where users click on an action, and they don't get feedback from the server, so they click again on the action.  One example of this is doing a "reaction."  Short of doing a full-blown local-echo implementation for these type of things, I wonder if it makes sense for us to have some kind of general mechanism for preventing click spam.  Basically, it would be a thin layer that caches the key aspects of the server call for a couple seconds, and if a redundant request comes in a second later, we just ignore it.  This way we don't spam the server, and we avoid double-updates in the frontend, as well as making it easier for us to do `blueslip.error()` on real logical errors without getting false alarms for double clicks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-24 19:47 UTC

yeah, that's a good idea.  I think in retrospect that specific issue could have been a side effect of f3af0fe63516377f754c13650c25317269472fae (where the reaction would _never_ echo until you reload), but I think a little "ignore duplicate clicks if within 3s and we haven't gotten a response from the server" module that we could use might make sense.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-24 19:54 UTC

Just to be clear, the current behavior is that we don't have any crazy bugs, but we still have to wait for the server to render the reaction, correct?

  4     var url =  '/json/messages/' + message_id + '/emoji_reactions/' + emoji_name;

  6     if (in_flight.pending(fingerprint)) {

 10     in_flight.start(fingerprint);

 20 }

## settings lazy load

*2017-04-06 to 2017-04-06 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/settings.20lazy.20load/with/186039)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-06 21:08 UTC

@Tim Abbott I added more commits to #4429, and now `settings.js` is pretty well organized to implement lazy loading.  There are a couple possible schemes.  Each section requires three phases to load:
* render the section (done via partial now)
* render the data within the section (some sections actually have separate code to fill in the guts)
* start up click handlers

If we're **too** lazy about loading sections, then we just move the sluggishness to each section, which may actually feel worse to users than just having the up-front cost.

Right now the scheme is all sections are there, but we hide all but one.  We could go to a scheme where we swap out the HTML every time.  That might be kind of sub-optimal, too.

We can also just put the loads in a `setTimeout(f, 0)` call so that the initial page loads quickly.

Finally, we can have the page do all the outer renders at once, but lazily do the 2nd/3rd steps on an as-needed basis (and probably only once per visit to the gear menu).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-06 21:17 UTC

I think swapping out the HTML every time isn't super useful as an approach

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-06 21:22 UTC

I agree--the only advantage of that it minimizes stale data, but I think it would degrade browsing your settings.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-06 21:23 UTC

I'm mostly inclined to just lazily call the foo.set_up() method the first time the foo section is visited during a visit to settings.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-06 21:24 UTC

We could arguably pre-fetch the other sections, but I think that's mostly overkill.  Probably the only expensive section are uploads and muted topics (for long-time users), and we could optimize those individually later.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-06 21:27 UTC

yeah that approach works for me

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-06 21:28 UTC

the basic lazy approach, correct?  (not the pre-fetch)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-06 21:36 UTC

Yep

**Raghav Jajodia** · 2017-04-06 22:14 UTC

Awesome! Apart from improving the performance, this would also make it easier to navigate through the "settings" code
