**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-13 13:43 UTC

@Tim Abbott I just did some research on the mysterious trailing bookend sub/unsub buttons.  The repro is pretty simple.  Narrow to some stream, then have the other user subscribe you to a new stream.  This will go through `stream_events` to call `message_list.update_trailing_bookend`, which only checks that you're in a narrow.  That function doesn't verify that you're in the narrow that's related to stream event.  Instead, it just creates a button for your current narrow.  (It's not even passed in a stream parameter.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-13 20:15 UTC

If click on a topic in the left sidebar, @Tim Abbott, we need to figure out the desired semantics.  Here is what I propose:

* compose box closed: we should leave it closed, as agreed in #3886
* compose box opened but clear: I think we should just close it (but we could leave it open and update the recipients, which inconveniences readers in order to encourage writers)
* compose box has content: I think we should save a draft then close it (or we could leave it untouched, which risks a mix,  or we could save a draft and change the recipients)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-13 20:35 UTC

for compose-open-but-clear, I'm not sure.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-13 21:14 UTC

Ok, so then I think the basic logic we are agreeing to is this:

* closed -- leave closed
* clear -- make it closed
* has content -- leave it alone

Which essentially boils down to `if open-but-clear: close`.

So, there's been some problems with our frontend markdown renderer and I think I've narrowed the problem down to the `block.paragraph` regex in `third/marked/lib/marked.js`.

Pretty much, messages like `T\n#a` are broken into two paragraph tokens `T\n` and `#a` whereas messages like `T\n@a` aren't broken into two paragraph tokens, thus, breaking user mentions after line breaks.

However, I don't know how to solve this issue, so that `T\n@a` will also be broken into two paragraph tokens `T\n` and `@a`. Any suggestions are welcome :)

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-07-18 04:35 UTC

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-07-18 04:37 UTC

I changed the lines here:
```js
 748     if (cap = this.rules.usermention.exec(src)) {
 749       console.log("CAP: ");
 750       console.log(cap);
 751       src = src.slice(0, cap.index) + src.slice(cap.index + cap[0].length);
 752       // src = src.substring(cap[0].length);
 753       console.log("usermention SRC: " + src);
 754       out += this.usermention(cap[2] || cap[3], cap[1]);
 755       continue;
 756     }
```
which fixes the `src` issue, but `out` is now not in the right order..

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-07-18 05:34 UTC

We need something like `InlineLexer.prototype.inlineReplacement` for usermentions

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-07-18 06:35 UTC

I fixed it!!!!! @Tim Abbott @Steve Howell it ended up being a really trivial change

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-07-18 06:35 UTC

The usermention regex used to be `usermention: /^(@(?:\*\*([^\*]+)\*\*|(\w+)))/m`

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-07-18 06:36 UTC

But the `m` at the end kept on matching it on new lines, so all we had to do was discard that `m`

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-07-18 06:36 UTC

The new usermention regex would just be `usermention: /^(@(?:\*\*([^\*]+)\*\*|(\w+)))/`

Notes: It looks like IE9 + IE10 is at most .1% according to https://www.w3schools.com/browsers/browsers_explorer.asp. It also seems like Microsoft EOL'd them a while ago, and other SAAS companies started dropping support for them sometime last year.

## css selectors

*2017-05-04 to 2017-05-05 · 73 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/css.20selectors/with/195644)*

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-05-04 14:47 UTC

When skimming through a css file, I encountered this:
```.css
ul.filters i {
    padding-right: 0.25em;
    /* Make filter icons the same width so labels line up. */
    display: inline-block;
    width: 13px;
}

ul.filters .arrow {
    position: absolute;
    right: 2px;
    top: 2px;
    right: 4px;
    font-size: 0.8em;
    display: none;
}

ul.filters li:hover .arrow {
    display: inline;
    cursor: pointer;
    color: #888;
}
```
To me, it seems that `ul.filters` gets assigned a different value for the `display` property in every rule-set. Is this correct / what is its purpose?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 14:52 UTC

Those are scoped selectors.  `u.filters i` is a single selector, not a list of selectors, and its `{ ...}` section is defining the format for any `<i>` tag inside of a `<ul>` with the class of `filters`.

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-05-04 14:53 UTC

Aah, right, thanks. Now I remember, a list has to be separated by commas, right?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 14:54 UTC

Yep, and in our coding convention, you do this:

``` css
.blue1,
.blue2,
#blue3 {
    color: blue;
}
```

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-05-04 14:56 UTC

Something like the BEM methodology is useful http://getbem.com/introduction/

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-05-04 14:57 UTC

But even more simply, you should almost never have a complicated selector. Like in 99.9% of the code bases I've seen, the specificity of the selectors is higher than optimal (and 0.1% is lower, I guess ;) )

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-05-04 14:58 UTC

Instead of writing `ul.side-panel div li#something` you just write `.stream-active` and then the div itself has this very concrete class

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-05-04 15:00 UTC

Yes, that sounds reasonable!

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 15:04 UTC

Yep, nested selectors are very brittle.

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-05-04 15:05 UTC

Also, no ID selectors like `#stream` but all should be `.stream` - performance is the same. On the other hand, having long selectors is detrimental

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-05-04 15:06 UTC

In most cases, perf difference doesn't matter much, but maybe in a long chat window, it will. I know that GitHub had serious CSS selector perf issues for their code formatted views.

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-05-04 15:08 UTC

Wouldn't it theoretically be possible to precompress all IDs and classes into some short IDs before sending the page to the user?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 15:08 UTC

We've definitely had performance issues in the past related to the message pane.

With other things, like our sidebars, the issues haven't been performance so much; it's been more that we accidentally break stuff.  You think you're only changing the font size for something in the left sidebar, but then it actually also changes the buddy list.  Those kind of errors are really annoying, and we don't really have a good way to protect against those errors with tests currently, so we need to be better about the CSS organization itself.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 15:09 UTC

The string length of the IDs have almost nothing to do with performance.  It's more about how the browser has to represent these complicated rules internally to figure out how to render stuff.

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-05-04 15:10 UTC

Not the string length but the selector length: `.a .b .c .d` is way slower than `.more-specific-class`

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 15:11 UTC

The browser has a much easier time with this:

~~~ css
.topic-list-active-item-unread-count { ...}
~~~
 than this
~~~ css
.tl .al .uc { ...}
~~~

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-05-04 15:12 UTC

Hmm, yeah, makes sense.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 15:16 UTC

BEM is basically a win-win.  It's easier for the human to reason about, and it's more performant for the browser.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-05 01:34 UTC

I don't think that BEM is actually more performant at all.

Why would the browser have an easier time with `.topic-list-active-item-unread-count` than `.tl .al .uc`?

If you think about it from an algorithmic perspective, the former could literally be *any node in the DOM*, whereas the latter has to be at least three levels deep. That means that the long class name has to search exactly every node in the DOM whereas the second only has to search all nodes three or more levels deep.

Some browsers *may* (not certain) cache what nodes belong to a particular class which would give the first example a bit of a leg up, however the difference is inconsequential and completely unstandardized. Not all browsers even cache nodes by ID.

Aside from that, I've seen lots of sources that state that CSS selectors are not any kind of bottle neck. Rendering/layout, etc is.

Here's some JS examples of times for selectors:
https://benfrain.com/css-performance-revisited-selectors-bloat-expensive-styles/

This is very much one of those things where you should 100% do what is easiest to developers and not care about perf implications – because there are basically none.

Aside from that, there's also basically no point in pre-compressing stuff. With our code base it'd be basically impossible because we'd have to comb over javascript, css, and our templates (both handlebars and jinja) to do so. This would likely yield less than a percent or two savings in space. This kind of compression is what gzip is for, and we already use it!

But aside from that, the examples above with slow rendering has nothing to do with CSS selectors and everything to do with bad CSS – as in the message pane was slow not because of selectors but because for example `transform: scale` was used on emojis.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 01:47 UTC

@Brock Whittaker When the browser initially renders a document, it has to traverse all the nodes to render the document.  For each element it can do an O(1) lookup on the class to find the CSS  for its class.  But it has to navigate a more complicated data structure to find out all the nested selectors.

And then as the app runs, typically you're modifying individual nodes, and again the browser can do an O(1) mapping of class to the simple selector for that class.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 01:50 UTC

Also, we all agree that we don't need to pre-compress stuff.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-05 01:58 UTC

The browser does tons of tree updates all the time. You're making the assumption that classes are stored in some sort of dict/linked list form. I don't know if that's a valid assumption.

The reason why people use IDs is because they are supposed to be O(1). The issue is that you can have many of a class scattered around the document and it doesn't really mean they're connected at all, and as far as I've seen, I haven't ever found any docs saying that is the case.

Other perf tests here: https://jsperf.com/id-vs-class-vs-tag-selectors/2

Show that IDs are the fastest followed of course by tags and classes which would be implemented similarly I'd imagine.
The important take away here is all of these are still incredibly fast. Currently on my zulip page there are only 13,000 nodes, of which I can query all in 1ms. The most expensive selector I can create:

```js
$(".app .app-main .column-middle .tab-pane .message_list#main_div .message_table .recipient_row [zid]");
```

Takes 1ms to query 274 things. This also includes the huge cost of creating a new inner reference to the prototype that jQuery returns when sizzle is performed. CSS selectors are likely an order of magnitude faster.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 02:05 UTC

I'm making the very reasonable assumption that when a browser ingests this type of CSS...

~~~ css
#id1 { ... }
#id2 { .... }
.class1 {...}
.class2 {...}
~~~

...the browser creates a hash table mapping `.class2` -> `{...}`.

So whenever it encounters an element with class of `class2`, it can quickly style it.

You are probably correct that the browser is basically fast for all of this, but it seems incredibly logical to me that non-compound selectors are going to be more performant than compound selectors.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-05 02:17 UTC

There's no difference in the layout computation between those however, because think of it like this:

If we have the structure:

```html
<div class="a">
  <div class="b">
    <div class="c a_b_c"></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

The browser *still* has to go up the chain and apply all styles.

This means regardless of whether you do: `.a_b_c` or `.a .b .c`, it will still fetch the styles associated with either (as you stated), and then fetch the properties of the parents `.b` and `.a`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 02:29 UTC

It won't need to **incrementally** fetch the styles related to a and b, because in its depth-first traversal, it will already have figured out the styles for the outer elements that get applied to children.  The **incremental** problem is to figure out which styles apply to `.c` and `.a_b_c`.  It will do a hash lookup on both of those classes to find relevant CSS sections.  The hash values will be some kind of data structure that is going to clearly be optimized for finding `.a_b_c` more easily than `.a .b. .a_b_c`, and, then, on top of that, when it finds the simple rule for `.a_b_c`, it doesn't need to do any more computation.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 02:35 UTC

When you write this CSS:

~~~ css
.a .b .c .d .e { color: blue}
~~~

The browser creates a data structure like this:

~~~
.e -> {
  more_checks: [.d, .c, .b., a.]
  if_all_good: {color: blue}
}

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 02:37 UTC

In contrast to...

~~~ css
.no_nesting { color: red}
~~~

~~~
.no_nesting -> {color: red}
~~~

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-05 02:44 UTC

Yeah I definitely agree with the logic provided. I think it already is doing `more_checks` with everything however.

If you think about the example of common nesting where you have `header` inside of `section` inside of `article` for example, it still has to do `more_checks` essentially at every step, and the semantic `if_all_good` would always happen.

This is because color could be set by the `article` which is valid, but it inherits all those props, along with `header` as well. It's basically creating a struct with props that are valid and those get re-set at every new level deeper (unless !important).

So there's two different processes:

One in which starts at the lowest level (the node `.c.a_b_c` for example) and the only difference between nested selectors is that it WILL look up the tree (in a list of course) for `.b` and `.a`, which it won't do to apply `.a_b_c`, but it is already doing `more_checks` as a semantic on every node from the body downwards.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 02:50 UTC

Yeah, all I'm really saying is that the `more_checks` semantic is cheap for a simple selector.  Let's say your node is at `.world .north_america .us .ca .sf .soma .berry-street`.  If your CSS only has `.berry_street` in its hash table, it's a super-quick lookup.  Imagine instead your CSS looks like this:

~~~ css
.world .ca .berry_street { ...}
.world .or .berry_street { ... }
.north_america .soma .berry_street { ...}
~~~

The browser is going to have to evaluate all of those selectors to determine whether they get applied.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-05 03:38 UTC

I really just think of it like this:

There is a struct that is created that is set to default browser properties. It matches with `.article .section` and sets to `color: blue`. Then it matches with `.foo-header` and sets those properties which overwrites the color previously set. Then it sees `.article .foo-header` which is more specific and once again overwrites that selector's color property. The rule is approximately that the closest selector (in distance) to the node you are styling is the most powerful. If they're the same distance, the one with the most selectors closest to the node wins.

If you are narrowed to a topic, the selected item will have the signature `li.topic-list-item.active-sub-filter`.  And then this a typical selector ancestry working from the bottom up:

* li.topic-list-item.active-sub-filter
* ul.topic-list

* ul.filters

* #streams_list.zoom-out

* .left-sidebar

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-05 15:28 UTC

Okay, I was curious about this, so I tested it. Here's the JS:

```js
let article = document.querySelector("article");

for (let x = 0; x < 10000; x++) {
    document.body.appendChild(article.cloneNode(true));
}


const tests = {
    time: (callback, num) => {
        let d = new Date();
        for (let x = 0; x < num; x++)
            callback();
        return new Date() - d;
    },

    selectAll: () => {
        return tests.time(_ => document.querySelectorAll("*"), 100);
    },

    selectAllSections: () => {
        return tests.time(_ => document.querySelectorAll("section"), 100);
    },

    selectEasyClass: () => {
        return tests.time(_ => document.querySelectorAll(".c"), 100);
    },

    selectComplexClass: () => {
        return tests.time(_ => document.querySelectorAll("article div .c .r"), 100);
    }
};

let keys = Object.keys(tests);
// remove `time` from the iterable list.
Object.keys(tests).shift();

keys.forEach(testName => console.log(tests[testName]()));
```

And the markup: 

```html
<article class="article">
    <section>
        <header>
            <h1><span>Test</span><p>Test</p></h1>
            <blockquote cite="http://">
                test
            </blockquote>
            <p>Test</p>
        </header>
    </section>
    <div class="">
        <div class="c">
            test
            <a href="#" class="r">test</a>
        </div>
    </div>
</article>
```

Keep in mind this code creates a total of 110,000 nodes (currently 7x what Zulip has). Each of these selectors is run 100 times successively (something that cannot be cached by the browser), and you can see by the linear performance. Here's the results:

**selectAll:** 6.4ms/selection
**selectAllSections:** 2.0ms/selection
**selectEasyClass:** 2.1ms/selection
**selectComplexClass:** 2.8ms/selection

With CPU throttling on Chrome, we get linear performance degradation that correlates almost perfectly with the CPU throttle ratio; as we'd expect.
Modern phones would be the worst with dealing w/ these kinds of things and they're around 3-4x slower than my laptop (the average laptop is about 2x slower than mine; phones don't fall that far behind).

Now let's scale this back to Zulip. Since Zulip operates with around ~15,000 nodes at a given time in the DOM (starts at around 12,000 and increases when you open settings/admin, etc), and the search performance is linearly correlated to the number of nodes in the DOM, we can assume that a `$("*")` selection is around 1ms, and the rest of them are around 0.3ms per selection.

The most important thing here is that the **selectComplexClass** method *is* slower, but only by about 30% on something that takes less than a half a millisecond in my browser.

If we scale this to my computer on Zulip:

**selectAll:** 0.91ms/selection
**selectAllSections:** 0.28ms/selection
**selectEasyClass:** 0.30ms/selection
**selectComplexClass:** 0.40ms/selection

To a normal computer:

**selectAll:** 1.82ms/selection
**selectAllSections:** 0.56ms/selection
**selectEasyClass:** 0.60ms/selection
**selectComplexClass:** 0.80ms/selection

Phones like the iPhone 6/7, Galaxy S6/S7, Pixel, etc., are all as strong CPU-wise as the average laptop today. For older phones such as the iPhone 5s (released 4 years ago!) and modern not-top-of-the-line androids, they're about 2-3x slower, so:

**selectAll:** 4.55ms/selection
**selectAllSections:** 1.40ms/selection
**selectEasyClass:** 1.50ms/selection
**selectComplexClass:** 2.00ms/selection

So none of them at all are anywhere near 20-30ms, and barely start approaching an order of magnitude lower.

This of course neglects to mention that most of our queries aren't even done from the DOM level but rather the level of for example the left sidebar, which may only be 450 nodes, so you can cut down the cost to 1/30th of the previous assessments.

Selector query time is a huge non-issue, especially because we actually have real performance issues due to less-than-great CSS and some inefficient JS.

I'm not as passionate either way about adopting something like BEM. I see the merit in it, but we should absolutely not do it under the guise of performance.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 15:35 UTC

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-05 15:41 UTC

Correct, but the algorithm for determining which CSS matches a node is approximately the same for finding a node in the DOM, just backwards.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-05 15:42 UTC

So it's a pretty good bellwether of CSS selector performance, except it's likely much faster because you aren't mallocing large arrays, producing JS objects, and all that nonsense.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 15:45 UTC

The algorithms are actually quite different, I believe.  When you try to find DOM nodes that match a selector, all you have to do is basically walk down a tree.  When you try to find CSS nodes that apply to a given DOM node, you have the problem of determining for each CSS node whether it's selector matches the DOM node, which can be pretty deeply nested.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 15:46 UTC

And even if you can do the lookup for each node in, say, 200 microseconds, for 1000 nodes that adds up to 200 milliseconds, which gets you in the non-negligible range of performance.

*2017-05-16 to 2017-10-11 · 30 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/typescript/with/203666)*

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-05-16 18:47 UTC

There is a push for more frontend test coverage at PyCon. What do you think about over the long term migrating to typescript? It would allow static typing on the frontend js assets. We could do it in a gradual way similar to how we did with python types.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-05-16 18:50 UTC

yeah, so one of the projects that could be good to push on at PyCon is using webpack more fully, which would enable doing that sort of thing

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-16 18:59 UTC

@Paul Weaver Any thoughts on typescript vs. flow?  (I haven't used either, and the only JS transpiler I've really worked with is coffeescript.)

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-05-16 19:09 UTC

Both are good :)

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-05-16 19:16 UTC

I have never really used flow but here is my understanding of the advantages and disadvantages:

**Typescript**
* A compiler and has more powerful syntax and potential for leveraging types
* Has better editor support
* Has much better external library definitions (we have to write definitions for any external libraries we use which don't already have them)

**Flow**
* Just a static checker
* Slightly closer to existing javascript syntax
* Easier to insert piecemeal into an existing app

The seem to have similar syntax. Both of them are similar to or use ES6/7 syntax in terms of functionality.

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-05-16 19:20 UTC

I think I would make a decision on which one to use based on:
How easy it would be to partially migrate js files to typescript and how many of our external dependencies have flow or typescript definitions.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-16 19:21 UTC

I'm not super concerned about our external dependencies, apart from jQuery support.  I think the ability to partially migrate would be the bigger deciding factor.

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-05-16 19:22 UTC

Typescript Types:
https://github.com/DefinitelyTyped/DefinitelyTyped/tree/master/types
Flow Types:
https://github.com/flowtype/flow-typed/tree/master/definitions/npm

**Shayan Toqraee** · 2017-05-16 19:24 UTC

See this blog post: https://blog.mariusschulz.com/2017/01/13/typescript-vs-flow
Also read the comments at the end. There is a small and good discussion there.

**Shayan Toqraee** · 2017-05-16 19:25 UTC

Last time I read that, I concluded that there is no disadvantage of using typescript.

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-05-16 19:28 UTC

In terms of tooling, Typescript works best with VSCode while Flow works with Nuclide (IDE build on top of Atom)

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-05-16 19:31 UTC

@Steve Howell The reason external dependency types are important for checking that calls to those libraries type check correctly (or at all). If we use an external library and there aren't type files specified, we have to write our own, which can get very obnoxious for some libraries. It makes the migration process harder.

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-05-16 19:34 UTC

Yep, for TypeScript, the existence of DefinitelyTyped is *definitely* an advantage

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-16 19:34 UTC

Yep, make sense.  I will rephrase a bit:

* jQuery is by far our biggest external dependency
* I think we can mostly wrap other external dependencies
* My gut says that the static type checker will mostly help us deal with refactorings and merge conflicts that deal with internal interactions among the ~130 Zulip modules.

My gut is that typescript would be better choice and the biggest risk is figuring out how the transition would work without being disruptive.

## compose box

*2017-06-13 to 2017-12-11 · 97 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/compose.20box/with/226011)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 13:29 UTC

We've had two separate threads of conversation about the compose box recently, so I thought it would be useful to explain how the compose box works currently.
* Two of our users were surprised that the compose box stayed open with the message-in-progress while switching to a PM narrow.
* New users often can't figure out how to reply to a new message.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 13:34 UTC

First,  I'll enumerate the ways to open the compose box:
* Click on a message to reply.
* Hit enter or "r" to reply.
* Hit "c" or "C" to compose a stream/private message.
* Click on a user's name in the buddy list.
* Choose one of the first two options in the popup menu when you click on a user.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 13:35 UTC

Once the compose box is open, we leave it open, even after you send a message.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 13:36 UTC

The user can explicitly close the compose box using these actions:
* hit escape
* click the "x" icon in the compose box
* click somewhere else in the app

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 13:37 UTC

The cause of all this is very simple. It is that we violate the principle: 'Do not surprise your users with your UI'.
While I was impressed with Joshua's command of the hot keys, the majority of people do not use them. 
Also the majority of people even who use Zulip do not live in it, like we do.
As such, you should consider yourself as the outlier among outliers (not only you are a dev working on Zulip, but you've used and shaped it for years)

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 13:38 UTC

The number of ways a user can do a thing is irrelevant. Relevant is if any of these ways are obvious. So 5 ways to do it none if them obvious is worse than a single way, but obvious. Even better is many ways, most of them obvious, others easily learnable.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 13:39 UTC

Generally the reasons that a user will explicitly close the compose box fit into the following categories:
* The user wants more screen real estate to read messages.  (This is especially important on small devices.)
* The user wants to page through the feed with page up and page down.
* The user wants to use hotkeys like "n" to advance to the next topic.
* The user wants to ensure that they don't send a message accidentally (and, of course, we create a draft, in case they change their mind).

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 13:39 UTC

UI is hard, because even with good intentions, and desire to teach the user, users already 'know' how to use similar apps. What is easy to them is what is familiar. If we don't have good reason to change how a thing works compared to a different app, we shouldn't. And my argument is that in that case we don't have a good reason to.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 13:40 UTC

If you choose certain narrowing actions, the system will close the compose box automatically, to prevent "mixes," which are generally just mildly annoying, but which can occasionally be embarrassing.

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 13:41 UTC

Screen real estate is very easily solvable. The compose box takes about 4 lines of text and it can take 2 with minimal code changes, and one with a bit more (ala FB Messenger on mobile)

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 13:42 UTC

To become two lines: 
* default height of text input becomes one line instead of two (as any other chat app)
* buttons below it go to the top right taking single line with 'recipient'

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 13:44 UTC

There are two main aspects of Zulip that make it different than other chat apps:
* We emphasize asynchronous communication, so it's often the case that folks are spending time catching up on 100s of messages, so reading is more important than sending messages.
* Our threaded model lends itself more to interleaved views where there is a danger of "mixing."

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 13:48 UTC

There's obviously some tension between different user needs.  And, as always, there are probably things that we can do to improve everybody's experience that don't involve serious tradeoffs.  But some decisions will have tradeoffs, so we should be thoughtful about changing the app's current behavior, as a lot of thought went into the way it currently works, and that thought process was influenced by literally thousands of users using the app on public forums that we monitor.

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 13:53 UTC

(deleted)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 14:01 UTC

If we want to experiment with a different paradigm, then we should decide a couple things for the experiment:
* Do we force the users to keep the compose box open all the time and disable all of our hotkeys?
* Do we keep the compose box open all the time, but allow users to defocus the compose box so they can do paging and use the hotkeys?  (And maybe allow users to clear the compose box when they're abandoing a message.)
* How do we prevent mixes?

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 14:06 UTC

* Yes. Hotkeys can be Ctrl+same key when you are in the compose box
* Yes. All chat apps allow defocus
* Have three 'modes':
  * send to current narrow
  * send to stream (current New Topic)
  * PM

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 14:07 UTC

Let's take a specific issue.  If I'm in  a narrow and I want to page back in the conversation, are you proposing that I have to hit control-page-up to scroll up?

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 14:13 UTC

This specific issue: Page-up can also be enabled to do the same even if you have focused the compose box input.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-13 14:13 UTC

Does this mean you can't use page-up inside the message when composing a long message?

**Boris Yankov** · 2017-06-13 14:14 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-14 00:05 UTC

> All chat apps allow defocus

This surprised me, so I did a quick check: in Slack, although if you click outside the compose box it does change appearance so that it looks defocused, in reality if you start typing, what you type goes right back in the compose box. Effectively, it's always focused. And all their hotkeys require keychords, with a couple of odd exceptions (like "up" for editing the last message sent.)

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-14 00:10 UTC

In general I agree with Steve that having an always-open compose box would probably require serious compromises to our reading / catching-up experience, because of the screen real estate (on smaller screens) and because of the interference with hotkeys.

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-14 00:12 UTC

Or if it's not always focused, that that would be likely to be very confusing for a lot of users. Because an unfocused compose box is going to look a lot like a focused one, I worry it'd risk being a cause of confusion and friction permanently, even after someone has used Zulip for a while.

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-14 00:26 UTC

We've gotten the feedback a number of times that many people are puzzled at how to send a message when they first use Zulip, so I definitely think this is an important area to improve.

But I think it's a problem that is specific to when a user is first getting started -- I haven't yet seen any reason to think that once a user gets going with sending messages (replies, new topics, and PMs) it's at all common to have any trouble with it thereafter. Conversely, I think the user experience that we have now for users who have figured out the basics is a really good one.

And, crucially, this is an app meant for people to use through the day, every day. So a typical user spends many, many more hours in the "have figured out the basics" state than minutes in the "figuring it out" state. I think we should therefore be very reluctant to make significant compromises in the main experience for the sake of the onboarding experience.

I'd much rather focus on solutions that are specific to the onboarding experience. I think there are still a lot of things for us to try there -- we've just gotten started.

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-14 00:31 UTC

s/hotkeys/keyboard navigation/g above -- I just saw Steve's remark this morning at  https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/frontend/subject/roadmap/near/226382 , and I'm 100% in agreement :)

## development processes

*2017-06-13 to 2017-06-16 · 39 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/development.20processes/with/226174)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 17:02 UTC

One of the major things I want to talk about during this meeting is our development processes for the frontend

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 17:02 UTC

Just to give context, I probably spend 3x as much time doing review work on a frontend change of a given size as I do for a similar backend change

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 17:04 UTC

There's a few reasons behind this:
* Backend has really awesome test coverage, where'as the frontend doesn't
* Frontend changes have more subtle details that impact the user experience, just by their nature
* There's UI to discuss in addition to just the code part of the system
* The frontend codebase is a bit messier than the backend codebase
* The web frontend is under more active change than the backend

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 17:04 UTC

But I'd like to talk with the group about how we can make frontend changes move more quickly, since I think it's really important to the overall success of the project that we can do so

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 17:05 UTC

Some ideas that I've come up with for accelerating things include:
* Increasing test coverage (we've been working on node, but we could also do that on casper)
* Having multiple people work on a given component so that they can review work with each other
* Developing better habits for sharing screenshots/brief videos of changes to make it easy to review the UI without checking out the code

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 17:05 UTC

I'd love to discuss these and also hear other folks' ideas

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-06-13 17:09 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 17:10 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 17:10 UTC

But Casper is great for UI elements, like the emoji picker

It encourages you to use module importing instead. This is the pain point with the migration to webpack. We have to make sure every existing gl …
i'm a little bit confused - are you saying that there is a way for webpack to bundle and transpile our javascript files without having to have their dependencies declared through ES6/CommonJS?

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-06-14 03:43 UTC

Yes, normally when you declare a webpack bundle there is one entry point which imports the rest of the files.
In our case every file is an entry point. Since they are declared in order all we need to to have webpack properly export all global variables currently exported and the transpiled javascript will function the same as the current one under closure.

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-06-14 04:00 UTC

There are currently three ways to do this. 
* script-loader just loads the file without any compilation. We use this to load minified third party assets (and skip expensive compilation steps), katex, jquery, zxcvbn
* expose-loader sets the module to a global variable. This allows exporting to the global scope modules like Util or debug.
* If a function or object is set on the window object directly, it will be exposed to the global scope. (This is basically what expose-loader does internally)

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-06-14 04:03 UTC

If this seems a little hacky, that is because it is. Our javascript currently loads all modules in order, modules set global variables and other modules consume them. It can be a little fragile which is why we want to move to a es2015/commonjs import, but it is important to break up this from the migration to webpack so it can be done in small steps.

**Paul Weaver** · 2017-06-14 04:13 UTC

Added a tracking issue at #5377

- variable identifiers from `const` declarations cannot be reassigned
- `let` prevents  sneaky bugs from the 'temporal dead zone', when variables are referenced prior to assignment due to hoisting

I wouldn't consider this to be high priority, but figured it would make sense to bring it up while webpack migrations are in progress.

not 100% sure, but what you're suggesting makes sense to me

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-06-21 19:23 UTC

Our default value of 0.5 is an overkill. `zxcvbn` rejects most passwords (unless it is really large) without a warning message when it is at 0.5.  We should probably make it 0.3 or something. @Rishi Gupta

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-06-21 19:24 UTC

#3190 is a relevant PR to this issue where we introduced minimum value for quality for the first time.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-06-21 19:29 UTC

>The scenario Zulip uses is one where an the attacker breaks into the Zulip server and steals the hashed passwords; in that case, with a slow hash, the attacker would be able to make roughly 10,000 attempts per second.  E.g. a password with quality 0.5 (the default), it would take an attacker about 16
 hours to crack such a password in this sort of offline attack.

We have to choose between security and user friendliness(ease of on boarding) here :)

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-21 19:34 UTC

zxcvbn and min_password_length are turned off by default (commented out in the default settings file shipped with zulip), so 0 makes sense as the default.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-06-21 19:37 UTC

Okay makes sense.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-21 19:37 UTC

I agree that empirically, zxcvbn does not seem production ready at the .5 level, and as some evidence in that direction, dropbox itself doesn't enforce the zxcvbn recommendations. **Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-21 19:40 UTC

And nice find on the original PR, was looking for it earlier :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-26 20:47 UTC

Note that we have default set in DEFAULT_SETTINGS.  You folks should read http://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/settings.html for a full explanation, but our settings model is that anything that's commented out in `prod_settings.py` has a default in DEFAULT_SETTINGS.  (and maybe we should make that doc clearer)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-26 20:48 UTC

@Greg Price would you be up for doing an analysis for what quality level we want to make the default?  I think it's possible we want to have a weaker threat model be what we secure against by default, but this is something that requires some care.

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-26 20:49 UTC

Sure

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-27 02:57 UTC

haha, I did read that documentation page in trying to understand this. I'll add a sentence or two to update it.

For zxcvbn, I understand it better now, and I think the problem can probably be solved with a better error message + communication as to what is going on (I can think through what the right thing here is). 
https://github.com/dropbox/zxcvbn#usage is useful reading. Our current default setting of $$.5$$ corresponds to $$10^{8.7}$$ guesses.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-28 03:54 UTC

Reading the prod_settings_template file, there seems to be a healthy mix of optional settings where:
* `SETTING_NAME = default_value`, where `SETTING_NAME = default_value` in `settings.py` (e.g. MAX_FILE_UPLOAD_SIZE)
* `SETTING_NAME = default_value`, where there is no corresponding setting in `settings.py` (e.g. SSO_APPEND_DOMAIN)
* `# SETTING_NAME = default_value`, where `SETTING_NAME = default_value` in `settings.py`(e.g. PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH)

It seems like we should stick to one or two of the three patterns? Maybe 1 and 2? Or 2 and 3? I think that would make the story behind the settings file clearer both for people installing zulip, and developers.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-28 19:37 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-04-14 00:54 UTC

We just merged #18075 which switches our translation library from i18next to [FormatJS](https://formatjs.io/). (This is the same library at the core of React Intl, which is already used by zulip-mobile, but without the React layer.) This changes the syntax of translated strings in frontend JavaScript modules and Handlebars templates. FormatJS uses the standard ICU MessageFormat, which notably interpolates variables with `{braces}` instead of `__underscores__`, and the HTML escaping details are different. See our [documentation](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/translating/internationalization.html#frontend-translations).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-14 01:11 UTC

This change is really valuable; I'm glad we managed to get it in before the 4.0 release.

One thing I'd like to highlight is that all PRs that use `i18n.t` will need to be modified when rebased across this change.

We actually scroll the stream into view, even if you're narrowed to a specific topic.  We may want to actually only ensure that the topic is in view. ## huddle sorting

*2017-07-04 to 2017-07-05 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/huddle.20sorting/with/242584)*

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-07-04 21:26 UTC

I've been working on #5612 today, but have gotten a bit stuck on finding an efficient way to do it. I was thinking maybe carry around a list of recent group pms, though it could be annoying in that you have to account for the order (e.g. `alice,bob,charlie` is the same as `bob,charlie,alice`)

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-07-04 21:26 UTC

Any thoughts? (or is this even a feature worth the extra code clutter)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-04 21:48 UTC

@Cory Lynch I'm not sure.  We area already keeping track of recent group PM threads for other elements in the UI, and if we track them as a set of user IDs, I imagine it wouldn't be too hard to compute those group PM threads that only contain users in your search so far and for typeahead purposes just sort any users in the group that are not already used.  E.g. if you're autocompleting Aa,Bb,Cc,Dd,Ee, and the user's typed `Aa,Bb,D`, you're offer `Aa,Bb,Dd,Cc,Ee`

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-04 21:49 UTC

I feel like we should strive for really simple behavior here.  Find your last 10 huddles and show them in recency order and filter by what you've typed so far.  Trying to do fancier things than that might not only complicate the implementation; they might also not really help the user.

    var stream_groups = stream_sort.sort_groups(get_search_term());

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-07-06 02:12 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-06 02:21 UTC

I just looked at all my drafts, and they're all jibberish.  So I'm not really on board with #5591.  I think we want to be pretty passive about opening drafts, like it should only be when you open the compose box on a narrow that was super recent.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-06 02:22 UTC

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-07-06 02:22 UTC

**Cory Lynch** · 2017-07-06 02:22 UTC

hmm

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-25 14:56 UTC

I think what's happening is that mousenter event on the plus icon causes the tooltip to render, which hides the plus icon, which simulates a mouseleave event, which closes the tooltip, which makes the mouse appear to be over the plus icon again, which triggers the mouseenter event, which causes the tooltip to render, and yada yada yada.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-25 14:59 UTC

It seems that changing `width` to `max-width` is the trick.  The `tooltip` library has to do a lot of pos/height/width calculations to avoid this, and I think setting the width to 600px messes up situations where the toolbar would be to the left of the widget.

## send_message_socket

*2017-07-11 to 2017-07-11 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/send_message_socket/with/247594)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-11 18:03 UTC

@Tim Abbott I am starting to resurrect Mahim's PR on send timeouts, and I'm wondering if we want to move to just once mechanism for sending messages.  Right now we have this:

~~~ js
304 exports.transmit_message = function (request, success, error) {
305     delete exports.send_times_data[request.id];
306     if (page_params.use_websockets) {
307         send_message_socket(request, success, error);
308     } else {
309         send_message_ajax(request, success, error); 
310     }                
311 };
~~~

I wonder if we should decide which mechanism is better in terms of reliability/performance/maintainability and just go with the better option.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-11 19:27 UTC

@Steve Howell unfortunately, I believe we have some users who need to use the `send_message_ajax` code path because of issues with their networking environment.  So we need to keep both code paths.  We could probably refactor them to have minimal differences, though.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-11 19:29 UTC

If send_message_socket is hard is less reliable, should we just always use `send_message_ajax`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-11 19:40 UTC

## JS timeouts

*2017-07-13 to 2017-07-13 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/JS.20timeouts/with/249750)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-13 17:30 UTC

Do we agree that short-duration JS timers aren't really worth canceling if you can properly handle state at the end of the timeout?

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-07-13 17:37 UTC

Can you elaborate on what you mean by "properly handle state"? And by cancel do you mean `clearInterval`/`clearTimeout`?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-13 17:43 UTC

I mean `clearTimeout`.  By being able to properly handle state, I just mean that after 5 seconds, I can easily determine that everything that was supposed to happen did happen, and early-return.  (The concrete scenario is making sure that we get get messages acked, and there are two things that need to happen in the 5 second interval, in possibly different orders.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-13 17:45 UTC

I think it probably depends on the situation, but I can certainly imagine cases where rather than clearing a timeout, we set some state that is checked afterwards.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-07-13 17:45 UTC

Why aren't we just using flags to check if the callbacks have both finished and then actually calling back?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-13 17:47 UTC

I think that's what is being suggested as an alternative to clearing timeouts?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-13 17:47 UTC

Let's say you are waiting for apples, oranges, and carrots to arrive, and they all have to be there in the hour.  The simple approach is set your phone timer for an hour, and at the end of the hour, make sure you have all your food.  Or, as each fruit/veggie arrives, you could take inventory and cancel your alarm.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-07-13 17:47 UTC

Is there positive benefit to this action happening sooner than an hour (or 5 seconds), or does it not matter?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-13 17:48 UTC

The only benefit that I can think of is just cleaning up some JS memory for timers.  But it comes at a tiny bit of complexity, and my gut feeling is that JS's timers are super cheap.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-13 17:49 UTC

I think using `clearTimeout` is important for cases like the typing notifications, where one also has to worry about duplicates.  But that doesn't apply in this context, which if I'm not mistaken is the context of alerting if a message wasn't confirmed delivered?

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-07-13 17:49 UTC

You don't have to worry about GC with `setTimeout`.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-07-13 17:50 UTC

They are automatically cleaned up once executed or once you use `clearTimeout`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-13 17:50 UTC

Ok, I feel like we're all on the same page, more or less, so I'm gonna go the not-clearing route for now.  It shouldn't be too hard to change our mind on this.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-07-13 17:51 UTC

The only issue with the class is with `setInterval`, for obvious de-referencing reasons.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-13 17:52 UTC

The only GC concern is holding on for memory for 5 seconds when I could theoretically release it in 1 seconds.  I'm doing this for multiple events (every message sent), but not nearly enough to worry about.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-07-13 18:00 UTC

GC doesn't run that rapidly in the browser anyways generally, so I really don't think it matters.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-17 12:55 UTC

@Tim Abbott Do we want to limit the number of messages we'll locally echo to some small value like 3?  Right now the limit is 100, which is mostly a quirk of the implementation.  Unless somebody is a really fast typist, getting ahead by 4+ messages usually indicates you are in a somewhat bad state.  Even if you're only on a really slow network connection, and you're otherwise fine,  it's probably good to slow down just to be able to wait for other incoming messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-17 18:11 UTC

possibly; I think it's a low priority compared to giving people clear feedback when their messages are failing to send.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-17 18:17 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-17 18:19 UTC

If you have a locally echoed message get an actual failure response from the server, we currently have the red "x" icon to cancel the message....

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-17 18:20 UTC

..and it works at first.  Only on the subsequent sent message do you have problems, caused by reusing the id, I believe.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-17 18:22 UTC

Here is the code that naively re-uses the id when you abort a failed message:

~~~
 39 function get_next_local_id() {
 40     var local_id_increment = 0.01;
 41     var latest = page_params.max_message_id;
 42     if (typeof message_list.all !== 'undefined' && message_list.all.last() !== undefined) {
 43         latest = message_list.all.last().id;
 44     }
 45     latest = Math.max(0, latest);
 46     return truncate_precision(latest + local_id_increment);
 47 }

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-17 18:23 UTC

Here is the code that lets 100 messages queue up, and which we could fix with a one-line fix:

~~~ js
106     var next_local_id = get_next_local_id();
107     if (next_local_id % 1 === 0) {
108         blueslip.error("Incremented local id to next integer---100 local messages queued");
109         return undefined;
110     }

~~~

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-17 18:42 UTC

Hmm, yeah, we should definitely fix the reuse bug regardless :)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-17 18:50 UTC

A fix that would work for both is say that next_local_id = floor(max_id) + 0.01, and then just punt on local echo if the id has already been used.  This simplifies the code and prevents several problems:
* It prevents you from re-using an aborted local id.
* It prevents you from getting too far ahead of the server, which leads to confusing reordering.
* It prevents some subset of runaway-local-id scenarios.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 18:09 UTC

I am 75% sure that `everyone` is an alias for `all`.  Since mentions only apply to messages, and messages can only go to recipients, I think mentions are inherently limited to stream recipients when you send the message to a stream.

If you want to get the attention of everybody in your realm, you want to use a stream where nearly everybody is subscribed, which is conventionally the #**announce** stream.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 18:26 UTC

@Cory Lynch is cleaning up some of our stranger jQuery idioms as part of the jQuery upgrade.  One of my pet peeves is that we say `$foo.toggleClass('yo', true)` instead `$foo.addClass('yo')`. **Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 18:28 UTC

## perfect scrollbars on /help

*2017-08-23 to 2017-08-23 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/perfect.20scrollbars.20on.20.2Fhelp/with/271697)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-08-23 00:49 UTC

We currently use perfect-scrollbar on https://chat.zulip.org/help, which means that searching for something (via browser search) in the left sidebar doesn't scroll the view. 

Readthedocs just doesn't put a visible/clickable scrollbar there: http://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

Thoughts on what we should do about this? I think "search not jumping to the link in the left sidebar" is a pretty high cost to pay, and possibly not having a scrollbar at all is indeed better.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-23 00:51 UTC

@Rishi Gupta agreed, I'd rather have no scrollbar there than have search not working.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-23 00:52 UTC

@Brock Whittaker is there a better alternative to perfectScrollbar that we can use on /help/?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-23 00:52 UTC

(Also, I don't really understand why perfectScrollbar would break browser search?)

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-08-23 00:52 UTC

Because perfectScrollbar changes the position to absolute and then uses transformations to change the position. A browser won't know to do that to see an item. It will just see that it is "locked" in absolute position.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-08-23 00:52 UTC

It's just not semantically correct.

**Shayan Toqraee** · 2017-08-23 07:35 UTC

I think that it means that the prefectScrollbar is broken. I have seen customized scrollbars in many websites, they didn't have such problems.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-23 07:37 UTC

Yeah, I think we need to use something else for that page.

Fixed
```diff
diff --git a/static/styles/zulip.css b/static/styles/zulip.css
index a8445a0..f8d058e 100644
--- a/static/styles/zulip.css
+++ b/static/styles/zulip.css
@@ -1860,9 +1860,6 @@ nav a .no-style {
 }
 
 #search_arrows {
-    margin-left: -4px;
-    margin-bottom: 5px;
-
     /* Bootstrap wants font-size: 0 to eliminate space between
        the buttons.  We need to inherit the font size, so we
        remove the button gap by adjusting "letter" spacing. */
```

@Craig Rodrigues thanks for looking into this stuff!  I think we basically have a few options:

* Switch our CasperJS backend to SlimerJS, which is an existing alternative to PhantomJS
* Invest effort contributing a Headless Chrome backend to CasperJS

## local echo timestamps

*2017-09-26 to 2017-09-26 · 24 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/local.20echo.20timestamps/with/287477)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-26 16:47 UTC

I am seeing this data in my dev environment when I send messages and add some consoles to the local echo code:

~~~
INSIDE process_from_server  echo.js:217:9
client 1506444332.509  echo.js:220:13
server 1506444333  echo.js:221:13
diff 0.4909999370574951  echo.js:222:13
INSIDE process_from_server  echo.js:217:9
client 1506444336.822  echo.js:220:13
server 1506444336  echo.js:221:13
diff -0.8220000267028809

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-26 16:51 UTC

A couple observations:
* Even on a fast local connection, the server's response can easily arrive in the next one-second interval, as demonstrated by the first set of data.
* If the client uses decimal precision and the server uses integer precision, the server message can appear older than the client message.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-26 16:55 UTC

For the decimal precision thing, it probably makes sense to round timestamps to integers on the client, since we don't ever show timestamps with more than one-second granularity, and since ordering is based on message id, not timestamp, for any two messages sent in the same second.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-26 16:58 UTC

Then, if we compare messages at one-second granularity, I know that there will be some cases where the server timestamp matches the client timestamp, but most messages will cross the one-second boundary due to being either sent "late in the second," or being sent over a slow network, or being slow to render, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-26 17:00 UTC

So I'm wondering if it makes sense to just always re-render messages once the server sends us message events.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-26 17:01 UTC

There are a few different approaches we can take:
* always re-render full messages
* re-render full messages if either content or rounded timestamp changes
* only re-render for content changes, and more surgically fix timestamps by poking into the dom

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-26 18:19 UTC

So the local-echo code is still kinda hard to read, but I found out where it updates timestamps in the UI.  It does it via `ui.show_local_message_arrived`, which does some strange throttling to update timestamps.  The function `echo.process_from_server` either bulk-renders the new messages (if any of them have updated content) or calls `ui.show_local_message_arrived`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-26 18:19 UTC

Hmm, interesting question.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-26 18:20 UTC

I think we shouldn't poke the DOM for timestamps, because the `timerender` objects (which are used to handle things like date changes) don't really expect to be edited via poking.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-26 18:20 UTC

So I'd probably go for option 2 (there are significant benefits to not re-rendering the full message in most cases)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-26 18:20 UTC

In particular, I think the browser flickers the avatar when it rerenders a message.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-26 18:20 UTC

~~~ js
105 var local_messages_to_show = [];
106 var show_message_timestamps = _.throttle(function () {
107     _.each(local_messages_to_show, function (message_id) {

110         });
111     });
112     local_messages_to_show = [];
113 }, 100);
114 
115 exports.show_local_message_arrived = function (message_id) {
116     local_messages_to_show.push(message_id);
117     show_message_timestamps();
118 };

~~~

        var cur_window_size = this._render_win_end - this._render_win_start;                      
        if (cur_window_size < this._RENDER_WINDOW_SIZE) {                                         
            var msgs_to_render_count = this._RENDER_WINDOW_SIZE - cur_window_size;                
            var slice_to_render = messages.slice(messages.length - msgs_to_render_count);         
            this.render(slice_to_render, 'top', false);                                           
            this._render_win_start -= slice_to_render.length;                                     
        }                                                                                         
    },                                                                                            
```

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 14:14 UTC

I just modified a test in our js node test suite, and stumbled over zjquery. For someone who never touched these frontend tests, it felt counterintuitive to see normal jquery functions applied in surrounding code,  while the own jquery calls (in my case `append` failed. Would it make sense to elaborate on this in http://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing-with-node.html?

Additionally, it might be worth mentioning why normal jquery calls don't work (which was not immediately clear to me). http://quaintous.com/2015/07/31/jqery-node-mystery/ helped me for understanding the latter.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:21 UTC

We want to document zjquery better eventually.  Part of the issue here is that it's completely new--we mostly built it at the PyCon sprints, and the only a few of us have had focused time to work on it.  It's good to get some feedback here on what's tricky.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:23 UTC

@Robert Hönig Can you give this a quick read?

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/frontend_tests/node_tests/zjquery.js

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:24 UTC

I'm not sure exactly what you mean by "counterintuitive to see normal jquery functions applied in surrounding code".  Do you mean in the test code or the actual code?

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 14:26 UTC

That was part of my initial confusion: I saw jQuery-ish code in the tests and wondered why my jQuery calls wouldn't work. I hand't realized yet that those calls are actually for zjquery.

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 14:26 UTC

So in the test code.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:29 UTC

Hmmm, we should figure out a way to make that more obvious.  We're a little bit constrained by wanting to mimic the `$` namespace, since we're essentially doing deep stubbing.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:30 UTC

The modules that do deep stubbing have this at the top:

~~~
set_global('$', global.make_zjquery());

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:33 UTC

For situations where zjquery gives you a false negative, there are usually two possible resolutions:
* In some cases, `zjquery` simply is incomplete, and you need to add new functionality there, and I can help with that.
* You may be using a jquery idiom in the actual code that's different from the rest of the codebase.  Even though your actual code may be correct, it's possible there's a simpler or more Zulip-conventional way to do what you need.

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 14:34 UTC

So I think the second case should be covered by the linter?

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 14:36 UTC

> In some cases, zjquery simply is incomplete, and you need to add new functionality there, and I can help with that.

Yup, that's the second issue I had. In my case, I tried to use the `append` function that essentially does smt like `element.innerHTML += ...`. I didn't really know how to add it to `new_elem`, since it didn't have an `innerHTML` attribute, and `html` was just an empty stub.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:36 UTC

Assuming it's the second case (for your particular situation, we don't know yet, of course), we'll want to analyze it a little further before using the linter to lock things down.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:38 UTC

For `append`, I think what we generally do is just directly stub out `append` in your own test, so that you can make assertions about what's being appended.  Let me see if I can find an example of that...

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 14:39 UTC

That's what I did in the end :)

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 14:39 UTC

Reading through `node_tests/zjquery.js`, it seems quite similar to https://github.com/cheeriojs/cheerio in functionality.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:40 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/frontend_tests/node_tests/stream_list.js#L91

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:44 UTC

I think `cheerio` is solving a slightly different problem, and it mostly seems like an alternative to JSDOM.  We might want `cheerio` for our template tests, where we just want jquery-like helpers to quickly inspect that we wrote the DOM correctly.  For all of our other tests, we are more interested in the browser-interaction part of jquery, which is why we made zjquery.

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 14:49 UTC

Re: 
> In some cases, zjquery simply is incomplete, and you need to add new functionality there, and I can help with that.

It would also be helpful if we could overwrite the default error `TypeError: $(...).append is not a function` one gets now to a more specific `zjquery does not yet support the function ...`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 14:52 UTC

We should solve that generically, although it would take me a while to track down the JS equivalent of Python's `__getattr__`.

For `append`, I think we actually want a specific message that directs you to create your own `append`function in the tests.  (We specifically make `zjquery` stupid about DOM, so `append` is sort of hard to emulate in `zjquery`.)

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-10-16 15:04 UTC

If this is anything we intend to iterate on, what I found for generically overriding an objects getter is making the object a [Proxy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Proxy). All its fundamental operations can then be overriden as needed.

For `append`, this should go easier, since we could just directly specify a custom getter.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-16 15:07 UTC

yep, `Proxy` would be the way to go here.  I don't want to make `Proxy` sound too hard to get working--I've played with it before, and it's a fine way to solve these types of problems.  I just don't have much experience with it.

*2017-10-30 to 2017-10-30 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/reaction.20id/with/306866)*

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-10-30 21:24 UTC

I am working on the reaction api migration, the backend part of which is complete(PR #7026). Only webapp is remaining to be migrated. For completing it I need to be able to compute an `data-reaction-id` sort of thing which can uniquely identify a reaction in a message. `emoji_name`, `emoji_code` and `reaction_type` are the three parameters that identify a reaction uniquely within a message. I need to define a two way mapping, i.e., if I have ID then I should be able to find all the three parameters and vice-versa. What would be the preferred way of doing this?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-30 21:25 UTC

@Steve Howell you may have good thoughts on this.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-10-30 21:28 UTC

For context, `emoji_name` is a sequence of words joined by `_`(for e.g. `gree_apple`), `emoji_code` is a sequence of words joined by '-'(for e.g. `2199-FE0F`) and `reaction_type` is also a sequence of words joined by `_`(for e.g. `realm_emoji`).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-30 21:35 UTC

`emoji_code` probably will eventually be just a number for realm emoji, right?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-30 21:35 UTC

(like, the ID in the database table?)

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-10-30 21:36 UTC

Yeah, it will be a number once we are done with the realm emoji migration, for now it is same as realm emoji name.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-30 22:04 UTC

I think `Dict` is fine for this.  Do we need to have some side of integer sequence on the JS side to create the `data-reaction-id` value?

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-10-30 22:06 UTC

I basically need a way by which I can map these three values to id and vice-versa.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-30 22:07 UTC

I think the default solution is something like this:
* forward mapping: generate integer keys sequentially
* backward mapping: encode key as <name>,<code>,<type>

There might be a better encoding for <name>,<code>,<type>, but you want to avoid things like JSON that aren't deterministically encoded.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-10-30 22:10 UTC

Would it be fine to use a string delimited with commas in `data-reaction-id`?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-30 22:10 UTC

That might be fine, assuming your data never has commas or brackets.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-30 22:10 UTC

Is any of the data user-entered?

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-10-30 22:11 UTC

Nope, all of it is validated by the server.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-10-30 22:11 UTC

Thanks @Steve Howell that seems to solve my problem.

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2017-11-27 08:57 UTC

We have to use `(name)[url]` format for link insertion, so we can not directly convert text to link(in compose mode). If we want to go with `Ctr+v` then 
* First when user press `Ctr+v` we have to check whether `pasted_text` is an url or not
* If it's url then we can covert it to `(selected_text)[pasted_text]` directly
* If it is not url then the `selected_text` will be replaced by `pasted_text`(default behavior for `Ctr+v`).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-27 16:52 UTC

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2017-11-30 13:30 UTC

After a bit search for implementation, these are the options:
**For `Ctr+v`**
* We have to override all `copy`,  `paste`,  `cut` operations for implementing this. Cause it's required to fetch data from clipboard(the url which user has copied). And for security reason browser(also include chrome) do not allow. To make it work user have to manually enable the setting in browser.
* one more thing, that we have to check the content is url or not. This can be bit confusing to user, if our parse function mismatch/match content to url, in case if it is/not.

Or we can do like GitHub. When user press shortcut for inserting link it will automatically convert to `[selected_text](url)` where `url` will be selected. User can directly press `Ctr+v` and paste the link by replacing `url`.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-01-04 19:25 UTC

I am working on the front end of the `/remind`
So regarding the frontend I am currently doing it like this
* [Some one types in the message](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/56/VApkAnyWPgUIpmpnu68K6oiM/pasted_image.png) 
* [Hits enter and sees something like this](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/c7/is771TkUPgiO6SxjtJbTNt0U/pasted_image.png)

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-01-04 19:25 UTC

Now the way I am currently doing this will make the hitting send take following course of action
* Disable the message box for typing.
* Display something like `Scheduling Message...`
* Now in the code we would have made a request to transmit the message to server either by the socket or AJAX.
* We wait for the response to get back us from server upon which we show the notification above the compose box about success of scheduling the message or failure. (In case of failure we don't clear up the compose box.)
* We enable the compose box for further message composition or editing in case of failure.

Now there are a lot of cases in which this sort of mechanism will be a problem. Like server restarts, user can't do rapid fire scheduling (Don't know whether that is even ever required?), compose box gets blocked until we receive a response from server.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-01-04 19:25 UTC

compose box getting blocked can be solved by changing the way we show success or failure. We can display the success or failure in a modal at the top which would essentially be similar to what happens when we lose internet connection or server restarts.
In that modal we can later add links to edit or retry scheduling the same message.

hm, I think we figure out a general way we want to handle errors from backend bot handlers, and use that for /remind and most other @bot commands. I imagine it to be an extension of how we currently handle backend errors from the server.

For remind in particular: I think very quickly we'll want to support things like replying to messages with `/remind 20 minutes` or even just replying with `/remind`, where we want it to be as fast as possible. (Such a response would mark the message as unread in 20 minutes, or something similar). Currently in case of failure something like this happens.

@Rishi Gupta

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-01-05 12:46 UTC

Yes @Steve Howell I have been thinking scheduling as something built into the Zulip Core. Like we have a ScheduledMessages table where everything is stored. We have a `deferred_message_handler` function just around our `send_message_backend` handler which is used to interrupt  normal flow of sending message and to schedule one. Then on front end side we just have a function which the compose_box's `compose.finish()` calls in case of a message which begins with `/remind` to appropriately handle its delivery to backend and also handle the front end aspects of the message, ie. we do not try to do local echo of the message (Currently though I am thinking about having all the scheduled messages tracked as well with a local id).
Finally there is (I mean I am gonna build this today) this management command which will be totally on the same lines as of `deliver_email.py` which will try deliver scheduled messages.

So the workflow for delivery will be like this:
* Management commands finds a scheduled message is due to be delivered.
* Message is then extracted from the Scheduled message table by the management command and send to `Check_send_message` function of the actions with appropriate parameters. Essentially this is what is finally called when a new message is actually sent by a user.
* Message is delivered to everyone in a way similar to what happens when user actually sends a message. The difference here is user might have scheduled a message long before it is actually delivered. UI experience is same for all the others than the user who scheduled the message. For the user who scheduled a message, what happens is a new message arrives which shows as sent by the user itself. But actually it was sent long before.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-01-05 12:46 UTC

Have I got it all wrong?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-05 13:32 UTC

> For remind in particular: I think very quickly we'll want to support things like replying to messages with `/remind 20 minutes` or even just replying with `/remind`, where we want it to be as fast as possible.

@Rishi Gupta I think your statement above illustrates that we haven't completely fleshed out the use cases here, at least on the front end.  There are two types of situations where you want scheduled messages:

* outgoing (@Aditya Bansal is mostly working under this paradigm, I believe)
* incoming (which @Rishi Gupta alludes to above)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-05 13:40 UTC

For **incoming** messages, I may get a Zulip message from Alice at noon with a link to the agenda for the 3pm meeting, and I want to re-send itself to myself at 2:45pm.  I could quote/reply the message, prepend with "/remind 2:45pm", and re-address to myself, but that's so awkward I'd probably just update my calendar instead. :)

I think it's much better if we just plan to have dedicated UI support for "snooze" reminders on incoming messages.  Put something in the message caret menu that gives me a popup with a timepicker widget, and then have the JS code hit the backend endpoint that Aditya's developing.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-05 13:43 UTC

Another reason for dedicated UI is that the **incoming** experience kind of precludes bots and API clients from helping here.  There's no precise way to tell a chat bot **which** message you want to act on.

I think it's a general question of whether we think `/remind <time>`, `/help private streams`, `/saleseforce customer foo` etc should be UI blocking or not until the backend returns. 

My feeling is that we should not make them blocking. One proposal for how that could work for /commands and bots in the general case is:
* For messages that are not going to add anything to the message feed, have a sticky "Sending .." in the green bar above the compose area, until the message is acked by the backend
* In case of success, either do some relevant action (open a modal so they can choose their saleforce customer from a list), or if there is no relevant action show a success message as Aditya has currently done
* In case of error .. a slick thing could be: if they haven't changed narrows, do what Aditya has currently done. If they have changed narrows, maybe save the message as a draft, replace the green bar with a red "Error: foo. Click to edit message", and clicking on it just recovers the last draft.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-01-07 16:20 UTC

I think the main important things are
* Some interaction may need to happen that doesn't send anything to the channel
* We have to allow the backend to throw errors (e.g. "your salesforce api key was revoked", "no such salesforce user was found", "can't understand en veinte minutos"), and that may be a relatively common case
* It should work really well for power users, and e.g. should not need the mouse. Any given bot will only be used by small fraction of users, but those users will often be senior people and power users, and a decent fraction of their interaction with zulip will be through that bot. 

I think a good case study might actually be a /github command. E.g. if we had a really slick /github, you could imagine doing a lot of github stuff from within zulip rather than switching to github. E.g.
`/github search issues bankruptcy`
`/github open 1234` (would open a new tab with #1234)
```
/github new issue
left sidebar: Put the foo above the bar

Currently the foo is below the bar, which causes ...
```

The use case for github is less compelling than for salesforce since the github UI is pretty okay, but one could imagine much worse pieces of software where one needed to regularly do similar sorts of actions.
