## autosubscribe

*2018-01-19 to 2018-01-22 · 30 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/autosubscribe/with/456551)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 19:59 UTC

So, I know @Alena Volkova has been looking into removing the synchronous API call to `/json/subscriptions/exists` in the compose code path (when `autosubscribe` is passed in as true), and I wanted to talk about this to see what we should do.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 20:00 UTC

The only code path that passes `autosubscribe=True` is the `narrow_stream` code path, which is primarily used for embedding a single-stream Zulip chat into another website (e.g. as a click-to-chat style integration).

Copying @Reid Barton since he's one of the experts on that feature.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 20:01 UTC

The intent of that `autosubscribe` feature is to make it the case that a user who starts sending messages in one of those single-stream integrations gets subscribed to that stream, so they might see replies to what they sent in their home view.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 20:01 UTC

I'm trying to figure out whether there's a way to remove that synchronous check without removing the feature.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 20:02 UTC

I think the most obvious way to do it would be to just do an asynchronous subscribe request, and pass in a callback to complete the "attempt-to-send" logic once the asynchronous request returns.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 20:04 UTC

Which might require some somewhat complicated refactoring...

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 20:05 UTC

The other option would be to have the browser attempt to submit the "subscribe me" and "send message" requests in parallel (rather than in sequence with subscribe first...), but that seems harder to reason about...

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 20:05 UTC

`check_unsubscribed_stream_for_send` is the function in question if anyone's trying to read along.

**Alena Volkova** · 2018-01-19 20:23 UTC

> embedding a single-stream Zulip chat into another website (e.g. as a click-to-chat style integration)
Is there any way I could do something like this in a test mode? Just to get the idea what we’re talking about.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 20:49 UTC

@Alena Volkova yes, though it's take some work for me to recall the mechanism.  My hope is @Reid Barton can help with that.  To give him a couple days, I'd recommend focusing on other issues.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-19 20:57 UTC

I'd much rather do any async stuff here serially than in parallel.  We already have the complication of local echo, where we process both the server response and the message event, and that's a hard code path to reason about now (since either one can win the race).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 21:00 UTC

What is problematic about doing the async approach is that we may need to do a significant structural change to support that, which may not be worth it for a minor feature.  It's possible that we should keep the synchronous call (It's not a big problem) but replace the nasty endpoint with the autosubscribe option (which is a really ugly wart)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 21:01 UTC

@Steve Howell it might be worth half an hour of your time tracing the code path to see whether I'm wrong about whether the continuation approach is reasonable, but it feels pretty messy to me.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 21:01 UTC

(Maybe I'm missing something though!)

**Alena Volkova** · 2018-01-19 21:15 UTC

I might be way off here, but I just want to understand why we need two separate requests to subscribe a user to a stream and to send a message. Why can’t we just send a message, check if user is subscribed / can be auto-subscribed on the backend (we can pass `autosubscribe` option from the frontend if necessary), and then either send a message or return an error?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-19 21:17 UTC

@Alena Volkova That is the approach that I would favor.  It's not a trivial refactoring, but it's certainly possible.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-19 21:18 UTC

Basically, if "autosubscribe" is on, we want to bypass most of the validation path (or maybe "bypass" is the wrong word--it would be more like the flag is an "ezpass" that gets you past most of the checks).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-19 21:18 UTC

And then those messages would generally get through "normal" validation but get rejected on the back end.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-19 21:21 UTC

We'd be touching two pretty complicated codepaths:

* validation -- mostly just removing the sync check, but there are like four functions in the call stack that we'll need to reason about a bit more carefully than I've done after a quick look at the code

* message-send -- this will be a good opportunity to make sure our "rejected messages" error handling works well

And we'd probably just want to say no "local echo" for any messages that are autosubscribe-but-unknown-stream.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-19 21:22 UTC

@Tim Abbott Another question to ask before we get too deep here is whether we still live in a world where the frontend knows less about streams-we-could-subscribe-to than the backend.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 21:50 UTC

Oh, that's actually a great question.  So, this case of a single-stream window is certainly one where we should be able to know whether the user is subscribed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 21:51 UTC

(I think one use case may involve "autosubscribe" also auto-creating the stream when someone first tries to send?  Not sure)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 21:51 UTC

Agreed re: that local-echo point.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-19 21:52 UTC

It might require some changes (I'm not sure those single-stream windows process subscribe events normally), but I believe it should be possible to make them do so and thus ensure that we can check correctly in the frontend whether the stream exists.  Still, I believe the UX here might require capabilities like "create if doesn't exist", which would require this sort of hit-the-backend feature.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-19 22:04 UTC

@Alena Volkova My advice here is to spend lots of time manually testing the existing feature, so you're 100% solid on how it works now (and gradually insert print/console statements in various places to start understanding the code flow, with particular focus on when that sync call to the backend happens).

**Alena Volkova** · 2018-01-19 22:20 UTC

Sure, I’ll try to learn as much as I can about this feature. Thanks for the guidance!

**Reid Barton** · 2018-01-21 22:59 UTC

@Alena Volkova I only have a vague recollection of how this feature worked, but I do know that you can access it with a URL like https://chat.zulip.org/?stream=frontend

**Reid Barton** · 2018-01-21 23:01 UTC

I haven't read the discussion here carefully, but as far as I'm concerned it would probably be sufficient to just send the message and asynchronously subscribe the user to the stream, without those two things interacting at all.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-22 18:36 UTC

I think the only complication with that we need to check how the backend handles the user not being subscribed.

**Alena Volkova** · 2018-01-22 21:57 UTC

@Reid Barton Thanks for the link! I managed to reproduce this behavior.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 16:57 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 16:58 UTC

This section of `popovers.js` is what implements that feature:
```
    $('body').on('click', '.respond_button', function (e) {                                          
        var textarea = $("#compose-textarea");                                                       
        var msgid = $(e.currentTarget).data("message-id");                                           
                                                                                                     
        compose_actions.respond_to_message({trigger: 'popover respond'});                            
        channel.get({                                                                                
            url: '/json/messages/' + msgid,                                                          
            idempotent: true,                                                                        
            success: function (data) {                                                               
                if (textarea.val() === "") {                                                         
                    textarea.val("```quote\n" + data.raw_content +"\n```\n");                        
                } else {                                                                             
                    textarea.val(textarea.val() + "\n```quote\n" + data.raw_content +"\n```\n");     
                }                                                                                    
                $("#compose-textarea").trigger("autosize.resize");                                   
            },                                                                                       
        });                                                                                          
        popovers.hide_actions_popover();                                                             
        e.stopPropagation();                                                                         
        e.preventDefault();                                                                          
    });                                                                                              
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 16:59 UTC

So, what we'll want to do, is move most of the code (don't want to move the `e.stopPropagation` and `e.preventDefault`)  in that block into an exported function, with a name like `compose_actions.quote_and_reply`, and call that function both from here and from the new hotkey.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2018-02-07 18:09 UTC

@Ann K Sorry I missed your message here(you mentioned someone else with same name). This issue can  broken into smaller chunks as follows:
* Infrastructure changes: All the emoji related data is  produced using 'build_emoji' script. This issue will require changing that script so that we can populate the data structures with skin tone related information. All of the required is already present in the emoji-datasource package(https://github.com/iamcal/emoji-data). `build_emoji` simply consumes data from this package.
* Deciding the markdown syntax: We will need to think about the markdown syntax for emoji with skin tones. Slack uses `:<emoji_name>::<skin_tone>:`.
* Bugdown changes: We will need to update the bugdown for recognizing the syntax and rendering it properly(using the info from build_emoji script).
* Reactions: I think this will not require any changes as unicode code for emoji with different emoji codes is different, so we can just store the corresponding emoji code in the table.
* Change emoji and reactions picker: Finally we will need to make related changes our emoji picker.

Just a heads up, this issue is going to be somewhat complex with some other major changes also going on in the same area. You can start by familiarizing yourself with emoji infra code(if you haven't already) and then we can discuss on how to get this functionality implemented. :simple_smile:

I had implemented frontend feature for muting user, but the problem is on clicking it, multiple ajax requests are being sent.  I googled it and found that the problem might be related to the 'click' event handler, in the sense that multiple event handlers were being attached, which resulted in sending multiple ajax requests, the solution for which was to unbind the event handler after each time it was triggered.
Now coming to the real problem, 
```javascript
exports.mute_user = function(event) {
        var id = $(event.target).parents('ul').attr('data-user-id');
        var muted_id = Number(id);
        var muted_name = people.get_person_from_user_id(id).full_name;
        popovers.hide_user_sidebar_popover();
        muting_user_ui.unmute_user([muted_id, muted_name]);
        event.stopPropagation();
        event.preventDefault();
};
```
```javascript
  // Mute the user
        $('body').on('click.mute', '.user_popover .sidebar-popover-mute-user', function(e){popovers.mute_user(e);
    });
        $('body').off('click.mute', '.user_popover .sidebar-popover-mute-user');
```

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-02-14 22:44 UTC

@Aastha Gupta  got the solution at this link https://stackoverflow.com/questions/24933430/img-src-svg-changing-the-fill-color
```
.loader {
    background-color: black;
    -webkit-mask: url(static/images/loader.svg) no-repeat center;
    mask: url(static/images/loader.svg) no-repeat center;
}
```
The only caveat is it is not fully supported in browsers like IE, but probably we can exempt that, you now need to figure out to return to the original state when svg is no more needed, you don't want it permanently to be black, hopes that makes sense.

## numbered lists in marked

*2018-02-20 to 2018-02-20 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/numbered.20lists.20in.20marked/with/508478)*

**Weronika Grzybowska** · 2018-02-20 14:57 UTC

I am working on moving automatic numbering of lists from preprocessor to after a paragraph has been recognized. The backend implementation allows me to change the paragraph blockprocessor so that lists in block get renumbered before passing it back to the original `run` method (which inserts the text as a paragraph).

However, marked doesn't give access to individual parts of block-level lexer, like it does for the inline one, so I wanted to ask for suggestions where is the best place to insert the function - that takes otherwise unchanged text meant to be a paragraph and returns the same with changed numbers. Preferably, it would be inside the [`Lexer.token` method](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/80ff3d8da50d57e27e70520d75ed952da338afd6/static/third/marked/lib/marked.js#L160), because it's roughly equivalent to backend and keeps track of whether the paragraph is inside a blockquote (so that quotations aren't changed). I have considered either before a paragraph token is created ([link](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/80ff3d8da50d57e27e70520d75ed952da338afd6/static/third/marked/lib/marked.js#L403)) or iterating over tokens after the main loop ends.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-20 15:49 UTC

@Weronika Grzybowska It's fine to modify `marked.js` here, since I agree with you that it's better to do stuff like this in the tokenizing phase.  I think renumbering might make sense to do after the main loop ends, but I'm not really sure.

**Weronika Grzybowska** · 2018-02-20 16:12 UTC

If it's fine, then adding after the loop has the benefit that there is no need to modify every place where this type of token is created, at the cost of being slightly separate, though it should be apparent that tokens could be modified by looking near the return statement. The result doesn't change,  the difference is mostly in clarity.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-20 16:17 UTC

I like the post-processing approach, because you could probably isolate that to a function that we could add tests on directly, if we wanted to.

**Weronika Grzybowska** · 2018-02-20 16:28 UTC

That is, have a function that takes all tokens or just for a single paragraph?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-20 16:30 UTC

I was thinking "all the tokens."  But I don't know exactly how this works.

**Weronika Grzybowska** · 2018-02-20 17:33 UTC

On a closer look, it should be in `Lexer.lex`,  if done as post-processing, since `token` recurses differently than I thought. 

Renumbering alone is possible to cover by tests in `markdown_test_cases.json`.  Tests for choosing the correct tokens to modify would use ones like those created by lexer.  Then they wouldn't, for example, be affected by bugs/changes in blockquote rendering, but equivalents should still be present in the general ones, for backend - so I'm not sure if having separate ones makes sense. Still, it's going to be an isolated function anyway, so that can be added if needed.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-20 17:41 UTC

I am thinking you may want tests at both levels.  You **definitely** want the general styles tests, of course.  But it might also be nice to cover some of the numbering edge cases with more directed tests.  So I think we're on the same page here.

**Weronika Grzybowska** · 2018-02-20 17:50 UTC

Is there something that I would need to test for in marked, but not bugdown?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-20 17:56 UTC

Not necessarily.  I'm just saying that for some things, it might be easier to test the token-related code directly, rather than the end product.  But as long as you use simple markdown, it might be easier to do all the testing from the "end result" layer.

**Weronika Grzybowska** · 2018-02-20 18:16 UTC

It's just that if  I have a test directly on tokens, I can't write it the same way for backend, so I either leave a gap in tests for one implementation, or need to have a markdown to html case anyway. I was worried about having too many tests for the same thing,  but It might be useful for narrowing the causes if they fail.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-20 18:17 UTC

Yeah, I think this is a special case, where you might want a little extra testing on the JS side.

**Weronika Grzybowska** · 2018-02-20 18:19 UTC

OK. Thank you for your help.

## send message performace

*2018-03-11 to 2018-03-12 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/send.20message.20performace/with/534955)*

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-03-11 16:24 UTC

@Aditya Bansal and I were discussing the `send_message` function and had a small observation: we do the local echo before sending actual ajax/socket request.

If we could shave off the time taken before sending the message, currently where we do the local echo (markdown processing and DOM rendiering), we could see an overall reduction in the amount of time between pressing 'send' and the other person getting the message.

Instead of the current flow of control:

```
- do local echo
- get local_id
- transmit message
```

we could do:

```
- get local_id
- transmit message
- do local echo
```

Since the actual transmission is  asynchronous, so shoudln't impact the experience of the person sending the message much. However, we could remove the somewhat synchronous code paths from the total time taken.

Thoughts? Is there a way to profile this codepath to see if it is a potential bottleneck?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:17 UTC

I don't think it's worth the extra complexity.  In return for getting a server message sooner, you make the app feel less responsive to the user (who often really only perceives the local echo as the "delay").  Also, I don't think you actually end up saving that much time in the round trip, since the local-side processing should be reasonably quick.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:18 UTC

It's probably still worth profiling, just to see if there is something that seems slower than it should be.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-12 02:29 UTC

It would slightly help perf-wise, but would create a lot of complexity.  On perf, the "local echo" part includes markdown processing., which may take some time; initiating an HTTP request for transmitting the message probably doesn't consume much time at all.  That all said, I think our frontend markdown processor generally takes about 1ms to render a message, so I don't think the difference would ever be material.


## JS code style

*2018-03-12 to 2018-03-13 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/JS.20code.20style/with/536057)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 15:34 UTC

How do folks feel about `return undefined;` vs. `return;`.  Semantically these statements are equivalent.  The former is more explicit, the latter is more concise.  We are considering moving toward `return;` as the standard. Thoughs?

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-03-12 15:39 UTC

I am all for moving towards `return`.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 16:39 UTC

ok #8669 should be an easy one for anybody with a little bit of linter knowledge

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-12 18:29 UTC

Great :)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 18:46 UTC

Thanks for everybody's feedback!  I was not expecting such a unanimous decision. :smile:

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-03-12 18:52 UTC

I guess everybody finds `return undefined;` a bit ugly and just a `return;` looks far soothing to eyes.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 18:56 UTC

A similar debate is 'return' vs. 'return None' in Python:

~~~ python
>>> def foo(): return
... 
>>> foo() is None
True

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-12 19:15 UTC

In Python, I prefer `return None` for functions that are intending to use that as a special value (e.g. as a distinct state from `return user_profile` or whatever), and `return` for functions that never return anything.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-12 19:16 UTC

I'd probably be happy with the same convention in JavaScript, though I believe our existing Python codebase is pretty consistent about doing what I described, and I'm not sure what our JS codebase is doing on this point.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 19:49 UTC

Yeah, I think the forces are a bit different in Python than JS, so I don't feel compelled to change anything on the Python side.

**Boris Yankov** · 2018-03-12 20:59 UTC

That should depend on the function's return type. While `return undefined` and `return` are functionally equivalent, you should use it as if it was a typed language.

**Boris Yankov** · 2018-03-12 21:01 UTC

So, a function that might return something or nothing should have both `return 'hey'` and `return undefined;`. 
If a function's return type is like `void` (there is actually a little known feature in JS that has this keyword!) and you are using this as an early function exit, then use `return;`

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 21:24 UTC

Yeah, @Boris Yankov, you are basically echoing what Tim says for Python.  I think we can revisit this if we eventually add some more type checking to JS.

**Boris Yankov** · 2018-03-12 21:27 UTC

Looks like a nice idea to make sure these two files align sometime in the future:
https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/master/.eslintrc
https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/.eslintrc.json

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-03-12 21:32 UTC

Purely linting perspective: if we go the Python route, eslint has a built in rule for checking return values. Otherwise, we'll have to write a custom rule.

Also, we have 51 occurrences of `return undefined` in the complete codebase.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 21:42 UTC

Let's go with `return;` for everything.

**Boris Yankov** · 2018-03-12 21:45 UTC

https://eslint.org/docs/rules/consistent-return

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-03-13 12:17 UTC

Opened #8684.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-13 12:23 UTC

Merged!

## message_list.all

*2018-03-20 to 2018-03-21 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/message_list.2Eall/with/545340)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-20 21:55 UTC

@Tim Abbott Can you explain the purpose of message_list.all (vs. home_msg_list)?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-20 21:55 UTC

Yep!

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-20 21:55 UTC

`message_list.all` contains the messages we fetched from the server in a contiguous block.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-20 21:56 UTC

(It differs in content from `home_msg_list` in that it has muted messages in it)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-20 21:56 UTC

It's used as a source of messages when we narrow to attempt to pre-render that narrow in the browser before we fetch anything from the server.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-20 21:56 UTC

(It isn't even displayed like the other message list objects; it's just a cache)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-20 21:57 UTC

The important difference between it and `message_store` is that `message_store` is just a hash table  -- it isn't able to tell one anything about which message (IDs) are in a contiguous block, whereas `message_list.all` can.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-20 21:59 UTC

Ok, that makes sense.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-20 21:59 UTC

I'm still getting tripped up a bit on trying to suppress message inserts into message lists when we know we haven't fetched forward all the way.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-20 22:00 UTC

Since message_list.all is never rendered,we can probably just exempt it from that code.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-20 22:00 UTC

although hmm

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-20 22:01 UTC

I suppose we have similar concerns about it being contiguous, they're just not as direct as the other two lists.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-20 22:09 UTC

I think I need to do one of the following:
* just have home_msg_list and message_list.all share the same fetch status
* be sure to update message_list.all when we are backfilling "home"
* just ignore fetch_status in message_list.all (which seems like the worst option to me)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-20 23:06 UTC

I think the second probably makes the most sense to me?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-21 14:37 UTC

So I was thinking the second bullet makes sense too--basically just update both message_list.all and home_msg_list with two lines of code in various places.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-21 14:44 UTC

And then I discovered another interesting twist that is actually not 100% related to the forward-fill effort:
* In load_old_messages, we get the oldest message id of the current list as the anchor, which could be the home list.
* When backfilling in our idle loop, we use `message_list.all.first_id` as our anchor, but `home_msg_list` as the msg_list parameter

I think the idle loop is correct here.  Given the impending release, I think I'll just fix that directly, but it feels like long term we might want some sort of simpler data model, where maybe most data-side code just needs to talk to message_list.all, and then message_list.all has some kind of parent/child relationship with the home list that it manages.  It's possible that's just moving complexity around, so this is more just a reflection on the current code.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-21 17:17 UTC

OK, makes sense.

## keyboard help

*2018-03-28 to 2018-03-28 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/keyboard.20help/with/550997)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-28 22:27 UTC

An annoying aspect of our keyboard help is that you need the mouse (:mouse:) to view the second page.  That is not cool, haha!

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-28 22:27 UTC

I looked into a bit today, and it's not really a bug, per se, it's more a consequence of the tab interface.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-28 22:28 UTC

When we go into any of our tabbed interfaces, we focus the keyboard on the tabs themselves, so that you can use arrow keys to switch tabs.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-28 22:28 UTC

Of course, that means we don't focus the "body" portions of the tabs.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-28 22:30 UTC

It's more or less a one-line change to auto-focus the body part of keyboard/search/markdown tabs when you go to them, but that would break being able to navigate the tabs, which wouldn't be such a bad thing if that were our only tabbed interface.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-28 22:31 UTC

So what I'm thinking about is just making the down key and maybe the tab key move focus from the tab portion of the widget down to the selected tab.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-28 22:32 UTC

@Rishi Gupta Do you know any history behind this that I should be aware of?  I think for v1.8 the down-arrow key is pretty low risk.  And then longer term we want to make the "toggle" component (as it's currently called) a little more robust when it comes to keyboard navigation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-28 22:51 UTC

@Steve Howell I know the history here; I think your analysis is correct.  We just want to be able to switch tabs and scroll down.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-28 22:51 UTC

I think it used to be that scrolling down was more rare as a thing to need to do, but then we added more content.

Having a bit of a hard time tracking down how the checkboxes are actually working on Settings. @Armaan Ahluwalia It is done using some classic CSS hacks only, I've tried understanding why this hack actually works but my understanding is weak about this. BTW there is no javascript included which fires the change event for the hidden checkboxes.

**Shubham Dhama** · 2018-04-02 21:46 UTC

The state of our checkboxes are decided by the state of hidden checkboxes using `:checked` CSS.

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-04-02 21:49 UTC

Thanks for responding btw @Shubham Dhama

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-04-02 21:54 UTC

The thing that makes the sidebar so tricky to make intuitive is that it's not really a menu nor is it a tree widget.  It's not what I think of as a menu, because most menus are transient, whereas our sidebar is definitely sticky.  It's a bit closer to a tree widget in my mind, so I'd be inspired by things like file system widgets, except we're not a tree of arbitrary depth (so we should take advantage of  being just two layers deep) and there's sort of aesthetic concerns that we might not want +/- icons for expand/collapse.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-18 23:10 UTC

* let me to narrow to one of them

**Michael Seery** · 2018-04-18 23:18 UTC

Good question! Since a message node can't be assigned to multiple topics, I suppose it is more folder-like. I'm not proposing that as a change, I rather like enforcing linear streams. It forces the user to organize their thoughts a bit, painlessly. 

My point was, if I'm imagining streams as "folders" with topics being "files", with a maximum depth of 1, then I think of the "files" as being updated with unread information before I think of the "folder" being updated. The unread count location is what rung true for me with respect to your observation that we could take advantage of the max tree depth.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-18 23:22 UTC

Yeah, I think of our messages as basically being in folders (topics) inside of filing cabinets (streams).  Or files=topics and folders=streams.

Under the hood we really do just kind of count the number of unread messages within whatever bucket you're looking at (stream or topic), and since messages only live in one place, it ends up that count(stream) = sum(count(topic | topic in stream)).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-05 00:06 UTC

~~~ js
$element = $.create('element-stub');
$element.animate = function () { // stub code };
f($element);
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-05 00:08 UTC

if you look at the zjquery source code, you'll see that most of the function chain:

~~~ js
210             removeAttr: function (name) {
211                 attrs.del(name);
212                 return self;
213             },
214             removeClass: function (class_name) {
215                 classes.del(class_name);
216                 return self;
217             },
218             remove: function () {
219                 return self;
220             },
221             removeData: noop,
222             select: function (arg) {
223                 generic_event('select', arg);
224                 return self;

~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-05 00:15 UTC

@Armaan Ahluwalia Here's a more fleshed out example:

~~~ js
set_global('$', global.make_zjquery());

function f($element) {
    $element.removeClass('hide').addClass('show').animate({ opacity:1 }, 100);
}

var test_elem = $.create('element-stub');

var was_animated;
test_elem.animate = function (opts, delay) {
    was_animated = true;
    assert.deepEqual(opts, {opacity: 1});
    assert.equal(delay, 100);
}

f(test_elem);

assert(was_animated);

assert(test_elem.hasClass('show'));

~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-19 00:26 UTC

I think there's a lot of overlap between the concepts of description and pinned messages.  I could see a path like this:
* we add pinned messages to the top of the feed behind a feature flag
* people complain they take up too much space, so we make them easy to hide/collapse (via one of many possible mechanisms)
* once we have the collapse feature, we might as well treat the description as being like the "first" pinned message on a stream

My two cents is that our current treatment of Description makes it a fairly useless concept at the moment, but it's also nontrivial to find a place to put it on the main screen.

## narrowing

*2018-04-24 to 2018-04-24 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/narrowing/with/568722)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 00:51 UTC

So, my work on narrowing this weekend seems to have introduced a regression: we now always go to the backend for a `use_first_unread_anchor` query, even when that shouldn't be necessary.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 00:53 UTC

I think in order to fix this we need to combine https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/7096 aka https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/8552, and then use the unread count data in order to determine whether we can compute the correct anchor from data present in the frontend or not.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 00:53 UTC

@Steve Howell does that reasoning make sense to you?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 00:55 UTC

Actually, maybe it's simpler than that: We just use the logic we already have for filtering `all_msg_list`, and check the unread status on those messages.  If there's a transition from read->unread in that list, we potentially optimistically assume that's our anchor.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-24 09:32 UTC

Can you elaborate on the second approach?  I guess you're suggesting that even if the "optimistic" assumption is wrong, it's not the end of the world?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 17:19 UTC

Yeah, basically.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-04-24 17:46 UTC

The second approach makes sense to me, then.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-24 22:47 UTC

Anyway, in the meantime, I'm going to revert the narrowing changes.

*2018-05-03 to 2018-05-05 · 42 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/delay_render/with/574679)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-03 23:04 UTC

I am thinking we should kill off the `delay_render`flag as part of our activate cleanup.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-03 23:08 UTC

Reasons to kill it:
* It's kind of a hacky option to pass through various call chains.
* It's still a low-risk removal (only 5 places in the code).
* It doesn't solve a hard problem (filtering message ids is easy).
* An alternative solution could improve our narrowing performance.

For the latter point, it's predicated on the idea that we pre-launch the server fetch, which Tim is in favor of  keeping, and I'm actually thinking we take it a step further.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-03 23:12 UTC

If we create a simple function that is `(message_list.all, current_filter) -> ordinary list of messages`, which we call `get_narrow_msg_ids`, then we can do this:
* call `get_narrow_msg_ids`
* do stuff like make sure it's not empty, find the last id if we don't have a msg_id already, etc.
* start the fetch
* instantiate the message list with its fairly expensive/complex clear_table stuff
* add in our messages for the initial render (we'll re-filter them all to true, but that step is super cheap, and we could always pass in a flag that says they're pre-filtered)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-04 00:38 UTC

Just to understand the proposal a bit more, the idea is to basically call a function that returns a list of messages instead of doing a `delay_render` `message_list` initialization?  That could be cleaner; it depends a bit on whether details like muting complicate the story and make the replacement function add a lot of complexity.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-04 03:03 UTC

Unfortunately, I think the muting complications are probably just enough to make this a no-go for now.  You'd need the function to basically return a record with two lists, and you'd need to duplicate/extract this code as part of that:

~~~ js
    unmuted_messages: function MessageList_unmuted_messages(messages) {
        return _.reject(messages, function (message) {
            return muting.is_topic_muted(message.stream, message.subject) &&
                   !message.mentioned;
        });
    },
~~~

Another idea here would be more internal to MessageList--have the concept that you need to call something like `list.start_view()` where `list.start_view = function () { this.view = MessageListView(...)` and instead of `if !opts.delay_render` you check `if this.view`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:32 UTC

So I think probably `topic_generator` logic for finding the next unread non-muted thread may not be doing the right thing; either because it's in the "inactive" section or for some other reason.  @Steve Howell FYI :)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-08 22:35 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:41 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:41 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:41 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:44 UTC

OK, after reading some code, it's more subtle than that and actually not related to `dormant`

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:45 UTC

What's happening is that the `topic_data` data structure isn't populated from `server_unreads`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:45 UTC

So it thinks that there are no recent topics in the stream, and doesn't look at the unread state for those.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:46 UTC

i.e. I think the call to `topic_data.get_recent_names` inside `get_next_topic` should instead be a query on some `unread.js` thing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:47 UTC

Confirmed with @Rishi Gupta, who also had this state that `topic_data.get_recent_names` returned nothing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-08 22:52 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-08 23:45 UTC

The server unreads may create gaps in topic history as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-09 01:02 UTC

Yeah, so can we just make the server-unreads feature insert the topics into the `topic_data` structures?

* fetched message ids are stored per-topic
* historical topics are stored (but no message ids for them, just counts)
* topic edits can happen
* now we also have unread message ids (but without actual messages)

It's been unmaintained for years upstream (and we have about 15 patches to it...), and so it's a pretty unpleasant dependency for us to have.  I don't know to what extent bootstrap typeahead is tangled with other parts of bootstrap (and thus whether we can upgrade the rest without upgrading the typeahead), but my hope is that we can switch to something newer and better. ## search_pill

*2018-05-31 to 2018-06-02 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/search_pill/with/591223)*

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-05-31 16:43 UTC

There have been some talks about improving the search experience by using pills. Each search term would have its own pill. The pills can be editable the way pills in gmail are.

Some of the major tasks I can think of are:
- Extending current pills implementation to support editing (we may want to do this later on once we have a rough implementaion of read-only search pills ready)
- Create search_pill.js similar to user_pill.js
- Refactor the current suggestions code and make it more streamlined with maybe preprocessing and postprocessing steps so that suggestions from different sources follow a certain predefined flow.
- something like compose_pm_pill.js for making use of user_pill. I think composebox_typeahead.js is more like search_suggestions.js taking care of query matches + some typeahead handling.

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-05-31 16:44 UTC

@Tim Abbott What are your suggestions for moving forward?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-31 16:48 UTC

I would start by refactoring the current suggestions code, as I think retrofitting pills into the current code would be difficult and then the refactoring with pills involved would be even harder than doing it first.

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-05-31 16:50 UTC

Yeah, agreed.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-31 16:50 UTC

And as you suggest, the current code could probably have a nicer structure that is more like a pipeline so that each suggestion is more like a function of the prior terms, whereas now it's kind of monolithic and hacky for multiple terms.

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-05-31 16:53 UTC

The goal is to make adding a new class of suggestions easy for the developer.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-31 16:59 UTC

I've never been a big fan of our search bar.  Not because it's broken necessarily.  But because I think you should mostly narrow from the sidebars.  And then the text input box should just be for keywords and implicitly be within the narrows.  (And for the 3 times a year that I do advanced searches, we could have a modal instead of ugly autocomplete that never lists more than N people named Tim or Vijay or other common names.)  But that's just me. :smile:

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-05-31 17:07 UTC

I personally like the filtering interface in GitHub issues.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-31 17:12 UTC

Yeah, I think we could a lot worse than to emulate their "Filters" dropdown for things like "has:attachment", "is:mentioned", "is:alerted", and "sender:me".  If you had those things in the dropdown and implicit-search-within-narrow, the search could be simple and uncluttered (and then maybe V2 would be more about autocompleting search words using words from messages).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-31 17:16 UTC

Fortunately, I think a cleaner data model in search_suggestions will make any UI approach nicer to implement, whatever combination of dropdown filters, curated autocomplete, pills, modals, etc. we evolve to.

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-05-31 17:31 UTC

Yeah, that is something which can be done irrespective of the approach :smiley:

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-06-02 17:43 UTC

I've been trying hard on the refactor for the last 2 days, but I'm unable to get further than code cleanup :sweat_smile: .  [Here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/compare/master...shubham-padia:refactor_search?expand=1) is the work till done now.  I think it would best to review the cleanup if it seems okay and carry out the required refactoring while doing the feature. I would love some thoughts on this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-02 17:48 UTC

@Shubham Padia it's definitely a good idea to submit code cleanup as you have it ready, not trying to build the entire feature before getting things reviewed.  It looks like some of your cleanup commits change a lot of things in a single commit; what I'd recommend you do next is prepare clear, small commits that each clean up one thing, and submit that branch for review.

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-06-02 17:49 UTC

Okay, sounds good.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-02 17:49 UTC

Generally, the way larger projects fail is that folks don't get the preparatory refactors written clearly, completed and merged, and instead generate a giant branch that's hard to understand and is impossible to merge (e.g. because one of the early "cleanups" that everything else depends on is based on incorrect assumptions, and is hard to remove).


## translations

*2018-06-01 to 2018-06-01 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/translations/with/591903)*

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-06-01 11:09 UTC

Can anyone please explain how the website gets translated to different languages when we change the default language in settings, I read the doc on translation and also read the code in frontend and backend  for default language setting, but I am not able to figure out how exactly does it work? How the other language gets properly rendered (without violating the CSS rules) on the website ?

**Shubham Dhama** · 2018-06-01 13:04 UTC

@Tarun Kumar We basically use `Django.utils.translation` in backend and `i18next` library frontend for translation. Basically, you can find tranlsation.json files which contain string's translation in the different language in different files. 
Ahh. I think you should ask the specific question you have as this can go long.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-06-01 13:30 UTC

@Shubham Dhama yeah, I read about that. I just wanted to know how those translations are applied/injected on the website user sees, as in, when we click the default language button to select a different language, how the frontend and html incorporates the new language ?

**Shubham Dhama** · 2018-06-01 13:39 UTC

Basic structure template(i.e. template with `.html` are handled by the backend, django itself) and handlebar templates (and strings in js files) are handled by `i18next` library. They aren't updated dynamically, you need to refresh the page to see the page in changed language. For frontend you can see it as the process of key-value mapping process, we pass a `page_params.translation_data` object to the client which contains all the strings which is further handled by `i18next` library. It's all I know about this process if someone wants to add here it would be great :)
Important reads: `home.py`, `translation.js`, `i18n.py`, `templates.js`

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-06-01 13:45 UTC

Thanks for the insight! I will see the files to make more sense of the process involved!

## media queries

*2018-06-06 to 2018-06-06 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/media.20queries/with/595575)*

**Akash** · 2018-06-06 11:03 UTC

Does anyone know what convention we follow with the media queries? 
a) Do we put them in the bottom of the CSS file?
b) Or next to their base counterparts. For example, if I have a class called “bot-information-box”, I could put any necessary media query styles right below the definition of that class.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-06-06 11:16 UTC

We have a file called `static/styles/media.scss` for major media-related stuff, but I think you can put things next to their counterparts for some things.

**Akash** · 2018-06-06 11:29 UTC

For the context, I'm working on #9513. I wanted to update the `.bots_list .bot-information-box` when the window width is `< 480px`, so I thought I'll reuse the already added media query i.e. [line #501](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/static/styles/settings.scss#L501). But since the `.bots_list .bot-information-box` is in the bottom i.e. [line #781](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/static/styles/settings.scss#L781) so those media rules are getting overwritten. I see two options here -
a) Put the media query 480px in the bottom i.e. [line #501](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/static/styles/settings.scss#L501)
b) Duplicate the media query right after the `.bots_list .bot-information-box` class -
```css
.bots_list .bot-information-box {
    position: relative;
    display: inline-block;
    width: calc(50% - 10px);
    max-height: 220px;
    margin: 5px;

    border-radius: 4px;
    box-sizing: border-box;

    overflow: auto;
}

@media (max-width: 480px) {
    .bots_list .bot-information-box {
        // some style here
    }
}
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-06 15:56 UTC

Yeah, we generally do media queries in `media.css` for big layout changes, but I think for an individual sub-component like this (which has no reason to have the same breakpoints as anything else), it'd be reasonable to just do it right after the main declaration.

**Akash** · 2018-06-06 21:10 UTC

Hmm, in that case, we'll have multiple copies of same breakpoints i.e -
```sh
line #501 
@media (max-width: 480px) {
    #pw_strength {
        margin: auto;
    }
    // other styles
}
line #800
@media (max-width: 480px) {
    .bots_list .bot-information-box {
         width: 100%;
     }
    // other styles
}
```
Let me know if it's okay to go that way.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-06 21:45 UTC

Yeah, I think if it's at a standard breakpoint size, we should do it in `media.css`, but if you have something weird for a single component, it might make sense to do it in the current CSS file.

**Akash** · 2018-06-06 22:09 UTC

Make sense.

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-07-07 00:29 UTC

I guess what I’m saying is even though there may be a little bit of overhead with using mostly functional open source components, it often comes with certain benefits. More of a passing thought than a strongly held vIew.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-07 12:56 UTC

@Armaan Ahluwalia Thanks for clarifying.  Probably the most archaic aspect of our codebase (where archaic is relative to how fast technology has moved in the last N years) is that we don't have any kind of **virtual DOM** system, and it's not particularly easy to introduce those systems in a gradual, non-disruptive way (although I would certainly love to be proven wrong there).

The other issue is that we tend to have **long lists** in the app, starting of course with the message view, but also things like subscriber lists in stream settings.  We do **progressive rendering** for most of our long lists.  Most of our longer lists use a home-grown component called `list_render.js` that is pretty solid and scroll-aware, but  it can't really completely abstract away DOM changes.  And then the message view code is highly home-grown, and is too complex for `list_render`, because on top of having to render only small windows of messages at a time (to avoid expensive re-renders), there's a lot of corner cases that come up as new messages arrive, particularly in interleaved views that have the recipient bars.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-07 13:03 UTC

Also, there are plenty of places in our code where we would benefit from nicer generalizations.  A good example is popup menus, where basically each of them, in our codebase, is a fairly ad hoc collections of click handlers tied to specific DOM selectors.  It wouldn't be hard to make an interface for them where you past in a list of items, and each item has the html and handler.  A lot of the popups have items that are only shown under certain conditions, so it's not quite static enough to be completely data-configured, but we could certainly make it cleaner with some thought.

:thumbs_up:

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-07 13:20 UTC

*2018-07-03 to 2018-07-06 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/.239871/with/607474)*

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-07-03 17:45 UTC

Continuing discussion about #9871 to here:

When a narrow is reloaded, the following things happened:
1. `subs.initialize()` was called, which in turned called `streams_list.build_stream_list()`for the **first** time
2.  `hashchange.initialize()`calls `narrow.activate()`
3. `narrow.activate()` in turn calls `streams_list.handle_narrow_activated()`
4. `streams_list.handle_narrow_activated()`calls `streams_list.scroll_stream_into_view`, which correctly scrolls the stream into view.
5. However,`message_fetch.initialize()` calls `streams_list.build_stream_list()`again for the **second** time, which triggers `streams_list.update_streams_sidebar()` (which doesn't scroll the stream into view). 
6. Step 5 occurs 2 more times, and then nothing else gets called.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-05 17:45 UTC

If we go to the original approach, which I still don't recommend, we should rename the function.  If we go with your approach, I'd move most of that code into `stream_list.js` and call it `stream_list.update_after_fetch` or something similar.  I'd also spend some time thinking about the nuances here.  Most of the current code gets invoked when either the user is explicitly narrowing to a stream or when they wouldn't have scrolled away for any legitimate reason.  There's a real danger here of introducing the opposite problem that we have now.  If I open up the app in a narrow I'm not interested in (totally plausible if I'm just going off of some dumb browser autocomplete), I'm gonna scroll to find more interesting narrows, and we don't want to disrupt the user.  So we possibly want a new helper function that's more like `keep_selection_in_narrow` that only re-scrolls if you're still looking at the active narrow in the sidebar.  Or we may want to do something more like detecting that the user has already begun actively scrolling.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-18 18:36 UTC

@Rishi Gupta the advice is against muting too high a fraction of the total traffic you're receiving (whether via muted streams or topics), and the problems it causes are more around algorithms that optimize the experience for your most recent messages do an increasingly bad job if you're not actually reading your most recent messages.  E.g. which topics we show without clicking "more topics" and going to the server after the webapp loads, what messages we show without going to the server when you click a narrow, etc.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-07-18 19:39 UTC

also I was thinking of framing the advice more as you should be muting < 1000 messages a week, or < 150 messages/day. If you're only getting 50 messages/day muting half of it won't be a problem.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-18 20:32 UTC

We send all topics to the frontend if you click "more topics".  The stuff before you click that is driven by the browser's cache.

## #9982

*2018-07-21 to 2018-07-22 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/.239982/with/615316)*

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-07-21 02:40 UTC

This is a discussion to find the best solution for the scrolling bug in #9982.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-07-21 02:40 UTC

It turns out there's no JS affecting the scrolling. Instead, the subscriptions modal is initially half its size when hidden due to some fancy-CSS-styling (see below), and it gets grown to its full size when the modal is opened.

```css
.overlay.show .overlay-content {
    -webkit-transform: scale(1);
    transform: scale(1);
}
.overlay .overlay-content {
    -webkit-transform: scale(0.5);
    transform: scale(0.5);
    z-index: 102;
    transition: transform 0.3s ease;
}
```

Problem is, when we try to scroll the row into view, the modal is still half its size, so the element scrolling function calculates the scroll position while the stream row is half its width and height.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-07-21 02:40 UTC

Currently, I've added the following JS to track when the size-transform transition completes so that everything is full width/and height, and then scroll to the active stream row.

```js
        $('.subscriptions .overlay-content').on('transitionend webkitTransitionEnd oTransitionEnd', function () {
            var stream_row = $('.stream-row.active');
            if (stream_row) {
                scroll_util.scroll_element_into_container(stream_row, stream_row.parent());
            }
        });
```

The catch with this solution is that there's a noticeable ~0.5 second delay from initial modal launch to stream row scroll [gif](https://i.gyazo.com/ae0b40176d2d5b50cd2302a89be2a08b.gif)

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-07-21 02:41 UTC

Is the lag is negligible enough? Or should the CSS that's affecting the size transitions be modified to not change size/removed?

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-07-21 11:17 UTC

To be very honest I’m not a huge fan of this expanding animation. It’s extremely laggy on top of an already VERY slow modal initiation. My vote would be to lose the additional animation delay and just display the window or cut it down by a lot.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-07-21 15:02 UTC

agreed on cutting down the animation.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-07-22 03:14 UTC

I've removed the size animation changes, here's what it looks like now: [gif](https://i.gyazo.com/ac18fe123212bf230f898ac4f407fb11.gif)

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-07-22 23:41 UTC

So I know the purpose of that check @Joshua Pan 
The workflow goes something like this
* Jitsi is the default option and 'https://meet.jit.si/' is the default jitsi server url 
* This means jitsi chat is enabled by default. 
* Case 1 (We switch to google hangouts)
In this case there can be no way that `realm_google_hangouts_domain` is null or '' (We ensure that at switching)
* Case 2 (We disable jitsi )
This is the case where `jitsi_server_url` could be `null` and hence the check is in place for that.

Why we don't need it for google hangouts (Because if hangouts is enabled, the field for its domain can't be null or empty and if it is disabled then jitsi option must be selected. But you can disable jitsi by setting `'JITSI_SERVER_URL'` to`None` so the check is required in that case.

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-07-28 05:05 UTC

1.) What should happen when a user pastes a copied search pill, should the filter for that pill be immediately applied and narrowed accordingly?

2.) What should happen when a user does not use a typeahead to add a pill i.e presses esc to remove the typeahead and then presses enter, should the filter for that pill be immediately applied and narrowed accordingly? 
The problem with doing that currently is some race conditions. The pills in the case of typeahead not open are added by an event listener in `input_pills.js`. The narrow for the same has to be done in `search.js`, also using an event listener. Having both these event listeners causes some race conditions and weird things to happen.
(A potential solution for this is to allow specifying a function to be executed in the event listener in input_pill.js)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-30 01:34 UTC

**Nehal Sharma** · 2024-01-30 16:30 UTC

@Evy Just pulled down and tested out #26803. 

I think I have a solution to propose: Replace the call to `hide` at the end of `select` with a call to `lookup`, passing hideOnEmpty as true. This will make it so that post accepting and filling in a typeahead selection, the typeahead menu will continue showing if there is potential for more autocompletion, with those suggestions, else it will close. On testing locally, it seems to work just as intended, and also doesn't seem to break other typeaheads

**Nehal Sharma** · 2024-01-30 16:33 UTC

I also think this would be a good improvement to make in general, since it enables chaining autocompletions, which might be needed for `/call` to lead into @-mentions and timestamps (#**design>making calls**), for example

      var val = this.$menu.find('.active').data('typeahead-value')
      if (this.$element.is("[contenteditable]")) {
        this.$element.html(this.updater(val, e)).trigger("change");
        // Empty textContent after the change event handler
        // converts the input text to html elements.
        this.$element.html('');
      } else {
         ...
      }

      return this.lookup(true)
    }
```

And there are still some issues:

(1) `this.$element.html('');` still clears the text I added
(2) If I comment out that line, the cursor still gets placed at the start of the input.

If I switch back to this, then it works, because the search pills and text get completely reset on each selection, so the `this.$element.html` calls aren't necessary.

```js
if (this.$element.is("[contenteditable]")) {
        this.updater(val, e);
        this.$element.trigger("change");
}
```

Would you recommend adding an option to the typeahead for this for not updating the typeahead content on selection?

**Nehal Sharma** · 2024-03-07 19:28 UTC

Yes, that makes sense since the updater here already modifies the html as needed. :thumbs_up:

So it turns out this does break the topic typeahead  (#**issues>🎯 topic typeahead getting stuck** )

## Make keyboard shortcut pop-up printable?

*2018-08-06 to 2018-10-30 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Make.20keyboard.20shortcut.20pop-up.20printable.3F/with/626341)*

**Karl Fogel** · 2018-08-06 15:45 UTC

In Zulip 1.8.1, if you go to settings pull-down (upper right gear icon) and choose "Keyboard shortcuts", you get a helpful pop-up.  It offers three panes: "Keyboard shortcuts", "Message formatting" and "Search operators".

All three of the panes would be useful as printed refcards, but there's no way to print each pane's content reliably.  I tried Ctrl-P (this is in Firefox Quantum 61.0.1 on Debian GNU/Linux) while on the first pane.  The attached screenshot shows what happens -- you get a printout of exactly what the current browser tab is showing, which is basically the grayed-out main Zulip page (note I've redacted some confidential channel names in this screenshot) with whatever amount of the scrollable help pane happens to be showing at that moment:

[zulip-1.8.1-kbd-shortcuts-popup-print-attempt-ffox-quantum.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/c1/By3NpABMIoPL-DWoOjnQ_EZY/zulip-1.8.1-kbd-shortcuts-popup-print-attempt-ffox-quantum.png) 

**Suggested behavior:** Have a print button on the help pane, which when clicked causes the *entire* contents of that help pane (including the stuff currently scrolled off the bottom due to the browser window size) to be printed out.  Bonus if the printout is formatted in some ref-card-ish way, but even just printing the full pane contents using whatever print formatting the browser defaults to would be fine.

Thoughts?  I wanted to float this idea here before filing a ticket in the tracker.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-18 05:11 UTC

haha, yeah we recently fix this issue of multiple click handler with other modal.(#10156)

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-08-18 05:13 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-18 05:13 UTC

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-08-18 05:14 UTC

But every time modal opens `meta.loaded` flag set to `False` so every time click handlers get initialized at least once.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-08-18 17:03 UTC

Maybe it'd be worth using `.once` instead of `.on` for one-time click handlers?

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-08-18 18:20 UTC

we can use `.once` but then it only allows to submit form once. Like if you open a modal and try to submit form twice, `.once` click handler only called once, second time it won't submit form. One of these days we should probably document how settings does setup stuff every time you open the gear menu.  When we built that out (it was largely me, but my memory is already fuzzy on details of how it all works, and stuff has changed a bit since then), it was kind of a necessary evil to work around a few parts of the settings system being really slow.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-20 19:55 UTC

We use the `meta.loaded` approach for this sort of thing in a bunch of other places; I don't see why it shouldn't work here.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:33 UTC

And strangely, if you go to sort on "Size" then come back to "Date uploaded" it works!  So something subtle is going on.  This is a progressively rendered widget, which could explain some glitches.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:33 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:34 UTC

Here's the markup:

~~~
  5     <table class="table table-condensed table-striped wrapped-table">
  6         <thead>
  7             <th data-sort="alphabetic" data-sort-prop="name" class="upload-file-name">{{t "File" }}</th>
  8             <th class="active" data-sort="numeric" data-sort-prop="create_time">{{t "Date uploaded" }}</th>
  9             <th data-sort="mentioned-in">{{t "Mentioned in" }}</th>
 10             <th class="upload-size" data-sort="numeric" data-sort-prop="size">{{t "Size" }}</th>
 11             <th class="upload-actions">{{t "Actions" }}</th>
 12         </thead>
 13     </table>

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:35 UTC

So it's setting `data-sort` to `create_time` using `numeric` as the sort method.  Seems reasonable.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:39 UTC

Unfortunately `static/js/attachments_ui.js` doesn't expose any of its data, so I can't look at the data in the dev console, but I can find it in the "Network" tab, since the data comes from "/json/attachments".

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:42 UTC

In the response to that REST endpoint, all the items I looked at seemed to have POSIX-like values for `create_time`, i.e. huge integers.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:44 UTC

There's some possibility that the sort is actually working, but the dates being displayed are just wrong somehow.  I doubt it, though, the code to handle that is pretty simple:

~~~
 79     _.each(new_attachments, function (attachment) {
 80         var time = new XDate(attachment.create_time);
 81         attachment.create_time_str = timerender.render_now(time).time_str;
 82         attachment.size_str = bytes_to_size(attachment.size);
 83     });

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:45 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 18:59 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 19:06 UTC

I can also play around with these types of things in the console:

~~~
list_render.get('uploaded-files-list').sort('numeric', 'create_time', undefined, undefined, true)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 19:26 UTC

Well, apparently this all comes down to the fact that the column is marked as "active" even though it was never sorted.  And then there are various shortcuts in the code that simply reverse the list if the markup indicates the code is already in sorted order.  What made this really tricky is that the attachments are in mostly-sorted order from the server, apparently.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 19:31 UTC

My guess is that it broke in this commit from @Cynthia Lin in October 2017 (11 months ago), in which "active" was added to the template for the "Date uploaded" column, which fooled the widget into thinking it was already sorted:

6a4e7ad12e09d60836555cb10af19809aadb4b1d

I think the real problem, though, is that the underlying design is a bit brittle.  At the very least, the attribute should be something more specific, like "forward-sorted", instead of "active".  And we should probably just re-sort every time instead of assuming the list is in some order based on some DOM attribute.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-17 19:36 UTC

It's also a super annoying bug in that the symptom is less than obvious.  I bet dev data is naturally in order by create_time, so you'd never see this in dev, not to mention we don't have much test data.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-09-21 04:03 UTC

Man, that's really subtle.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-09-29 00:37 UTC

Just read over @Steve Howell 's comments; so is the primary issue that when initially rendered, the files aren't sorted by date uploaded as we initially thought but in a random order instead, so we need to sort by date when it's rendered?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-29 00:51 UTC

correct

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-29 00:52 UTC

I think we want to remove "active" from the markup in the template and do things more explicitly in JS code.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-29 00:53 UTC

You probably want to look at it a bit though before following my recommendation--I know what's broken but I'm a bit fuzzy on how to fix it in the most kosher way for the `list_render` mechanism.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-09-29 05:15 UTC

Alright, I think I know why the sorting is broken.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-09-29 05:15 UTC

This is the markup of the table headers:
```html
  5     <table class="table table-condensed table-striped wrapped-table">
  6         <thead>
  7             <th data-sort="alphabetic" data-sort-prop="name" class="upload-file-name">{{t "File" }}</th>
  8             <th class="active" data-sort="numeric" data-sort-prop="create_time">{{t "Date uploaded" }}</th>
  9             <th data-sort="mentioned-in">{{t "Mentioned in" }}</th>
 10             <th class="upload-size" data-sort="numeric" data-sort-prop="size">{{t "Size" }}</th>
 11             <th class="upload-actions">{{t "Actions" }}</th>
 12         </thead>
 13     </table>
```

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-09-29 05:15 UTC

This is our sorting code that gets called when we initiate a list render:
```js
        if ($this.hasClass("active")) {
            if (!$this.hasClass("descend")) {
                $this.addClass("descend");
            } else {
                $this.removeClass("descend");
            }

            list.sort(undefined, undefined, undefined, undefined, true);
            // Table has already been sorted by this property; do not re-sort.
            return;
        }

        // if `prop_name` is defined, it will trigger the generic codepath,
        // and not if it is undefined.
        list.sort(sort_type, prop_name);

        $this.siblings(".active").removeClass("active");
        $this.addClass("active");
```

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-09-29 05:15 UTC

By adding `class="active"` to one of the sort headers, we trick the table into thinking it's pre-sorted by that header's sort tpe, when it really isn't. Removing the class specification should theoretically solve the problem.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-09-29 05:16 UTC

I'm not sure if we want to have the attachments table presorted by using jQuery to click on a certain sort header (date uploaded/file size/name/etc.) though.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-29 09:21 UTC

I agree with the analysis here.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-09-29 16:38 UTC

Should we manually initialize a sort with a jQuery click when the tab is first launched? The sort arrow + behavior doesn't actually show up until you click on a header, so users might now know about the sorting behavior.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-29 18:07 UTC

I don't think you need to simulate a click to make the sort happen--there should be a way to do it by calling the list_render API (or if there isn't, you could change the code probably fairly easily).

It also occurs to me that if the natural sorting order here  is by date, then we should just sort the data before putting it in the widget.

And then to answer your question about making the feature discoverable, I view that as a would-be-nice here, not a strict requirement.

**Cynthia Lin** · 2018-09-29 22:05 UTC

My solution is just to call `list.sort('numeric', 'create_time');` on the generated list while keeping the active class on the Date sorted column (`<th class="active" data-sort="numeric" data-sort-prop="create_time">{{t "Date uploaded" }}</th>`) when it initializes then. Does that sound reasonable to you?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-29 22:40 UTC

That sounds reasonable.

## Add raw content with messages

*2018-10-22 to 2018-10-22 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Add.20raw.20content.20with.20messages/with/654309)*

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-10-22 01:17 UTC

I noticed that our quote-and-reply mechanism was a little *slower* than expected, and I found this piece of code:

```js
    channel.get({
        url: '/json/messages/' + message_id,
        idempotent: true,
        success: function (data) {
            if (textarea.val() === "") {
                textarea.val("```quote\n" + data.raw_content + "\n```\n");
            } else {
                textarea.val(textarea.val() + "\n```quote\n" + data.raw_content + "\n```\n");
            }
            $("#compose-textarea").trigger("autosize.resize");
        },
    });
```

It looks like we're sending a request only to get back the `raw_content` field. Is there a reason why we do not already have that field on the server?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-10-22 12:02 UTC

I think the reason we don't send raw_content is bandwidth.  We actually have some fairly complex code on the server that decides whether to send only one of either raw_content or rendered_content based on what the client requests.  I'm not sure whether this is set in stone, so I'd be curious to hear what @Tim Abbott says here.  I think quote&reply is relatively rare.

(The reason bandwidth is an issue here is that messages can get delivered to lots of users at once, at least on streams.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-10-22 17:08 UTC

Yep, that's correct; it's a bandwidth optimization to only send the HTML-rendered content.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-10-22 17:09 UTC

(I guess it doesn't feel slow to me, because I have a nice Internet connection to where our servers are; @Rohitt Vashishtha how long does it take for you?  It's possible we should have some sort of loading indicator or other transient state)

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-10-22 17:15 UTC

I pressed the k
> Yep, that's correct; it's a bandwidth optimization to only send the HTML-rendered content.
 ey and started typing this message. The delay is noticeable here on my network.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-10-22 21:38 UTC

OK.  We should probably do something like what we do with uploading files, namely, adding some placeholder content immediately and then swapping it for the final content once we've fetched it from the server.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-10-22 21:38 UTC

So that you can start typing immediately without that kind of issue.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-10-22 21:52 UTC

Filed as #10705.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-10-22 21:59 UTC

Great :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-27 00:02 UTC

The way we like to do things is to figure out a plan that lets us efficiently and at scale produce clean, mergable commits/PRs that are efficient to verify (e.g. it's a clear code change that just renames one variable and clearly doesn't break anything and you can check by grepping, etc.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-27 00:04 UTC

I'll have more thoughts later, but I think every improvement is potentially in scope eventually, we just need to figure out a strategic sequencing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-27 00:07 UTC

The things we have done that are worth making sure folks know about:
* `app_components.scss` and `components.scss` have a bunch of reusable button (etc.) styles used in many places across the app
* A bunch of components (sidebars, settings areas, etc.) have their own CSS files that have (hopefully) all of the custom styling for those components.
* We migrated to webpack with SCSS support.

A bunch of low-hanging refactoring fruit we have not done:
* Variables for popular colors
* Converting those component-level CSS files to use SCSS layering so that it's structurally obvious that e.g. `subscriptions.scss` doesn't effect anything outside the "Manage streams" overlay.  So far, it's been mostly a matter of discipline for ensuring that.
* Things like variable name styling standardization.
* A lot more things, but I'm out of time for composing more of this message right now :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-27 00:09 UTC

We should definitely do small tactical fixes to remove complexity while we're working through some such CSS codebase cleanup phase, but given that there's several folks interested in helping here, I think we mostly need to come up with a good strategy for organizing the work.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-27 00:21 UTC

E.g. perhaps a few good starter projects would be:
* For the variables concept, to pick a color we use in ~50 places (not huge enough to be a merge conflict issue) and convert just that to be a value in a `variables.scss` file, so that we can figure out how we want that to be hooked up.
* Do changes like 9efe907ef10c74ae676a140b04fdb68e48d7b412 to some of the individual CSS files we've already broken out (e.g. `static/styles/input_pill.scss`)

**Michel Tomas** · 2018-11-27 19:45 UTC

I agree, I hate BEM. Definitely, not for the `--` but for the double-underscore :), but I hate it.  
But in my experience http://thesassway.com/advanced/modular-css-naming-conventions has 2 issues. 
Say we have a `<button class="button dropdown-button left">I'm a button</button>`:   
* Readability: the relation between `button` and  `dropdown-button` isn't obvious. Much less than `button button--dropdown` - the single dash being reserved for components/children/sub  
* DX: if from my IDE I want to go to the related SCSS declaration for `.left`, my IDE won't know which `.left` it should go to: is it the `.button.left`, the `.menu.left` or the `.badge.left`? Using `u-left` makes it easy to understand. 

Using `button button--float u-left` makes it quite clear: it's a button, floating variant, aligned left. IDEs can easily go to any definition (even `&--float{}` is recognized), and it's still pretty easy to document (I wasn't planning on sending this link to people, I'd like to write this doc for us, as simple as the SASSway post)

**Michel Tomas** · 2018-11-27 19:47 UTC

Also the fact that modifiers like `--` are used in at least 2 naming conventions, one being BEM (still hate it but quite adopted nowadays), makes it a great candidate for modifiers :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-03 03:35 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-03 15:14 UTC

Here's the main logic to hide it:

~~~ js
 69     var candidate = rows.get_message_recipient_row(selected_row);
 70     if (candidate === undefined) {
 71         return;
 72     }
 73     while (true) {
 74         if (candidate.length === 0) {
 75             // We're at the top of the page and no labels are above us.
 76             exports.hide();
 77             return;
 78         }
 79         if (candidate.is(".recipient_row")) {
 80             if (candidate.offset().top < floating_recipient_bar_bottom) {
 81                 break;
 82             }
 83         }
 84         candidate = candidate.prev();
 85     }

~~~

@Tim Abbott I think my last series introduced a bug related to `ui_init` ordering.  The `muting` module now depends on `stream_data` earlier in the process.  Probably a two-line fix.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-15 18:51 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-15 19:06 UTC

#11053 should me merged before we deploy again

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-15 19:32 UTC

I have a pretty thorough commit message for the change that I made, but I wasn't super explicit about what happens inside `unread_ui.js`.  The `unread_ui.initialize` function causes `unread_ui.update_unread_counts` to happen, but it happens via `initialize -> consider_bankruptcy -> enable -> update_unread_counts`.  For the non-bankruptcy case, it's pretty easy to reason about.  For the bankruptcy case, I recommend doing a quick QA where you just hard-code the condition to `true` with a couple unread messages. (I did this and it seems fine.)

## #11016

*2018-12-18 to 2018-12-18 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/.2311016/with/673728)*

**Shoumorup Mukhopadhyay** · 2018-12-18 16:48 UTC

I'm new to Django and am not able to figure out how all the CSS is plugged into files (such as templates/zerver/email_log.html) that extend templates/zerver/base.html? I've googled a lot but am still at a loss. Maybe i'm missing something trivial?

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-12-18 16:49 UTC

So for each email, there are two source templates: the `.txt` version
(for plain-text format) as well as a `.source.html` template.  The
`.txt` version is used directly; while the `.source.html` template is
processed by `tools/inline-email-css` (generating a `.html` template
under `templates/zerver/emails/compiled`); that tool (powered by
`premailer`) injects the CSS we use for styling our emails
(`templates/zerver/emails/email.css`) into the templates inline.

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-12-18 16:51 UTC

Something useful I do whenever I'm stuck is to search [the documentation website](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) for keywords I think may be relevant. In your case email and css may have pointed you to that para?

There are lots of possible outcomes from this logic:
* defensive code that seems unlikely to me (last row should always be there)
* can't move the pointer up (**so warn user**)
* more defensive code that seems unlikely (zero message height?)
* user doesn't have focus (only relevant for messages from **other people**)
* popovers are active (so don't scroll, but probably only comes with **other people's** messages)
* user's already fine (message hasn't scrolled off screen yet)
* will autoscroll (so user **will** be fine once animation completes)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-01-04 17:00 UTC

I think we ignore the defensive cases.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-01-04 17:00 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2019-01-04 17:01 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2019-01-04 17:01 UTC
