**Steve Howell** · 2019-01-05 17:54 UTC

One thing I'd like to clean up is that we reverse-engineer whether the user was already in a scrolled-up state by subtracting out `new_messages_height` from `bottom_last_visible`.  This calculation is bogus due to the fact that `new_messages_height` only includes messages sent by you.  It's plausible that we should we should tweak the height of `new_messages_height` itself, but I think its intended purpose is to dictate how much we scroll, and that won't always correspond to the actual amount of new rendered content.  So...

**Steve Howell** · 2019-01-05 17:56 UTC

...in my mind it makes more sense to just calculate, right before rendering, whether the user is already scrolled up (or to put it another way, to calculate whether the bottom message is already offscreen), and then just pass that boolean to `_maybe_autoscroll`.  And that can short-circuit scrolling more easily, plus that will drive us to always tell the user to scroll down.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-01-05 18:06 UTC

A typical story here would be this:
* I zoom to topic (and maybe get caught up).
* I scroll up manually (with either mouse or keyboard) to a message a page back.
* Somebody sends a new message to the topic.
* At this point, I don't want to be distracted, and I certainly don't want the feed to scroll away from the message I'm reading.
* I start composing, and maybe another message comes in.
* Again, I don't want to be distracted, I don't want to be scrolled.  (some subtle indicator would be fine, though, especially since many folks don't have notifications on)
* I send the message.
* At this point, I'd argue not to scroll me yet (I may still want to read the paged-up convo ).
* But I do want the "Scroll down to see the message you sent" message.

## #11112 Multiuse link

*2019-01-09 to 2019-01-09 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/.2311112.20Multiuse.20link/with/680358)*

**Shubham Dhama** · 2019-01-09 18:28 UTC

This is in reference to #11112:
We are using stream names for `invite_users_backend` and stream ids for `generate_multiuse_invite_backend`. Any particular reason for that?
Actually I was thinking to make both APIs similar, i decide to for  `stream_id` for both methods as it seems more reasonable to use id than a string. Is this alright?
Then in frontend it would make easier to use stream_ids for both type of invitation methods(we can also go for stream name for both?)
If we decided to go for stream ids then we need to change `invite.get_invite_streams` to this :
```js
// stream_data.js
exports.get_invite_stream_data = function () {
    var filter_stream_data = function (sub) {
        return {'name': sub.name,
                'stream_id': sub.stream_id,
                'invite_only': sub.invite_only,
                'default_stream': stream_data.get_default_status(sub.name)};
    };
    var invite_stream_data = _.map(stream_data.subscribed_subs(), filter_stream_data);
    var default_stream_data = _.map(page_params.realm_default_streams, filter_stream_data);

    // union doesn't work on array of objects we are using below filter
    var is_included = {};
    var streams = _.filter(default_stream_data.concat(invite_stream_data), function (sub) {
        if (is_included[sub.name]) {
            return false;
        }
        is_included[sub.name] = true;
        return true;
    });
    return streams;
};


// invite.js
exports.get_invite_streams = function () {
    var streams = _.filter(stream_data.get_invite_stream_data(), function (stream) {
        var is_notifications_stream = stream.name === page_params.notifications_stream;
        // You can't actually elect to invite someone to the
        // notifications stream. We won't even show it as a choice unless
        // it's the only stream you have, or if you've made it private.
        return stream_data.subscribed_streams().length === 1 ||
            !is_notifications_stream ||
            is_notifications_stream && stream.is_invite_only;
    });
    return streams;
};
```
and some changes to backend.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-01-09 18:40 UTC

@Shubham Dhama We definitely want to move to `stream_id` over names whenever possible.  Some of the legacy code makes these refactorings slightly tricky, but it's well worth your time to clean those up as you see fit.  For this kind of cleanup you'll often need 2 or 3 commits to kind of shim your way around stuff.

I tend to work from back to front on these.  For example, if some function obnoxiously requires a stream name, you can make it take a stream id instead, and then convert back to name inside that function.  And the knot will slowly untangle.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-01-09 20:16 UTC

I believe we don't interact with invites in non-web clients, so we can change just the API to be an ID-based API here.

The tooling is in place and `dict.js`, a common module used in a lot of places is now `dict.ts`.  We'll probably be playing with the tooling and migration approach for the next few days before trying to move larger amounts of code; this is probably also something where we'll want to use TinglingGit to scan for and let us target JS files that don't have larger open PRs that we'll want to avoid conflicting with.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-21 17:59 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-21 18:03 UTC

I'd also love to hear ideas from folks on what strategy we should take for migrating.  My current thinking is that:
* We want the typescript migration to be as limited as possible in terms of making changes not part of moving to typescript, to simplify code review, since we're moving ~45K lines of code.  So ideally no functional changes, and potentially avoiding replacing `_.each` type calls with newer ES6 things in the first pass that churn the code.  It'll be easy to bulk-migrate those with `git grep` in a later pass.  Possibly we should take the same approach with `let` vs. `var` too.  We'll want to experiment a bit.
* We want to start with migrating a few smaller groups of files (e.g. we're doing `typing_*.js` next) just to get some experience before we tackle big things like `people.js`.

 @Steve Howell @Anders Kaseorg @Tommy Ip FYI

**Tommy Ip** · 2019-03-22 16:10 UTC

For reference here is the lodash implementation of each (alias forEach):
```js
function forEach(collection, iteratee) {
  const func = Array.isArray(collection) ? arrayEach : baseEach
  return func(collection, iteratee)
}

function baseEach(collection, iteratee) {
  if (collection == null) {
    return collection
  }
  if (!isArrayLike(collection)) {
    return baseForOwn(collection, iteratee)
  }
  const length = collection.length
  const iterable = Object(collection)
  let index = -1

  while (++index < length) {
    if (iteratee(iterable[index], index, iterable) === false) {
      break
    }
  }
  return collection
}

function arrayEach(array, iteratee) {
  let index = -1
  const length = array.length

  while (++index < length) {
    if (iteratee(array[index], index, array) === false) {
      break
    }
  }
  return array
}
```
So basically it just turns into a for loop. Underscore's implementation is simpler but their approaches are pretty much the same. Interestingly though they are no way near the performance of a plain for loop (https://medium.com/tech-tajawal/loops-performances-in-node-js-9fbccf2d6aa6), probably due to the etra function call in each iteration.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-22 16:43 UTC

> In any case where the `forEach` performance is a concern (I doubt there will ever be one) using a `for`loop is guaranteed to beat it and the custom `_.each` implementation.
I haven't benchmarked recently, but when we adopted `_`, the difference had a significant effect on the performance of common operations like narrowing.  I think it's valuable to be consistent about how we do loops in the codebase for readability (we'll probably want to add a linter rule for this), and I don't think there's a reason we'd want to migrate to `forEach`.  

Back to the actual TypeScript discussion, the main point I wanted to make is that we should avoid churning the codebase for `_.each` -> `for` in the same commit migrating a  file to TypeScript, because it adds a lot more complexity to what's changing and thus will takes 2-3x as long to review as doing those two changes in separate commits.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-22 19:10 UTC

There is an alternate way to make progress on TypeScript conversion in the presence of circular dependencies: we could write temporary `.d.ts` declaration files for enough of our own `.js` modules to allow their dependents to be converted, and remove the separate declarations once the conversion circles back around to those modules.

This comes with its own pitfalls: there’s no enforcement that the separate declarations remain in sync with the modules, so we’d need to pay attention to that when reviewing changes to those modules. And we do want to eventually banish circular dependencies anyway for a number of other reasons.

But this shortcut may still be worth considering in some cases, since having TypeScript could help us to more confidently perform the refactorings that remove the circular dependencies.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-24 22:19 UTC

Hmm, yeah, that does seem like an approach that will be useful once we get a ways through this.  I think the specific refactoring mentioned above is trivial (structurally, the file just has two unrelated sets of functions in it), but it seems likely to be useful for others.

Hi everyone, I'm fairly new to the Zulip and having a tough time wrapping my head around how data is flowing from backend to frontend. I want to understand how handlebar templates are getting data from the backend? I tried to look in `static/js` but didn't help much.
I tried to understand it by following this documentation as well  - https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/new-feature-tutorial.html#example-feature
Thanks!

PS: I'm coming from Reactjs  background

**Vishnu KS** · 2019-01-28 07:26 UTC

hmm. I think there are 3 main ways. When the app is loaded for the first time a bunch of data is loaded from the server as page_params. It contains information like the email of the user, emojiset, full_name, is_admin etc values that are used by the various javascript modules for rendering the UI (handlebars also usually use page_params for data). I think you can think of it as the state equivalent of a react component. But page_params would be global for all the javascript modules. There won't be any reactive rendering. You need to manually update the various elements like divs when the value of a key in page_params change. Type `page_params` in console.log to see what is contained in them.

Okay. Now we have the initial data stored in page_params. What happens when the value of a page_params change in the server? That is communicated via the zulip event system. A new event is sent using 'send_event` function from backend when the value changes and the value of page_params is updated in frontend. (send_event is kind of like socket.io if you have worked on that before) You need to manually add the code to change the value of page_params in frontend whenever an event happens. See server_event_dispatch.js for the code for that. If any UI change is required during the event that is also triggered usually from this file.

Finally, there are some data which you don't want to pass as page_params. Like the list of messages for example in the stream frontend. They are fetched using the Zulip REST API whenever required. 

See https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/events-system.html for more details :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-05 01:39 UTC

This is now test-deployed here; you can play with it using `Ctrl+M`.  It is very experimental; we're looking for super-early thoughts on direction.  Some things I notice:
* I like that it includes unread PMs at the top, with the user avatar beside them.  I think I like that it's full-height.  We'll need to figure out how to do a visual UI for toggling to the other view; not sure what to do there.  Reasonable options include a top-level toggle thing and having each view have a link to the other.
* It's a bug that muted streams/topics show up, in the "unreads" view; they should be excluded so that if you're "caught up" the view is empty.  Thought this bug is kinda handy for me testing right this moment :)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-04 20:16 UTC

Just to provide a little more clarity to the above statement.  It's definitely a good habit to flesh out issues on chat before filing them on GH, as often you can get immediate feedback that you just don't understand the feature, or we're never going to do it for X reason, etc.  But you never need to wait for core members to file an issue.  In fact, sometimes filing an issue is good for things that aren't completely decided. The mobile app is **strongly recommended** over mobile web.  But we still want mobile web to work.  It doesn't have to work great, but it should at least be usable, I think. ## data attributes

*2019-02-04 to 2019-02-05 · 28 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/data.20attributes/with/694019)*

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-04 20:05 UTC

I know we kind of oscillate on the tradeoffs here, but @Tim Abbott, do you have any objection to putting data attributes closer to click handlers (even though it makes the HTML a tad heavier)?  This is coming up for the "unread list" work, where the click handlers for topic popovers can basically only work in one location and are thus hard to reuse if we make different views.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-04 20:10 UTC

See #11449 for context.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-04 20:12 UTC

Even without the current motivation, I think the prior code is brittle.  We've definitely had bugs where well meaning designers cleaned up HTML/CSS and didn't realize it would break click handlers.  It's hard to protect 100% against that, but the PR above makes it a lot less likely.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-04 20:13 UTC

Amazingly, this is first prep "prefactor" commit for the mobile view.  (Although part of that is I'm too afraid to refactor any CSS.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-04 21:42 UTC

@Steve Howell What do you think about `build_topic_popover(stream_id, elt)` and having the caller be responsible for getting the `data-stream-id` object?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-04 21:45 UTC

I guess it's really cheap to have the data-stream-id in each topic object, and those are immutable.  It feels more silly with the topic name; I'd need to look at how topic editing works to see if that's going to cause problems for us where an object gets left with a stale data-topic-name, which is the class of bug this new approach generates.

I think the `.closest` approach we have currently is pretty safe (since designers are unlikely to remove the outer container) and it seems like we could achieve the same refactoring.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-04 21:46 UTC

(Or even `build_topic_popvover(elt, stream_id, topic_name)`

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-05 13:43 UTC

Actually one subtle thing I forgot to mention yesterday is that the structure of the unread list is flatter than the sidebar list.  The unread list is just a single list of items, where each item can be either pm, stream, or topic.  Whereas the left sidebar is a pm list, and then a stream list with nested topic lists.  I find the flatter list a lot easier to work with.

It's because of these differences that I don't want to borrow too much markup, because in the unread list a topic doesn't have a parent stream item (from an HTML hierarchy perspective).

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-05 19:53 UTC

Hmm, what's your thinking around not having that hierarchy?

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-05 19:56 UTC

I think flatter's nicer, basically.  In the left sidebar we only really ever had one nested list.  Having lists inside of lists can lead to wierd bugs where CSS selectors grab sublist items when you only want the parent items, etc.  The only tradeoff is that you just need a good sort function.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-05 19:57 UTC

It will also make it easier to add keyboard navigation to the list.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-05 19:58 UTC

I guess keyboard navigation makes sense.  But not having hierarchy will make it harder to do things like "highlight the parent stream row" if we ever want to do that sort of thing.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-05 20:01 UTC

> I guess keyboard navigation makes sense. But not having hierarchy will make it harder to do things like "highlight the parent stream row" if we ever want to do that sort of thing.
 
Yeah, I suppose.  The main time you care about a topic's parent is when you are talking about the current topic, and we can flag the corresponding current stream pretty easily so that it can be styled.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:15 UTC

So, Twitter has this issue where its open graph previews of stream narrows ends up being the preview of the Zulip server in question, eating the actual link.  See for example how this tweet looks in Twitter: https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/60-twitter/topic/zulip/near/696673

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:16 UTC

[pasted image](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/c2/TQp_FNjNvkQqweFUVjiXK4db/pasted_image.png) is what it looks like.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:16 UTC

Now, there's 2 parts of this problem that we can work on.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:17 UTC

One is that the open graph tags for an individual Zulip server's homepage, e.g. https://chat.zulip.org.  We should potentially make those homepages have open graph tags that explain which organization's server this is; that should be a pretty straightforward change that I'll open an issue for shortly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:18 UTC

The second problem, which is a lot more messy, is that we may want links to a specific narrow to have different open graph tags from the realm homepage.  If we want that, we'll need to change our default URL scheme for narrows to not use hashes, because those are invisible to the target webserver.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:19 UTC

Opened https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/11497.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:22 UTC

Possibly the right solution is to just not have Twitter/open graph tags for a Zulip community's homepage.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-02-08 17:26 UTC

and in the interim I think turning off open graph previews is pretty reasonable.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:27 UTC

(FWIW, Slack just doesn't do open graph tags for these pages)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-08 17:28 UTC

Changing the `#` is a significant project that we will probably end up wanting to do.  There's some annoying costs to doing so, but it should be possible to migrate with full backwards-compatibility.

## style guide

*2019-02-19 to 2019-02-19 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/style.20guide/with/703294)*

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:20 UTC

So here is a summary of how we style Zulip.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:22 UTC

Our default font size is 14px, which we use in the message body.  Other fonts are bigger (most sidebar text is 14.233px).  Some are smaller (individual names under "Private messages" are 12.82 pixels.  As I mention in the "font sanity" thread, we would probably benefit from more consistent choices.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:23 UTC

Padding is highly dependent on where you are in the screen layout, and we mostly intend to line things up and give a somewhat uncompressed feeling.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:25 UTC

The gutter below the navbar is 10px.  Messages are padded 4px on the top, 1px on the bottom.  The stream panel has a 4px gutter at the bottom.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:26 UTC

Our color scheme is basically to have fonts be black, blue, or green in the main screen.  If you turn off press-enter-to-send, you'll see the color of our "Send" button.  The "Invite more users" link is blue.  Things are different in night mode, of course.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:28 UTC

Most of the color on the page is actually driven by stream names, which are randomly chosen by an algorithm, but users can customize their stream colors.  A stream's color shows up in the "#" icon, recipient bars, and the border going down the side of the message pane.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:28 UTC

We also have green circles to indicate you're online.  A half-orange/half-white circle in the buddy list indicates you have been recently online.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:29 UTC

Our unread counts have a dark gray background in day mode.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:30 UTC

We generally prefer a more rectangular feel than a circular feel.  So, for example, all of our avatars are rectangular.  Typically things like buttons and unread counts are rounded with 4px-radius corners, but obviously this can vary with the size of the element.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:31 UTC

I don't think we ever use borders that are thicker than 2px.  The left border on the message pane is 2px, as is the blue box.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:32 UTC

Our message pane borders are actually box shadows, technically.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:35 UTC

Our popovers use bootstrap, and most have the default rounded border radius of 6px.  Many have a little white triangle that points to the launch target, but we hide that when we need to position the popover in different places to keep them onscreen or prevent obscuring certain elements.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:37 UTC

Our main font family is `'Source Sans Pro', 'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif`.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:39 UTC

We use hover in most places that you can launch popovers, and when you hover over an element, you'll see a chevron.  In the message feed you can also hover to get the smiley/pencil/chevron/star options.  You can open menus also by clicking on avatars and menu pills.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:40 UTC

For icons we generally use Font Awesome.  But some things, like the green circles, are drawn in CSS.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:41 UTC

The icon in the top left can be customized by organizations--I don't what our recommendations are there for sizing.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:42 UTC

For container titles like `STREAMS`, `USERS`, and `GROUP PMs`, we tend toward all caps and a gray-ish color.  They are actually the same font sizes as the items beneath them, generally.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:51 UTC

If, as a designer, you are creating a new element on the page, the best advice is to find similar items on the page and be consistent style-wise with them.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-19 15:52 UTC

If there are elements on the page that you feel have arbitrary style differences that should be fixed, a good process is to first collect data and say what the current style is.  Then, on #design, suggest the changes you want to make.  Or, if they're small, just create a PR right away, try to keep it as simple as possible, and provide before/after screenshots.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 16:34 UTC

So I want to give a little update on the work that @Vaibhav and I have been doing on cleaning up our message templates...

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 16:35 UTC

First, some very important pieces have already been merged, which are basically extracting partial templates.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 16:37 UTC

The main template that determines positioning of elements is now called `message_body.handlebars`, and it's a relatively slim 54 lines of template code.  It delegates some things out to partials:

* message_avatar
* me_message
* edited_notice
* message_controls
* message_reactions

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 16:38 UTC

The 5 partial templates are relatively cohesive--like we want to change how message reactions get displayed, it's likely that the changes would only need to happen within `message_reactions.handlebars` now, and that's a good thing.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 16:42 UTC

There are still several things that make it difficult to work with message templates:

* there are some structural things that are arguably just an accident of history
* there is the tricky issue of copy/paste
* there are complicated boolean expressions in the template that are hard to reason about and hard to test
* there's a lot of absolute positioning happening in the CSS
* it's hard to read the template and know which goes in the left column, top line, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 16:44 UTC

I think our next goal is to focus on `left_col`, `middle_col`, and `right_col`, which allows for some really nice CSS cleanup (as well as making it easier to just read the template and predict where things will show up).

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 16:45 UTC

@Vaibhav is going to work the PR to try to focus mainly on introducing that concept.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 16:46 UTC

And then if we can get that merged, we'll work toward some other goals, like removing absolute positioning when it's not really necessary.  (The complications here are copy/paste, where the order of things in markup is driven by more by copy/paste concerns than expressing visual hierarchies.)

## async and defer

*2019-02-27 to 2019-02-27 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/async.20and.20defer/with/709261)*

**Aditya Bansal** · 2019-02-27 22:00 UTC

Has there ever been discussion about use of async/defer as a way to load js files in parallel while browser is rendering our HTML.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-27 22:03 UTC

I don't think anyone's worked on doing that.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2019-02-27 22:03 UTC

From what I know we include js files at the top therefore browser first downloads them. But since we wrap everything up in $(function) nothing is executed until HTML is finished rendering. Therefore after downloading the js files browser continues rendering the html. Recently I read that specifying async/defer can make this happen in parallel which from my view point should boost the performance

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-27 22:04 UTC

There's a bunch of performance optimization approaches for achieving the goal of that (E.g. HTTP/2) that could be worked on.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2019-02-27 22:07 UTC

I don't know much about HTTP/2 I guess (or maybe can't remember it). I have definitely read about QUIC protocol and from what I remember these protocols were not implemented yet in browsers?

**Aditya Bansal** · 2019-02-27 22:10 UTC

Just did a quick reading and seems like I am talking about HTTP/3 when I say not implemented in browsers :sweat_smile:

**Aditya Bansal** · 2019-02-27 22:42 UTC

reading up a bit more it feels like doing both HTTP/2 and using async/defer of HTML would be beneficial. 
Basically async/defer of HTML instructs browsers to start downloading assets in parallel to rendering rest of HTML. If there are more than one asset requests HTTP/2 would speed up things by multiplexing it on a single connection.
From the outside it doesn't feel like it should be a very involved project to do since HTTP/2 doesn't change anything (the methods) which is visible to the developer

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-27 23:46 UTC

OK.  Probably a fairly low priority in that our startup JS isn't super slow to execute.

**Problem I am facing:**

## ws between span tags

*2019-03-06 to 2019-03-06 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/ws.20between.20span.20tags/with/714795)*

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:00 UTC

What is our preferred methodology for killing off whitespace between span tags?

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:01 UTC

I'm trying to line up some elements, and there's some whitespace between two spans that is causing like a 3px gutter that makes it really hard to line up stuff without introducing random or inconsistent padding.

**Boris Yankov** · 2019-03-06 22:03 UTC

@Steve Howell `<span>`s tend to be used for text so it makes sense for them to preserve the space.
`<div>`s inside a Flexbox container will definitely not have this issue (or spans for that matter)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-03-06 22:06 UTC

Can you simply delete the space from the source?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-03-06 22:08 UTC

If it’s in a Handlebars template, I think you’re aware of the `{{~` and `~}}` whitespace removal syntax.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:10 UTC

It's server-side, although it wouldn't be a ton of work to move it client-side.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:10 UTC

It's basically this:

~~~
  5             <li class="top_left_all_messages global-filter active-filter" title="{{ _('All messages') }} (Esc)">
  6                 <a href="#">
  7                     <span class="filter-icon">
  8                         <i class="fa fa-home" aria-hidden="true"></i>
  9                     </span>
 10                     <span>{{ _('All messages') }}</span>
 11                     <span class="count">
 12                         <span class="value"></span>
 13                     </span>
 14                 </a>
 15                 <span class="arrow all-messages-arrow"><i class="fa fa-chevron-down" aria-hidden="true"></i></span>
 16             </li>

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:11 UTC

For some reason the browser sees the space after the `.filter-icon` span, but not before the `.count` span.

**Boris Yankov** · 2019-03-06 22:14 UTC

`a => display: flex`

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-03-06 22:15 UTC

I get both spaces.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-03-06 22:17 UTC

I’d be more inclined to do something like
```html
<a href="#"
    ><span class="filter-icon"
        ><i class="fa fa-home" aria-hidden="true"></i
    ></span
    ><span>{{ _('All messages') }}</span
    ><span class="count"
        ><span class="value"></span
    ></span
></a>
```
than rely on weird CSS rules, especially ones that might slow down layout.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-03-06 22:18 UTC

Jinja also has various whitespace removal mechanisms that we could investigate.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:24 UTC

> `a => display: flex`

Introducing flex has some challenges with keeping the unread counts lined up.  @Boris Yankov Do you have a sec to play with the flex approach?

**Boris Yankov** · 2019-03-06 22:24 UTC

@Steve Howell sure.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:25 UTC

> Jinja also has various whitespace removal mechanisms that we could investigate.

This to me would be the most promising solution.  I googled earlier, and there is indeed stuff out there.  Just wasn't sure we had put any of it to use already in our codebase.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-03-06 22:29 UTC

Also `display: flex` would disturb the vertical alignment between spans of different height.

**Boris Yankov** · 2019-03-06 22:35 UTC

Hmm, not really, you can align the items vertically on any axis.

**Boris Yankov** · 2019-03-06 22:36 UTC

`align-items: flex-end` will probably simulate what is the default `span` behavior. 
On the other hand, other styles like `align-items: center` or `align-items: stretch` might be better (and that is why `flex` is way more flexible than  `inline`)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:41 UTC

To kill the space, this did the trick:

~~~
{%- if true %}{% endif -%}

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-03-06 22:46 UTC

You might be able to do the same with a Jinja comment: `{#- -#}`

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-06 22:55 UTC

> You might be able to do the same with a Jinja comment: `{#- -#}`

Yeah, that's what I'm going with for now.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-19 01:56 UTC

To elaborate, you should rebase your second commit to keep the tests passing (which apparently you know how to do, but you did it an a later commit, which is not atomic).  And then try to get the third commit passing.  And so on.  And then ideally, when you get stuck, you can point to a commit that changes very few things and fails the tests, while the prior commit passes the tests.  And then it's a lot easier to troubleshoot the problem.  Also, it's helpful to over-explain your changes in the commit messages, so that people reviewing your code can understand your thourght process.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-08 20:12 UTC

Hey folks, I'd like to discuss the UX question present in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/11797.  Basically, if you do a search in the right sidebar, under what circumstances do we want it to create a group PM with the set of users you'd selected vs. just the highlighted one (that you might have gotten from keyboard navigation).

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-08 20:13 UTC

I think there's a reasonable case to be made that if you use the `,` or `|` syntax to OR together multiple search terms, and you haven't moved the keyboard cursor, you might want the group PM case, but this may also be non-discoverable enough that it'd be effectively a misfeature in how people experience it.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-08 20:23 UTC

I don’t know this would be easier than using the compose box.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-03-08 20:24 UTC

I'm not sure I totally understand the `|` case. What's an example when it would be useful?

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-08 20:26 UTC

You might only want to track your three teammates in the buddy list?

**Wyatt Hoodes** · 2019-03-08 21:05 UTC

It seems like there would need to be some sort of tab-completion on a highlighted user or something, as typing out a search OR-ing together a  few users seems like a lot of work as compared to, as Steve was saying, using the compose box.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-08 21:48 UTC

There are other use cases; e.g. I think in the Recurse Center they put batch IDs in people's names, and can use this to look at the online status for everyone in one or more current batches.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-08 21:49 UTC

(One could imagine a fancy user group based way to do that, but that's a lot more complex in many ways)

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-03-08 22:25 UTC

I feel like the current buddy list model is not the right model, so I'm reluctant to add features like this to it, but don't have strong opinions I guess. For the RC example I think the right solution is to have better search over custom profile fields.

If we imagine the search over custom profile fields, having an `|` makes sense, but then I think I would expect that to still give me 1-1 PMs? The main reason being so that people aren't tempted to create group PMs wiht the 20 people in their batch.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-08 22:28 UTC

Yeah, that was my concern with anything that would make group PMs -- we don't allow them above ~12 users, and the cutoff behavior seems weird.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-08 22:28 UTC

I guess if we wanted to offer that option, we could have a button "create group PM with all these users", but I don't think that's super valuable.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-08 22:29 UTC

So I'm tempted to do nothing and close the PR.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-08 22:32 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-11 16:32 UTC

@Tim Abbott I think we should just eliminate the animation entirely here.  The code here uses naive code to detect changes in count, which causes us to flash the animation on every single list item when we do redraws.  We could clean up that logic, but I'm not sure it's a useful feature.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-11 16:34 UTC

The relevant code here is `unread_ui.animate_private_message_changes`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-11 18:18 UTC

This feature falls into the category of things added after a usability study years ago to help draw visual attention to new PMs so that folks are more likely to notice them, by having a subtle flash to draw the user's attention.  Of course, it's a hardcoded color that we neglected to adapt for night mode, and apparently we're also now flashing the entire PM area by accident, not just the individual row.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-11 18:19 UTC

@Rishi Gupta what are your thoughts on whether we should fix or remove this? currently it just opens/closes when we click the search icon. This is not bad, but I feel as though it could be better.
First of all,
 * I feel as though having some transition for this might be a good follow up.

And then one interesting thing I have in mind is this:
 * I feel as though having the search open (with slide) whenever we mouse over the empty part of the navbar would be a positive change in UX.
To clarify, if we're on home, then the search bar will be closed and the navbar will be empty except for the home icon, but then, as soon as we mouse over the empty part of the navbar (anywhere beyond just a slight margin after the home icon), we could open the search bar with a slide animation from the left.
  * v1 of this would be involved with doing this on the home page
  * v2 of this would be involved with triggering this as a mouse over on the "search-icon" ie immediately show the user the results of clicking the search button, even when they haven't actually clicked it, but if they were hovering over it as though they'd want to, and if they mouse out, quickly undo the change (close the navebar).


 * some technical details for this kind of UX (v1 only):
 If we decide to do the above, then it would make sense to ensure that the navbar is hidden and the search bar stays open if we select the search bar, but then also, consider if we:
hover over the navbar (let search open) -> select the search box -> type something (or don't) -> mouse out (maybe click somewhere else?)
the question is, after this, is the navbar still open?

## all_topics_in_cache

*2019-03-15 to 2019-03-15 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/all_topics_in_cache/with/719552)*

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 15:42 UTC

I pushed #11909 to restore 100% test coverage to stream_data.js.  I have some questions about the implementation.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 15:45 UTC

First, it seems that the condition `first_cached_message === undefined` is essentially unreachable, because we do on `message_list.all.empty()` check earlier in the function.  The comment claims this can happen because `message_list.all` is not initialized, but if that's the case, we should be trying to structure the overally page initialization to avoid that.  (I just added test coverage in a contrived way to work around this.)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 15:47 UTC

A deeper problem that I worry about, which is hopefully somewhat rare, is that if you do things like keyword searches, then `message_list.all.first()` could have an artificially low message id even though many of your older streams haven't been fully backfilled.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 16:11 UTC

@Tim Abbott FYI. ^^^^

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 16:19 UTC

It's fine to make the code being defensive in terms of `message_list.all` itself being undefined, which it already does.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 16:21 UTC

But then as soon as it's created, I believe we can rely on the invariant that as long as `list.empty()` is false, then `list.first()` will return an actual message, not `undefined`.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 16:21 UTC

So it's possible we should just remove the check in the code under test, instead of adding my contrived test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-15 16:25 UTC

`message_list.all` is by construction always a list of consecutive messages.  Older search would only add items to `message_store`, not `message_list.all`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-15 16:26 UTC

Oh, I think you're right; I think I had an order-of-operations issue when developing this and added the `.empty()` check after the other one.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 16:26 UTC

Ah, ok, it might be worth calling that out a bit more explicitly in comments at the top of `all_topics_in_cache`.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 16:28 UTC

Do you want me to fix the PR, or do you prefer to just make the change yourself at this point?  (remove dead code, re-enable the coverage requirement, and possibly add a comment about message_list.all invariant)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 16:29 UTC

Ha, I see you merged it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-15 16:33 UTC

I guess I'm sorta assuming that folks understand what `message_list.all` means, but a comment reminder on that would be valuable.  I'll add a quick commit for that.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-15 16:38 UTC

Sounds good.  I don't think it's gonna be super obvious to people that `message_list.all` has two interesting properties:
* it's contiguous, so we have to take care when populating it
* unlike other message lists, it's just a data holder (and we should arguably move it to be just `MessageListData`)

It's also somewhat confusing that `home_msg_list` is the message list we use for "All messages".  (It used to be called "Home", hence the naming.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-15 16:39 UTC

Yes.  Also in the future we will probably want to maintain multiple `MessageListData` objects for various stream/topic narrows.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-15 16:39 UTC

But we'll probably rename "all messages" and fix that naming issue that way.

@Steve Howell while debugging I observed something that was totally unexpected. When we hit `g` and gear menu opens, we can scroll through list via arrow keys. We were thinking that this kind of behaviour is produced by `hotkeys.js` and we need to fix that to get the same kind of behaviour when the gear menu is opened by clicking. But the thing is, in `open()` function inside `gear_menu.js` we focus on the very first item in the menu and then the handling of arrow keys is done by default browser features.
`$("#gear-menu").find("li:not(.invisible) a".eq(0).focus();` is the piece of code that focuses on the first list item.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-23 18:53 UTC

Which part -- the expiry or the UI?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-23 18:54 UTC

For expiry, the simplest implementation would involve syncing around the expiration data field when sending user status data (so that clients can automatically expire without a notification from the server when rendering a view).  I don't imagine that being super complicated.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-04-23 18:56 UTC

the expiry. oh, I didn't realize user status came with an expiry field. Would we need two expiry dates -- one for the availability (green, orange, etc) and one for the message (could be "1 week")?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-23 19:07 UTC

It doesn't come with one, I'm proposing we add one.  The point is that there's two models for how expiry could work:
* Server is responsible for monitoring for expiry and then notifying clients when a user's status expires.
* Client is responsible for doing this work.

And I'm saying the client being responsible is probably a simpler model.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-04-23 19:11 UTC

what happens if the expiry is a week from now?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-23 19:21 UTC

I'm not sure I understand how you imagine that would be different from it being in 10 minutes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-23 19:22 UTC

I'm imagining a model that works just like presence -- when rendering a component, the client checks if the expiry date is passed, and if so, it shows the "no status" state.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-04-23 19:33 UTC

I think I'm probably a little confused about how presence works, but also not important. Status message working like presence sounds good to me.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-23 19:34 UTC

The way presence works is that what we sync is is a pair (idle/active, timestamp for last data), and the "offline" state is how we handle cases where the timestamp is too old (and thus we know the client hasn't checked in recently).

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-04-23 19:36 UTC

the thing that's being sync'd is the data in the `UserPresence` table?

**Abhinav Singh** · 2019-04-29 13:58 UTC

@Tim Abbott I have the following plan. Save the time in the database and check it on the client whether it expired or not. I used the similar model when I was working on the birthday cake feature for practice and it was working fine.

**Abhinav Singh** · 2019-04-29 13:58 UTC

I will make a basic working pr so that you can check.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-29 17:45 UTC

@Abhinav Singh sounds good.

I did some more experimentation on the DllPlugin. **Tommy Ip** · 2019-06-12 05:15 UTC

> For, the sass-loader issue, I looked into fast-scss-loader the only problem with using that would be if we have same variable name across files it would cause issues since that plugin munges all the files into one and compiles them. sass-loader is slow because it calls native bindings for sass library for every single file.

I think all the variable names across our scss files are unique? If different elements are referred by the same name now wouldn't that already cause trouble since our webpack config concat all the compiled css to one file anyway?

**Priyank Patel** · 2019-06-12 20:36 UTC

Only variable names could be a issue, i.e.
```scss
// a.scss
$color: red;
h1 {
  color: $red;
}
```

```scss
$color: blue;
h2 {
  color: $color;
}
```

Depending on the order both variable either could be `red` or `blue`. Though now that I think about this, we don't use variable names in scss even after a year of migration to scss so we should be fine with this.

**Tommy Ip** · 2019-06-29 07:09 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-11 16:42 UTC

For backstory, we've been stuck on an ancient version of Boostrap basically since we started using it in 2013, and work towards upgrading it has been pretty unfun.  While I am confident that we can upgrade it to a modern version if we choose to, it would be a lot of work, and I think there's a good question as to whether the end result of that project is a world that we want.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-11 16:43 UTC

For example, we recently migrated from Bootstrap to TippyJS for our tooltips, and I'd be curious for others' thoughts, but I think a dedicated library for that purpose has been a much better experience for that specific part of our application.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-11 16:47 UTC

Further, we don't use Bootstrap intentionally for that much of the web app these days.  I think the set of features is basically this:
* Typeahead, which was removed in modern Bootstrap anyway.
* Popovers, including the gear menu, which we already plan to migrate to PopperJS (TippyJS's cousin).
* Modals and overlays.  It seems very likely that there's a high quality, 3KB, dedicated library for modals that we'd be happy to switch to.  And we've actually already done most of the work that would be needed to transition modal libraries through extracting `overlays.js` and `confirm_dialog.js`.
* Button styling, for which Bootstrap makes our life harder, rather than easier, since we've 90% overridden the Bootstrap styles anyway, and thus we just end up with Bootstrap leaking through in unexpected ways.
* Table styling, which we also heavily customize at this point.

When I look at that list, it doesn't really sound like we'll be happy in a world where we upgrade to the latest Bootstrap release.

**Ganesh Pawar (ganpa3)** · 2021-06-11 16:47 UTC

I think we should get rid of Bootstrap and migrate to modern specific-purpose libraries. Bootstrap being a large framework slows down upgrades as has been seen. Bootstrap 2 is unsupported and has been causing issues (e.g. race conditions in modals)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-11 16:51 UTC

One thing that will help us on the typeahead migration is that we're not really coupled to bootstrap's matcher/sorter/updater/highlighter regime.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-11 16:52 UTC

For example:

~~~ js
1029     $(selector).typeahead({
1030         items: max_num_items,
1031         dropup: true,
1032         fixed: true,
1033         // Performance note: We have trivial matcher/sorters to do
1034         // matching and sorting inside the `source` field to avoid
1035         // O(n) behavior in the number of users in the organization
1036         // inside the typeahead library.
1037         source: get_sorted_filtered_items,
1038         highlighter: content_highlighter,
1039         matcher() {
1040             return true;
1041         },
1042         sorter(items) {
1043             return items;
1044         },
1045         updater: content_typeahead_selected,
1046         stopAdvance: true, // Do not advance to the next field on a Tab or Enter
1047         completions,
1048         automated: compose_automated_selection,
1049         trigger_selection: compose_trigger_selection,
1050         header: get_header_html,
1051     });

~~~

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-11 16:55 UTC

I think a plan to remove bootstrap would look something like this:
* Figure out whether we need to migrate typeahead libraries (or if we can delete bootstrap and keep `bootstrap-typeahead`), and if so, do that.  It's only 473 lines of JavaScript, and I think it is written to be independent, so we may be able to defer dealing with this detail.
* Migrate the popover and modal/overlay libraries to modern special-purpose libraries.
* Switch the portico pages to using an upstream copy of Bootstrap obtained via NPM.
* Audit for any other bootstrap JavaScript components that we're using in the webapp.
* Then, migrate tables to styling we control (whether we grab a third-party library or just do it ourselves), and potentially delete the table styling from our copy of Bootstrap CSS to make sure we're not relying on it in unexpected ways.
* Do the same with buttons.
* Try deleting Bootstrap and fix everything that breaks; we may end up needing some CSS reset stuff in our base stylesheet.

**Isham Mahajan** · 2019-07-01 14:04 UTC

Hi! I was implementing 'Copy message link' on the mobile app, could anyone here guide me to where that feature is implemented in the WebApp so I could cross reference and use the same code for creating the link if possible? I tried searching the `zulip/zulip` repo for it, and I found this.

[Screenshot-2019-06-23-at-1.34.42-AM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/2/fVY5ezc3PSGVDB7G8Xg-tCVT/Screenshot-2019-06-23-at-1.34.42-AM.png) 

As [mentioned by @Greg Price ](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/pull/3412#issuecomment-505504746) on a PR,

**Vinit Singh** · 2019-07-01 14:07 UTC

It is in the `actions_popover` (chevron to the right of each message. 
`copy_link` is what you want to look for. I think you can find relevant code for both the popover and the click handlers in `static/js/popovers.js`

**Vinit Singh** · 2019-07-01 14:09 UTC

[ClipboardJS](https://clipboardjs.com/) handles the copying of the messages, I believe.

**Vinit Singh** · 2019-07-01 14:11 UTC

@Isham Mahajan

**Vinit Singh** · 2019-07-01 14:11 UTC

```js
    new ClipboardJS('.copy_link');

    $('body').on('click', '.copy_link', function (e) {
        popovers.hide_actions_popover();
        var id = $(this).attr("data-message-id");
        var row = $("[zid='" + id + "']");
        row.find(".alert-msg")
            .text(i18n.t("Copied!"))
            .css("display", "block")
            .delay(1000).fadeOut(300);

        setTimeout(function () {
            // The Cliboard library works by focusing to a hidden textarea.
            // We unfocus this so keyboard shortcuts, etc., will work again.
            $(":focus").blur();
        }, 0);

        e.stopPropagation();
        e.preventDefault();
    });
```

Relevant code.

        var args = {

## Handlebars filename syntax

*2019-07-11 to 2019-07-13 · 68 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Handlebars.20filename.20syntax/with/766766)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:42 UTC

Hey folks! We have a question I'd love to get a bunch of opinions on, about how we organize our handlebars templates.  https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/12761 has the context; basically, as part of moving to a nicer system where webpack knows which Handlebars templates are used where and can use that for optimization, we'll be switching to the `require` syntax for rendering templates, which roughly means this diff:

```
-        var html = templates.render("settings/custom-user-profile-field", {
+        var html = require("../templates/settings/custom-user-profile-field.handlebars")({
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:43 UTC

As you can see, a consequence of this change is that we're encoding the full filename, e.g. `../templates/settings/custom-user-profile-field.handlebars`, and we also no longer have the consistent behavior of having a function, `templates.render()`, that appears in each place where we render a template.  You would of course still be able to do `git grep /templates/` to find template render calls, so really not a big deal.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:44 UTC

But since doing this requires a bit of a migration where we're now encoding filenames (rather than just the template name) in a bunch of places, it's worth having a discussion about how we want to name these files.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:45 UTC

One minor detail is that we should probably fix the 6 ones that use `-` as the delimiter in the filename to use `_` for consistency:
```
(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ ls static/templates/*_* | wc
     95      95    4563
(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ ls static/templates/*-* | wc
      6       6     297
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:45 UTC

But there's several reason proposals, which I'll try to write as a poll.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:45 UTC

/poll How should we name our handlebars template files?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:47 UTC

(Folks should feel free to add other options.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:48 UTC

I'd love responses either in the poll or messages even from folks who aren't regular Zulip contributors to the webapp codebase, in that I think one of the more important aspects of naming is how intuitive it is for folks who aren't used to the status quo.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-07-11 19:53 UTC

I don’t think `.html` is a good idea. That would involve telling webpack to treat all `.html` files as Handlebars templates (which could prevent us from doing things with e.g. html-webpack-plugin in the future), or teaching it to treat different `.html` files differently depending on their directory (which is extra complexity that will confuse humans if nothing else). And it would probably involve telling Node to treat all `.html` files as Handlebars templates unconditionally, since you don’t get as many knobs there.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-07-11 19:54 UTC

The handlebars Node library doesn’t even have an option for installing Node handlers for extensions other than `.handlebars` and `.hbs`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-07-11 19:54 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-07-11 19:56 UTC

I guess `.html.hbs` is possible if someone wants to propose that, but I think it’s unnecessarily verbose.

Hmm, yeah, I didn't think about the fact that we no longer have anything specifying it's handlebars in the paths anymore.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:58 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 19:58 UTC

Well, `.html.hbs` is probably the most reasonable proposal containing `.html`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 20:05 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-15 16:30 UTC

I have found that there’s a single question that points the way toward solutions for a large fraction of software engineering challenges in this codebase: *“is this a problem that would have been solved by other people?”* Zulip was pretty innovative in 2013, but now we are entirely playing catch up in an engineering sense, even though we still have innovative user experience ideas.

So—*have other people have figured out how to write large UI codebases without tangled circular import graphs?* Yes. *How?* Encapsulation with components. *What’s a component?* Fundamentally, an object that manages part of a DOM tree. You initialize its state directly via constructors and method calls. When the user does something to it, it emits events; you register callbacks to receive these events. A component has no external side effects except by emitting events.

*Sounds like a lot of work. What are the advantages?*

* Reasoning. The component exposes a well-defined interface through which all of its interactions with the rest of the code can be explained.
* Reuse. The component can freely be instantiated elsewhere; it isn’t tied into a specific place in the control flow graph of a specific application.
* Testing. As one application of reuse, you can test the component without mocking all kinds of random functions elsewhere; you just instantiate one, poke it, and listen for its events.
* Isolation. As another application of reuse, we can create test pages that let us look at an individual component in an arbitrary state, without going to the effort of arranging for that state to occur in the real application.
* Imports. A component only imports other components that are direct children, and perhaps some purely functional utility libraries. This leads naturally to a cycle-free import graph.

This is something we can do; we can do it incrementally, and it will make our life better in many ways.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-04-15 18:08 UTC

A concrete example would be helpful here.  I know there are tactical reasons to prefer events over function calls, but I also think events are just an obfuscated way to replace explicit function injection. If you introduce events you just have a different problem with namespaces.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-15 18:46 UTC

Events for a component are not in a shared namespace. Each instance of each component has its own events.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-15 18:46 UTC

The simplest version is that they’re just callbacks provided to the constructor.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-15 18:49 UTC

Or for a component using the Web Components API, the component dispatches events using `el.dispatchEvent()` and the parent listens to them using `el.addEventListener()`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-15 18:52 UTC

Various other component frameworks have their own event systems, but they’re all shaped pretty similarly at a high level.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-15 18:53 UTC

The point they have in common is that your button component should not go and tell the app do a specific action; it should emit a `click` event.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-15 19:28 UTC

To pick an arbitrary example, consider `static/js/giphy.js` (which you had nothing to do with).

* It currently initializes itself by installing its own global `click` handlers. It should instead be an object that’s instantiated from within the compose box component and the message edit component.
* When you select a GIF, it currently makes a direct call to `compose_ui.insert_syntax_and_focus()`. It should instead emit a `selected` event; the caller should be responsible for deciding what to do when it receives that.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-04-15 19:56 UTC

That’s probably a really good use case, since it doesn’t have any legacy muck to sort through.

Yeah, I should clarify: my vision of using React is that the major places where we have very long lists of items would be the last things we'd attempt to migrate, if ever. That means the message list, and perhaps the right and left sidebars.

Those are performance-sensitive areas where it pays to invest effort in optimizing by hand, and where (at least for the message list) we have important custom optimizations. It'd only make sense to migrate those to React, or for that matter to any generic framework, if we find places in its API where we can customize those components' behavior to get equivalent optimizations, and spend the time to use them.

**Greg Price** · 2022-05-12 01:35 UTC

Where I think React would deliver the most value for us up front is in places where the ratio of how much UI surface area there is to maintain, against how sensitive it is to performance (from having giant lists of items) and/or how important it is to get the best performance, is much greater.

That means places like the settings UI. There is tons of surface area there, which could benefit a lot from being cleanly organized into components. Most of it has no giant lists at all, so the performance is unlikely to change much, if at all. And if it does, a performance hit doesn't matter much to any user's experience, unless it's a really severe hit.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-12 01:39 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-27 00:33 UTC

@Ankan Bhattacharya @Chandraprakash Darji @Yash Mittal I would recommend getting started by picking a module which doesn't have an open PR converting it to TypeScript (easy to find the <5 such open PRs via GitHub search, but since there's more than one person interested, the state may change) and has no dependencies that are still JS, and submitting a thoughtfully written, reviewable PR converting that module. (See our contributing guide for what we mean by reviewable).

The most important thing we'll be looking for is writing good PRs that are reviewable.

Feel free to use this topic to coordinate on what you're working on, ask for reviews from others interested in the TypeScript migration (without mentioning core contributors -- see our community guidelines for details), etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-03-02 02:37 UTC

(replying to SatVeer Singh)
> I mean, how will I know which type or what data is coming from backend. Because in typescript we need to define custom type aliases.
They are usually documented in https://zulip.com/api/; the vast majority of the data (`page_params`) comes from https://zulip.com/api/register-queue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-03-02 02:39 UTC

We have generally been working towards having `page_params` be disassembled in `ui_init.js`, with blocks of data popped out of it and passed to individual modules, and then live-updated within those modules rather than via mutating `page_params`. But it's an "as convenient when changing things" migration, and the realm/server settings properties in particular (most booleans and whatnot with names like `realm_` or `server_`) should generally be left as-is,  since we're likely to restructure the API response itself in a way that makes that nicer.

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> I think we should just replace all our `.safeOuterHeight()` calls with `.height() ?? 0`, or just `.height()` if we know the element exists, and get rid of this jQuery monkey patch.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-28 22:51 UTC

Yes. Use `.height()` on jQuery objects that are known to be non-empty, and `.height() ?? 0` on jQuery objects that might be empty (since `$("#nonexistent").height()` returns `undefined`). I don’t know why we would be calling height on jQuery objects that might be empty—this might be a historical thing that doesn’t happen anymore.

**Lalit** · 2023-03-29 15:28 UTC

Hi so I have raised #24909 for converting `overlays.js` now the next step is to convert `dialog_widget.js` so it is kind of a prep PR. So, my question is should I convert `dialog_widget.js` in the same PR in different commit or should open a new one after this prep PR is merged?

**xoldyckk** · 2023-03-29 18:06 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> Yes. Use `.height()` on jQuery objects that are known to be non-empty, and `.height() ?? 0` on jQuery objects that might be empty (since `$("#nonexistent").height()` returns `undefined`). I don’t know why we would be calling height on jQuery objects that might be empty—this might be a historical thi …

Knowing what jquery elements are defined or not would be hard, because they're dependent on css selectors that just by themselves tell nothing about nullability of an element. As far as I can see, the height and width functions are only used in arithmetic calculations to determine relative height differences and stuff, so using `height() ?? 0` wouldn't make it convoluted in any sense. 

 The thing about calling height on jQuery objects is a historical thing yes, prior to jquery v3, `outerHeight` and `outerWidth` used to return `number|null` instead of `number|undefined`, so arithmetic operations with `null` were possible, because it'd behave the same way as `0`. In v3, it changed to `number|undefined`, and using `undefined` in such operations would result in `NaN`. 

Though I do agree, using even `null` was a bad decision from the start, typescript for example prevents such bad decisions by default.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-03 22:33 UTC

So that question is about this change:

``` diff
-    $(`[data-on-page='${CSS.escape(location)}']`).addClass("active");
+    if (location) {
+        $(`[data-on-page='${CSS.escape(location)}']`).addClass("active");
+    }
```

I think this is a common enough class of pattern that it's worth talking about here. We have a line of code like the one in the diff block below, where TypeScript can't know whether the variable (in this case, `location`) set, because (say) it was read from the DOM. So if the page was implemented correctly, then the value should never be undefined, but if the page had a typo, it won't.

My claim is that this change to appease the typechecker is not constructive -- previously, we had code that would throw an error if the data was invalid, and we're changing it to code that will silently do nothing if the data was bad. Usually that's a much worse symptom.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-03 22:34 UTC

Is there a good general solution for what we should be doing instead?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-03 22:41 UTC

We can do `if (location === undefined) throw new Error(…)`. TypeScript knows how to narrow types based on control flow.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-03 22:47 UTC

By the way, as a general point, we should be preferring `if (foo !== undefined)`, `if (foo === undefined)`, `foo ?? default` rather than `if (foo)`, `if (!foo)`, `foo || default`, because the latter will trigger on unexpected falsy values like `0` and `""`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-04 01:09 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> We can do `if (location === undefined) throw new Error(…)`. TypeScript knows how to narrow types based on control flow.

Yeah, that's what I've been suggesting everywhere I've seen this; it was my preferred option before asking this question.

@xoldyckk @human @Lalit and others, can you go over your TypeScript PRs and update them for this issue and then report back here? I don't want to have to keep pointing it out in review.

I wanted to ask whether we should pass generic type for html elements in JQuery's $() function, something like this:-
```ts
const $divElements = $<HTMLDivElement>(".class1");
const $divAndSpanElements = $<HTMLDivElement|HTMLSpanElement>(".class2");
```
This generic type on jquery object itself won't have any effect, but when we access the raw dom element, something like `$divElements.get()[0]` here, the retrieved raw element will have type of `HTMLDivElement`, and it'll give us narrowed types and better type intellisense which apply only to div elements in html. This is one of the advantages of using typescript in frontend applications imo.

But this also looks hard to maintain because we're manually keeping track of what element `class1` will be applied to, it's possible the class needs to be applied to some element other than a div. That'd be dirty.

It also looks over engineered if we don't ever use the raw element, and only use jquery object to do stuff.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-30 20:33 UTC

We want to be able to separate the frontend from the server so that you can connect it to an arbitrary remote server. This will let us make the desktop app much more efficient, enable customized frontends and multi-organization frontends, and improve the frontend development experience. But in order to do this securely, the frontend needs to validate everything coming from the server. So we do want to parse all API responses with Zod.

**xoldyckk** · 2023-04-30 21:48 UTC

@Lalit zulip's openapi schema. It's present at `zserver/openapi/zulip.yaml`in the repo. Here's the [link](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/openapi/zulip.yaml).

**xoldyckk** · 2023-04-30 21:55 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg I've personally never seen this approach of validating server responses on client side. The arbitrary remote server you're talking about, as long as it is in sync with openapi-schema, the types generated and being used on clients will never lie. The client types are not limited to typescript btw, openapi generator has generator for differerent client side programming languages. 

Zod's validation exists at runtime, so it is an overhead. The only value zod provides here is knowledge of the fact that something on the api side changed. Also, with zod you will have to manually write the validators for api responses for each endpoint, each http method and each http response code. Not only that, there's also the need for validation of request body, url query, url dynamic path.

The same benefit is provided by using generated types in client side code, except there's no overhead because the types get purged at runtime and it's all automated, there's no manual work. The mental model here is that the compile time checking needs to be enforced strictly, and we trust that at runtime it will never break, which should be the philosophy when using typescript.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-04-30 22:33 UTC

> The arbitrary remote server you're talking about, as long as it is in sync with openapi-schema,

We have no way to know that it is. It could be running with arbitrary code changes, even malicious ones, or just an older or newer version where we’ve slightly changed the API. To ensure security, we can’t blindly trust anything that goes across a security boundary.

(Also, I would bet that even our unmodified server doesn’t fully comply with our OpenAPI schema. We don’t have any static guarantees connecting them, just a test suite that only checks specific test cases, as any test suite must.)

> Not only that, there's also the need for validation of request body, url query, url dynamic path.

This makes no sense in context—we are talking about the client parsing responses from the server, not about requests.

**xoldyckk** · 2023-05-01 08:40 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-30 18:15 UTC

> Although null checks are performed before calling the function, TypeScript still issues warnings about null values. Therefore, assertions are added to the variables to address these warnings.

An assertion is something that will blow up — throw an exception — if your assumptions turn out to be violated. For example:
```js
  if (a === null) throw "a was null";
```

That can be a good way to handle a situation where the type-checker warns you about a situation you believe is impossible.

(Though in many cases, including this one as @Anders Kaseorg's later comment pointed out, the better solution is to write the types differently so that the type-checker can verify that the situation is impossible.)

**Greg Price** · 2023-10-30 18:16 UTC

In this code, the logic was instead:
```js
  // Setting default value to 0 if a or b is null or undefined
  const aValue = a !== null && a !== undefined ? a : 0;
```

That's not an assertion. If your assumptions turn out to be wrong, that code would just silently behave nonsensically. That's basically never a good solution. If you believe a situation is impossible, but you can't find a way to express that in the types, then it's usually best to have a real assertion that will throw.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-03-02 02:49 UTC

This seems like a common issue people run into, so posting this here: if you’re seeing that `$foo.val()` has a type `string | string[] | number | undefined`, that’s because you haven’t convinced TypeScript that `$foo` is an input element (as opposed to a multiselect, slider, or something else). Resist the temptation to add an assertion or a `.toString()` or something here. The right solution is to make `$foo` have type `JQuery<HTMLInputElement>`, not `JQuery` or `JQuery<HTMLElement>`. This type can be built by changing `$("#foo")` to `$<HTMLInputElement>("input#foo")`. (Note that the actual selector string is changed here to guarantee this construction is safe at runtime, even though TypeScript won’t check that for you.)

**Greg Price** · 2024-03-25 17:40 UTC

I haven't looked at the specific code in question, but in general: in a JavaScript codebase without a type-checker, it's very common for test code to have some test data that is missing fields it should have, or has the wrong type for some fields, etc.

(This isn't *good* — it's better to have the test data be representative, because when it's bogus that tends to cause a lot of noise failures in the tests. You refactor the code being tested, it starts calling some other function that cares about a field that this particular code hadn't previously cared about, and now all its tests are failing and it's entirely the tests' fault. It's not good, but without a type-checker it's hard to systematically avoid.)

So if some test code that hasn't been getting type-checked has some data that doesn't fit the types you have, then it's very likely that the types you have are right and the tests are wrong.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-25 17:45 UTC

Yeah, agreed. Our node test codebase in general should be making use of functions with the broad structure of `make_user` that are designed to accept a few parameters specifying details of the user that the test cares about, and fill out the rest of the type with such fields.

Sadly, we didn't write such functions, and until we do so, there will be a lot of tests with incomplete objects, and the short-term fix is to tweak the tests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-25 17:47 UTC

But I think it would be a very good project to write functions of that form in `web/tests/lib/` that can generate user/stream/messages, so that bad test code like:
```
const test_user = {
    email: "test@example.com",
    user_id: 101,
    full_name: "Test User",
};
```

can become something like:
```
const test_user = make_test_user({
    email: "test@example.com",
    user_id: 101,
    full_name: "Test User",
});
```

With that `make_test_user` being a single function we write that fills in the rest of the fields.

```

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Yeah, agreed. Our node test codebase in general should be making use of functions with the broad structure of `make_user` that are designed to accept a few parameters specifying details of the user that the test cares about, and fill out the rest of the type with such fields.

Yeah, I definitely recommend this pattern. In mobile we have a fairly extensive "example data" module (which we import as `eg`) that's made up of exactly this sort of function, and it's worked very well for us.

**Greg Price** · 2024-03-25 19:18 UTC

A related pattern I like is to have the test code avoid talking about specific user IDs, message IDs, etc., as magic constants; instead it deals with whole user objects, message objects, etc., and when it needs the ID it gets it from the object, just like the normal application code would do.

(Sometimes there's a test where the IDs get really intensively used in some data structure and it becomes more readable to make them literals like 1, 2, 3, etc.; but those can be an exception.)

To facilitate that, the example-data functions make up random IDs by default. Here's from the zulip-flutter version of `eg.streamMessage`:
```dart
/// A fresh message ID, from a random but always strictly increasing sequence.
int _nextMessageId() => (_lastMessageId += 1 + Random().nextInt(100));
int _lastMessageId = 1000;

/// Construct an example stream message.
///
/// If the message ID `id` is not given, it will be generated from a random
/// but increasing sequence, which is shared with [dmMessage].
/// Use an explicit `id` only if the ID needs to correspond to some other data
/// in the test, or if the IDs need to increase in a different order from the
/// calls to [streamMessage] and [dmMessage].
///
/// See also:
///  * [dmMessage], to construct an example direct message.
StreamMessage streamMessage({
  int? id,
  // …
}) {
  // …
  return StreamMessage.fromJson(deepToJson({
    // …
    'id': id ?? _nextMessageId(),
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-06 23:03 UTC

I expect ESLint to flag more of these violations as we migrate more code. The most common issues have been:

- `new Map()` is of type `Map<any, any>` unless TypeScript infers a better type from the same line (it will not infer backwards from later usage). Provide the needed generic arguments: `new Map<string, number>()`.
- jQuery `$el.data("foo")` is of type `any`. Try to convert this to `$el.attr("data-foo")` (for a string) or `Number($el.attr("data-foo"))` (for a number), but be careful to convert all reads and writes to `.data("foo")` for that `foo` **in the entire codebase** at once, because `.data()` does not sync with `.attr()` after the first access of `.data`. ([Documentation for `.data`](https://api.jquery.com/data/).)
- jQuery `event.currentTarget` is of type `any`. Convert the event handler to a non-arrow function and use its `this`, which is equivalent.
  - For a delegated handler, you might need to annotate the type of `this`: `$("body").on("click", ".foo", function (this: HTMLElement, e) {…})`.
  - If you need a more specific type than `HTMLElement`, also edit the selector string to guarantee that it satisfies that type at runtime: `$("body").on("click", "input.foo", function (this: HTMLInputElement, e) {…})`, since TypeScript won’t check that.
- jQuery `event.target` is of type `any`. Carefully consider whether `event.currentTarget` is what was intended instead, and then do the above. (See documentation for [jQuery `event.target`](https://api.jquery.com/event.target/), [jQuery `event.currentTarget`](https://api.jquery.com/event.currentTarget/), [MDN `event.target`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/target), [MDN `event.currentTarget`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/currentTarget).)
- `xhr.responseJSON` is of type `any`. Validate it with Zod.
  - If this is an error handler, it’s always possible you’ll get a different error that doesn’t have the format you were expecting, so use Zod’s `safeParse` to check whether it matches rather than throwing more errors.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-06 23:21 UTC

Another rule we should probably re-enable at some point is `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition`, which likely indicates either types missing `| undefined` or overdefensive checks.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-12 04:10 UTC

The `any` results from a TypeScript error; you want to resolve the errors from `tsc` before the ones from `eslint`. In this case, `.next()` on `Iterator<T>` returns `{done: false; value: T} | {done: true}`, so the error is that you need to check `!done` before reading `value`.
