**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-16 03:24 UTC

I’m going to enable [`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#exactOptionalPropertyTypes) in #30106, to prevent an evil type safety problem I noticed while developing the above PRs. We’ll need to be more precise about the difference between `{prop?: T}` (maybe missing) and `{prop: T | undefined}` (maybe present with a value of `undefined`) and `{prop?: T | undefined}` (maybe either of those).

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-16 16:02 UTC

Cool, yeah that's probably a form of precision that's worth the bit of fuss involved in it.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-16 16:42 UTC

Glad to see that development. That's one of the distinctions Flow has always made, that it's seemed unfortunate that TypeScript glossed over.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-16 21:50 UTC

As a general note for fixing `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` errors, it will almost always be simpler to change the type rather than the code, if it’s a type that we control (even if it’s in a different file). For example, to fix this error:

```ts
type Options = {left?: boolean, right?: boolean};
function mirror(options: Options): Options {
    return {left: options.right, right: options.left};
}
```

rather than contorting the return value into `{...(options.right !== undefined && {left: options.right}), ...(options.left !== undefined && {right: options.left})}`, prefer changing the type to `{left?: boolean | undefined, right?: boolean | undefined}`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-05-16 21:54 UTC

There are only a few cases in #30106 where I contorted the value like that, having to do with a type with an optional property being spread into another type where that property is not optional.

export function the<T>(items: T[] | JQuery<T>): T {

so we can replace the common patterns `$element[0]!` and `$element.expectOne()[0]!` with `the($element)`.

export function access<T>(arr: T[], idx: number): T {

`arr[idx]` is not forbidden; it’s just correctly typed `T | undefined` now. So you can use `nullthrows(arr[idx])` if that’s the effect you want. **Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-29 20:54 UTC

**Afeefuddin** · 2024-07-29 20:54 UTC

Yes, but it has an additional key `is_system_bot` which is always true.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-29 20:56 UTC

`CrossRealmBot` is a subtype of `User`.

```ts
export const cross_realm_bot_schema = user_schema.and(
    z.object({
        is_system_bot: z.boolean(),
    }),
);
export type User = z.infer<typeof user_schema>;
export type CrossRealmBot = z.infer<typeof cross_realm_bot_schema>;
```

So `User | CrossRealmBot` is identical to `User`, as far as TypeScript is concerned.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-29 20:58 UTC

(That `z.boolean()` could be strengthened to `z.literal(true)`, but the conclusion would be the same.)

**Afeefuddin** · 2024-07-29 21:04 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-29 21:05 UTC

You can’t access `.is_system_bot` on `User | CrossRealmBot` either.

```ts

```ts

const user = get_by_user_id(1) // returns  User

here

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-29 21:11 UTC

That’s a TypeScript bug (if perhaps an intentional one), since `{...user, is_system_bot: 123}` is a valid instance of `User` and a valid instance of `User | CrossRealmBot`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-29 21:13 UTC

Anyway, we don’t use `if ("is_system_bot" in user)`, and we don’t want to since that’s ugly. So in this case we want `is_system_bot` to be an optional field of `User`, and I don’t see any reason to have a `CrossRealmBot` type.

We might want a `CrossRealmBot` type if we were storing additional data that only exists on cross-realm bots, but I don’t think we are.

## excessive spans

*2019-07-13 to 2019-07-13 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/excessive.20spans/with/767688)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-13 18:29 UTC

Does anyone have ideas for whether there's a way to fix https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/12778/files without adding a bunch of extra spans?

**Vaibhav Rabber** · 2019-07-13 19:54 UTC

A solution (which actually could be more work) is that we shift the avatar from the popover title to the body. And then just setting the display of popover-title for message-info-popover to none so that any title we add does not appear inside the popover.

**Vaibhav Rabber** · 2019-07-13 19:59 UTC

Currently the avatar is set this way, setting the title inside js:

```javascript
    popover_element.popover({
        content: render_user_info_popover_content(args),
        // TODO: Determine whether `fixed` should be applied
        // unconditionally.  Right now, we only do it for the user
        // sidebar version of the popover.
        fixed: template_class === 'user_popover',
        placement: popover_placement,
        template: render_no_arrow_popover({class: template_class}),
        title: render_user_info_popover_title({
            user_avatar: "avatar/" + user.email,
            user_is_guest: user.is_guest,
        }),
        trigger: "manual",
        top_offset: 100,
        fix_positions: true,
    });
```

Any `title` attribute we set takes more preference over the title we set here. So, we shift the avatar template inside the popover template and remove the title from here. Using CSS we hide the title for the popover (because when we'll set the title to `User profile (u)`, it will appear in the popover).

**Yash RE** · 2019-07-16 19:42 UTC

I was working with:
```
    $("#stream_message_recipient_topic").typeahead({
        source: function () {
            var stream_name = compose_state.stream_name();
            return exports.topics_seen_for(stream_name);
        },
        items: 3,
        fixed: true,
        highlighter: function (item) {
            return typeahead_helper.render_typeahead_item({ primary: item });
        },
        sorter: function (items) {
            var sorted = typeahead_helper.sorter(this.query, items, function (x) {return x;});
            if (sorted.length > 0 && sorted.indexOf(this.query) === -1) {
                sorted.unshift(this.query);
            }
            return sorted;
        },
    });
```

## mysterious lightbox error

*2019-07-22 to 2019-07-23 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/mysterious.20lightbox.20error/with/771248)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-22 22:27 UTC

We've been seeing this error in production exceptions for a long time.  It's fairly common (several people hit it every day), and I'd love it if someone can figure out how to debug it.  Here's the error:
```
Lightbox for unknown message undefined

Stacktrace:
Error
    at Object.e.error (https://example.zulipchat.com/static/webpack-bundles/app.4f7c38d16142be420044.js:6:16776)
       = ./static/js/blueslip.js line 271 column 1

    at Object.e.open (https://example.zulipchat.com/static/webpack-bundles/app.4f7c38d16142be420044.js:313:490005)
       = ./static/js/lightbox.js line 140 column 1
```

This comes from this code in `lightbox.js` inside `exports.open`:
```
        if (is_compose_preview_image) {                                                                                  
            sender_full_name = people.my_full_name();                                                                    
        } else {                                                                                                         
            var $message = $parent.closest("[zid]");                                                                     
            var message = message_store.get($message.attr("zid"));                                                       
            if (message === undefined) {                                                                                 
                blueslip.error("Lightbox for unknown message " + $message.attr("zid"));                                  
            }                                                                                                            
            sender_full_name = message.sender_full_name;                                                                 
        }                                                                                                                
```

The "lightbox for unknown message" was added previously as part of trying to debug this.  The mystery is in what view we're opening the lightbox on an object that is neither in a compose preview nor inside a message body (which is where the `zid` attribute comes from).

I've tried investigating "message edit history" and "drafts", but neither of those seems to show previews.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-22 22:27 UTC

If anyone can find a reproducer or code path that could trigger this, I imagine it's not actually hard to fix.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-22 22:28 UTC

This is https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/9549

```scss
.a { color: white; }

    @extend .b;
}
```
compiles to
```css
.a { color: white; }
.b { background-color: blue; }
.c { color: white; }
.c { @extend .b; }

dart-sass output:

.a, .c {
  color: white;
}
.b, .c {
  background-color: blue;
}

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-12 21:46 UTC

Hi :)
I want to work on this [issue](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/13093) but it doesn't have the 'help wanted' label, also I don't know which part of the code I should read to debug.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-12 21:49 UTC

I haven’t investigated, but static/js/search.js may be a good place to start looking.

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-12 21:54 UTC

Thanks, I gonna read it

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-16 00:49 UTC

I have opened a PR to solve it, I have explicated more about it in a comment in the issue and in the PR, but I haven't claimed the issue yet because of the labels

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-19 21:33 UTC

The main problem currently is that we can't differentiate between users that use an input tool (as Google Chrome input tool) and the ones who don't. Because when we type characters in Unicode, in general, we use composition, so to type á we type ' and then a, depending on the keyboard and keyboard language this is done automatically, but in some cases is necessary to use an input tool. But when the users use an input tool, an auxiliary input bar appears for him, the events on this bar are propagated for the Zulip search bar so he maybe pressed enter just to move a word from the input tool to search bar instead of wanting to search for it, to handle this case, currently in the search bar code, if it's detected a composition event some hacky variable is used and the search is not triggered, so if the users use an input tool and types Unicode he won't trigger the search, but if you don't use you would need a second enter (kind of simulating the input tool) to do the search.

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-19 21:34 UTC

I don't see who to handle properly both cases in such a way that both work with the enters in a good way.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-19 21:36 UTC

I claim the main problem is that we trigger search on `keyup` rather than `keydown` (to work around some other bug). The logic behind the hacky variable used to ignore certain `keyup` events is subtly wrong, but it wouldn’t be necessary at all if we used `keydown`.

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-19 21:40 UTC

But if we triggered always on `keydown` the users with input tool would trigger a search for every word they type.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-19 21:40 UTC

I don’t think so—the `keydown` event should to the input tool, just not the `keyup` event for the last press (since the corresponding `keydown` for that press has already closed the input tool).

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-19 21:43 UTC

Both events will be triggered by the input tool, but to choose a word in the input tool you need to use a enter and this enter would trigger the search on `keydown` when you have not necessarily finished what you want to search

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-19 21:44 UTC

If that were the case, every website ever would have the same problem. It wouldn’t be possible to type anything into a form using an input tool without submitting the form.

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-19 21:46 UTC

That's a good point

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-19 21:55 UTC

Okay, I tried to simulate  and in fact the enter doesn't pass from the input tool to the search bar, well, I was sure that I had tested it before, but now it doesn't make sense to me the reason of using the hacky variable

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-19 21:58 UTC

Anyway, I will try more simulations later and see the results of changing the code

**Felipe Mota** · 2019-09-24 00:36 UTC

Well, I don't understand why on zulip we need to suppress the enter from input tool, even I testing on a lot of other sites, all of them stayed fine. And in fact it was even described in this [comment](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/422325454866fe3f060bc3f369096423fc0f5268/static/js/search.js#L124) on github that the code is used to suppress the enter from input tool.

~~~ py
 54 exports.highlight_query_in_phrase = function (query, phrase) {
 55     let i;
 56     query = query.toLowerCase();
 57     query = query.replace(/[\-\[\]{}()*+?.,\\\^$|#\s]/g, '\\$&');
 58     const regex = new RegExp('(^' + query + ')', 'ig');
 59
 60     let result = "";
 61     const parts = phrase.split(' ');
 62     for (i = 0; i < parts.length; i += 1) {
 63         if (i > 0) {
 64             result += " ";
 65         }
 66         result += exports.highlight_with_escaping_and_regex(regex, parts[i]);
 67     }
 68     return result;
 69 };
~~~

## unit tests in TS

*2019-10-15 to 2019-10-15 · 27 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/unit.20tests.20in.20TS/with/791865)*

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 21:26 UTC

I was chatting with a friend who works on a TypeScript codebase, and explained the story -- as best I understand it -- of how we've found the migration to it tricky because our unit tests are full of mutating other modules to mock or stub them out. I was curious how they handled that need.

Her answer was: oh, that was easy, we use `sinon`. Which appears to be this: https://sinonjs.org

I'm going to guess that that library's existence isn't news to y'all, and that in any case its implementation isn't doing anything particularly magic that we couldn't have done for ourselves. But I feel like I don't fully understand what the difficulty has been, because I don't know why that library isn't a solution to it. I would be curious to understand it better!

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-15 21:41 UTC

https://github.com/sinonjs/sinon/issues/1711

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-15 21:46 UTC

The basic difficulty is that both Babel and TypeScript compile
```
export function foo() {
}
export function bar() {
    foo();
}
```
to
```
function foo() {
}
exports.foo = foo;
function bar() {
    foo();
}
exports.bar = bar;
```
which leaves you with no way to test `bar` while mocking `foo`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-15 21:47 UTC

Or if you’re compiling to native ES6 modules, module bindings are immutable, leaving you with no way to mock `foo` at all.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:03 UTC

> ```js function foo() { } exports.foo = foo; function bar() { foo(); } exports.bar = bar;
which leaves you with no way to test `bar` while mocking `foo`.
```

Ah, I see -- whereas the pattern we have in our frontend app code is more like
```
// ...
function bar() {
    exports.foo();
// ...
```

Is that the key difference between what Babel and TypeScript emit, and what we've been doing in the status quo?

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:06 UTC

So in our status quo, we're effectively having a given module's exports object serve a dual purpose, as a site for dependency injection *into* the module, to mock out pieces of itself in order to test other pieces of itself.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:09 UTC

That also explains why we so often say `exports.foo`! Usually we write things so that we don't have any other name for it anyway (that is, we write
```
exports.foo = function () {
}
```
rather than
```
function foo() {
}
exports.foo = foo;
```
)... but even that choice effectively serves as a way of enforcing that internal references consistently look like `exports.foo` rather than plain `foo`, so that the dependency injection works and doesn't end up confusingly only affecting half the call sites it was meant to.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:12 UTC

OK, so popping the stack from that:
> which leaves you with no way to test `bar` while mocking `foo`.

This sounds like something that would be a pretty mainstream need!

... Unless... this is one of the reasons that JS libraries usually seem unreasonably intent on breaking everything up into as tiny modules as possible, like one 20-line function per file.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:15 UTC

Let's suppose for a moment that most people just give up on compiling *to* native ES6 modules, so they don't have the problem that module bindings are immutable.

How do most people who are writing "modern JS" or TS, and are using `sinon` or otherwise writing unit tests that involve mocking, deal with the problem? Is it just that they do all their mocking between modules? (And, perhaps, take that as a reason to cut their modules up extremely finely.)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-15 22:24 UTC

Yeah, I don’t really know how other projects deal with that and I’d be curious to know. `babel-plugin-rewire[-ts]` is the only existing solution I’m aware of but it doesn’t seem to be used all that widely.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:25 UTC

Yeah -- if I understood your comment correctly over on the TS-migration PR, it didn't even exist until a couple of months ago!

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-15 22:25 UTC

`babel-plugin-rewire` is older but the TypeScript-supporting fork is new, yeah.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:25 UTC

Ah got it

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-15 22:31 UTC

I have heard a number of random folks complaining that it's really hard to write tests for their JavaScript code.  I would not be entirely surprised if the answer was that you need to write your code a special way for testability and cross-module testing like we do in many of our node tests isn't commonly attempted.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-15 22:31 UTC

Though I'd be a little surprised -- it seems like such a basic aspect of reasonable testing.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:32 UTC

Hmm, I wasn't sure if the friend was referring to work-work or to their open-source LED-art tools in her answer -- but on looking at the latter, there are very few tests (a reasonable choice), so they must have meant the former and I can't trivially just look through that code to get an answer :slight_smile:

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:33 UTC

> that you need to write your code a special way for testability and cross-module testing like we do in many of our node tests isn't commonly attempted.

As best I've understood it, it's the inverse -- it's testing *within* a module, i.e. testing part of a module while mocking/stubbing out another part, that can't be done with widely-used tooling

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-15 22:36 UTC

There’s a separate question about how you test something that imports an external module while mocking the external module. But I think the existing frameworks have answers to that question.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:36 UTC

And it seems like the special way you need to write your code, or at least a special way that suffices, is:
* Break everything up into the smallest modules you can -- preferably ludicrously small, like <=1 function and <= 30 lines per file
* Compile away ES6 modules into older JS constructs (at least for running tests?)

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:37 UTC

One form of data that I think corroborates this story is that this style:
> * Break everything up into the smallest modules you can -- preferably ludicrously small, like <=1 function and <= 30 lines per file
is what I do actually observe most of the time when looking through the source code of a hip JS library.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-15 22:39 UTC

An independent reason you might want to write ludicrously small modules is so that users can be selective about which parts of your library they pull into their bundles. This reason will become obsolete with ES6 modules and tree shaking, but the ecosystem isn’t good at that yet.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:40 UTC

Yeah. That's the reason I'd known about, and had assumed was the reason people did it that way.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:40 UTC

But even if that's the primary reason people write in that style, a side effect is that they don't really have a need for within-module mocking for tests.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 22:42 UTC

(A classic example of that style, which I happened to be looking at yesterday for other reasons: `date-fns`. Here's [the source of `isThursday`](https://github.com/date-fns/date-fns/blob/f49acbcf1/src/isThursday/index.js), and [the list of functions](https://github.com/date-fns/date-fns/tree/f49acbcf1/src). (They don't appear to mock stuff for tests, though -- which seems an appropriate choice for their domain.))

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-10-15 22:53 UTC

A library that provides `isThursday` in addition to a `const THURSDAY = 4` would be a little curious. A library that provides `isThursday` *instead of* a `const THURSDAY = 4`is totally bewildering.

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 23:21 UTC

Heh, yeah, I would not call this awesome API design.

I think one thing that's going on here is that they've cloned part of their API from JS's standard `Date` prototype. So `getDay` is just a composition of [their `toDate`](https://github.com/date-fns/date-fns/blob/f49acbcf1/src/toDate/index.js) -- which I guess recently stopped doubling as a string parser, but the API is surely shaped by the previous assumption that `toDate` had a complicated job -- with the standard [`Date.prototype.getDay`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/getDay).

**Greg Price** · 2019-10-15 23:22 UTC

And then... I guess they didn't totally think things through when someone had the idea to make the API friendlier so your code didn't have to know whether the convention was 0 -> Sunday or what.

Thinking through at a fine-grained level the steps needed for sharing the emoji autocomplete code:
1. Move `get_emoji_matcher` (and its deps) to shared -- that's #13739
2. Move `typeahead_helper.sort_emojis` (and its deps) to shared
3. Perhaps add a doc comment on each of those to say what the interface is? I think I have some idea from staring at the implementations, but it'd be good to make explicit
4. Add `.js.flow` files so mobile can use these and have types
5. Bump the version in `static/shared/package.json` and upload to NPM
6. Bump the version called for in mobile's `package.json`
7. Replace the mobile implementation with calls to the shared version

Happily none of these are hard or much work, which is why we chose this as a place to start.

I think it makes sense for us mobile folks to handle 4-7, though 4 and 5 are in the zulip.git repo. I should probably augment `static/shared/README.md` (or some other form of docs) with more about these steps, too.

For those, I think the way I'd like to extend this plan is:

* Webapp maintainers do the refactoring needed to cut those dependencies: dependency injection, or getting data as arguments instead of calling a dependency for it, etc.
* For interesting cases, we probably chat here first about possible interfaces.
* After it's free of dependencies and moved to the shared package, mobile maintainers/contributors send any follow-up PRs for further interface changes that simplify our usage in the mobile code.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-12-23 21:19 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg @Tim Abbott One thing I've discovered today in working on search is that `people.get_all_persons` does an O(N) pluck from our person `Dict`.  I don't know how expensive it actually is for even a 10k list of people, since it's just copying pointers, essentially.  But it wouldn't be hard to cache that somehow.  One option is to make a variant on `Dict` called `FastDict` that uses a little extra memory to cache keys and values as separate lists, since we often tend to just need the list of ids or the list of objects for people.

Another option is to just manage some separate arrays in `people.js`, or do the caching there.

I prefer to do it in `FastDict`, because it could manage dirty flags automatically, and we'd get more code reuse.  Plus, we could easily swap back to regular `Dict` on a case-by-case basis.  But wondering what your thoughts are.

## startsWith

*2020-01-28 to 2020-01-28 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/startsWith/with/812813)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-28 14:02 UTC

It would be nice to have a case-insensitive startsWith helper in our codebase for typeaheads.  Right now the best we can do is this: `item.toLowerCase().startsWith(lowerQuery)`, which has the disadvantage of iterating every character in `item`when the query itself may only be two or three characters (and may not even match on the first character).

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-28 14:06 UTC

I searched SO for insight, and there are a few issues:
* Naively slicing item by lowerQuery.length does not account for cases like German where you have straße/STRASSE.  (Although there's possibly some weaker invariant that we could rely on there that would help.)
* Doing regex matches would require us to sanitize the query.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-28 14:07 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg @Greg Price I am wondering if either of you has an idiom/library that you would trust for this.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-28 15:35 UTC

Somewhat of an aside, but I just noticed that our heavily used `prefix_sort` method doesn't do diacritics.  So it treats "c" as a match for "C" (although placing it below actual "C"), but it views "ç" as a complete mismatch.  This isn't necessarily wrong behavior.  A use case would be deciding which of these two names is a better match for "sean": Seán or DeSean?  The former matches on prefix, but the latter matches on not having the accent.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-01-28 18:22 UTC

* I would not be surprised if even naive slicing adds enough allocation overhead so as not to be worthwhile unless the strings are really big.
* We have `_.escapeRegExp` for inserting strings into a regexp correctly.
* Unicode case folding would be more correct than `toLowerCase`, but I'm not sure if we've pulled in a library for that.

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-28 18:24 UTC

> * I would not be surprised if even naive slicing adds enough allocation overhead so as not to be worthwhile unless the strings are really big.

I share this intuition.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-28 18:34 UTC

The tradeoff is allocating 2n tiny strings of uniform length vs n big strings of varying length.  I would think most memory allocators are pretty fast for the former.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-28 20:01 UTC

I was curious, so I ran some numbers.  For stream descriptions, you get about 1.5x speedup with slices and about 2x speedup with regexes.  For people names, the slice memory allocation does actually make slice slower, while regex stays faster.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-28 20:01 UTC

~~~ js
function time_it(f, label) {
    const t1 = performance.now();
    for (i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) {
        f();
    }
    const t2 = performance.now();
    console.log(label, t2 - t1);
    console.info(f());
}

var prefix = 'stuf';

function f1() {
    return _.filter(stream_data.subscribed_subs(), (s) => {
        return s.description.toLowerCase().startsWith(prefix);
    });
}

function f2() {
    const len = prefix.length;
    return _.filter(stream_data.subscribed_subs(), (s) => {
        return s.description.slice(0, len).toLowerCase().startsWith(prefix);
    });
}

~~~ js
var prefix = 'st';

function f1() {
    return people.filter_all_persons((p) => {
        return p.full_name.toLowerCase().startsWith(prefix);
    });
}

function f2() {
    const len = prefix.length;
    return people.filter_all_persons((p) => {
        return p.full_name.slice(0, len).toLowerCase().startsWith(prefix);
    });
}

function f3() {
    const regex = new RegExp('^' + prefix, 'i');
    return people.filter_all_persons((p) => {
        return p.full_name.match(regex);
    });
}

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-15 00:30 UTC

The big difference I'm thinking of is this:
* In the webapp, the app's state is stored in mutable objects, and the various parts of the application look at it through references to those mutable objects (either direct references to the raw data structures, or getters which have them in their closures.)
* In the mobile app, nearly all the app's state is managed with [Redux](https://redux.js.org/introduction/three-principles). This means that it all lives in *immutable* values; there's a single mutable object (the "store") at the root of the tree, which basically has a mutable pointer to the value that is the current value of the entire immutable global state. (Which is a giant tree of nested objects, typically sharing most of its subtrees with the previous value, and the one before that, etc.)

  And virtually all the app's code that handles such data is given either the current immutable global state, or various immutable pieces plucked from within it.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-15 00:34 UTC

Am I right that so far none of the code that we have shared (including the pending markdown changes) don’t yet force us to confront mutability issues?  Sincere question, just trying to figure out where we stand now

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-15 00:36 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-15 00:37 UTC

That was a good solution there, and not a lot of work, because it was such a small set of data it needed

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-15 00:38 UTC

Then the caller takes responsibility for laying hands on the data in the way it needs, which it does in the webapp case by invoking the getter itself, and it does in the mobile case by pulling it out from the immutable-global-state object it was passed

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-15 00:39 UTC

In the markdown, case, in the "helpers" interface in #13899, this comes up with a getter like `get_user_by_name`. That's an API that fits well in a context where the mutable store is readily sitting around -- the markdown code can get passed `get_user_by_name: people.get_by_name`, giving it one of those getters that has a reference to the mutable state

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-15 00:41 UTC

It’s a function

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-17 19:52 UTC

BTW speaking of test setups for JavaScript, I've found Jest (which we use on mobile) to be pretty great. Dearest to my heart are the things it does to make tests run fast:
* it automatically parallelizes to use all your cores
* given a list of files you've changed, it can compute exactly which test files could have been affected (based on the module import graph, I assume), and run only those!

  In particular you can tell it to compare to a given Git ref, e.g. like `--changedSince upstream/master`, and consider files that differ from that.

  So what we do is have our `tools/test` script pass it that option by default, so that running tests in development is super fast; and then in CI we run `tools/test --full`, and that runs the full suite just to be sure.

So if/when at some point we start putting tests in the shared package, one thing we could do is make that a playground for using Jest as a shared test framework.

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-25 03:41 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> Passing in page_params from show_email’s callers moves the problem to their callers. Where do they get page_params from? Their callers?

This would actually be quite parallel in usages on web and mobile.
* In either case, if the caller is itself one of these leaf-y, pure, product-detail-encapsulating functions that makes sense to share, then it gets the value from its own caller.
* Otherwise:
  * On web, it gets it from the global state. It does this by saying `page_params`, same as the code generally does now.
  * On mobile, it gets it from the global state. In many cases it'll do this by saying `state.realmConfig` (or `state.pageParams` or whatever we might call it), where `state`, the global state, is something the code gets from its caller. It's a consequence of the Redux architecture that a large number of different points where app code gets invoked by framework code have the (current, immutable, value of the) global state passed in as a parameter.

   In other places, it'll be convenient to have a caller extract a few pieces off of the global state and pass just those to a callee, with the `page_params`-alike object being one of those. This is a very common pattern for lots of other pieces of the global state too.

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-25 03:42 UTC

(It seems there's a Markdown bug; please pretend that last paragraph is indented to be part of the inner, "On mobile, ..." bullet rather than the outer one.)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-25 04:01 UTC

For state that is basically global could we just agree on a convention of where to put it without passing it down the stack?  Like have an object that stores the subset of page_params that webapp and mobile share?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-02-25 07:07 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> (It seems there's a Markdown bug; please pretend that last paragraph is indented to be part of the inner, "On mobile, ..." bullet rather than the outer one.)
I don't think is a markdown bug, exactly; many markdown and CommonMark implementations expect that if you mean to continue a bullet, you need to indent every line until you're done with the bullet.

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-25 19:32 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> For state that is basically global could we just agree on a convention of where to put it without passing it down the stack? Like have an object that stores the subset of page_params that webapp and mobile share?

No -- there really is no equivalent in the mobile app. It's a difference in architecture, not just naming.

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-25 19:39 UTC

One reason for that difference is that the mobile app lives on as you switch from looking at what you see as one user, logged into one org, to looking at what you see as a different user logged into a different org; whereas on the web, you do that in a new tab with a completely new instance of the app. That means that data that the webapp gets at startup, and can treat as a constant, will actually vary within the mobile app and so it's important to use the right value at the right time.

Moreover, in the future we'll want to do more than we currently do with handling data for two *different* user identities (i.e. typically in two different orgs) at the same time. Currently for the most part we only handle one identity/org's data at a time, but that causes problems in the user experience for people who use several orgs routinely.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-25 19:44 UTC

Well, webapp data changes on every server event.  For certain things, like settings, that data is simply kept in `page_params` (and modified as needed).  All I'm saying is that in the middle of some user action there's a canonical place to find each type of data.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-25 19:46 UTC

Anyway, I should just withdraw my question for now.  I still think `show_email` is kind of a bad example.  I'd rather focus on bigger chunks of code, like markdown, that have basically a single entry point, where the architectural differences between the apps are pretty small.

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-25 21:16 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> Well, webapp data changes on every server event. For certain things, like settings, that data is simply kept in `page_params` (and modified as needed).

Ah, well, that's an additional architectural difference, then :-) -- we don't mutate data.


> All I'm saying is that in the middle of some user action there's a canonical place to find each type of data.

But this is the thing that just cannot be true when handling data for several different user identities at the same time. Which is a thing that the webapp doesn't need to do, and the mobile app does.

For example, the user might be an admin in one org and not the other -- so there is no one value for `is_admin`. The only way for a piece of code to get the right answer for `page_params.is_admin` is to be passed by its caller one of
* (a) the value of `is_admin`
* (b) some object like `page_params` that contains (a)
* (c) some kind of key that identifies the user+realm (among all the other accounts the person is logged into on different realms), with which to look up (b) or (a) in a global data structure

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-25 22:04 UTC

Ok, thanks for the clarification.  Obviously, for any nontrivial piece of code we share that is basically a one-call API, it's no big deal at all to pass in some kind of context thingy.  (Like, for markdown, we pass in a pretty big structure of thingies.)

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-25 22:10 UTC

Yeah, agreed.

I think we should move toward this goal, but I have several concerns that I think we need to address in the short term. **Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:23 UTC

```
  2 import i18next from 'i18next';
  3 import localstorage from './localstorage';
  4
  5 window.i18n = i18next;
```

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:24 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg What's your vision here, before I get too into the weeds?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-02-26 23:29 UTC

If we provide an empty `page_params.translation_data` in the global Node tests environment, or make `translations` check whether it exists, then the Node tests don’t have to change.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-02-26 23:30 UTC

I don’t see what this has to do with mobile. Mobile doesn’t have any interactions with `page_params` or `i18next`.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:32 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> I think the interaction with mobile is that if there's code that wants to invoke translations, and we start sharing it, then it needs to get the translations in a way that mobile can also provide it with.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-02-26 23:34 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-26 23:34 UTC

Which will basically look like passing it some appropriate parameter.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:34 UTC

Interesting idea.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:40 UTC

My main goal for the node tests is to have most tests pretend like it's not there.  Setting `translation_data` to empty would basically accomplish that, I think.  At some point I think we had concerns that simply requiring the module was slowing us down, but that might either be fuzzy memory or obsolete constraints.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-02-26 23:43 UTC

The [commit I was reacting to](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/14026/commits/492a94df6defcbec5bed6be7899e0e403de60d26) had the problem that whenever we want to get any information from e.g. `create_stream_policy_values` (even just a single integer), we’d have to rebuild the entire structure each time, including re-internationalizing the strings.

Maybe a better structure, if we want to add the ability to pass `i18n` data functionally for the sake of mobile sharing, would be
```js
exports.create_stream_policy_values = {
    by_admins_only: {
        order: 1,
        code: 2,
        description: i18n => i18n.t("Admins"),
    },
    …
};
```
rather than
```js
exports.get_create_stream_policy_values = i18n => ({
    by_admins_only: {
        order: 1,
        code: 2,
        description: i18n.t("Admins"),
    },
    …
});
```

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:44 UTC

Those calls aren’t expensive

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:50 UTC

Nor are they ever called in a loop, if that’s your optimization concern.

Well that would also let you get `create_stream_policy_values.by_admins_only.code` without having `i18n` data at all.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:50 UTC

Yeah that’s fair

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-26 23:52 UTC

But these really are cheap calls the 2nd or 3rd times, correct?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-27 22:38 UTC

Does anybody have interest in prototyping an alternative to Casper?  For folks who have never heard of Casper, it's similar to Selenium, and it's the tool that we use to do full-stack testing of our webapp.  CasperJS is a screen-scraping test framework build on top of the headless browser PhantomJS.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-27 22:40 UTC

We are interested in replacing Casper because both it (https://github.com/casperjs/casperjs) and its main dependency (https://phantomjs.org/) are no longer being actively maintained.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-27 22:43 UTC

Zulip's requirements for doing full-stack testing of the webapp aren't much different than any other similar webapp:
- start up the dev server (we do this now, no need to reinvent)
- run the headless browser
- simulate things like clicks and data input with the headless browser
- screen-scrape results
- make assertions about what's on the screen

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-27 22:44 UTC

So if you've done similar things on another project (even a personal project), it might take only a few hours to whip up something for Zulip that we can use as a starting point.

**Yash RE** · 2020-03-11 01:07 UTC

```javascript
const puppeteer = require('puppeteer');
const assert = require('assert');
async function run() {
  const browser = await puppeteer.launch({
    args: [
      '--window-size=1400,1024',
    ],
    defaultViewport: null,
    headless: false,
  });
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.setViewport({
    width: 1400,
    height: 900,
  });
  await page.goto('http://localhost:9991/devlogin/');
  const cordelia = "#direct_login_form > div > div > div:nth-child(2) > p:nth-child(3) > input";
  await page.waitFor(cordelia);
  await page.$eval(cordelia, a => {a.click();});
  const buddy_data_selector = "#user_presences > li > div > a";
  await page.waitFor(buddy_data_selector);
  
  const buddy_data_urls = await page.$$eval(buddy_data_selector, anchors => { return anchors.map(anchor => anchor.href) })
  assert.equal(buddy_data_urls[0],'http://localhost:9991/#narrow/pm-with/8-cordelia');
  
  // open message box
  await page.keyboard.type('c');

  const compose_box_stream_input = "#stream_message_recipient_stream";
  await page.waitFor(compose_box_stream_input);
  await page.$eval(compose_box_stream_input, a => {a.value = "test";});

  const compose_box_topic_input = "#stream_message_recipient_topic";
  await page.waitFor(compose_box_topic_input);
  await page.$eval(compose_box_topic_input, a => {a.value = "test topic";});

  const compose_box_body = "#compose-textarea";
  await page.waitFor(compose_box_body);
  await page.$eval(compose_box_body, a => {
    a.value = "test message";
    // prep for pressing enter
    a.select();
  });

  // send the message
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');

  const last_message = "#zhome101";
  await page.waitFor(last_message);
  const message_body = await page.$eval(last_message, a => {a.textContent;});
  
  // commented as will fail if not run on a fresh build
  // (ie if other messages had already been sent)

  // assert.equal(message_body, "test message");

  browser.close();
}

run();
```

Yup -- that's #11767

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-05 21:21 UTC

Basically, the server currently has a bug where for a wide range of modern emoji, it corrupts them. It tries to translate them into Zulip's emoji universe, but it doesn't understand the full range of ways emoji can exist in Unicode, and so it ends up converting just the first part of the emoji. Then the other parts remain in Unicode, but left dangling because the thing they're meant to modify or combine with is gone (having been translated into a Zulip-style emoji object.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-22 22:48 UTC

Yep, I know.  One of the things that's important in our goals for this is to be able to support email/mobile notifications for topics the current user recently participated in.  So we're not looking to do just a frontend-only feature.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-22 22:49 UTC

(Because part of our goals for notification settings is to be able to configure email/mobile notifications for messages in topics you've participated in).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-22 22:49 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-22 22:50 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-22 22:53 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-22 22:54 UTC

## css utility classes

*2020-03-24 to 2020-03-25 · 29 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/css.20utility.20classes/with/838467)*

**Vishnu KS** · 2020-03-24 18:38 UTC

So I  and @Shubham Gupta were trying to simplify some CSS in activity.css file. We found out that the following three classes can be replaced with one class without affecting the styling much.

```diff

-.support-discount-form {
-    position: relative;
-    top: -50px;
-}
-
-.support-plan-type-form {
-    position: relative;
-    top: -25px;
-}
-
-.scrub-realm-form {
-    position: relative;
-    top: -50px;
+.support-form {
+    margin-top: -25px;
 }

```

This is great but we find it annoying that we have to create a special class called `.support-form` just to apply ` margin-top: -25px;` There should be many classes out there like this which were created just for applying a single CSS style.  

What about creating utility classes for cases like this? So instead of creating a class called `support-form`, a class called `-m-25` is created and used here. Folks can reuse classes like this anywhere else as well. 

There is a CSS framework called [tailwind](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/margin/) which has predefined utility classes like this. I don't think we need it at the moment. We should be fine for now by defining our own utility classes if we think this is a good direction to pursue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-24 19:57 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-02 22:18 UTC

Yeah, that's a gesture. By "available" I mean: take the "New private message" button in the compose area, just because it's a nice large button. Mouse-down near one end, move to the other end, and mouse-up.

You'll find that the effect is a click.

If you do the same with something like a long link (in a browser), you'll instead find the effect is a drag.

In the case of the button, there's no such thing as dragging a button. (In this context, anyway, and I think most any other outside a UI editor.) So no matter how much you moved the mouse around while down, the mouse-up becomes a click.

We only instantiate one copy of `drag`:

~~~ js
const drag = (function () {
    return {
        start: function (e) {
            // ...
        },

        end: function (e) {
            // ...
        },
        val: null,
    };
}());

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-05 12:51 UTC

As long as we only use that in one context, we're fine:

~~~ js
 47     $("#main_div").on("mousedown", ".messagebox", function (e) {
 48         drag.start(e);
 49     });
 50     $("#main_div").on("mouseup", ".messagebox", function (e) {
 51         drag.end(e);
 52     });

~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-05 12:51 UTC

But if we use this for multiple elements, you have the risk of mixing up `start` and `end`calls across different elements.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-05 12:53 UTC

The most incremental change here is something like this:

~~~ js
function drag_tracker() {
    return {
        start: function (e) {
            // ...
        },

        end: function (e) {
            // ...
        },
        val: null,
    };
}

const message_box_drag_tracker = drag_tracker();

$("#main_div").on("mousedown", ".messagebox", function (e) {
    message_box_drag_tracker.start(e);
});
$("#main_div").on("mouseup", ".messagebox", function (e) {
    message_box_drag_tracker.end(e);
});

~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-05 12:54 UTC

But, really, what we ideally want here is just a higher level abstraction.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-05 12:55 UTC

There's nothing wrong with `drag_tracker` itself--that's a nice tiny component that makes perfect sense.  But it should be used in a bigger abstraction that just lets you attach handlers to an element for higher level things like `on_local_click`, `on_long_tap`, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-06 21:41 UTC

You can think of commit almost like financial transactions.  You can have multiple financial transactions, but each transaction should leave the person square:

* commit #1: Alice gives Bob an apple, Bob gives Alice a banana (good!)
* commit #2: Alice gives Bob a dollar (incomplete!)
* commit #3: Bob gives Alice some popcorn (incomplete!)
* commit #4: Alice gives Bob two wheels, a frame, some components, and some money, and Bob gives Alice a bike (good!)

Notice how we can easily squash #2 and #3.   And we can't break down #4, despite all the pieces involved.  The size of the commit kinda depends on what you're doing and how much you can break down the work.

## out-of-order local ids

*2020-04-09 to 2021-07-17 · 45 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/out-of-order.20local.20ids/with/850456)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-09 16:23 UTC

Here's a fun bug going back to 065fcf1a1b5682b3066e3603a817ecb60aaaeb21 (March 2014):

~~~ js
// Turn the 10.02 in [11, 10.02, 12] into 11.02
var decimal = parseFloat((msg.id % 1).toFixed(0.02));
~~~


It just returns 0 there.

~~~
> msg = {id: 10.02}
{ id: 10.02 }
> parseFloat((msg.id % 1).toFixed(0.02))
0
> parseFloat((msg.id % 1).toFixed(2))
0.02

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-09 16:26 UTC

More context:

~~~
363     // Returns the index where you could insert the desired ID
364     // into the message list, without disrupting the sort order
365     // This takes into account the potentially-unsorted
366     // nature of local message IDs in the message list
367     _lower_bound: function (id) {
368         const self = this;
369         function less_func(msg, ref_id, a_idx) {
370             if (self._is_localonly_id(msg.id)) {
371                 // First non-local message before this one
372                 const effective = self._next_nonlocal_message(self._items, a_idx,
373                                                               function (idx) { return idx - 1; });
374                 if (effective) {
375                     // Turn the 10.02 in [11, 10.02, 12] into 11.02
376                     const decimal = parseFloat((msg.id % 1).toFixed(0.02));
377                     const effective_id = effective.id + decimal;
378                     return effective_id < ref_id;
379                 }
380             }
381             return msg.id < ref_id;
382         }
383
384         return util.lower_bound(self._items, id, less_func);
385     },

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-09 17:13 UTC

This code is also doing a binary search when I'm guessing we're always inserting near the end of the list, too.  And binary search kinda relies on the invariant that your list is sorted, which is contradicted by the comment mentioning the "potentially-unsorted nature...".

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-09 19:04 UTC

The whole floating-point ID hack needs to be shot.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-09 19:05 UTC

It's such a pain.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-09 20:36 UTC

The hack does solve the problem of "We might need an ID in between two consecutive real message IDs".  But it's potentially the case we'd be better off with "messages not acknowledged by the server are always re-sorted to the bottom", which would let us remove the floating point behavior, and replace it with a very large made-up number (or something like it).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-09 20:37 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-09 20:37 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-09 20:56 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> We don’t need to make up numbers. We have, like, an entire programming language worth of more suitable data types.

Yes, but if a goal is for them to sort as just after a given message ID, it does make sense to just make them a number fitting that description.  Sort-to-end is a different situation, but there is a benefit to every message object visible in the frontend to have a `message_id` with a number type, rather than supporting two types.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-09 20:58 UTC

I would love to see a PR for a different approach here, even if it's only like 85% working, just to get an idea for the scope of a rewrite here.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-09 20:59 UTC

I don’t agree. It saves us having to write a two-line helper function for that one sorting operation, while making everything else involving message IDs more confusing.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-09 21:01 UTC

If we sorted by timestamps, that reduces the problem to dealing with generating approximate server timestamps for the not-yet-acked local messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-09 21:04 UTC

Sorting by timestamps would be problematic for invariants around things like "When you get to the top of the feed, and fetch more messages, we know all the new messages go on top".

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-09 21:04 UTC

So I don't think it'd be a good idea to change that.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 19:15 UTC

I think the first step here is to make a product decision that all messages with `locally_echoed=true` get put below all the normal messages.  And then we sort by either `id` or `local_id`, so that the key for sorting is basically the tuple `(m.locally_echoed ? 1 : 0, m.locally_echoed ? m.local_id : m.id)`.  Once we have that in place, we could at least have a sane sorting operation.  I doubt a binary search is actually needed here, and it may even be inferior.  We do call `message_range` in a scroll handler, but that's throttled at 50ms.

And then the next step would be to remove the float/fixed hacks.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 19:15 UTC

(I am bumping this conversation due to #19253.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 19:21 UTC

What does the product currently do?  I think it might be the case that in practice that code does the same thing as a normal sort by ID.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 19:24 UTC

In normal circumstances, even a fast typist rarely gets too far ahead of the server, so I usually see the message that I just sent show up at the bottom of the feed.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 19:26 UTC

I would assume that any behavior other than putting non-acked messages at the bottom of the feed is an unintentional quirk of the algorithm.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 20:02 UTC

Well, these code paths are mainly for where you have unreliable Internet.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 20:03 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell (showell))
> I would assume that any behavior other than putting non-acked messages at the bottom of the feed is an unintentional quirk of the algorithm.

There's utility in having your message not jump around unnecessarily; I feel like we might have intentionally arranged to have those messages stay put as new messages to that topic come in, and have them move at most once (when acked by the server).  I don't recall whether that's actually the case, but I remember that tradeoff being discussed.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 20:05 UTC

The algorithm I propose would only move the messages when they are acked.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 20:06 UTC

(Unless you count when “prior” messages come in.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 20:51 UTC

Right, when messages sent by other clients appear, your algorithm will push down existing messages, rather than adding new messages at the bottom.  The alternative proposal of "just sort using the temporary ID we generated" would do the opposite.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 23:15 UTC

Let's say Bob has a fast connection and is sending messages at rapid-fire speed to Alice, who has a slow connection.  Let's say he's sending a message every 2 seconds, and they're getting the server almost immediately.  At t=20, then Bob will have sent messages with real DB ids of 1001, 1002, 1003, ...1010.  Let's say that Alice is 10s "away" from the server, so she has only seen message 1005 from Bob when she hits send.  She is likely to get 1011 as the message id from the server, even though our current algorithm will probably assign 1005.01 or something like that as the message's local id.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 23:16 UTC

In my mind the desired behavior is that as messages 1006, 1007, 1008, 1009, and 1010 finally arrive from Bob, Alice's message will keep staying at the bottom of the feed.  And then when her message finally gets acked, it's likely to be 1011, and her feed should reflect the server's order, where the server is sort of the "independent observer" of the conversation.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 23:18 UTC

I understand there can be funny races here, but I don't think there's actually one perfect ordering system for the messages, so my vote is to keep it simple.  And I think most of the time the right thing will just naturally happen, even if Alice has a much slower connection than Bob.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-07-15 23:20 UTC

I tend to agree, though I can understand the counterargument that the unsent message should remain between 1005 and 1006 until it’s acknowledged, for the purpose of avoiding the multiple visual jumps each time one of 1006, 1007, 1008, 1009, and 1010 come in.

Neither view explains why you would ever get a situation like [11, 10.02, 12], though.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 23:21 UTC

If Carl is on the same stream, he will likely see the messages in the order that they hit the server, since he has no local info about which message Alice is actually responding to.  And I think if I were Alice, I would want to know which view Carl has of the world, so that you can resolve confusion accordingly.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 23:24 UTC

I think we could mitigate the visual jumps by doing the right thing from a scrolling perspective.  And some sort of visual weirdness could actually be considered a feature--make it clear to Alice that's she behind on the feed.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 23:26 UTC

~~Another possibility is that if a message list has any unacked messages, we queue up incoming messages until the messages get acked, and then do a single redraw.~~ (probably not a good idea)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-15 23:40 UTC

There is some benefit to not letting unacked messages scroll off the top of the screen.  (As an aside, I think we should make it a little more visibly obvious that your message hasn’t actually been acked.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 23:49 UTC

I don't think there is a right thing we can do visually to avoid jumping in that case; fundamentally, your "local message" that you're sending would be having other messages appear between the previous message and it, so either the previous message or the local message has to jump.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-16 01:08 UTC

When any incoming message arrives, you are gonna perturb the view no matter what the paradigm is.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-16 01:10 UTC

If you hold the screen position of the first unacked message as a constant, the I don’t really see how putting the previous message above it necessarily has to feel wrong.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-16 12:08 UTC

I'm willing to back down on this argument.  If we decide that Alice's respond message to Bob's message 1005 should stay between 1005 and 1006 until the server acks it with a real server-side message_id, then what are the next steps here?

I feel like we've done enough reasoning about the desired behavior here that we shouldn't invest tons of time in reverse engineering the algorithm.

I am curious how motivated @Anders Kaseorg is to just fix this code, with the understanding that the current implementation is frustrating on many levels.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-16 12:11 UTC

I can imagine a tiny first step here would be to have a do-not-merge commit that makes it easy to simulate something like this:
* every message that Cordelia sends gets delayed 3 seconds outbound
* every message that Cordelia receives (including from peers?) gets queued up for 3 seconds on the inbound side
* every time Hamlet sends a message, we actually send 10 copies of the message over 30 seconds or so
* we hack the UI code to make message ids (and local ids) clearly visible in the message

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-16 12:13 UTC

I am willing to fight this battle in the coming weeks, but I don't really have any special historical knowledge here that I couldn't easily communicate to somebody else.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-16 12:14 UTC

This relatively tiny (but super complex) piece of code has been perplexing me since ~2017, and I think it's one of the few remaining reasons we don't have 100% line coverage on an otherwise pretty-testable module.

**Greg Price** · 2021-07-17 00:37 UTC

This seems like a situation where there is no algorithm that's ideal from a product/UI perspective, basically because there's fundamentally a race in what's really happened: the time that you wrote the message and hit send on it, and the time when it actually reaches the server, are at different points in the final sequence of messages. There are some messages that come after one of those times but before the other.

So for example in the current behavior, if you have a message that's trying to send and then some more messages come in, we'll show your message above those -- but at this point we know that the reality is that your message will come after them if/when everyone else sees it. So we're showing a less faithful representation of what things will look like than we could.

**Greg Price** · 2021-07-17 00:37 UTC

I see how it's arguable that the current behavior has advantages over just always showing the pending messages at the end. But it doesn't seem at all clear that it's actually better and not worse.

**Greg Price** · 2021-07-17 00:39 UTC

Given that, and because its implementation involves this complex bit of code that's been perplexing Steve for years and that puts an asterisk on the fundamental concept that is a message ID, it seems like it'd be an improvement to drop that complexity and switch to just putting the pending messages at the end.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-07-17 11:28 UTC

Well said, Greg.  I am still basically of the position that we can decide on either product decision, and know that neither one is ideal, and then have someone clean up the code.

Greg articulated my position better than I could, but I am actually on the fence here.

I really mostly think this is an edge case.  When in doubt, do the simple thing.

I have been investigating the laggy scrolling on the Chrome mobile web for the last few days and I have drawn several conclusions (as I posted before [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/65-checkins/topic/hashir/near/932275)).
 
Until now I have tried the following fixes but none of them were successful, unfortunately:
* Refactor HTML and CSS to lessen the composite layers that are being created (reference [article](https://www.html5rocks.com/en/tutorials/speed/layers/))
* Use `will-change: transform` CSS property with main app container (reference [article](https://developers.google.com/web/updates/2016/09/re-rastering-composite))
* Tried to eliminate the overlapping margin and padding as I mentioned [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/6-frontend/topic/multiple.20composite.20layers.20in.20chrome.20mobile/near/937937)
* Commented all the styling properties in `zulip.scss` and uncommented them one by one. I couldn't find any property that drastically affected the scrolling performance. The performance kept on decreasing as I increased the CSS properties.

Does anyone have any other idea about how this can be fixed? Using `will-change: transform` with `.app` is the closest solution IMO as it makes scrolling absolutely smooth by enforcing the entire layout into single composite layer but this doesn't allow any static content in the screen like `column-left`, `column-right` etc (as shown below).

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-14 10:02 UTC

But then `maybe_add_local_messages` has some other side effects that you probably don't want--the main thing it does is call:

~~~ js
 343 function load_local_messages(msg_data) {
 344     // This little helper loads messages into our narrow message
 345     // data and returns true unless it's empty.  We use this for
 346     // cases when our local cache (message_list.all) has at least
 347     // one message the user will expect to see in the new narrow.
 348
 349     const in_msgs = message_list.all.all_messages();
 350     msg_data.add_messages(in_msgs);
 351
 352     return !msg_data.empty();
 353 }
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-14 10:03 UTC

And, just to be clear, this is only populating your `MessageListData` object with messages that the client has already fetched.  To get older messages you would need to do `channel.get(...)`.

## Maintain undo history after typeahead

*2020-04-14 to 2020-05-04 · 34 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Maintain.20undo.20history.20after.20typeahead/with/853852)*

**Jivitesh Jain** · 2020-04-14 23:03 UTC

As detailed by #14311, currently, the browser undo history is lost when any typeahead is applied. This is because programmatically editing the text behaves this way.

Possible fixes include:
1. Using `document.execCommand`, a (still) popular choice, but now deprecated
2. Implementing a custom undo stack
3. A third party editor library (which doesn't use `execCommand` under the hood!)

None of these options sounds optimal. The first is extremely easy to implement, but it is deprecated and may have compatibility issues. The other two are hard to implement.

Looking for better options.

@Tim Abbott FYI

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 00:29 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-16 19:33 UTC

(replying to Jivitesh Jain)
> There isn't even much mention of it being obsolete, except the MDN page I linked. But I believe MDN pages are reliable.

MDN is pretty great, and is definitely the best place to start for a lot of things. I do a lot of Google searches where I put `mdn` in the query so I can quickly go straight to the MDN article.

But it's also not always reliable. It's basically about at the level of some of the higher-quality areas of Wikipedia (which can also be pretty great!). And that's not a coincidence -- MDN itself is a wiki.

So, just like Wikipedia, when you want to be sure of something that MDN is telling you, you have to go to its sources. In the case of MDN, those sources are generally the specifications, which are linked from a prominent box toward the bottom of each article.

This adds the selection action to the undo stack as well, so when you undo, in the first step the typeahead changes go, and in the second, all the earlier text gets selected.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-04 12:23 UTC

I think it's generally good practice to have just one handler, since as Tim mentions, having multiple handlers for the same event can be tricky with `stopPropagation`, plus it can be hard to reason about which order the handlers will run it (if it's even deterministic at all).

What you can do, however, is create two helper functions in the handler, especially if there are two pretty distinct things that need to happen for the event.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-28 15:19 UTC

I think what you're proposing is certainly feasible.  There are three major moving parts, probably listed below in increasing order of complexity:
* Have MessageListData encode data gaps (or encode "fetched chunks" if that fits your mental model better)
* Have message-fetching logic be able to consult MLD to find out what's missing (with `fetch_status` possibly as an intermediary)
* Have the UI handle scrolling when it gets to gaps

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-28 15:20 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-28 18:26 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-28 18:43 UTC

So from MLV's perspective, when you get to message 799 and page down, it think it's going to do exactly what it did for the last chunk:
- ask the server more data
- start the spinner
- get the server response
- stop the spinner
- draw the next chunk of records

But we'll short-circuit some of the server work with our `FetchStatus` structure.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-28 18:45 UTC

So we'd save the most expensive bit of re-work (asking the server for messages that it already gave us) but we'll still do a bit of re-work (like re-rendering the messages).  The data layer is easy to make smart; the UI layer is more messy, where it might be good to keep it dumb.

**rinwa** · 2024-02-16 14:33 UTC

Passing `oldest`, `first`, and `newest` to `then_select_id` didn't update the view.
**Research and Solution:**

After looking into this, I discovered that `final_select_id` expects a numerical  value to fetch the first message. 

**Explanation:**
* `target_select_id` passes `-1` to `final_select_id`.
* `final_select_id` then receives its actual value and triggers a switch statement.
* Based on the received value, `final_select_id` might assign `oldest` to the `anchor` variable.
* If `oldest` is assigned, the first message is fetched for the view.
* Similarly, passing `LARGER_THAN_MAX_MESSAGE_ID` fetches the latest message.

**rinwa** · 2024-02-29 13:07 UTC

```
case -1:
 // This case should never happen in this code path; it's
 // here in case we choose to extract this as an
 // independent reusable function.
 anchor = "oldest";
 break;
```
 However, due to an external requirement when fetching messages from the API, we need to pass `id_info.final_select_id: -1` even if it's not ideal. This forces the anchor to be set to "oldest" for fetching the oldest messages.

**rinwa** · 2024-02-29 15:27 UTC

**rinwa** · 2024-03-01 11:10 UTC

I apologize for the previous unclear explanation.

In the `narrow.activate` function, the `switch` statement handles different cases. Ideally, the `case` where `id_info.final_select_id` is assigned `-1` should not be reached in this specific code path.

However, to fetch the first ever message in the view, we need to pass `id_info.final_select_id: -1` even though it's not ideal. This forces the `anchor` to be set to `"oldest"` to fetch the first message in the view.

## i18next library usage in i18n.js

*2020-04-18 to 2020-04-18 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/i18next.20library.20usage.20in.20i18n.2Ejs/with/856389)*

**Pranay Shah** · 2020-04-18 02:07 UTC

Hi, @Rohan Prashant and I are trying to test the i18next library's pluralization functionality. We decided a good place to begin would be the i18n.js node test. We saw that the translation data is loaded into the ```page_params``` variable, and tried to add our own mappings to it. We are doing this to get acquainted with the i18n library to resolve https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/1286.

We realized that using i18next's complex features like nested keys (https://www.i18next.com/translation-function/essentials) and plurals (https://www.i18next.com/translation-function/plurals) do not work by adding mappings to the page_params variable. Calling ```i18n.t(look.deep)``` from the example linked does not return the nested mapping, it literally returns "look.deep". Similarly, calling ```i18n.t('key', {count: 100}); // output: 'items'`` (from the internationalization.md docs at https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/docs/translating/internationalization.md#frontend-translations) does not return the plural form, it simply returns "item" instead of "items".

Are we modifying the wrong variable (```page_params```) in the test? Do we need to initialize the i18next library in some way? Any help would be appreciated.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-18 02:21 UTC

You probably want to look at our configuration in `static/js/i18n.js`. In particular, the `interpolation` setting means you need to use `i18n.t("__look.deep__")`.

**Pranay Shah** · 2020-04-18 02:34 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> You probably want to look at our configuration in `static/js/i18n.js`. In particular, the `interpolation` setting means you need to use `i18n.t("__look.deep__")`.
`i18n.t("__look.deep__")` seems to be returning an empty string after adding ```"look": { "deep": "value of look deep"}``` to `page_params`

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-18 02:36 UTC

Variables aren’t interpolated from `page_params`, they’re interpolated from the model you pass as the second argument to `i18n.t`.

**Pranay Shah** · 2020-04-18 02:49 UTC

I see, I got it to work by passing a model called "look" as the second argument. Thanks!

I was under the impression that the translation data can hold nested keys as shown in https://www.i18next.com/translation-function/essentials We were trying to get that to work as a first step -- is there a way to make the example work? Or do we necessarily need to use interpolation and pass a model in the second argument?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-18 02:54 UTC

Oh I see, we’re talking about keys, not variable interpolation.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-18 02:56 UTC

That’s because we set `keySeparator: false`.

**Pranay Shah** · 2020-04-18 03:21 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg  Thanks, that seems to explain it! Still learning the ropes 😅

Our main goal was to get the pluralization working, but using the example with the keys given in the internationalization.md docs (https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/docs/translating/internationalization.md#frontend-translations) does not seem to work. For instance (in the context of the linked doc), ```i18n.t('key', {count: 0})'``` returns ```item``` when it's supposed to return ```items```.  The "_plural" does not seem to have an effect on whether the singular/plural version of the translation is chosen. I've added the example keys from the doc to ```page_params```.

Would you have any idea about this? Is it something in ```i18next.init()```, or maybe something with the locale code?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-18 03:44 UTC

Not sure, but perhaps the default `pluralSeparator` `'_'` interacts badly with our `interpolation` setting?

**Pranay Shah** · 2020-04-18 14:03 UTC

Seems like it was an issue with setting the language code ```lng``` in the ```i18next.init()``` function.

Originally, ```lng``` was being set to ```lang```. Setting ```lng: 'en'``` and making the appropriate change in the ```resources``` object within ```i18next.init()``` makes the plurals behave correctly. I guess the key parsing for plurals is specific to each language.

How can we dynamically update these options outside of ```i18next.init()```  so that the appropriate translation data is used instead of the ```lang``` for pluralization?

**Pranay Shah** · 2020-04-18 20:31 UTC

Edit: figured it out. ```i18n.language("en")``` can update the language being used by the i18next library. Will soon make a PR for the following issue: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/1286

Currently working on a test to simulate the usage of i18next's pluralization functionality.

@Steve Howell reverting back would be a straight forward one. Will probably just add a new class for the CSS relying on that property. Will make a PR for that. Should I also try making a PR for changing the code in copy and close according to `readonly="readonly"`. I mean, it should be that instead of `readonly=""`.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-19 14:39 UTC

I don't know this issue well enough to have an opinion.

**Vaibhav Raj Singh** · 2020-04-19 18:43 UTC

Ok, so there are two separate bugs here.

First, the bug I mentioned is basically that the copy and close icon is not clickable. You can test it here itself on CZO. Turns out it isn't because of the readonly property I mentioned above, but rather because of opacity = 0.5. Sending a PR for it.

Second, the one reported in #14640 is not related to what I reported since the OP was able to click the button. Seems like clipboard.js didn't work in his case. However, I was unable to reproduce this one.

## Viewport height on mobile browsers

*2020-04-23 to 2020-04-29 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Viewport.20height.20on.20mobile.20browsers/with/860880)*

**Jivitesh Jain** · 2020-04-23 09:38 UTC

#11324 talks about modals such as stream settings being shifted down on Chrome and Safari mobile. The reason is that WebKit and Blink browsers do not consider the address bar while calculating the `vh` unit, so `100vh` is around 60 pixels taller than the visible screen when the address bar is visible. This is however, not the case with geko browsers like firefox. For more details, look at the issue comments.
One way to fix this is to use `document.innerHeight` to get the true viewport height on all platforms, and export that as a CSS variable, as implemented by #14552.
We are however, looking for pure CSS based solutions. The problem here is to apply different styles for WebKit and blink based browsers on mobile, and different styles for geko based mobile browsers and all web browsers. Browser sniffing, unfortunately, can be unreliable. Looking for suggestions.

FYI @Tim Abbott

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-23 19:36 UTC

@Jivitesh Jain I unfortunately don't have better ideas for how to do.  Maybe someone else does?  

It seems like it would be valuable to figure out a nice solution here.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-23 19:57 UTC

What is wrong with `100%`?

**Jivitesh Jain** · 2020-04-23 20:35 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg 100% of what? I am not sure how `100%` behaves when applied to an outermost element, but as far as I know it would be 100% of the viewport height itself.
Moreover, I remember trying this but it didn't work :(
Will look into it once more though.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-23 21:06 UTC

Comparing https://andersk.scripts.mit.edu/test/zulip/100vh.html and https://andersk.scripts.mit.edu/test/zulip/100percent.html in my mobile Chrome, the latter works as expected and the former doesn’t.

**Jivitesh Jain** · 2020-04-29 08:03 UTC

Oh, thanks!
