## <hr> tags

*2020-04-24 to 2020-04-26 · 30 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/.3Chr.3E.20tags/with/862282)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 21:26 UTC

If we were to standardize on a format for '<hr>' tags, what would people prefer?
* <hr>
* <hr/>
* <hr />

I'll make a poll, but feel free to answer outside the poll.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 21:27 UTC

/poll tag style preference?
* <hr>
* <hr/>
* <hr />

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-24 21:29 UTC

Examples in the HTML spec use `<hr>`:
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/grouping-content.html#the-hr-element

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 21:31 UTC

[Prettier](https://prettier.io/) prefers `<hr />`.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 21:31 UTC

I unvoted, not because I don't have a preference here, but because I'm mostly concerned about consistency.   (I doubt anyone's gonna vote for '<hr/>', though.)

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-24 21:34 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> [Prettier](https://prettier.io/) prefers `<hr />`.

Hmm, is that the same Prettier that [wants to write](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/blob/master/tools/formatting.eslintrc.yaml) conditionals like
```js
  if (someLongConditionOfEightyColumnsAndMore()) return;
```
? :stuck_out_tongue:

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-24 21:35 UTC

("Doing what Prettier likes" can be a fine pragmatic choice -- I just don't give it much deference on the question of how it *should* be, given other choices I've seen it make)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 21:35 UTC

The HTML compatibility guidelines of XHTML 1.0 required `<hr />` over `<hr/>`; HTML5/XHTML5 and modern browsers don’t care, but that’s the reason the space made its way into most stylistic conventions.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 21:42 UTC

(BTW, Prettier is also happy with
```js
  if (someLongConditionOfEightyColumnsAndMore()) {
    return;
  }
```
which seems like a good set of preferences to me.)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 21:43 UTC

This isn't entirely scientific, but it shows how Zulip developers have voted with the feet over the year.  I'm not positive this reflects actual preferences in all cases, as some folks may have been pressured into a style they didn't like depending on whether we thought XHTML or HTML5 was better at the time.

~~~
(zulip-py3-venv) ~/zulip (showell-node)$ git grep '<br />' | wc -l
87
(zulip-py3-venv) ~/zulip (showell-node)$ git grep '<br>' | wc -l
84
(zulip-py3-venv) ~/zulip (showell-node)$ git grep '<hr />' | wc -l
18
(zulip-py3-venv) ~/zulip (showell-node)$ git grep '<hr>' | wc -l
9

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-24 21:45 UTC

Yeah, I've been writing `<br />` in large part because of memory from the XHML 1.0 era.

**Ray Kraesig** · 2020-04-24 21:48 UTC

I can't say I'm a fan. It has semantic implications that just don't hold in HTML5 – `<hr></hr>` is invalid, not just verbose.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 21:48 UTC

FWIW our markdown processor writes '<br>' in a few places.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 21:52 UTC

The (anti)symmetry holds: `<span />` is also invalid, not just terse.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 21:53 UTC

We are now preventing '<span />' tags fwiw.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 22:03 UTC

Other practical benefits of the `<hr />` convention:
* We can copy SVG code in and out of HTML without switching conventions.
* Tools like the template indentation checker can work entirely syntactically.
* We could decide to start serving XHTML5 for stronger validity guarantees. (Remember that time some translator accidentally wrapped our entire app in a `<strong>` tag?)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 22:06 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> Other practical benefits of the `<hr />` convention: * We can copy SVG code in and out of HTML without switching conventions. * Tools like the template indentation checker can work entirely syntactically. * We could decide to start serving XHTML5 for stronger validity guarantees. (Remember that time …
I mostly agree with points 1 and 3, but the template checker already does semantic checks, since it knows that div, span, etc. don't make sense as '<foo />' tags.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 22:07 UTC

The historical Markdown behavior is no longer a barrier for that, now that we parse all historical Markdown in `clean_user_content_links` (which I’d like to evolve into a real abstraction/security layer).

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 22:08 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> The historical Markdown behavior is no longer a barrier for that, now that we parse all historical Markdown in `clean_user_content_links` (which I’d like to evolve into a real abstraction/security layer).
Yeah, and it's a pretty weak data point to begin with.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 22:12 UTC

I’ve mentioned before that I’d prefer to delegate the semantic checks to a real validator, rather than making up our own rules. (I realize this will take work.)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 22:12 UTC

FWIW we also have lots of tags of the style `<img src='...' />` and `<input ... />`.  We also have SVG tags, but I mostly consider them a non-issue, as I think we'd want to accept both styles for those, since they're often copy/pasted (and it's super easy for the template checker to ignore them).

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 22:14 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> I’ve mentioned before that I’d prefer to delegate the semantic checks to a real validator, rather than making up our own rules. (I realize this will take work.)

I don't think there's anything blocking us having both things:
* use Zulip's checker on the source templates (and let us be even pickier than the "real" validators about stuff where we're finicky)
* use a third-party validator on the output (probably in backend tests at first?)

Obviously, to truly validate a template, you want to exercise all its code paths, which is not impossible, but not trivial either.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 22:15 UTC

Yeah. We have coverage collection for templates now, which helps.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 22:17 UTC

It's probably not a ton of work to at least extract all the HTML that gets generated in the backend tests, correct?  It's theoretically like a 20-line change once you find the right place to hook in.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-24 22:20 UTC

Even a one-time hack here would be interesting.  If we're producing any HTML that's invalid, I would be curious what we're doing wrong.  And it would be probably easy to get immediate fixes in either the template checker or our regex linters.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-24 22:24 UTC

@Greg Price The resizing code was written in 2013, when all of our customers were pretty small organizations.  Let's say you have 30 streams, 10 users, and 28 lines on the screen.  The reasonable values would be:
- 14/14: just naively pick 50%, but then you don't show 16 streams and have awkward whitespace
- 18/10: show all your users, keeping 12 streams below the fold (and then jitter when somebody joins)
- 21/7: go proportional, showing most of streams, most of users

It's not the most obvious compromise.  The forces have changed a lot since then--we do the have the extreme long tails now with instances like czo, for example.

So, We have this code block in `topic.py`:
```python3
def update_messages_for_topic_edit(message: Message,
                                   propagate_mode: str,
                                   orig_topic_name: str,
                                   topic_name: Optional[str],
                                   new_stream: Optional[Stream]) -> List[Message]:
    propagate_query = Q(recipient = message.recipient, subject = orig_topic_name)
    if propagate_mode == 'change_all':
        propagate_query = propagate_query & ~Q(id = message.id)
    if propagate_mode == 'change_later':
        propagate_query = propagate_query & Q(id__gt = message.id)
    messages = Message.objects.filter(propagate_query).select_related()

    update_fields = {}

    # Evaluate the query before running the update
    messages_list = list(messages)

    # The cached ORM objects are not changed by the upcoming
    # messages.update(), and the remote cache update (done by the
    # caller) requires the new value, so we manually update the
    # objects in addition to sending a bulk query to the database.
    if new_stream is not None:
        update_fields["recipient"] = new_stream.recipient
        for m in messages_list:
            m.recipient = new_stream.recipient
    if topic_name is not None:
        update_fields["subject"] = topic_name
        for m in messages_list:
            m.set_topic_name(topic_name)
    messages.update(**update_fields)

    return messages_list
```

def update_to_dict_cache(changed_messages: List[Message]) -> List[int]:
    """Updates the message as stored in the to_dict cache (for serving
    messages)."""
    items_for_remote_cache = {}
    message_ids = []
    for changed_message in changed_messages:
        message_ids.append(changed_message.id)
        key = to_dict_cache_key_id(changed_message.id)
        value = MessageDict.to_dict_uncached(changed_message)
        items_for_remote_cache[key] = (value,)
    cache_set_many(items_for_remote_cache)
    return message_ids
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-16 22:55 UTC

I think the backstory here is that at some very early point in Zulip's development, Tornado did effectively a `get_message_by_id()` query to memcached to get data on a message before sending an `update_message` event, and we wrote that code to update the cache for that situation, where it was important that the cache actually have a fresh/current copy of the Message body so that Tornado didn't have to go to the database for that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-16 22:55 UTC

Long ago, we removed those database queries from Tornado, which were always a bad idea; now, it just passes through the data constructed on the server in the event to the client.  (The client already knows about the `Reactions`s on the message, for example).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-16 22:57 UTC

So I think there's limited benefit to doing anything with these messages other than deleting the stale entries from the caches (if present); the `GET /messages` logic for fetching them already has a properly optimized process for hydrating the data that only uses bulk queries.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-16 22:58 UTC

That said, there is some benefit; anyone who was looking at the topic that is about to be moved for a `change_all` or `change_later` propagation mode is going to have their client automatically renarrow to the new location.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-16 22:59 UTC

And so if there are a ton of those people, there may be a bit of a "thundering herd" fetch of that set of messages that might end up being inefficient (because all of the processes fetch from the database and then all store into the cache).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-16 22:59 UTC

I don't think there being a lot of such people is actually a very common outcome, so it's unlikely to have much impact on total load given that topic editing is also a relatively rare event.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-16 23:02 UTC

So maybe it's worth the bit of work to let us fill the cache.  I think all we need to do is use the bulk `get_raw_db_rows` code path like `messages_for_ids` does rather than doing it a loop.

~~~ py
 292     @staticmethod
 293     def get_raw_db_rows(needed_ids: List[int]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
 294         # This is a special purpose function optimized for
 295         # callers like get_messages_backend().
 296         fields = [
 297             'id',
 298             DB_TOPIC_NAME,
 299             'date_sent',
 300             'last_edit_time',
 301             'edit_history',
 302             'content',
 303             'rendered_content',
 304             'rendered_content_version',

 307             'recipient__type_id',
 308             'sender_id',
 309             'sending_client__name',
 310             'sender__realm_id',
 311         ]
 312         messages = Message.objects.filter(id__in=needed_ids).values(*fields)
 313
 314         submessages = SubMessage.get_raw_db_rows(needed_ids)
 315         sew_messages_and_submessages(messages, submessages)
 316
 317         reactions = Reaction.get_raw_db_rows(needed_ids)
 318         return sew_messages_and_reactions(messages, reactions)
~~~

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-07 06:07 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-20 22:06 UTC

Now that Zulip 4.0 is out, one of my top priorities is integrating the [Web public streams feature](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/18532).  I'm starting a thread here to discuss some of the decisions about how it should work in terms of the webapp implementation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-20 22:06 UTC

(@Aman Agrawal (amanagr) FYI)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-20 22:09 UTC

One of the major questions is what to do with UI elements, like the widget to star a message, that are not available to "web public visitors" aka someone browsing an organization without having logged in.  (Opinions on terminology appreciated; the main thing we've decided is not to use the term "guest" for this, since that already is a role in Zulip.  I can also see "anonymous users" being a sensible choice; that's what Django uses to refer to the concept of a visitor who isn't logged in).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-20 22:11 UTC

There's a few ways we can achieve the goal of having these elements not be there (since they will be confusing/distracting):
* Add `if` statements to all the templates to make them not appear in the DOM.
* Add a CSS class, e.g. `web-public-visitor-hidden`, to those elements, and have that class defined as `display: none !important;` for web-public visitors. 
* Leave them there but have trying to use them pop up a modal or something asking you to login.  (Which I'm sure we'll have for some actions).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-20 22:13 UTC

My comments on the PR argue for the CSS class approach, because it involves minimal churn to the templates, feels readable, and means we don't have to worry about auditing live-update JavaScript for those elements that might have `expectOne()` assertions to check that they're actually changing what they're supposed to.  (Many of these elements will be static for web-public visitors, but it's nice to not have to think about whether this feature will result in an element not existing when writing new JavaScript code to render/update an element)

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-05-21 00:22 UTC

I recall @Steve Howell (showell) was against the css technique and wanted to not have the elements rendered.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-05-21 00:24 UTC

Adding a css class has the same problem with events, we need add the class every time element renders. So, we have to have the class be part of the template. So, doing it in JS won't make sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-21 00:25 UTC

Well, what I'm imagining is just having the CSS class statically in the template, with it not doing anything if you're not a web-public-visitor.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-05-21 00:26 UTC

Okay, that makes sense.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-05-21 00:26 UTC

Yup, that would be lot simpler.

**Greg Price** · 2022-01-13 22:32 UTC

(replying to Alex Dehnert)
> Relatedly, if the markdown format changes over time, does an old post get rendered with the old markdown parser or the new one? (I'm not sure what Zulip does right now.)

Generally the answer to this right now is that old messages keep the rendered HTML that they got when they were first sent.

The basic reason for that is that as long as we're making any changes to the Markdown syntax at all, it's very hard to be sure that they don't break old messages. And nobody's "maintaining" the old messages -- nobody's going to go back and fix their syntax up to work with the changes -- so any breakage would just mean corrupting the old data so that reading old conversations becomes hard.

**Greg Price** · 2022-01-13 22:38 UTC

The one time that a client really needs to parse the Markdown of a message is immediately after sending, for the "local echo" that we show in the message list before we hear back from the server with its authoritative rendered version.

In order to support that, we need the Markdown syntax to be implemented in JS (for web and mobile) as well as in Python (for the server). I'm not sure what zulip-terminal currently does, but because it's in Python it could use the same implementation as the server.

I think it's OK if random things that aren't a full-blown, high-effort Zulip client don't have local echo. So we need two implementations (as we have now for our current syntax) but I think it's fine for our design to mean (as it does now) that having another implementation would be quite a bit of work.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-13 23:17 UTC

I can imagine a design where we'd store details like a reference to any data that was required to render a given message alongside the message (E.g. the user IDs that were looked up in mentions) such that it would be possible to re-render a message from its stored raw content when we update the markdown processor. But without some mechanism like that, you have the problem that data-dependant features like mentions of streams could produce a different result if rendered today (E.g. after an organization renamed all their streams) than it did when originally typed, which makes it difficult to design a "correct" rerendering algorithm.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-13 23:18 UTC

So while in the early days of Zulip circa 2013, we did routinely rerender all historical messages from their raw markdown input because we'd changed our mind about how the markdown processor works, that's no longer something we can safely do.

|`***~~italic bold strikethrough 1~~***`|***~~italic bold strikethrough 1~~***|
|`~~***italic bold strikethrough 2***~~`|~~***italic bold strikethrough 2***~~|

- To better clarify

## microinteractions / animations

*2020-05-12 to 2020-05-12 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/microinteractions.20.2F.20animations/with/874633)*

**Yash RE** · 2020-05-12 12:32 UTC

**background info:** I've been speaking to designers and product leads, I've them about microinteractions because it's an idea that fascinates me a lot. Definitions vary but essentially you could simplify it down to "animations" + context. The theory of user delight has 5 stages in this order: availability > performance > functional > useful > delightful. Animation features are what would fall into "delight". (Where as stuff like positioning / layout / color would not).

**problem:** I feel like we have very very little work in this category, which is something we could improve upon. There's about 35 different places (I got 21 off the top of my head) where we could have animation related features.

Also, these would all be things we'd tag as "good first issue".... so, how do you think we should handle this kind of work?
* How should we track these areas?

Should I name each of the areas I know about, and create a separate issue for them, and then create new issues as the come?
* How should a contributor submit ideas?

Do we need to prototype every interaction? Do we need to test deploy every interaction?
* Are there any best practices in terms of design?

Can we find and share research related to them?
* Are there any best practices in terms of code/implementation?

eg https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/14561#discussion_r407572012
* How important is work in this direction? Will it get attention?

**Thomas Fini Hansen** · 2020-05-12 12:56 UTC

(replying to Yash RE ✨)
> * How important is work in this direction? Will it get attention?

Much, I'll say. In our  ongoing "Slack or Zulip" discussion the topic of general "niceness" keeps cropping up. It's mostly aimed at the visual design in general, but I think that well implemented animations really takes things from "nice" to "awesome".

**Wyatt Hoodes** · 2020-05-12 17:52 UTC

I can resonate with this.  Zulip has such amazing features and functionality, it just needs some attention to the pizazz while being an octopus keeping track of dozens of conversations with ease.

**Yash RE** · 2020-05-12 18:06 UTC

*I've talked to them about...

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 19:04 UTC

I think there's a few generic considerations on animations:
* We should make sure they don't get in the way of usability -- e.g. adding a significant delay to something users do a lot and want to be fast.
* It's a lot less design work to reuse a handful of patterns that we like repeatedly than to come up with fresh animations for each thing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 19:05 UTC

I'd generally focus on working on animations in the most visible places where we think they'd be an improvement.

## adding new elements to DOM

*2020-05-12 to 2020-05-12 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/adding.20new.20elements.20to.20DOM/with/875041)*

**Clara Dantas** · 2020-05-12 18:48 UTC

Is there a way or convention to add classes on newly added elements on the DOM, that prevents it from breaking the rest of the code? I saw two bugs, not that much time apart from each other, caused because a new div was added and someone used a class that was already being used by some other sibling of that element, so some behaviors are broken because the selector finds the wrong element. Maybe it would be nice to have some more frontend tests that assure selectors are getting the correct nodes or something? Or maybe a protocol of some sort that people can follow and would minimize those types of errors?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 19:00 UTC

It's a good question.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 19:02 UTC

In general, the strategy we try to take is being thoughtful about the selectors and CSS class names we use to make sure they have the right level of specificity (E.g. if it's a reusable widget, use a class, not an ID, and attach event handlers specific to this instance of that widget using a selector that includes its container)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 19:02 UTC

I think it's hard to do automated tests for this sort of thing; but I think we could work harder on having clear conventions to discourage this sort of issue.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-12 22:09 UTC

I tried to build tooling for this kinda problem a few years ago, but it can be tricky to distinguish accidental collisions from intentional reuse, and the tooling had too many false alarms to be worth maintaining.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-05-12 22:11 UTC

I think this is one of several problems that would be solved if we decided to become religious about using [CSS modules](https://github.com/css-modules/postcss-modules).

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-12 22:11 UTC

I would have tried harder to maintain the tooling if it were a really pervasive problem, but usually good judgment was enough to prevent lots of issues, and the bugs were often pretty shallow and easy to discover and fix.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-12 22:15 UTC

Also just to be clear I am not saying my aborted experiment means it’s a lost cause—I totally agree with the problem statement and support rethinking here.

## prefetch old topic names

*2020-05-13 to 2020-05-13 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/prefetch.20old.20topic.20names/with/876793)*

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-05-13 18:55 UTC

Is there any reason we don't prefetch the all the topic names in a stream, or at least last 100 or so? Being limited to just the messages currently loaded cripples the stream>topic typeahead. I've found myself quickly using the search function to load some message from the topic I want to link to and then use the typeahead to select the topic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-13 18:57 UTC

Yes, because it's expensive to compute that data set :).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-13 18:57 UTC

It is definitely possible to fix it being expensive; we just haven't done so.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-13 18:58 UTC

I still would love a topic table.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-13 19:08 UTC

It's important to understand that a topic table wouldn't solve this problem in the case of private streams, because the current user might not have access to all of the historical topics in that stream.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-13 19:09 UTC

But there's definitely an opportunity for at the very least a memcached cache for "what are all the topics within stream ID x" that gets updated whenever one sends a message to the stream, and gets used extensively for streams with `history_public_to_subscribers` (which get the vast majority of message receipts) to make things fast.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-13 19:21 UTC

A UserTopic table could work, too.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-13 19:27 UTC

Or add topic_id to user_message.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-13 19:48 UTC

If we had proper topic ids we could mostly hydrate them from memcached on the server and cache misses would be a dead simple dB hop.  Our message caches could be smaller.  Our clients could work with topic ids.  I know there are trade offs, but I think we underestimate the upside of topic ids. It’s database design 101, and it makes a certain class of problems more straightforward to solve.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-13 19:49 UTC

Certain indexes would also use less memory and be faster.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-13 19:51 UTC

Features like pinning topics or adding detailed topic descriptions would be easier.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-13 22:07 UTC

The `topic.lower()` string works as an ID; I don't think a numerical ID makes any difference in the ability to do that.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-13 22:15 UTC

It seems to cause us friction for creating new features, and I don’t think there’s any controversy that numerical ids are at least more compact than topic names.  I understand the join counter argument, of course.

## User search

*2020-05-17 to 2020-06-30 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/User.20search/with/880340)*

**Plankter** · 2020-05-17 21:46 UTC

Reporting a problem  with the user search in the browser version:

When you want to send a message to a user, you might first do a search to find the user in the list. The search is likely to use a part of the user's name or email, e.g. "Jeff", "Smith", "gmail".

There are two places where the search might be done:

1) In the search box located above the list of users, on the right hand side of the screen (search 1),
2) In the "To" box above the compose field (search 2).

It seems that a search done in each of these boxes might give different results. For example, if I search for "zulip", search 1 only returns users whose email begins with "zulip". Search 2 only returns users with "zulip.org" emails.

I would expect to get the full list for both searches. 

-----------

Another thing: we have recently installed zulip on a local server, for testing purposes. I noticed that on this installation, search 1 only returns users whose names begin with the given search snippet. For example, "Smith" will not return "John Smith", but "John" will. Is there a way an admin can control the search filters? We have full access to the server.

Thanks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-18 04:41 UTC

It's known that we use different algorithms in those two places (I'd expect the compose one to be better in general), but the domain issue you mention is interesting/new.  Anyone have time to look into it tomorrow?

**Plankter** · 2020-05-18 08:03 UTC

Apart from the domain issue, I think a partial search should be implemented on the names (and ideally on emails or other relevant fields identifying the users). For example, if you are looking for a "McDonlald", but are not sure how the Mc/Mac bit  is spelt, you should be able to search for "donald".

Right now, a search for "donal" will return  "Ben Donaldson" and "Donald Langhorne", but not "Jared McDonald". In my view, all three should be in the list. Otherwise you have to keep changing your search snippet.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-18 16:49 UTC

@Plankter If you look for `exports.build_termlet_matcher` in `static/js/people.js`, you can probably change `startsWith` to `includes` to get more aggressive matching for the termlets that you use in the right sidebar search.

**Plankter** · 2020-05-19 15:21 UTC

Thanks!

**Plankter** · 2020-06-19 20:35 UTC

Revisiting this issue

Doing the same  search in the app and in the browser version gives different results. Whereas the browser version uses 'startsWith', the app uses 'includes', i.e. a search on a partial text, which to me seems the correct approach. The result is that the user gets different results in different places and on different devices.

The  'startsWith' approach strikes me as a design mistake. If you use someone's surname in the search on the right, you will not find them and might think that they do not have an account. Later they might show up in another search and you will conclude that the software  is buggy.

To recap, in my view, this is an important issue from the UX perspective. It should work as expected by the user and it should be consistent. I expect it would be easy to modify, though I'm embarrassed to say I couldn't do it. 

[In retrospect, I realise I should have put this in the feedback stream.]

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-19 21:00 UTC

@Plankter This is a fine place to register this complaint.  It's a tricky issue.  If you use `includes`, you can introduce too much noise.  If you use `startswith`, you can prematurely reject suitable names.

**Gittenburg** · 2020-06-20 06:38 UTC

For me searching for surnames works in the User search on the right.

**Plankter** · 2020-06-30 17:35 UTC

It works for me too. However, not quite as it should: if you try to search for "**donal**" in the list of users of chat.zulip.org, you will get different results for the browser, desktop and app versions. On the app, you'll get three names; on the Linux desktop and browser versions, you'll get two. Since they refer to the same list, they should return the same results. The same search on the compose box also gives three names. 

The argument that `includes` introduces too much noise does not convince me, because the list returned by the search quickly shrinks as you add letters to your search text.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-30 17:44 UTC

I would be happiest if we used our algorithm for mentions, which has definitely gotten the most attention of these, for the right sidebar search.

(My view is that you want to look at these various algorithms, but prioritize more exact matches over less exact ones, which is what the mention algorithm does)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-15 19:21 UTC

@Alya Abbott @Mateusz Mandera @Wesley Aptekar-Cassels Let’s discuss possible improvements to the poll widget, including a separate “election” widget.

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-06-15 19:30 UTC

A proposal: polls should have "settings", which the original sender can change. These settings could include:

* Allow anyone to add options
* Hide usernames
* Number of votes allowed per person
* End date?

Settings could be easily implemented as an additional submessage type.

The UI for this could be a small gear in the corner of a poll, which opens a popup for settings.

I think it's cleaner (from a user understanding perspective) to have all of the poll-like-things be invoked with the same /poll command, and to be fundamentally the same category of thing. While I'm not particularly happy with the technical implementation of polls, I'm not sufficiently unhappy that I think we should try to build a new thing instead.

Implementing anonymous polls on top of the current architecture will be hard, but not impossible — it'll just require the server not sending a user ID (or sending some sentinel  user ID) if it detects that the poll is in anonymous mode.

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-06-15 19:31 UTC

Notably, we can't have truly "anonymous" polls so long as we have presence indicators, since people can see who's online when a poll option changes, but I don't think that's something we should try to defend against, personally.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-29 01:01 UTC

The other thing to note is that whenever we call `inplace_rerender`, which I think can happen for pretty common things like reading a message, which tweaks your topic's unread count, we are currently using this strategy:

* find its "new" position
* insert the row after its "new" previous neighbor

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-29 18:59 UTC

One quick question for @Tim Abbott: When we put `fetch_status` on MLD, we still need to mostly retrieve it (for now) from the ML that holds the MLD.  Do we want to make the API be something like `message_list.get_fetch_status()`?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-29 19:02 UTC

@Ryan Rehman So there is usually a 1:1 correspondence between `MessageList` and `MessageListData`, where an instance of the former contains an instance of the latter.  There are times where we actually create the `MessageListData` object first, and work with it directly for a couple small thing, and then we wrap it with a full `MessageList` when we're actually ready to display it.  Here's some context for that:

~~~ js
  8 exports.MessageList = function (opts) {
  9     if (opts.data) {
 10         this.muting_enabled = opts.data.muting_enabled;
 11         this.data = opts.data;
 12     } else {
 13         const filter = opts.filter;
 14
 15         this.muting_enabled = opts.muting_enabled;
 16         this.data = new MessageListData({
 17             muting_enabled: this.muting_enabled,
 18             filter: filter,
 19         });
 20     }

~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-29 19:03 UTC

As you can see from the above code, you can either pass in an existing MLD instance as `opts.data`, or else ML will just create a new one for you.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-29 19:05 UTC

And here's some example code from `narrow.js` where we first make the data object, do some stuff to it (purely data-related, of course), and then finally create the `MessageList` object that wraps the data object:

~~~ js
208     let msg_data =  new MessageListData({
 209         filter: narrow_state.filter(),
 210         muting_enabled: muting_enabled,
 211     });
 212
 213     // Populate the message list if we can apply our filter locally (i.e.
 214     // with no backend help) and we have the message we want to select.
 215     // Also update id_info accordingly.
 216     // original back.
 217     exports.maybe_add_local_messages({
 218         id_info: id_info,
 219         msg_data: msg_data,
 220     });
 221
 222     if (!id_info.local_select_id) {
 223         // If we're not actually read to select an ID, we need to
 224         // trash the `MessageListData` object that we just constructed
 225         // and pass an empty one to MessageList, because the block of
 226         // messages in the MessageListData built inside
 227         // maybe_add_local_messages is likely not be contiguous with
 228         // the block we're about to request from the server instead.
 229         msg_data = new MessageListData({
 230             filter: narrow_state.filter(),
 231             muting_enabled: muting_enabled,
 232         });
 233     }
 234
 235     const msg_list = new message_list.MessageList({
 236         data: msg_data,
 237         table_name: 'zfilt',
 238         collapse_messages: !narrow_state.filter().is_search(),
 239     });

~~~

**Ryan Rehman** · 2020-05-29 20:40 UTC

I Understood. Every `MessageList` instance has a `MessageListData` instance.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-29 21:46 UTC

Yep!  And our plan in #15131 is to only keep MessageListData objects, not MessageList objects, as the persistent structures.

## displaying time

*2020-06-02 to 2020-06-02 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/displaying.20time/with/892626)*

**Cyphase** · 2020-06-02 10:00 UTC

**TL;DR:** Having investigated and written the below, I'm pretty sure the second option with `stringify_time` is the best one; but I'm happy to hear different if I'm wrong.

I'm working on #15171 (edit history timestamps don't respect the time format setting), which is pretty simple on its surface, except I'm still familiarizing myself with the code and code style. [Here's the code in question](https://github.com/cyphase/zulip/blob/master/static/js/message_edit.js#L780-L785) in `fetch_and_render_message_history`, which is currently using `moment` for formatting:

```javascript
                // Format timestamp nicely for display
                const timestamp = timerender.get_full_time(msg.timestamp);
                const item = {
                    timestamp: moment(timestamp).format("h:mm A"),
                    display_date: moment(timestamp).format("MMMM D, YYYY"),
                };
```

I've looked at this and other time display code, and I'm not certain how I should go about fixing this; there's more than one way to do it.

* The current code uses `timerender.get_full_time` to get an ISO 8601-formatted string which it passes to `moment` for formatting. The problem is that it doesn't respect the time format setting in `page_params.twenty_four_hour_time`. The most immediate solution is probably something like this (or with an if/else if ternarys are discouraged):
```javascript
                // Format timestamp nicely for display
                const timestamp = timerender.get_full_time(msg.timestamp);
                const time_display_format = page_params.twenty_four_hour_time ? "HH:mm" : "h:mm A";
                const item = {
                    timestamp: moment(timestamp).format(time_display_format),
                    display_date: moment(timestamp).format("MMMM D, YYYY"),
                };
```
* There's `timerender.stringify_time`, which takes an `XDate` (at least), and which is used [here](https://github.com/cyphase/zulip/blob/master/static/js/message_list_view.js#L107) and [here](https://github.com/cyphase/zulip/blob/master/static/js/message_list_view.js#L175) in `message_list_view.js` and [here](https://github.com/cyphase/zulip/blob/master/static/js/drafts.js#L215) in `drafts.js`. Using that would look something like this, if `item.display_date` was changed to also use the `XDate`:
```javascript
                // Format timestamp nicely for display
                const time = new XDate(msg.timestamp * 1000);
                const item = {
                    timestamp: timerender.stringify_time(time),
                    display_date: time.toString("MMMM d, yyyy"),
                };
```
* The user info popover and user profile modal use `people.get_user_time(user.user_id)`, which calls `people.get_user_time_preferences(user_id)`, which calls `settings_data.get_time_preferences(user_timezone)`, which essentially returns `page_params.twenty_four_hour_time ? {timezone: user_timezone, format: "H:mm"} : {timezone: user_timezone, format: "h:mm A"}` (pardon the one-lining). One could write a version of `fetch_and_render_message_history` that used `settings_data.get_time_preferences`, but I don't think that would be correct.

Having investigated and written all that, I'm pretty sure the second option with `stringify_time` is the best one. That also jibes with what (replying to Tim Abbott)

> This likely just requires using some of the logic in `timerender.js` when rendering the edit history UI.

But I've come this far, so I might as well send this and make sure. :slight_smile:

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-06-02 10:14 UTC

I like the second option here but prefer we move everything to moment.js eventually.

I think we should invest in cleaning up this area so there's one authoritative way of doing this.

**Cyphase** · 2020-06-02 10:25 UTC

I'll proceed with the second option then in order to fix the immediate bug. Anyway, I don't think moving this away from `moment` for now will have any more than a nominal effect on a refactoring effort later.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-06-02 11:34 UTC

Yeah, I'm in favor of the second approach here. Any further refactoring can just replace moment in one function, anyway. :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-02 19:36 UTC

Yeah, that sounds right to me.

## unknow function params

*2020-06-17 to 2020-06-17 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/unknow.20function.20params/with/906824)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-06-17 06:50 UTC

I often find that in our js code there are functions which just take in `opts` or `params` and then that function passes it to another function or uses some keys in opts and passes the rest to another function. 
Like this:
```js
    append: function MessageList_append(messages, opts) {
        const viewable_messages = this.data.append(messages);
        this.append_to_view(viewable_messages, opts);
    },
```
It is super unclear what values does `opts` contain by giving a look to this function and could scare away a new contributor. I would very much like to work on improving these parts of our code (maybe after a couple of weeks). What would be the best of doing this?
I see these docs sometimes in other repo codes:
```js
/**
 * @param {very_long_type} name           Description.
 * @param {type}           very_long_name Description.
 */
```
Which look useful in these cases. Is there a reason we don't use them or is it because they are hard to maintain?

One could always console.log these args but they take time and are not reliable.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-06-17 06:56 UTC

Tests can also be helpful in figuring out args. Anyway I would like to know if this is worth doing?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-17 06:56 UTC

That sort of documentation is certainly helpful, but I'd prefer to use TypeScript for this sort of thing long term.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-06-17 07:05 UTC

Yes, that makes sense.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-06-17 07:34 UTC

@Steve Howell and I discussed this recently, in the context of the `list_render` widget. We might have a lot of options, of which certain combinations are preferred. We somewhat like this approach of self-documenting code:

```js
// ----------------------------------------------------
// This function describes (programatically) how to use
// the list_render widget.
// ----------------------------------------------------

exports.validate_opts = (opts) => {
    if (opts.html_selector && typeof opts.html_selector !== 'function') {
        // We have an html_selector, but it is not a function.
        // This is a programming error.
        blueslip.error('html_selector should be a function.');
        return false;
    }
    return true;
};
```

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-06-17 07:35 UTC

This simple example equates to `Optional[Callable]` in python, but we think such an approach makes sense for more complex cases where we can assert combinations of different optional parameters.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-17 11:02 UTC

I think the example that @Aman Agrawal posted, which I will re-post for convenience, is particularly hard to read and reason about, since `append` passes on the `opts` to `append_to_view`, so you really can't deduce what the contract is for `append` unless you go read the other function.

~~~ js
    append: function MessageList_append(messages, opts) {
        const viewable_messages = this.data.append(messages);
        this.append_to_view(viewable_messages, opts);
    },

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-17 11:09 UTC

This pattern has always bothered me, too.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-17 19:56 UTC

In that particular case, it just looks at this one value in `opts`:
```
    append_to_view: function (messages, opts) {                                            
        opts = { messages_are_new: false, ...opts };                                       
                                                                                           
        this.num_appends += 1;                                                             
        const render_info = this.view.append(messages, opts.messages_are_new);             
        return render_info;                                                                
    },                                                                                     
```

and my guess is that we wrote it this way mainly so that it'd be visible in the calling code that we're passing `messages_are_new=true`, not just `true`.  If this were Python, I'd make that function take a single keyword-argument and it'd be nice.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-17 19:57 UTC

I wonder if there's a good way to clean this sort of thing up in the JS codebase without blocking on moving the file to typescript.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-17 20:06 UTC

This is totally possible to do in current JS.  Just never pass your parent's opaque version of opts to the child.  Instead, always explicitly copy the fields the child needs.  And you can enforce this discipline starting from the child, then fix the parent, fix the grandparent, etc.  It's a bit more verbose, but the verbosity makes it so that anybody reading a function can understand it locally.

Another discipline is that you have a non-trivial function (maybe 10 lines or more), then explictly do this at the top:

~~~
const foo = opts.foo;
const bar = opts.bar
const baz = opts.bz
~~~

This will helps us when it comes time to move to TS, as well.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-17 20:07 UTC

Finally, for things like `list_render`, as @Rohitt Vashishtha pointed out, you can explicitly validate `opts` at the top, including more semantic checks like preventing mutually exclusive options.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-17 20:07 UTC

Yeah, I think that sort of refactoring would be helpful today.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-06-17 20:16 UTC

I generally like things like `const { foo, bar, baz } = opts;`, but outside of validation, its helpful when reading the code to see what variable was passed to the function and what was calculated by the function. `opts.*` is a reliable indicator for that.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-17 20:21 UTC

I think this might be something where we use different idioms depending on whether the functions is small, medium, or large.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-06-17 20:26 UTC

`function (messages, {foo, bar, baz}) { … }` is also a thing.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-06-24 20:11 UTC

But, that means we want to have things like:

```
--left-sidebar-background: hsla(something);
--settings-background: hsla(something);
```

For all our initial themes, they'd be the same (suppose). In that case, we're redefining `something` twice, and I just want to make that centralized.

By writing:

```
$something: hsla(something);
--left-sidebar-background: $something;
--settings-background: $something;
```

we achieve two things at once:

1. We do not repeat ourselves. We have a LOT of UI elements if we want to break our CSS vars by UI element.
2. We have a link between them. Anyone reading the code knows that it is an explicit decision to make the left sidebar and settings have the same background.

*2020-06-26 to 2020-06-26 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/unknown.20user.20IDs.20in.20update.20events/with/916686)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-26 18:02 UTC

We've been getting a somewhat puzzling exception in the `server_events` code path when a new user joins certain large organizations:

```
Error: Unknown user_id in get_by_user_id: 25
 at Object.blueslip_error [as error] /static/js/blueslip.js:245
 at Object../static/js/people.js.exports.get_by_user_id /static/js/people.js:50
 at Object.update [as update_person] /static/js/user_events.js:7
 at Object.dispatch_normal_event /static/js/server_events_dispatch.js:260
 at dispatch_event /static/js/server_events.js:77
 at get_events_success /static/js/server_events.js:83
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-26 18:03 UTC

I finally figured out the reproducer for this: It's what happens when you copy existing settings when creating your account from a user that had uploaded an avatar; we end up sending a "changed avatar" event before sending the "new user" event.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-26 18:03 UTC

The fix is to just suppress the "changed avatar" event when we call the internal function to setup the copied avatar.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-26 18:21 UTC

Fixed in a5be2a30fa464fce5e568636da140f8e90b5d7b1.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-26 18:21 UTC

This bug accounted for >50% of all JavaScript exceptions seen in zulipchat.com, so I'm pretty happy to have tracked it down.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-26 18:31 UTC

:tada:

```js
function update_table_stream_color(table, stream_name, color) {
    // This is ugly, but temporary, as the new design will make it
    // so that we only have color in the headers.
    const style = color;
    const color_class = exports.get_color_class(color);

    const stream_labels = $("#floating_recipient_bar").add(table).find(".stream_label");

    for (const label of stream_labels) {
        const $label = $(label);
        if ($.trim($label.text()) === stream_name) {
            const messages = $label.closest(".recipient_row").children(".message_row");
            messages.children(".messagebox").css("box-shadow", "inset 2px 0px 0px 0px " + style + ", -1px 0px 0px 0px " + style);
            $label.css({background: style,
                        "border-left-color": style});
            $label.removeClass(exports.color_classes);
            $label.addClass(color_class);
        }
    }
}
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-29 19:23 UTC

It seems like it might be a modest performance optimization for low-network users.  But of course it's likely more or less immaterial in comparison to `message_inline_image` objects, which tend to be much larger images.  I guess what I'm not sure about is whether this optimization is actually helpful.  It's kinda nice in Zulip that as you scroll around you don't really see grey squares for avatars, and I'd like to be sure whether we're improving the situation with this sort of change (or whether the browser was already doing the right thing).  

@Priyank Patel FYI.

Yeah, this is mostly helpful for cases where avatar images are not cached and one is one a bad network. Although that is more of a case for large organizations such as this one.

I guess doing this for the user sent images (as you mention) might be more of an improvement. But I am not sure of the UX; I don't think just doing the grey images or leaving it blank would be nice but I haven't tried it out so I am really not sure.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-07-09 07:35 UTC

We have our own version of `marked.js` library which have modified significantly for our own use, but its  regex are broken for `em`, `strong` etc.; they don't get noticed since we instantly replace the markdown with the one fetched from the backend, which also lowers our appeal for improving them for the brief period when message is in local echo state. **Steve Howell** · 2020-07-09 11:08 UTC

@Aman Agrawal I think we're pretty committed at this point to always showing (client-rendered) markdown during local echo.

We should just fix the regexes for `em` and `strong`.  We have mechanisms in our test system where we can validate them using the same fixtures as the server's parser, so once we fix the problem, we can make regressions less likely.

## multiple composite layers in chrome mobile

**Hashir Sarwar** · 2020-07-16 03:09 UTC

Hi everyone,  I am working on optimizing Zulip on chrome mobile web. I recently found out that Chrome is creating many extra composite layers when being run on a mobile device. The easiest way to reproduce this to enable "Layer Borders" from Chrome Dev Tools and toggle the device toolbar.

Does anyone have an idea why Chrome behaves this way (particularly for Zulip) when we run it on a mobile device and what will be the right fix here?

Right now the closest solution I could determine was to add `will-change: transform` to the `.app` element (as suggested by an article [here](https://developers.google.com/web/updates/2016/09/re-rastering-composite)).

## prettier

*2020-07-17 to 2024-04-20 · 23 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/prettier/with/943010)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-07-17 22:40 UTC

We’ve just reformatted all our JavaScript files with [Prettier](https://prettier.io/) in #15797. If you have open PRs with many frontend changes, it may be hard to rebase them across this reformatting in the normal way, but it’s easy with these commands:

```sh
git fetch https://github.com/andersk/zulip.git prettier-prep
git rebase FETCH_HEAD
FILTER_BRANCH_SQUELCH_WARNING=1 \
    git filter-branch --force \
    --tree-filter '/srv/zulip/node_modules/.bin/prettier --write "**/*.{js,ts}" tools/check-openapi' \
    --commit-filter 'git_commit_non_empty_tree "$@"' \
    "FETCH_HEAD^..HEAD"
```

## compose box accessibility

*2020-07-24 to 2020-08-28 · 62 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/compose.20box.20accessibility/with/953872)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 22:37 UTC

I'd like to discuss the issues around compose box accessibility raised in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/15914

Our current situation is definitely problematic, in that it's not possible to `tab` to any compose box elements other than the Send button, so one has to use the mouse to use the emoji picker, file attachment picker, add a view call, etc.

However, it does one thing well, which is make `Tab + Enter` trigger sending a message, which is how a large number of users send messages in Zulip (I'd go so far as to say I think it's the most common mechanism for folks not using "Press Enter to send").

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 22:38 UTC

The original proposal in #15914 is to do the most natural thing from an accessibility perspective, namely having `tab` iterate between elements in the order they appear in the DOM (which matches the visual order).  This breaks Tab+Enter, because you would need to hit tab like 7 times to get to the "Send" button.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 22:39 UTC

One potential option is to swap the "Send" button to the left of the compose box, which is the new proposal in #15914.  That has design implications that may not be great (it's definitely intentional that it's on the right based on usability studies).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 22:40 UTC

Other options include:
* Using a `tabindex` hack and/or the existing JS that controls how tab proceeds; while positive `tabindex` is a bad pattern, that doesn't mean it cannot be a good solution in some situations.
* Changing the markup/CSS to preserve the current visual appearance but have "Send" appear earlier in the DOM than the other buttons with appropriate positioning CSS.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 22:41 UTC

Thoughts on how to proceed here?  I think we should treat it as a constraint that "Tab+Enter" will send messages (that feature is in fact part of what makes people comment they like Zulip's keyboard accessibility), but beyond that I don't have strong feelings on how this should work.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-24 22:42 UTC

For me the extra-tabbing wouldn't be annoying, because I hit control-enter.  But I respect that tab-enter is a pretty hard constraint here.

I also agree that having Send on the left would just feel weird.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-24 22:44 UTC

Why not put the controls before the edit box?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 22:44 UTC

Yeah, I agree.  I think the right keyboard UI is that tabbing past "Send" takes you through the UI widgets on the bottom, and we just need to arrange that in an appropriate way.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 22:44 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> Why not put the controls before the edit box?
I don't think that helps -- for the same keyboard UI reasons, we want tab from the topic to go to the compose box.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-24 22:48 UTC

I'm up for trying that.  (I was about to say the same about the press-enter-to-send-checkbox, but that's just a visual thing; it's something that you almost never toggle.)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-07-24 22:49 UTC

Have we looked at Discord/Slack?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-24 22:49 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> I'm up for trying that. (I was about to say the same about the press-enter-to-send-checkbox, but that's just a visual thing; it's something that you almost never toggle.)
Yeah, that one is a little weird -- it's something that a ton of folks toggle just once during their first 5 minutes, and usability studies suggested it's really important folks can find it.  But folks don't change it much after that.

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> I wonder we could reduce the `Tab`+`Enter` problem by increasing the visibility of `Ctrl`+`Enter`? ``` Send with ⚪ Enter ⚫ Ctrl+Enter ```

I'm not sure this solves it -- Tab+Enter is a thing that works with most webforms on the Internet, and doesn't require two hands to do things at the same time, so it's potentially simpler to execute.  But this is at least somewhat helpful.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-27 19:29 UTC

> There are the accessibility best practices

I disagree with the claim that accessibility best practices require that tab order matches the visual display order.  Accessibility best practices require that we make this important component highly usable for someone using a screenreader; technical details like "avoid using `tabindex`" as to how that is achieved are secondary to achieving the actual accessibility goal.  And in any case, "avoid using X" doesn't mean "never use X when there's a good reason".

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-27 19:31 UTC

In this case, all of the proposed ideas for changing this component to avoid use of tabindex reduce its actual keyboard accessibility in comparison to what we would get were we to just ensure that tabbing past `send` takes you to the UI elements in the bottom-left of the compose box.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-27 19:32 UTC

There are certainly problems with `tabindex` (it's a maintenance headache among other things), but no rule in computer science is absolute; we have to apply our reasoning to our particular situation, at least when it's an important part of the UI.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-27 19:34 UTC

So I think how I'd like to proceed here is merging a commit to make tabbing past "Send" go to the additional compose button elements, and then ask some users we know who actually use screenreaders to test the user experience and see if they find it ergonomic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-27 19:36 UTC

(This is the only place in Zulip we use positive `tabindex`, so this is really is a discussion about this single specific UI element, not our general practices which are indeed to avoid positive tabindex)

(replying to Tim Abbott)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-27 23:35 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-07-27 23:40 UTC

> But not at all our only major problem with the accessibility of Zulip ... which is frankly so bad that it is ridiculous that we claim to follow best practices.

Certainly that's an aspirational goal; I was not aware of our making that claim about Zulip today.  

But looking now I see we have an accessibility claim on /features, not just on the accessibility goals page: https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing/accessibility.html.  I think that is certainly a source of confusion here.  For context, the goals page was written in collaboration with some folks who work on accessibility on EdX and has good content, but then the contributors who were planning to actually implement the changes suggested by those tools got busy and never did that work.

I see that was added in 0b8956152411bf0a353d28cf2da86d380e36eea6, so not clear exactly how that happened :/.  I think we should remove that /features claim in any case, as it's not accurate today (though I'd very much like us to make it accurate).

**Sahil Batra** · 2020-08-03 21:44 UTC

Issue here is that we rerender the sidebar only when the sorted stream groups are not same before and after the change. Previously we were storing stream names in the stream group list and thus list was being rerendered correctly as the rename of a stream changes the stream group list, but now we have changed it to store stream-ids, the sidebar is built again only if the order of stream ids changes, which does not happen in some cases of stream rename.

## bootstrap upgrade

*2020-08-13 to 2020-09-02 · 39 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/bootstrap.20upgrade/with/985429)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-13 06:26 UTC

I think it's getting to be time to do the unpleasant work on upgrading bootstrap.  The background here is that we have a somewhat forked version of bootstrap; most of our changes were to bootstrap typeahead, which is removed in modern bootstrap entirely and we've extracted as `static/third/bootstrap-typeahead`, so in theory that shouldn't be relevant for upgrade work.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-13 06:31 UTC

We currently are using 2.1.1 (slightly forked) for most of the site but 2.3.2 (the last 2.x series release) for our landing pages to get the carousel feature.

So I'd start with (1) computing a diff between `static/third/bootstrap` and Bootstrap 2.1.0 to see what changes we need to investigate and figure out what to do with, and then use that to prepare a commit where we switch to using stock 2.3.2.

(And then iterate from there).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-13 06:32 UTC

E.g. looking at `git log -p --follow css/bootstrap.css` we can see we have a dozen or fewer commits where we incorrectly changed bootstrap CSS rather than our own code; we should look at each of those, figure out if they still do anything, and then ideally migrate that file to the original Bootstrap CSS (with any overrides we need to do moved into `components.scss` or the appropriate file).

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-08-13 06:36 UTC

I expect after moving to 2.3.2 we will want to upgrade to 4.5.x and then upgrade to the next 4.x or 5.x as they come along. Also, make a rule to never modify bootstrap files.

There are 20+ commits in bootstrap.js too which will have to be taken care of.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-13 18:47 UTC

Yeah the goal is to just be getting bootstrap from `npm`, which would make modifying bootstrap files impossible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-08-13 18:48 UTC

Bootstrap is one of the last big pieces of hacky management of dependencies that we need to clean up (the other is `marked`)

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-08-14 13:25 UTC

>  The background here is that we have a somewhat forked version of bootstrap; most of our changes were to bootstrap typeahead, which is removed in modern bootstrap entirely and we've extracted as static/third/bootstrap-typeahead, so in theory that shouldn't be relevant for upgrade work.

This is actually half the work since we moved the js part to typeahead.js but tweaked the bootstrap.css file for the css part, so we need to override all the dropdown-menu css and then match it with what we want the css to finally look like.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-08-14 13:26 UTC

This also means that everytime we upgrade bootstrap, even the minor releases, we will have to makes updates in for the typeaheads atleast.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-02 15:48 UTC

To find deps, I hack `.eslintrc.json` to remove all the global exclusions, and then I run this program:

~~~ py
import glob
import subprocess
import re

cmd = ["./tools/lint", "--groups=frontend", "static/js"]
result = subprocess.run(cmd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
lint_lines = result.stdout.decode().split("\n")

deps = {}
fn = None
for line in lint_lines:
    m = re.search("static/js/(\S*).js", line)
    if m:
        fn = m.group(0)
        deps[fn] = set()

    if fn:
        m = re.search("'(.*?)' is not define", line)
        if m:
            deps[fn].add(m.group(1))

fns = glob.glob("static/js/*.js")

for fn in sorted(fns):
    others = deps.get(fn, set())
    if "$" in others:
        continue
    if len(others) <= 2:
        print("*", fn.split("/")[-1], others)
~~~

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-09-02 19:42 UTC

Which I suppose is why Steve is excited about targeting leaf modules.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-09-02 19:43 UTC

Enabling `import/no-cycle` in ESLint seems like a good idea, although it won’t help with implicit circular dependencies that run through `window` mid-transition.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-02 20:01 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Which I suppose is why Steve is excited about targeting leaf modules.

Yeah, I still think this is the best strategy.  I think if we take `i18n` and `blueslip` off of `window`, then we'll have a few modules that are low hanging fruit (or low hanging "leaves", if you will).  And then we convert them.  And then eventually I think quite a few dependencies will mostly fall like dominoes, but we'll eventually get to tricky modules.  And I think tricky modules that are dependency violators should be broken up.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-02 20:03 UTC

It would be nice to find out which `window` vars get accessed during import time.  If we can clean those up, then I think it allows us to be more aggressive about converting modules to es6 that still have indirect ties to `window`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-09-02 20:06 UTC

We can maybe extract that information by using `imports-loader` to bind `window` to a `Proxy` object.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-02 20:19 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)

Yeah, like maybe after `ui.initialize` or something similar runs?  Is that along the lines of what you're thinking?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-02 20:20 UTC

or right before, I suppose, would be closer (sort of distracted, thinking out loud)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-09-02 20:21 UTC

The check would go at top level in `ready.js`. Doesn’t need to be as late as `ui_init.initialize_everything`, since that’s in a `$()` callback which guarantees all the modules are already loaded.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-09-02 20:27 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> The check would go at top level in `ready.js`. Doesn’t need to be as late as `ui_init.initialize_everything`, since that’s in a `$()` callback which guarantees all the modules are already loaded.

Make sense.  I think it's worthwhile to track this down.  My hypothesis is that we'd only see things of the nature of `util.js` get accessed that early.

In the latest version of chrome we have weird outlines all the over the app on clicking some buttons etc due to  this https://blog.chromium.org/2020/09/chrome-86-improved-focus-highlighting.html

[Screenshot-2020-09-26-at-8.42.14-PM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/b8/G-GkUUDG1RD10m9ZLtuFh995/Screenshot-2020-09-26-at-8.42.14-PM.png) [Screenshot-2020-09-26-at-10.41.04-PM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/ed/b5uXuAmR6C2VPzR2M6a-tvrT/Screenshot-2020-09-26-at-10.41.04-PM.png) [Screenshot-2020-09-26-at-10.41.27-PM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/0/zdllzyk3T6wMVBDFk2deQuJ6/Screenshot-2020-09-26-at-10.41.27-PM.png) 

(There are more)

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-09-26 17:16 UTC

Should I fix them or do they really have assistive value?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-09-29 23:54 UTC

@Gittenburg FYI for this thread.  We likely want to change the ones that don't have assistive value, but not the ones that do.  It's kinda a tricky case-by-case situation, but often we want to avoid having outlines if the user focused the element by clicking around the UI (especially for things like the menus, where we should likely have moved focus to the menu itself, not the toggle for the menu), but have the outlines if they got there by tabbing around the UI.

**Gittenburg** · 2020-10-02 05:05 UTC

Yeah I think Firefox handles this better by only showing the outline after you shift focus with Tab once. To remain accessible we definitely should have focus outlines when using Tab to navigate around ... so I seriously don't think we should totally remove outlines on input elements. Maybe we could emulate Firefox's behavior by adding an `tab-a11y` class to `body` once the user pressed `Tab` and do sth like:

```scss
input, select { outline: 0; }
.tab-a11y {
   input, select {
    outline: 1px dotted #212121;
    outline: 2px auto -webkit-focus-ring-color;
  }
}
```
That's just what comes to my mind ... there might be better ways. I don't have time to work on this.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-10-02 06:35 UTC

Thanks for input. I will find time for this next month maybe.

## comfortable mode  #16595

*2020-10-22 to 2020-10-29 · 36 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/comfortable.20mode.20.20.2316595/with/1044638)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-10-22 14:15 UTC

I deployed an approach for creating comfortable mode in https://nightly.zulipdev.org.  PR #16595

We convert font-size and padding from px to rem units. Then, we set font-size to 110% for `<html>` in comfortable-mode. We could also opt for explicit font sizes of 14px and 15.4px for compact and comfortable mode, so that we have more control over what we are showing to the user.

This PR is at a state of minimal effort. 

Issues noticed:
- [ ] There is a common issue that text / icons are a little lower than middle alignment level.

Script used for conversion:

```python
import os, re

def ctorem(matchobj):
    return str(int(matchobj.group(1))/16) + 'rem'

def rep(matchobj):
    return 'padding: ' + re.sub('(\d+)px', ctorem, str(matchobj.group(1))) + ';'

for dname, dirs, files in os.walk("."):
    for fname in files:
        if fname[-3:] == 'css':
            fpath = os.path.join(dname, fname)
            print(fpath)
            with open(fpath, 'r') as f:
                s = f.read()
                x = re.sub(r'padding: (.*);', rep, s)
                print(x.strip(), file=open(fpath, 'w'))


```

Deployed on https://nightly.zulipdev.org/

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-10-26 14:29 UTC

In the past few days, I tried like many ways to make this approach possible but it is not because this breaks media queries.

why?

because media queries don't depend upon root element font size in chrome (it does in safari) when using rem units. They depend upon the default browser font-size. So, media queries' max/min-width don't get affected when css/js changes the font size of html or root.

I researched a bit more about using this approach in a complicated webapp like ours. To make something like this work, we have scale our app vertically without scaling it horizontally when changing font-size. This will make sure our media queries don't break on font size changes. This isn't simple to accomplish :sweat_smile: Just converting our vertical padding / margin / height units to rem isn't going to solve this.

So, I was thinking we should rather work on Tim's initial proposal of adding just a comfortable-mode to our webapp. I will try my best to make sure it isn't a pain to maintain.

## CSS migrations: rem

*2020-10-29 to 2021-02-02 · 29 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/CSS.20migrations.3A.20rem/with/1051751)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-29 23:27 UTC

There's a couple CSS migrations that @Aman Agrawal has been working on that perhaps deserve a broader discussion on naming and other details.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-29 23:28 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/16640 migrates out font sizes from `px` to `rem`, and I'd like to have a bit of a discussion of whether we want to do that as a complete sweep or do something more subtle.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-10-30 06:14 UTC

(Bringing discussion here from PR) 
Tim:
> I think we'll want to write in our CSS style guide somewhere the logic around when to use rem vs. px vs other units and why -- can you write down your reasoning for why we should convert all font-size values to rem rather than em or keeping them as %s? I can see potential use cases for % for compone …

rem, em and % I feel are fine as units for font-size. We don't want to use px for reasons because they are set in stone, don't respect user font-size preferences (accessibility) and are not scalable. Bootstrap 4 has also migrated to use rem, em and % units for their font-size. 

I personally find em and % confusing to work with. We don't have any modular components here which are used in multiple places. They are not dependable.

I migrated % units to rem in the PR because the ones using it all depend on the body font-size  right now and can easily be done now. For `em` units I don't think we can we even migrate them to rem without spending a lot of time and are probably not worth it.

We are doing this as part of adding a comfortable mode that is easier to maintain.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-10-31 02:38 UTC

Yeah, I think that strategy is reasonable; I suppose we don't actually reuse components at different sizes right now.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-11-03 00:34 UTC

I'm not sure I'm a fan of the editability consequences of this migration:

```
-    font-size: 9px;
+￼    font-size: 0.5625rem;
￼```
