**Alya Abbott** · 2021-11-01 21:05 UTC

In Chrome on a Mac, the new message count in the favicon is very hard to read on my computer. Comparing with how it looks on @Tim Abbott 's screen, perhaps there's a missing background to display the number on top of? @Yash RE FYI, since you're working in this general area.

 [Screen-Shot-2021-11-01-at-11.59.34-AM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/50/DCWi6DDO1Al5qo9zxpo1NIl4/Screen-Shot-2021-11-01-at-11.59.34-AM.png)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-01 22:17 UTC

For comparison, here's mine for a realm with a very large unread count:
[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/a0/w65Iy7cWUQHpdxSeV2IeIyZc/image.png)

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-01 22:23 UTC

It looks like if we put the count on a little pill with its own background, that would probably help the legibility a lot.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-01 22:24 UTC

The most conspicuous difference between Tim's screenshot and Alya's is that Tim's browser is apparently using more pixels for the tab's icon. I think that's probably the main reason it's more legible on Tim's screen than Alya's.

(Though it's hard to say for sure without seeing the actual displays in person.)

**Alya Abbott** · 2021-11-01 22:55 UTC

Yeah, a pill would be great. Especially with the work in #20088, which will result in logos we have no control over behind the number.

**Alya Abbott** · 2021-11-01 22:55 UTC

@Tim Abbott thought his tab already had a pill, but maybe that's an illusion.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-01 22:59 UTC

Yeah, in that screenshot I think there definitely isn't. You can see the blue-purple of the logo between the 4 and the 7 and the K.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-01 23:00 UTC

There is a white border, or stroke, around each letter and digit. That helps, but not as much as a pill that covered the space between them (and some padding around) would.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-02 19:56 UTC

There’s only so much you can cram into ⅙ of an inch at 96 DPI. (Tim’s screen is 192 DPI.) The numerals do get larger if you have a one- or two-digit unread count. I figured that when you have more than 99 unreads, it’s more important to convey “a lot” at a glance than to try to convey the exact count. Before the SVG icon we just wrote “99+” there.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-02 19:59 UTC

Adding a background pill would destroy whatever recognizability the logo has left in this state, since the top half of our logo is hard to distinguish from a featureless rounded line.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-02 20:02 UTC

Looking at Alya's screenshot, I'm not sure the bottom part of the logo has much visibility as it is.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-02 20:03 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> I figured that when you have more than 99 unreads, it’s more important to convey “a lot” at a glance than to try to convey the exact count.

I definitely agree with this. Perhaps there's a way we can do that with fewer symbols again? "99+" might feel less detailed than "24K".

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-02 20:38 UTC

What I’m saying is that the length of the number already conveys 99+ without having to actually go and read the actual digits.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-02 20:40 UTC

If you care about being able to easily read the number of unreads, you should, like, read some messages and have fewer unreads.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-02 20:41 UTC

Or look at the title bar, which has the exact count at a normal font size.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-02 21:40 UTC

When we have a specific number there, it conveys an expectation that we're communicating information we expect the person to be able to read. It's frustrating to have the app presenting information to you, and then not be able to read it because of the design choices the app made.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-02 21:53 UTC

I think it's a pretty hard problem with a low-DPI screen here, and we shouldn't beat ourselves too much over not being perfect, even if we think we can do better.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-02 21:54 UTC

True.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-02 21:55 UTC

And also Gmail's looks even harder to read to me, so it's not like this is a solved problem.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-02 21:55 UTC

(I'm a bit puzzled at the low-DPI screen on a Mac. Is that on an external display?)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-02 21:55 UTC

Yes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-02 21:55 UTC

That said, I do think it's worth experimenting with whether a background pill or increasing the size of the number or something lets us increase readability without a material change in the visibility of the logo.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-02 21:57 UTC

The three-digit number already takes up the entire available width. The size already does increase for one- or two-digit numbers.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-02 21:59 UTC

Yeah, so maybe the only option available is the background direction.

please i need help.i have been working on this issue #20046 and  have had a few problems.

so i tried using media_queries in settings.css  but that doesnt work as well. please can anyone help? [image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/b1/jgNZON4k7-TmLAJ16LoDoUeq/image.png)

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-03 22:51 UTC

**Morgan Njaw** · 2021-11-03 23:01 UTC

OK, i am trying to make the gear_menu component responsive by including scroll bar.
So I used the "simplebar" on the ul-list but it won't make it scrollable. I then, tried out media queries but it won't reduce the size of the ul-list when the screen reduces in size. It still cut's off the content of the gear_menu components

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-03 23:02 UTC

(replying to Bang-Kwe Morgan Njaw)
> So I used the "simplebar" on the ul-list but it won't make it scrollable.

What did you do specifically? Pasting the code, in a code block, might help.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-11-04 05:49 UTC

I see this is a problem after we added "About / Support Zulip" buttons. It can just edge out on some mobile / table (landscape) screens. Since the gear menu has `position: absolute`, it will be hard to make it scrollable since it won't respond to `overflow`.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-11-04 05:50 UTC

We can hide some buttons on small screens so that atleast `Log out / in` is accessible.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-11-04 05:54 UTC

We can hide buttons like `Usage stats / Desktop and mobile apps / Integration / API documentation`. Stats page is not readable on mobile and docs pages can be accessible outside the app too.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-11-04 05:56 UTC

550px height seems like a good point to do so.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-11-04 05:57 UTC

[Screenshot-2021-11-04-at-11.27.13-AM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/2/WVmmBt1f4QR997yTlwujSkwQ/Screenshot-2021-11-04-at-11.27.13-AM.png)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-04 05:58 UTC

There’s no reason you can’t have an absolutely positioned element with overflow. Something like `overflow-y: auto; max-height: calc(100vh - 51px)` should work fine. (This may need some adjustment if an alert panel is open.)

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2021-11-04 06:01 UTC

Yeah, the `max-height` is the tricky part to calculate.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-04 06:03 UTC

Maybe Tippy can help.

**Morgan Njaw** · 2021-11-04 08:00 UTC

ok thank you all for the tips and help.

**Morgan Njaw** · 2021-11-04 08:03 UTC

here is what i came up with as a working solution. i added a new class and edited the zulip.css

```  @media( max-height: 600px) {
        .scrollMenu { 
            overflow-y: scroll;
            height: calc(100vh - 100px);
        }
    } ```

## drafts synchronization

*2021-11-10 to 2023-06-06 · 33 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/drafts.20synchronization/with/1279224)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 20:14 UTC

Since we've had an API for syncing drafts for a few months, I want to start a discussion about the technical issues involved with syncing drafts.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 20:15 UTC

First, we have API documentation for the API endpoints involved: https://zulip.com/api/get-drafts and friends.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 20:17 UTC

There's a few things that need to happen for this sort of feature:
* Sending existing local drafts without a remote draft ID to the server.
* Adding to the local drafts data structure any drafts present on the server.
* Deleting drafts on the server when a message is sent or its draft deleted.
* Dealing with situations where a draft exists on both the server and the client and they're different, which is the hard part.  One mostly wants to prefer whichever version is newer using timestamps ... and maybe once we have something kinda working, we'll need to think about corner cases.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 20:20 UTC

I think this is the kind of feature that is probably best developed with a flag `drafts.synchronization_enabled` that can probably equal `page_params.development_environment` in its initial version, so that we can merge parts of this behavior incrementally without having any effect on production.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-10 20:30 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> * Adding to the local drafts data structure and drafts present on the server.

(s/and/any/?)

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-10 20:37 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> * Dealing with situations where a draft exists on both the server and the client and they're different, which is the hard part. One mostly wants to prefer whichever version is newer using timestamps ... and maybe once we have something kinda working, we'll need to think about corner cases.

This basically means situations like the following, right?
* I start writing a draft, on device A. It gets synced up to the server.
* I keep writing. My later edits don't get uploaded, because I lost network or something.
* On another device B, I open up the draft and find the old version.
* On device B, I write some more again, and that gets uploaded.
* Later, I return to device A, with a working network again. There's the version from A and the version from B.

I think in a case like this where the history has diverged, the right thing is probably actually to make a new separate draft with the other version. That way the user has both versions, and can choose between them -- or even copy-paste parts of one to combine with the other.

If on the other hand we pick just one, that's unavoidably going to mean situations where the user loses work, because it gets clobbered by the one that we judged to be newer. For example the newer version could be their incomplete attempt to frustratedly retype from memory a longer, better version they'd drafted earlier.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-10 20:38 UTC

(A fancier thing would be to attempt to merge the edits into one draft, like a Dropbox Paper document. But that's a lot more complex than I think would make sense for this feature.)

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-10 20:40 UTC

Then the key is that:
> I think in a case like this where the history has diverged, the right thing is …

we need to know when what happened is that the history diverged, vs. when what happened is just that the server has an older version that the client's version was based on, or vice versa.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 20:42 UTC

Yeah, I think diverging the draft is probably ideal in that sort of situation; annoying but better to leak a draft than anything else.  Making that work might require adding an algorithm to detect such situations, which I think might be as complex as the rest of this implementation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 20:43 UTC

So I'd be tempted to first build in a turned-off mode an implementation that doesn't do that, and then do focused work on that async problem, as a way of having the early steps be things that don't require a lot of careful thought to do.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-10 21:13 UTC

There’s an extremely simple algorithm from which this behavior emerges automatically:

* Drafts are content-addressed; they don’t even need IDs. (Here I define “content” to include both the text and the recipient.)
* Each client-side draft consists of two contents: the current local content, and the old content that was previously sent to the server.
* Each server-side draft consists of one content.
* To sync a draft from a client to the server, the client sends its old and current content. The server deletes a draft with the old content (if present) and adds a draft with the current content. The client sets its old content to its current content.
* To sync a deletion from the server to a client, the client deletes a draft whose current and old content both match the deleted content (if present).
* To sync an addition from the server to a client, the client creates a draft with its current and old content both set to the added content.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 21:19 UTC

I like that idea.  I think the only downside of that sort of system is it'd make any sort of rewriting of draft objects complicated.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 21:19 UTC

Like, if we wanted to run a database migration to edit existing drafts to use updated syntax for X, which I'm not sure we'd ever want to do, I guess we'd need the content addressing logic to understand that in some way that's probably going to end up ugly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 21:20 UTC

Oh, the other UX question is if you currently have a given draft open, I guess the algorithm would replace an existing open draft if and only if the server-side "old draft" it received were the same as what's in the compose box?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 21:23 UTC

I guess the final thing to think about is how drafts should interact with topics being renamed.  At present, if a topic is renamed, and you are typing a message to the pre-rename topic, we live-update your compose box to the new recipient.  If we wanted to live-update unfinished drafts as well, which would be the consistent thing to do, I guess we'd potentially want to require the server to send "update draft" events that replace "old_topic,body" with "new_topic,body"?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 21:25 UTC

I guess that algorithm doesn't work, because clients that are offline won't be updated properly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 21:26 UTC

I guess that could be patched if the client-side persistent state includes an `on_server` flag, and when the client starts up, and draft with `on_server` that is not present on the server when the client starts up are assumed to have been deleted by another client?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 21:26 UTC

I think that algorithm would work.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-10 21:28 UTC

No flag is needed; the client thinks that a draft is on the server iff its old content equals its current content.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-10 21:30 UTC

(One could special-case such drafts to use less storage, as long as one is careful not to introduce different behaviors for states that should be conceptually equivalent.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-10 22:00 UTC

Sure, yeah, I guess a function with the right name for that check would do rather than an explicit variable.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-10 22:35 UTC

In that algorithm, what happens if the client uploads a new version of a draft, the server gets it, but the response doesn't make it back to the client?

If the client only updates its old content when it gets the response, then when it later retries, that will create a duplicate.

(And if it updates before it gets a response, then things go wrong if the server didn't get the request. That seems worse.)

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-10 22:35 UTC

That might be a mild enough problem in practice, and it's nice that the algorithm (and the data model) is simple.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-10 22:38 UTC

Yeah, that bug can be addressed by having client-side drafts store a *list* of old contents, but I suspected it’s rare and mild enough that it’s not worth complicating the algorithm.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-11-11 20:01 UTC

I've been looking at what's been implemented for the drafts re: the api and the events; particularly the parameters and return values as there's an issue with how they're being rendered in the documentation.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-11-11 20:01 UTC

And it looks like the 'id' that's generated by the server is the key for communicating what draft has been created, updated or deleted/sent. So the algorithm you all are discussing would be a change to that? Correct?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-11 20:11 UTC

Any aspect of the existing implementation is subject to change.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-11-11 20:13 UTC

Of course, I wanted to make sure I'm following the thought process.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-11 20:14 UTC

Yes.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-11 20:19 UTC

There are still lots of details to work out; for example, we might decide to optimize the content addressing using hashes or UUIDs, in which case we might still end up with something that’s called an ID but it’s a string that changes each time you edit.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-13 01:02 UTC

Yeah, the current `ID` field is an incrementing database row ID, but as Anders says, we can change anything about the existing implementation freely, since it's not used in production yet.

**Cyphase** · 2023-06-04 00:45 UTC

Any news on this (#3775) since late 2021? Does any work since then change things or make this easier?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-06-06 00:18 UTC

I think we just haven't had the attention to think more about the API we want here.

## CSS nesting

*2021-11-17 to 2021-11-19 · 24 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/CSS.20nesting/with/1283355)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-17 19:39 UTC

@Tim Abbott When we were talking yesterday about solutions to our CSS modularity mess, you mentioned CSS nesting yesterday as a solution, e.g. wrapping the entirety of `left_sidebar.css` in `#left-sidebar`. So I want to point out why that doesn’t solve the problem.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-17 19:39 UTC

Suppose `.foo-widget` and `.bar-widget` both have a `.title` subelement. If they both write

```css
.title {
    /* styles for foo-widget title */
}

.title {
    /* styles for bar-widget title */
}
```

at top level, obviously these are going to conflict and cause a mess.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-17 19:39 UTC

No problem, you say—we’ll fix this with nesting:

```scss
.foo-widget {
    .title {
        /* styles for foo-widget title */
    }
}

.bar-widget {
    .title {
        /* styles for bar-widget title */
    }
}
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-17 19:40 UTC

The issue is that *these will still conflict* if we happen to put a `.bar-widget` inside a `.foo-widget`, because `.foo-widget .bar-widget .title` matches both `.foo-widget .title` and `.bar-widget .title`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-17 19:40 UTC

The only solution is to not use generic names like `.title` at all, ever. Scoping needs to happen in the class names, not in the nesting structure. This is the motivation for systems like BEM.

```css
.foo-widget__title {
    /* styles for foo-widget title */
}

.bar-widget__title {
    /* styles for bar-widget title */
}
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-17 19:50 UTC

Similarly for bare element selectors: the same problem arises with `.foo-widget h3` and `.bar-widget h3`.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-17 22:15 UTC

I think there are cases where nesting can work to get some isolation. But that is a good illustration of why it doesn't work as a general solution.

One example in yesterday's discussion was the left sidebar. If everything that's meant to affect only the left sidebar is nested inside a `#left-sidebar { … }`, then it won't affect anything that's not in the left sidebar.

If that's done for areas like "left sidebar", "right sidebar", "modals", then those areas aren't ever going to nest inside each other, and so it does successfully isolate those areas' styles from each other.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-17 22:17 UTC

That doesn't make it a working strategy for how we'd want the styles to be organized as an end state. But even just isolating some of those broad swaths of styles from each other could be quite useful, both for making the styles somewhat more maintainable immediately and for making it more tractable to refactor further into a good end-state organization.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-17 22:23 UTC

In addition to the point you raise with that example -- that widgets can nest inside one another, and then the styles that were meant to be local to the outer widget start conflicting with the styles that the inner widget was trying to locally apply -- there was one that came up in yesterday's discussion, that also demonstrates how nesting doesn't provide a working general solution for getting isolation of styles.

That example was that sometimes you have a coherent group of styles that you want to apply in a couple of places that don't usefully share a single ancestor element. It was @Tim Abbott who described a specific real example of this, and I didn't catch the details of it -- I think it was something about things that appear in a couple of different kinds of popups and/or modals.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-17 22:29 UTC

What one really wants at a source-code level, as I think you were saying first, is that the HTML-template code should have to specifically point to what styles it wants to apply. There's a few different ways one could imagine that working, in terms of what the source code looks like and what it ultimately compiles to in order to implement the intended semantics. One would be that it produces class names like those `.foo-widget__title` and `.bar-widget__title`.

(One could also write class names like that directly in the source, but that seems like it'd (a) be annoyingly verbose, and (b) require quite a lot of discipline to do systematically.)

**Yash RE** · 2021-11-18 00:28 UTC

I'll just mention that BEM has the potential to reduce style recalculation costs and hence improve performance.

**Yash RE** · 2021-11-18 00:29 UTC

but that's only tangentially related to this conversation.

Performance is certainly something to think about in any longer-term rearchitecture of the CSS, and I would believe that flat selectors could be faster than nested ones. Do you happen to know of benchmarks demonstrating this?

## function parameter destructuring for (opts)

*2021-11-23 to 2021-12-19 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/function.20parameter.20destructuring.20for.20.28opts.29/with/1285735)*

**Yash RE** · 2021-11-23 15:46 UTC

I've noticed that the frontend follows a pattern where we receive function params as an `opts` object and later assign them to variables.
```js
function foo (opts) {
    let bar = opts.bar;
    let baz = opts.baz;

    bar+=1
    ...
}
```
notice that I'm using `let` in the above example, a line declaring `const` meaningfully conveys that the variable is constant.  ^^

Here are some examples in relatively unrelated places:
- [export function get_person_suggestions(query, opts) {](https://github.dev/zulip/zulip/blob/b3c58f454f0dce8a88c696305945bac41f9786bc/static/js/composebox_typeahead.js#L450)
- [view.remove_reaction = function (opts) {](https://github.dev/zulip/zulip/blob/b3c58f454f0dce8a88c696305945bac41f9786bc/static/js/reactions.js#L386)
- [export function create(opts) {](https://github.dev/zulip/zulip/blob/b3c58f454f0dce8a88c696305945bac41f9786bc/static/js/input_pill.js#L14)

I feel like this is an anti-pattern because:
(1) It obfuscates the function signature and prevents one from learning at-a-glance "what values does this function need?".
(2) It generally adds about 1 to 3 lines where we're just saying `bar = opts.bar`:
(3) Obfuscating the function signature is a good way to hide the code smell of "functions taking 3 or more parameters". ^

A change that we could make is to move towards function parameter destructuring:
```js
function foo ({bar, baz}) {
    bar+=1
    ...
}
```
(4) One additional benefit here is that we can handle "undefined" via defaults (null, "" and other falsey values would be handled differently), so, stuff like the following is possible:
```js
function foo ({bar = "alpha" , baz} = {bar: "beta", baz: "gamma"}) {
    console.log("bar: " + bar + ", baz: " + baz);
}
```
```js
foo(); 
> bar: beta, baz: gamma
```
```js
foo({baz: "omega"});
> bar: alpha, baz: omega
```
Although I don't expect us to be doing things as complicated as the above... in fact, I don't think we use defaults a whole lot to begin with.

^ The code smell of 3 or more params is bad because it implies (1) a high number of combinations to test (2) likely trying to do more than one thing. Now, chapter 3: "Functions", Page 43,  heading "Argument Objects", of Clean Code says:
> Reducing the number of arguments by creating objects out of them may seem like cheating, but it’s not. When groups of variables are passed together, the way x and y are in the example above, they are likely part of a concept that deserves a name of its own.

And I agree, but I just don't think `opts` is a very good name in most cases. There's also nothing preventing functions like:
```js
function foo ({bar, baz}, qux) {
    bar+=1;
    corge(qux);
    ...
}
```

^^ So, what about `const`?
well... we can still use destructuring, it just wouldn't be in the function parameters, in the case that we have both mutable variables and a constants, it'd look like:
```js
function foo ({baz, ...opts}) {
    const {bar} = opts;
    console.log("bar: " + bar);
    baz+= " alpha";
    console.log("baz + alpha: " + baz);
}
```
```js
foo ({bar: "a", baz: "b"})
> bar: a
> baz + alpha: b alpha
```


but that might not actually be worth refactoring, so we should look at how often each case happens.
```
(zulip-py3-venv) re@DESKTOP:~/zulip$ grep -rE "let ([a-z]+) = opts.\1" "./static/js/" | wc -l
1
```
```
(zulip-py3-venv) re@DESKTOP:~/zulip$ grep -rE "const ([a-z]+) = opts.\1" "./static/js/" | wc -l
21
```
```
(zulip-py3-venv) re@DESKTOP:~/zulip$ grep -rE "\((.)*opts\) {" "./static/js/" | wc -l
96
```
```
(zulip-py3-venv) re@DESKTOP:~/zulip$ grep -rE "opts." "./static/js/" | wc -l
590
```
```
(zulip-py3-venv) re@DESKTOP:~/zulip$ grep -rE "opts(\)?) =>" "./static/js/" | wc -l
1
```

So... from those numbers it seems as though in most cases we just use `opts.a` directly, we don't declare a const and there may be some cases where we could improve function signatures...
...Do you think it would be worth it?

Further reading: https://javascript.info/destructuring-assignment#smart-function-parameters.

**Yash RE** · 2021-11-23 16:00 UTC

A couple of more thoughts:
- I'm not sure if this will make typescript-ification any easier but I don't think it would make it harder?
- The reason we aren't already doing this probably has to do with not having access to ES6 features due to phantom/casper in the past.
- It'd have to be done by hand, I don't think it could be automated.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-23 19:15 UTC

We should usually prefer the modern pattern `function foo({bar, baz})` or `function foo({bar = "alpha", baz} = {})`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-23 19:16 UTC

A top-level default other than `{}` would be incredibly confusing, don’t do that.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-23 19:17 UTC

`const` is not very important; since `const` is shallow in JS and locally inferable, it doesn’t add much information.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-23 19:19 UTC

I did some cleanup of this particular pattern in #17806 and #19013, in cases where the ability to use defaults saves a lot of noise.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-11-24 14:45 UTC

(replying to Yash RE)
> - The reason we aren't already doing this probably has to do with not having access to ES6 features due to phantom/casper in the past.

The `opts` pattern definitely comes from pre-es6 days (and not just casper, the actual app).  The more modern idioms are definitely to be preferred here

**Steve Howell** · 2021-11-24 14:49 UTC

On a related note we have an anti-pattern where `opts` can be completely opaque to a function that's in the middle of the call stack.  Even in a pre-typescript world we can do things to make things more explicit.  Suppose A calls B with 5 options, and then B calls C where only 3 of the 5 options matter to C.  We should have B explicitly build a new `opts` that's relevant to C (or possibly just do the right thing in ES6 to make the contracts between functions more explicit).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-24 19:48 UTC

Yeah, also these things were kinda hard without types -- the more times you copy a bundle of parameters with string names (especially pre-ES6) the more times you have opportunities for typos and the like.  We shouldn't feel that we need to copy patterns developed at an early stage startup back in 2013 to make development reasonably fast with an early codebase which has essentially no frontend testing at the time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-24 19:48 UTC

I'd argue that in many cases the ideal thing to do would be to define an object with a type to be used in contracts between functions, and create an object of that type, etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-24 19:49 UTC

But that's essentially the typescript migration project.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-24 19:50 UTC

Which @Priyank Patel did some really good work on this summer; we're now a 7% TypeScript codebase, which might seem small, but doing the first N modules is always the hardest.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-24 19:54 UTC

TypeScript makes it easier to share the types, but Steve is arguing (correctly, I think) that the types should *not* be shared in this case.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-24 19:57 UTC

One should not add a keyword argument to every function in a call tree, both depth-wise and breadth-wise, just because it’s used in a single place. Each function should be explicit about which arguments are used in its part of the call tree, and not pass on irrelevant ones.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-29 21:12 UTC

A type-checker makes it easy to share the whole `opts` type, but also makes it easier to share a subset of the `opts` -- you can copy through some of the properties without worrying about typos in their names, and also you can avoid worrying about whether there is actually some code path deep in one part of the call tree that was expecting a property that you took out. So I think TypeScript will indeed make it easier to avoid the anti-pattern Steve is describing.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-11-30 00:58 UTC

Yeah, I agree with Greg here that TypeScript (TS) would make this better.  I think the antipattern here had solutions way back in ~2014, and the solutions get better and better as we get options from es6 and TS to improve both syntactical elegance and type safety.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-11-30 01:00 UTC

@Yash RE Do you want to take a stab at fixing the `remove_reaction` example?

**Yash RE** · 2021-11-30 19:39 UTC

I'd like to, as soon as I get a chance, but in case anyone else wants to give it a shot please don't block on me.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-11-25 17:05 UTC

**Enis Tara** · 2021-11-26 20:02 UTC

(deleted)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-26 21:25 UTC

`{{~ display_recipient ~}}` does work. The left `~` deletes all of the whitespace between `{{/if}}` and `{{~`, while the right `~` deletes all of the whitespace between `~}}` and `</a>`.

Note however that deleting the whitespace between `{{/if}}` and `{{~` has no effect, since that deleted whitespace always follows some non-deleted whitespace in the template output.

Note however however that the leading whitespace doesn’t matter to begin with because we’re at the beginning of a block element, where leading whitespace is ignored. The trailing whitespace matters because in the actual code, we’re not at the end of the block element. And also, in Firefox, even trailing whitespace at the end of a block element becomes visible if the user highlights it (but that’s not something I would nitpick about in isolation).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-11-29 23:50 UTC

I think whitespace in selections is important in the message feed but likely not elsewhere.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-30 04:54 UTC

(replying to Oliver Pham)
> For total number of messages and number of messages in the last 30 days, I think I can use [this logic](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/76afb31196bab8833268b98260d5a6adf08b94cc/static/js/stats/stats.js#L596) to get the string.

```js
        const total_string = plot_data.total.toString().replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g, ",");
```

That appears to be a rather arcane way of formatting a number with commas as thousands-separators: turning e.g. the number 1234567 into "1,234,567". It wouldn't necessarily be a good idea to copy that -- in addition to being pretty dense to read, it doesn't respect the user's locale. (In some places it's conventional to use other separators, like `.` instead of `,`. In other places it's conventional to do something other than powers of 1000 for separating digits in large numbers.)

But in any case I think more interesting than how to turn the number into a string is how to get the number in the first place.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-30 05:02 UTC

(replying to Oliver Pham)
> For getting the number of users, I actually haven't come up with a neat way to get it. However, I think [this logic](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/76afb31196bab8833268b98260d5a6adf08b94cc/static/js/stats/stats.js#L758) can be useful. Do you think I can use this somehow?

It looks like that line is inside an `on("plotly_hover", …` callback -- so it's tied to the details of the API of the Plotly library we use for making the graphs. In particular the data it's handling comes from the argument to that callback, so it's in the shape provided by that library. I don't think you'll want to use that logic itself.

However, that is a good step on the way of tracing that data! When you hover on the far right-hand end of the users graph, that line processes exactly the number we want here, so that demonstrates that this is a point where that data passes through. You'll just want to get the data from somewhere upstream of this point -- Plotly has the data in the first place only because we pass it the data, so the next step upstream would be where we do that.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-11-30 06:10 UTC

Better solution, for the record: `(1234567).toLocaleString() === "1,234,567"`.

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-30 18:40 UTC

And to demonstrate how it can vary:
```
$ LC_ALL=en_US node -e 'console.log((1234567).toLocaleString())'
1,234,567

$ LC_ALL=de_DE node -e 'console.log((1234567).toLocaleString())'
1.234.567

$ LC_ALL=en_IN node -e 'console.log((1234567).toLocaleString())'
12,34,567

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-30 18:41 UTC

Plus:
```
$ LC_ALL=ar node -e 'console.log((1234567).toLocaleString())'
١٬٢٣٤٬٥٦٧

**Oliver Pham** · 2021-11-30 18:58 UTC

Thanks a lot, @Anders Kaseorg and @Greg Price ! It was hard for me to figure out what the regex does, so I just trusted it (please excuse my bad practice). Can I open an issue to suggest refactoring that line of code?

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-30 20:07 UTC

No problem :smile: Good to ask!

I think changing that to use `toLocaleString` would be good. It's more than a refactor, because it'll change how the page behaves -- its behavior will be different depending on the user's locale.

One thing to be careful of is that we'll want to make sure all the numbers on the page switch to using `toLocaleString`. Having a mix would actually be worse than consistently doing the `en_US` thing of commas at thousands, because then it'd be hard for the user to be sure which convention applies to a given number they're looking at, and when you're not sure of that it becomes ambiguous: if your browser is set to `de_DE`, then "12.345" could mean either approximately twelve (if it's using the `en_US` convention) or approximately twelve thousand (if it's using `de_DE`.)

**Greg Price** · 2021-11-30 20:08 UTC

So making the whole page use `toLocaleString` would be a good issue to file.

**Oliver Pham** · 2021-12-01 21:54 UTC

## text-wrapping of ordered lists

*2021-12-04 to 2021-12-07 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/text-wrapping.20of.20ordered.20lists/with/1291737)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-12-04 21:03 UTC

I've run into an interesting frontend issue that I'd like folks' feedback about. @Alya Abbott  posted #20440 and asked me to look into it as it seemed related to an issue I fixed the week before (#20342) where ordered list items were not text-wrapping as expected. At the time, the fix that worked was adding a blank line between the list items in Markdown. But as Alya noticed, that fix doesn't work on an ordered list of a single item.

The summary from my looking at the issue is that I noticed that adding a space between the list items in Markdown changes the way it's parsed into html. And I found this mentioned in [Daring Fireball's Markdown Syntax section on Lists](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/syntax#list):
> If list items are separated by blank lines, Markdown will wrap the items in <p> tags in the HTML output.
But, when a list is only one item long, the item isn't  wrapped in the <p> tag, even if there is a blank line following the list item in Markdown. Normally, this shouldn't be a problem and it isn't for example with [unordered lists on Zulip's help pages](https://zulip.com/help/using-zulip-for-a-class).

But for ordered lists, we've created a css rule (see `static/styles/portico/markdown.css`) that depends on that <p> tag being there. For ordered lists, we're using a styled `::before` pseudo-element instead of the `::marker` pseudo-element. Here's a [CodePen](https://codepen.io/chriscoyier/pen/Yppeoz) from a [CSS-Tricks blog post](https://css-tricks.com/style-list-markers-css/) that's doing something similar to what we're doing. In the CodePen, if you edit the html text for a list item so that it wraps to the next line, then you can see the text wrapping behavior we're seeing without the <p> tag.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-12-04 21:11 UTC

My inclination is that ideally there would be a way for the css to not depend on the <p> tag to be there as it also breaks if / when someone doesn't format the list in Markdown to be separated by blank lines.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-12-06 20:36 UTC

Upon reflection, maybe this is an issue that should be in #**design** ?

**Alya Abbott** · 2021-12-06 20:39 UTC

Is there a question here about what we want the result to be from the user perspective (i.e. someone using the Help Center)? If not, this seems like the right place.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-06 22:10 UTC

Yeah, this is the right place, since it's a purely technical issue, not a "what is our goal" question.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-06 22:11 UTC

(replying to Lauryn Menard)
> My inclination is that ideally there would be a way for the css to not depend on the <p> tag to be there as it also breaks if / when someone doesn't format the list in Markdown to be separated by blank lines.
I agree that'd be ideal.  I'm not sure I know an easy way to address that; this isn't an area I have a lot of experience with.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-06 22:11 UTC

I certainly don't think we have a strong reason to be using `::before` rather than `::marker`, so @Lauryn Menard it'd be well worth your trying to switch that if you think that'll fix this bug.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-06 22:12 UTC

Certainly https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/::marker seems much more clearly to be intended to be used for this purpose than `::before`.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-12-07 13:41 UTC

Agreed that switching to `::marker` would be the ideal solution and what that pseudo-element is intended for. But I think some of the properties we need to keep the same style for our ordered lists in the documentation are not yet supported by Safari.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-12-07 13:45 UTC

Looks like [Chrome started supporting the `content` property](https://web.dev/css-marker-pseudo-element/), as well as other styling properties, just over a year ago.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-12-07 13:49 UTC

From the 2016 blog post about using the `::before` element, there was a comment that addressed the text wrapping issue. So I could try to implement that for now knowing that it's supported by all the browsers. And we keep an eye on the [webkit issue for Safari support](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=204163) to do the ideal fix when that's resolved?

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-12-07 13:52 UTC

I haven't done any editing yet of Zulip's CSS. Is there a style guide or guidelines / preferences for what units to use for spacing (like margin or padding).

**Lauryn Menard** · 2021-12-07 19:13 UTC

I've got #20500 up for review on this issue. I kept the `::before` pseudo-element due to the browser support issue for `::marker`.

I didn't get any feedback about what units for spacing in CSS rules so I stuck to `px` :smile:

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-07 19:51 UTC

I think we use `px` primarily in the portico pages right now, so that seems certainly fine as a choice.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-12-07 19:53 UTC

Merged.  Thanks for the detailed investigation!

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-16 22:34 UTC

Apparently most of our sorting happens in `typeahead_helper.js`.  The sorters get dispatched in `composebox_typeahead.js`:

~~~ js
1032 export function sort_results(completing, matches, token) {
1033     switch (completing) {
1034         case "emoji":
1035             return typeahead.sort_emojis(matches, token);
1036         case "slash":
1037             return typeahead_helper.sort_slash_commands(matches, token);
1038         case "stream":
1039             return typeahead_helper.sort_streams(matches, token);
1040         case "syntax":
1041             return typeahead_helper.sort_languages(matches, token);
1042         case "topic_jump":
1043         case "time_jump":
1044             // topic_jump doesn't actually have a typeahead popover, so we return quickly here.
1045             return matches;
1046         case "topic_list":
1047             return typeahead_helper.sorter(token, matches, (x) => x);
1048         default:
1049             return undefined;
1050     }
1051 }
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2021-12-16 22:35 UTC

`sort_streams` is at the bottom of `typeahead_helper.js`:

~~~ js
387 export function sort_streams(matches, query) {
388     const name_results = typeahead.triage(query, matches, (x) => x.name);
389
390     const desc_results = typeahead.triage(query, name_results.rest, (x) => x.description);
391
392     // Streams that start with the query.
393     name_results.matches = name_results.matches.sort(compare_by_activity);
394     // Streams with descriptions that start with the query.
395     desc_results.matches = desc_results.matches.sort(compare_by_activity);
396     // Streams with names and descriptions that don't start with the query.
397     desc_results.rest = desc_results.rest.sort(compare_by_activity);
398
399     return name_results.matches.concat(desc_results.matches.concat(desc_results.rest));
400 }

~~~

**Alya Abbott** · 2021-12-16 22:53 UTC

I see, so then it uses:
```javascript
function activity_score(sub) {
    let stream_score = 0;
    if (!sub.subscribed) {
        stream_score = -1;
    } else {
        if (sub.pin_to_top) {
            stream_score += 2;
        }
        // Note: A pinned stream may accumulate a 3rd point if it is active
        if (stream_data.is_active(sub)) {
            stream_score += 1;
        }
    }
    return stream_score;
}
```

And `stream_weekly_traffic` is the tie-break, which is what determined the order in the case I had.

**Nehal Sharma** · 2024-03-08 22:48 UTC

The commit message / PR description does explain this, but to be even more clear, here's exactly how activity scores are assigned to streams now (in decreasing priority):
- 8 - Stream being composed to
- 7 - pinned unmuted active stream
- 6 - pinned unmuted inactive stream
- 5 - unpinned unmuted active stream
- 4 - unpinned unmuted inactive stream
- 3 - pinned muted active stream
- 2 - pinned muted inactive stream
- 1 - unpinned muted active stream
- 0 - unpinned muted inactive stream
- -1 - unsubscribed stream


## pasting rich text

*2021-12-17 to 2022-01-03 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/pasting.20rich.20text/with/1299163)*

**ben** · 2021-12-17 09:38 UTC

Hey hey, do tell if this belongs elsewhere (like a github issue)
What would be your thoughts on supporting pasting rich text? For example, if you copy something like:

Hello `this` is *text* with some [formatting](https://example.com)

...into a program like teams, or gmail, or [Hemingway](https://hemingwayapp.com/), you'll see they don't just copy the text, but also the markup. Could there be interest in supporting some subset of that?

**ben** · 2021-12-17 09:44 UTC

For reference, in the `paste` event there's a `clipboardData` which contains what was pasted. For html there are two pieces of data in that event: `text/plain` for "just the text", and `text/html` which contains the html that's [`getData`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/DataTransfer/getData)

From there, it's conceivable to either wing it and turn the html into markdown, or a library like [turndown](https://github.com/mixmark-io/turndown). Looking at how Hemingway does things (as it imo has the best result), it seems like they rely on Draft.js' [`convertFromHTML`](https://draftjs.org/docs/api-reference-data-conversion#convertfromhtml) (but that could be less applicable here, as it converts html into Draft.js specific data structure)

**ben** · 2021-12-17 10:01 UTC

aaahhh from looking at the code it [looks like there's some implementation](https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/zulip/zulip@0b454dda1207c24ba19d51d7cd5839ea3c349f67/-/blob/static/js/copy_and_paste.js?L273), but it's [behind a dev flag](https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/zulip/zulip@0b454dd/-/blob/static/js/copy_and_paste.js?L322). The code is years old, and a good start and can use some love. Any chance of talking on how to make it more worthy of primetime?

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-17 21:32 UTC

I regularly paste things where I would appreciate this feature.

Just getting

would go a very long way.

**Greg Price** · 2021-12-17 21:35 UTC

One feature we don't have in our Markdown, which if we did would help quite a lot in being able to make a not-super-buggy version of this, is escaping.

As is, if the text you're copying has some brackets or asterisks or other punctuation in it, it's going to get interpreted as Markdown formatting. That interferes with getting the formatting that the original text had.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-06 13:22 UTC

@Alya Abbott See my question above.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:19 UTC

The converse question sort of also applies.  We could, in the edit-subscribers tab, use our current nice pill interface, but don't send stuff to the server until you have done all your edits.  My question is mainly driven by wanting to keep the code simple, but it would also mean that we never have to explain how adding/removing subscribers works differently at creation time than edit time.

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-01-07 17:21 UTC

What's the user impact of this decision? Is it mostly that different things happen if you get disconnected in the middle of what you're doing?

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:22 UTC

The first proposal or the second?

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:28 UTC

The advantages of batching stuff before you send to the server apply at both creation time or when dealing with an existing stream, but in different degrees:

* you allow all users that you add to start participating at the same time
* you can do things like add all users from stream X to stream Y, but exclude Alice, if, for example, you are planning a surprise party for Alice or doing year-end peer reviews or whatever
* if anything goes wrong, it's all or nothing, so you don't have unintentional partial participation

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:28 UTC

The advantage of doing things immediately
* instant feedback
* if you get disconnected halfway through, at least you helped some folks

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:35 UTC

FWIW usually when I create streams, I just subscribe myself, and then go to the Subscribers tab in edit mode, but my use cases may be somewhat unrepresentative:
* I may want to set up topics or intro content before adding people.
* I may be starting with only one or two peers, in which case I don't even add them through Managed Streams.
* The czo process is kinda busted now for adding subscribers to the stream, so I have learned all the workarounds.
* I rarely if never actually need the add-everyone-but-Alice workflow.

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-01-07 17:40 UTC

Mm, yeah, with the bulk-add method, you definitely want the opportunity to remove people before anything goes through. (Both when creating and editing.)

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:42 UTC

(replying to Alya Abbott)
> Mm, yeah, with the bulk-add method, you definitely want the opportunity to remove people before anything goes through.

And that would motivate my second proposal, which would be this (where bold is new)
* at create time continue to do things in batch but use **nice pills**
* at edit time continue to use nice pills but **only send to server when user confirms all changes**

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-01-07 17:44 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell (showell))

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:45 UTC

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-01-07 17:47 UTC

Yeah, or lots of other scenarios, like creating an engineering discussion channel for your team, where you start with the full team and remove the PM, the designer and the boss's boss from the subscribers list.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:48 UTC

(replying to Alya Abbott)
> Hrm, it seems generally reasonable, but (as perhaps you're alluding) it's important to be able to create and populate a private stream without being a member of that stream yourself.

I have no real practice with that, so it wasn't part of my thought process, but that's a reason to prefer bulk at create time (and possibly edit time as well).

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:51 UTC

It's worth noting that for the admin-wants-to-admin-private-stream-without-participating use case, we currently allow admins to edit subscribers even after creating time, which would suggest that any consistent approach should be made to work here.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 17:55 UTC

* at create time, the person creating the stream is auto-subscribed, but admins can opt out with a checkbox
* I hit "Create Stream" button and the stream is immediately created with 0 or 1 participants

* I can decide to come back later if I want

That sounds reasonable to me.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 18:17 UTC

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-01-07 18:25 UTC

Sounds good! Happy to have others chime in in the meantime.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 22:38 UTC

One annoying factor for existing streams is that you can multiple people trying to add/remove subscribers to the same stream at the same time.  It's not just a theoretical race, since you often have two people talking that want to add the third person to the stream, and they both jump on it as soon as they agree on the idea.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 22:40 UTC

In our current scenario, it's usually a pretty harmless race condition, since if we're both trying to add the same person, the race winner doesn't undermine the race loser, and the window for confusion is pretty small.  The race loser will get back something like "Carol was added to the stream.  Dave was already subscribed."

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 22:41 UTC

If we were to go to the batch-editing paradigm for existing streams, the race window goes from a second or two to possibly a matter of minutes.  The backend will still kinda sort things out properly, but it's a little more difficult for the UI to mitigate confusion.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 22:46 UTC

Let's say that Alya and I both agree we want to add 5 new users to our existing stream, and we don't clearly communicate to each other that we're both doing it now.  She starts to do it, takes about 10 seconds in the UI, and then hits Send.  I do it too, but four seconds in, the teapot boils, and I walk away.  When I walk back a few minutes later, the two users I added locally will now be officially added to the list of subscribers on my Subscribers panel, as well as the three users that I didn't add yet.  As long as I can clearly see what happened, I can just leave the UI knowing Alya won the race.  If it's not clear, I do six extra seconds of work and spam the server.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 22:51 UTC

(The context above is that we were to move to a more batch approach for existing streams.)

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 22:53 UTC

With the same scenario currently (Alya and I agree to add 5 people, but Steve needs to turn off the teapot), you still get some races and confusion.  You almost want something akin to typing indicators here, so that I can see "Alya is managing subscribers...", and then I can just abort.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-07 23:04 UTC

I do think that the likelihood of this race, in practice, is inversely proportional to the amount of pain it causes (in a good way).  If two folks decide to add a hundred new people to a stream, they will probably spend more time coordinating it so that one person is clearly in charge of the task.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-12 00:23 UTC

I briefly skimmed the whole thread above, but wanted to note that historically, we've wanted to subscribe users in the same API request that created the stream.  If one doesn't do that, the "new stream created" notification to the "stream events" topic will not be received by the "initial" subscribers, which feels buggy.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-12 00:24 UTC

I also think it's probably nicer for one to stage a set of changes and then do a single submit to batch-modify the membership, in that it might feel easier to undo planned changes that you realize you don't actually want to make.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-12 00:24 UTC

(E.g. if you accidentally select the wrong stream to copy members from in the typeahead, that might prove difficult to reverse).

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-12 19:10 UTC

I had a chance to talk to @Alya Abbott about this, and my stance is still basically that we should change the edit-subscribers experience for existing streams to be batch-oriented.  But she had to jump to another meeting, so she probably needs to think about it, and I'm still not 100% sure myself what the best approach is here.  I am leaning toward consistency, all other things being equal.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-12 22:21 UTC

I think such a change would be reasonable in concept; but we would need to figure out a good visual design pattern for it.

**Alya Abbott** · 2023-03-23 16:35 UTC

> I have concluded that when the DMs section is open the tooltips appear on the bottom only when there is one DM present otherwise when there is more than 1 DM both the tooltips appear at the top itself.

Is this the behavior just in your PR, or in `main` as well? If the latter, was it intentional?

**Satyam Bansal** · 2023-03-23 17:33 UTC

It's in `main` as well. The [flip](https://atomiks.github.io/tippyjs/#placements) property in Tippy.js is unintentionally causing the tooltip to move to the bottom when only one DM is present. This is because there isn't enough space for the tooltip (just space of 1 DM) to appear at the top. However, when there are multiple DMs, space becomes available at the top and the tooltip appears there instead.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-03-23 20:37 UTC

The new enter-sends toggler in #20530 has an construction for translators. Structurally, we want translators to translate the string `{key_combination} to send`, where `{key_combination}` is the HTML, and not have to deal with the specific HTML details that we may change in the future.                                         <span class="enter_sends_false">

                                            {{#tr}}

                                            {{/tr}}                                                      
                                        </span>

## stream_topic_history_util.get_server_history

*2022-01-27 to 2023-09-28 · 26 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/stream_topic_history_util.2Eget_server_history/with/1317162)*

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-27 20:04 UTC

Do we want to call `stream_topic_history_util.get_server_history` as soon as you enter a stream narrow?  I think there's a pretty strong argument that we want to be somewhat lazy about getting full topic history for every stream, but I could see us being a little bit more eager.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-27 20:05 UTC

(for specific streams that the user is clearly interested in during their current usage)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-27 20:45 UTC

I've resisted doing that because that database query is I think more expensive than the one for just displaying the contents of a narrow.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-27 20:46 UTC

But it is very possible that neither of those database queries is particularly significant anyway.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-27 20:46 UTC

Also, this would be limited to 1/stream/user, not 1/topic/user, since you only need to do it once per stream.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-27 20:49 UTC

Yeah the query only ever happens once per stream per reload, since we track the fact that we have retrieved topics for a stream.  (I am omitting some nuances, but that’s the gist.)

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-27 20:54 UTC

A good sanity check would be to look at logs while you do something in the UI for some stream like #**general** that causes us to ask the server for historical topics.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-27 20:56 UTC

I think we’re on the same page that my proposed change would be mostly invisible to users, and the concern here is server load, correct?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:44 UTC

Yeah, that's right.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:45 UTC

(I think if we added such a call, we'd still keep the calls we have elsewhere for typeahead, though maybe we'd get to remove the one that happens when you click "more topics"... but we might not want to because of callback complexity reasons).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:48 UTC

Based on server logs, I think this would be at most a 10x increase in calls to `/api/v1/users/me/{stream_id}/topics`.  Specifically, we currently have calls to `/json/messages [stream,topic]` or  `/json/messages [stream,topic]` about 10x more often than to `/api/v1/users/me/{stream_id}/topics`.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-28 01:48 UTC

I think it’s fine to call this in multiple places, since we short circuit any redundant calls.  But I would like to know how expensive these calls are before making them too eagerly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:48 UTC

The statistics might be substantially different right after a server reload.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:50 UTC

For both queries, the typical request returns in <50ms.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:50 UTC

(With a long tail on both classes of requests -- some requests take a couple seconds in both filters I looked at)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:51 UTC

The one caution is that streams without shared history -- but those are rare in practice so it likely doesn't affect scaling considerations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:52 UTC

So I think we can probably just change this and it'll be a slightly nicer experience and nobody will notice.  One specific fact is that these requests are currently like 800x less common than presence requests, and take about as much time to process normally, with a long tail.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:53 UTC

So moving them to something <80x less frequent is probably fine.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-01-28 01:54 UTC

I would add a comment for the "more topics" call if you change this, that notes the quirk that we very likely already have the data unless the user clicks "more topics" immediately, in which case we'll end up asking the server for the data twice, which is OK performance-wise and avoids extra callback gymnastics.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-01-29 18:07 UTC

I agree that in the long run presence requests would drown these out (especially since they're cached), but immediately after the server reload I do think having these happen on any narrow might slow things down a bit.  I am gonna hold off on changing anything for now.

**Jonathan van Clute** · 2022-01-31 01:33 UTC

This has bit me a few times, and I think I may have finally narrowed down why/how it happens.  Here's the situation:

User joins as a full member, and at some point leaves and is deactivated.  Then later, they come back again but through a different level of access, where they should be a Guest with access to just a few specific streams.  When they are reactivated, Zulip appears to show (via Manage Streams) that they are not subscribed to any stream.  They can be added to any/all of them. We have fixed the behavior of `Manage streams` UI to show that the reactivated user is subscribed to the previous streams and refresh is not required anymore.  But the user will be subscribed to all the streams that they were subscribed to before deactivation irrespective of the role change.

**Yash RE** · 2022-02-09 06:26 UTC

```
(zulip-py3-venv) re@DESKTOP:~/zulip$ git show 1b5a16bd1f2 
commit 1b5a16bd1f2d695de5562d87ea5b64677aecc415
Author: Aryan Shridhar <53977614+aryanshridhar@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Sat Apr 10 06:36:27 2021 +0530

    click_handlers: Prevent compose opening when copying code blocks.
    
    Previously, clicking the codeblock copy button also
    triggered the compose box to open.
    
    This is because of the fact that ClipBoard.js lacks the
    ability to stopPropogate the event when clicked.
    
    Rectified by explicitly defining the copy click event
    within `is_clickable_message_element`, which disallows
    the triggering of reply box.
    
    Effectively a workaround for
    https://github.com/zenorocha/clipboard.js/pull/475.
    
    Fixes #17861.

diff --git a/static/js/click_handlers.js b/static/js/click_handlers.js
index 3428d8bedf..20bbc6b205 100644
--- a/static/js/click_handlers.js
+++ b/static/js/click_handlers.js
@@ -132,6 +132,13 @@ export function initialize() {
             return true;
         }
 
+        // Ideally, this should be done via ClipboardJS, but it does't support
+        // feature of stopPropagation once clicked.
+        // See https://github.com/zenorocha/clipboard.js/pull/475
+        if (target.is(".copy_codeblock") || target.parents(".copy_codeblock").length > 0) {
+            return true;
+        }
+
         return false;
     }
 ```

**Yash RE** · 2022-02-11 18:13 UTC

I'm a little confused why this would happen.

On main if you apply this patch:
```spoiler patch
```diff
diff --git a/static/js/people.js b/static/js/people.js
index ed965eaad8..83e69ab9ab 100644
--- a/static/js/people.js
+++ b/static/js/people.js
@@ -13,6 +13,7 @@ import * as reload_state from "./reload_state";

```
ie just import user_status in people.js, and then try to log into the dev. realm, the login will fail and the following error will show up in the run-dev.py logs:
```
2022-02-11 18:07:51.221 INFO [zr] status=403, data=b'{"result":"error","msg":"CSRF error: CSRF token missing or incorrect.","reason":"CSRF token missing or incorrect.","code":"CSRF_FAILED"}\n', uid=6@zulip

This is a typical symptom of circular imports being resolved in a different order.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-15 20:32 UTC

Obviously we’re never going to have a `<form>` that directly submits to the server in our single-page application, but a `<form>` `submit` handler is still a convenient way to group all the ways one should be able to submit (`Enter` in a control or clicking on a submit button), and it’s also useful for HTML5 constraint validation.

There is now a way to nest the controls belonging to different forms without nesting the `<form>` elements themselves: the [`form` attribute](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#attr-fae-form) ([caniuse](https://caniuse.com/form-attribute)).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-15 21:04 UTC

You’re not wrong.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-15 21:07 UTC

But it’s also reasonable to think of this in the same way as `<label>User <input id="user"></label>` vs. `<label for="user">User</label> <input id="user">`, with the former being a convenient abbreviation when the association happens to coincide with the DOM nesting, and the latter being available when it doesn’t.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-15 21:09 UTC

So if you need to nest an inner `<form>` in an outer `<form>`, grumble, convert the outer `<form>` to attribute style, and move on, I guess.

## lint for $obj.data()

*2022-02-24 to 2022-02-25 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/lint.20for.20.24obj.2Edata.28.29/with/1334626)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-24 23:48 UTC

Should we add a linter rule to ban `$(foo).data("user-id")` in favor of `$(foo).attr("data-user-id")`?  The jQuery `.data()` function has unexpected behavior (in that it doesn't change the `data-user-id` field when writing, but reads it when reading, which can often lead to bugs), is worse for `git grep data-user-id`, and also is a jQueryism that we will want to purge as part of moving off jQuery more generally.

I constantly see folks adding new code using it.

https://github.com/dgraham/eslint-plugin-jquery/blob/master/rules/no-data.js seems like it has a weird error message (recommend `WeakMap` when usually we want to just not use that feature), so we may need to do our own thing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-24 23:50 UTC

I suppose we could even try just converting the the native https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/HTML/Howto/Use_data_attributes and get rid of `$(foo).attr("data-user-id")` if we're doing this sort of sweep.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-24 23:50 UTC

```
$ git grep '[.]data[(]' static/js/ | wc
    109     525    9438
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-24 23:50 UTC

We only need to worry about the two-argument setter, not the one-argument getter.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-24 23:51 UTC

```
$ git grep '[.]attr[(]"data-' static/js/ | wc
    149     709   14600
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-24 23:51 UTC

Only that 2-argument setter is an issue for correctness; but the 1-argument getter is still an issue for greppability.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-24 23:52 UTC

I guess the native dataset attributes are a problem for greppability too, so maybe I don't want to use that.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-24 23:53 UTC

The jQuery methods are apparently some [30× slower](https://www.measurethat.net/Benchmarks/Show/9389/0/modern-dataset-vs-old-getattribute-vs-jquery-data-vs-jq).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-24 23:54 UTC

Actually maybe I don’t believe that benchmark code.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-24 23:56 UTC

This [more reasonable benchmark](https://www.measurethat.net/Benchmarks/Show/14432/0/getattribute-vs-dataset) suggests that `getAttribute` is 6× slower than `dataset`, which makes sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-25 00:38 UTC

Makes sense, but may not actually matter; essentially all of our `data-` field accesses are responding to clicking on something, since we generally store real state directly.

## dark-mode-single-file-css

*2022-02-26 to 2022-02-28 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/dark-mode-single-file-css/with/1335565)*

**Tushar 👾** · 2022-02-26 14:51 UTC

Following from some [earlier](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/101-design/topic/Images.20in.20a.20line.20vs.20row/near/1335561) discussion, are there good reasons to why we have a single file dark theme stylesheet? I think we should look at arguments for and against and consider moving to a multi-file structure which *could* be better to navigate around and more generally applicable.

**Vlad Korobov** · 2022-02-26 23:54 UTC

It's not that obvious guys. Sometimes its better to have all styles about a "thing" next to that "thing".
Having styles of 1 things spread across multiple files can cause "bugs"

**Vlad Korobov** · 2022-02-26 23:54 UTC

I suggest to go the path of encapsulating styles... and then bundle them

**Vlad Korobov** · 2022-02-26 23:55 UTC

so styles about Header all in the same place and styles about users all in the same place

**Vlad Korobov** · 2022-02-26 23:55 UTC

Think more like "components"

**Vlad Korobov** · 2022-02-26 23:55 UTC

It is also helpful to unwind the legacy with bootstrap.css

**Steve Howell** · 2022-02-27 01:28 UTC

The proposal here is to include dark theme CSS￼ rules inside the same modules as their corresponding day theme rules.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-02-27 01:55 UTC

The idea is to not have styles for a single element spread across two files.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-28 20:53 UTC

There's tradeoffs here, and I'm not sure what would be best. The specific file structure we have today was because of constraints around CSS priority, but for some categories of CSS rules, it is nice to have them together for some development work.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-28 21:03 UTC

There’s no such priority-related constraint. A selector `body.dark-theme foo bar` will always override a selector `foo bar`, no matter where it is located. We should switch this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-28 21:04 UTC

There was also at least at some point some preprocessing logic run for the `automatic` color scheme; I can't remember if that has been replaced.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-02-28 21:05 UTC

The other thing I'd want to do before splitting them up is making use of some sort of SCSS variables for the colors that are repeated a million times.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-28 21:06 UTC

Yes, we’d need to copy these five lines into the relevant files.

```scss
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
    body.color-scheme-automatic {
        @extend body.dark-theme;
    }
}
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-02-28 21:08 UTC

Common color variables are good but I don’t see a particular reason to do that before or after this restructuring.

> I'm also curious about `is_search()` though I'm not sure if that's at all related to the idea of this view being a search view.
This is probably a confusing term. Conceptually `is_search` could refer to either "Is this a search view" (of any sort), or specifically "Is one of the operators a full-text keyword search)". It means the latter:
```
    is_search() {                                                                                        
        return this.has_operator("search");                                                              
    }                                                                                                    
```

I propose doing a preparatory PR renaming that function to `is_keyword_search`, since that's what it means.

Here's the code for the functions used in the two situations:
```
export function filter_and_sort_mentions(is_silent, query, opts) {                                       
    opts = {                                                                                             
        want_broadcast: !is_silent,                                                                      
        filter_pills: false,                                                                             
        ...opts,                                                                                         
    };                                                                                                   
    return get_person_suggestions(query, opts);                                                          
}                                                                                                        
                                                                                                         
export function get_pm_people(query) {                                                                   
    const opts = {                                                                                       
        want_broadcast: false,                                                                           
        filter_pills: true,                                                                              
    };                                                                                                   
    return get_person_suggestions(query, opts);                                                          
}                                                                                                        
```

`filter_pills` is just whether the private message typeahead should exclude users you've already added.
