## time limit settings

*2022-08-31 to 2022-09-01 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/time.20limit.20settings/with/1428567)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-08-31 12:07 UTC

I am cleaning some settings code related to message edit settings, specifically to avoid sending the setting value which has not changed. We currently send all the setting values in the message edit section in the `PATCH /realm` request, even when only one setting is changed.

While working on this, I noticed that we have some different behavior in showing save-discard widget.
For `Delay before sending message notification emails` setting in `Default user settings` section, when changing setting from say "1 hourt" to "custom", we do not show the save-discard widget unless the value in custom input-box is changed, since the input value is initially set to "60" (minutes) which is same as "1 hour".

But for message edit and delete limit settings, we show the save-discard widget even when the input value is "60".

Sharing GIFs to depict the above behavior.
[time-limit.gif](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/5a/bGf9YF2iMywcNPQ4U01-0lrj/time-limit.gif)

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-08-31 12:08 UTC

We should make it consistent. I think showing the save-discard widget only when input value is changed should probably be fine since setting value is not changed unless the input value is not changed. Though not sure if it may be confusing for users to not show save-discard widget when changing dropdown.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-31 22:17 UTC

Yeah, I think correct behavior is to show the save/discard widget only when there are actual changes to save; i.e. the message edit/delete settings are the ones we should fix.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-31 22:17 UTC

It seems more confusing for it to suggest saving would change something when it won't than the other way around :)

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-09-01 06:26 UTC

@Tim Abbott 's proposal makes sense to me!

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-09-01 16:27 UTC

Cool, I will add this in my next PR.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-03 21:18 UTC

The zjquery mock wasn’t intended to define best practices. It has a very limited understanding of how jQuery is supposed to behave, that was sufficient at the time for the purpose of stubbing out the jQuery parts of mostly non-jQuery code so it could be unit tested.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-03 21:23 UTC

Unfortunately, as people started trying to drive up the test coverage metrics, they started writing zjquery tests for UI-heavy code. This doesn’t actually verify anything of value—if you want to demonstrate that your code runs correctly with jQuery, running it with zjquery is completely irrelevant to that goal. But it does entangle the code with the tests in a way that makes it very difficult to change either.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-03 21:24 UTC

You should feel free to alter the tests to support whatever UI code you need to write, and uh, I wish you the best of luck.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-04 02:31 UTC

If you want to test UI code in a way that actually tests anything, write Puppeteer tests. If you want to stub out UI code in order to unit-test something else, the `$(…).remove = …` advice is probably among the least worst options.

## reload local storage bug

*2022-09-16 to 2022-09-22 · 29 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/reload.20local.20storage.20bug/with/1436756)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 17:23 UTC

So in #22832, we apparently have a pretty silly bug where if you have multiple browser tabs open to the same Zulip server, a race will clear the metadata from local storage needed for other tabs to restore their state.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 17:26 UTC

I think it's pretty important that we fix this; but I'm wondering if the right way to fix this would be to rewrite `reload.preserve_state` to just store an actual object rather than having the legacy "Serialize to a single URL" system, and then that object can have a date flag and the auto-clearing logic can just clear any that are older than some amount of time (in theory, the time between reload token generation and use should usually be <30 seconds, but I can see i being useful to save this metadata for up to like a week in case a tab fails to load or something ... and of course we'd also delete the tokens from local storage after a successful reload).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 17:29 UTC

If we want to be nice, we can preserve logic for parsing the old format, so that we don't have a 1-time loss of narrowing/compose state when upgrading.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-09-16 17:30 UTC

I feel this bug is fairly important, since its seems like it could lose compose box state in addition to narrow and scroll position.

## Generating types from OpenAPI

*2022-09-23 to 2022-09-23 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Generating.20types.20from.20OpenAPI/with/1439837)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-09-23 00:12 UTC

It looks like we can get benefits from generating types from our OpenAPI Spec. There are codegen tools that support OpenAPI -> TypeScript client code conversion.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-09-23 00:14 UTC

The potential downsides of this are
- We have to rely on a set of third-party tools to get it working properly
- This adds a dependency on a routinely generated client library. It can be problematic in terms of version control
- Needing to tune the generated code somehow if it does not suit our need

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-09-23 00:19 UTC

https://github.com/drwpow/openapi-typescript

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-23 00:21 UTC

Yeah, I share the concern about the developer experience with generated TypeScript files. Another way that might work better is to generate an OpenAPI spec from TypeScript—not to replace our hand-generated spec, but rather for the purpose of statically checking in CI that the hand-generated spec is a subtype of the generated one. I’m not sure what kind of tooling exists in that direction.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-23 00:27 UTC

And ideally we could do the converse check against a second generated spec from our Python types.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-09-23 00:35 UTC

https://github.com/grantila/typeconv/ does that, but I'm not sure if generating a spec from typescript is a reliable way to test the compatibility of the spec.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-09-23 00:37 UTC

The good thing about generating the client from OpenAPI is that we don't have to repeat writing helpers for API calls, as long as the client is properly versioned.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-09-23 00:43 UTC

Oh, there was a similar request in [zulip-js](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-js/issues/74) a while back. Some PRs got made but were not merged.

## parseOneAddress perf

*2022-10-04 to 2022-10-28 · 34 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/parseOneAddress.20perf/with/1444654)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 22:13 UTC

So I've been noticing that switching views is a bit slow on chat.zulip.org. Today I did a round of browser profiling and determined this is indirectly caused by the new private messages section #**design>private messages section #20870**. Specifically, there's about 100ms of work that gets done in `pm_list.update_private_mesages` here:
* Most of the time is, at the lower level, in `hash_util.pm_with_url` calls inside the `get_conversations` loop in `pm_list_data.js`. 
* That calls `people.emails_to_slug` , which is this function:

``` js
export function emails_to_slug(emails_string) {                                                          
    let slug = reply_to_to_user_ids_string(emails_string);                                               
                                                                                                         
    if (!slug) {                                                                                         
        return undefined;                                                                                
    }                                                                                                    
                                                                                                         
    slug += "-";                                                                                         
                                                                                                         
    const emails = emails_string.split(",");                                                             
                                                                                                         
    if (emails.length === 1) {                                                                           
        slug += parseOneAddress(emails[0]).local.toLowerCase();                                          
    } else {                                                                                             
        slug += "group";                                                                                 
    }                                                                                                    
                                                                                                         
    return slug;                                                                                         
}                                                                                                        
```

Within that, all the time seems to be in `parseOneAddress`, aka the library function we're using the split the local name from the domain. 


[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/3a/R9yFhExcZzv9sTp8PUsdURtP/image.png)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 22:14 UTC

Apparently each call to `parseOneAddress`, in this profile, takes like 3ms; so we're spending that much time for each entry in the sidebar list;  somehow that adds up, in part because we also seem to be calling `update_private_messages` more than once in this code path.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 22:15 UTC

What I'm not sure about is what the correct fix to make here is. One option would be to cache the `pm_with_url` values on user objects in `people.js`, so we only compute those once (at least between email address changes); though I suspect it'd probably be a bad idea to just compute that for 10k users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 22:15 UTC

Another option would be to look at whether there's a better way to do the parsing that doesn't involve that library. I'm not 100% sure whether what I'm seeing with this function being slow isn't some sort of profiling artifact.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 22:16 UTC

We also can try to figure out how to avoid needing to do an apparently expensive call to `update_private_messages` whenever we load messages -- we're doing so every time we fetch messages from the server, apparently, even in cases where 0 of those messages had been private messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 22:19 UTC

Trying to frame things as a set of items to fix:
* We're calling `update_private_messages` in the `message_fetch.process_result` code path, i.e. every time we bulk-fetch messages from the server, regardless of whether the messages received could impact anything. Opened I opened #23141 and #23142 for this.
* The `update_private_messages` function does not have the capability to do an incremental update of just values that have changed, and just always does a full rerender.
* The `update_private_messages` full rerender of the left sidebar private messages list appears to be be expensive, in part due to the `emailaddress` library function.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 22:59 UTC

I think the parsing algorithm for narrow URLs would be totally fine with our replacing `{user_id}-{encoded_email}` with `{user_id}-{encoded_name}`:
```
export function slug_to_emails(slug) {                                                                   
    /*                                                                                                   
        It's not super important to be flexible about                                                    
        PM-related slugs, since you would rarely post                                                    
        them to the web, but we we do want to support                                                    
        reasonable variations:                                                                           
                                                                                                         
            99-alice@example.com                                                                         
            99                                                                                           
                                                                                                         
        Our canonical version is 99-alice@example.com,                                                   
        and we only care about the "99" prefix.                                                          
    */                                                                                                   
    const m = /^([\d,]+)(-.*)?/.exec(slug);                                                              
    if (m) {                                                                                             
        let user_ids_string = m[1];                                                                      
        user_ids_string = exclude_me_from_string(user_ids_string);                                       
        return user_ids_string_to_emails_string(user_ids_string);                                        
    }                                                                                                    
    /* istanbul ignore next */                                                                           
    return undefined;                                                                                    
}                                                                                                        
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-04 23:06 UTC

So changing the `emails_to_slug` encoding is probably the best path forward; it'll require some care to handle special characters/capitalization/etc. in a reasonable way, but I expect no real compatibility issues.

## Fine-grained script detection

*2022-10-05 to 2022-10-12 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Fine-grained.20script.20detection/with/1445241)*

**Aaron Muir Hamilton** · 2022-10-05 23:55 UTC

I frequently write messages with mixed language content, in English, Japanese, and Chinese. Japanese and Chinese fonts differ regionally, and while in general it is acceptable to use the default han character font on the platform to render characters, even if the font is not appropriate for the specific language, there are cases where this can look really hideous. Particularly if say, you are in Taiwan and are reading a piece of Japanese text (mixed kana and kanji) on a computer configured to prefer Taiwanese fonts: you will see a mix of Taiwanese fonts on some of the kanji, Japanese fonts on some of the variant kanji that are only used in Japan (e.g. 說 vs 説), and kana rendered in a proper japanese font, or possibly from a Chinese font other than the one displaying the rest of the common unified han characters, which happens to have kana (e.g. MS KaiTi).

Furthermore, screen readers often struggle with multilingual text, or even just text that doesn't have a plausible language tag; you may be lucky and be in a situation where the defaults make sense, but you can also end up with a situation where the screen reader will read Japanese kanji as pronunciations of the most common Mainland Chinese pinyin for the given character, in an American English accent with no tones.

I have a relatively lightweight library (a ~5k nugget of js) that I've used to solve this segmentation problem before, it is general and consults the browser environment (via `navigator.language` and `navigator.languages`) to resolve ambiguous situations (e.g. a word on its own that is common between CJK languages and regional scripts; or a sequence of generic latin script). If I were to make a clean PR for tagging likely regional script boundaries on the web frontend, and rendering them into spans with `lang` attributes, and the additional size and runtime were considered negligible, how likely is it that this would be merged?

P.S. If there is a similar source of locale preferences available to the mobile apps, it should be applicable there as well; and provided the language information can be provided through the platform accessibility APIs, the accessibility issues should be resolved through that on mobile as well, or at least on iOS (I think RN doesn't use `accessibilityLanguage` properly on Android, and doesn't have upstream support for `LocaleSpan` [the Android approach to spans with language tag information]).

[cross-posted at advice from github issue]

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-06 00:09 UTC

The GitHub issue in question is #23131.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-06 00:11 UTC

@Aaron Muir Hamilton can you give some examples and also explain what you have in mind as to at what phase the "tagging likely regional script boundaries" would occur? I'm not sure whether the right layer for this sort of thing is in the HTML for individual message that'd be shared between users (perhaps with Markdown syntax of some sort for overriding something?) or something else entirely.

**Aaron Muir Hamilton** · 2022-10-06 00:11 UTC

I can gladly produce examples, and after untangling the code nugget I can put together a demonstrator to show what my existing code for this can do, and why it's defensible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-06 00:11 UTC

In part because I don't know what a "regional script boundary" is :)

**Aaron Muir Hamilton** · 2022-10-06 00:17 UTC

Ah yes, so for some languages, the browser/platform's font selection depends on the language tag information for the text. Particularly with Chinese characters, many of them are common to most Chinese dialects, Japanese, and Korean (though chinese characters are less common than hangeul writing in Korean today). The fonts can render the same unicode grapheme quite distinctly by region, and sometimes variants are coded as separate unicode scalars, even though they are interchangeable (e.g. the example 説[jp] vs 說[tw,cn] in the post above).

What I am calling "regional script boundaries" here is similar to the general concept of a script boundary (i.e. a boundary between two scripts, like latin and hebrew), but with the added information about which regional variant that chunk of text is most at home in.

**Aaron Muir Hamilton** · 2022-10-06 00:22 UTC

As for what phase this is introduced at, I am thinking it would be right before rendering. In most cases, a message is going to have one likely regional script detected for the whole message, if this is the same as the page `lang` then no work need be done; if it differs from the page `lang`, maybe it could be introduced to the element surrounding the message content.

In more complex cases, with mixed script usage, sequences that can be safely split into spans without interrupting font shaping (e.g, the boundary between Latin script, with or without whitespace, and Chinese script or Japanese mixed script [chinese characters, kana, and embedded standard digits and punctuation]]) would be split into such spans, and tagged with a plausible `lang`based on hard rules, heuristics, and the environment (locales preferred by the browser/platform, etc.).

**Aaron Muir Hamilton** · 2022-10-06 00:24 UTC

as in `"something something何々"` => `<message lang=en-US>something something<span lang=ja-JP>何々</span></message>` as the 々 kanji iteration character, particularly this style, is essentially only used in Japanese, and maybe because the two contiguous characters are CJK or CJK-adjacent, and `ja-JP` is higher than `zh-TW` in `navigator.languages`, and `en-US` is `navigator.language` or the configured language.

**Aaron Muir Hamilton** · 2022-10-06 00:29 UTC

It is a complicated and tuning-sensitive process, and there are many things to consider, like when to continue to suspect that chinese characters are being used in a Japanese context, even when interrupted. My code has some heuristics for this, but it's not always right. It will tend to "give up" and make bigger contiguous spans, or not try to tag a span, when things get too complicated.

**Aaron Muir Hamilton** · 2022-10-06 00:30 UTC

TL;DR on "when": right before rendering, not on the server.

**Aaron Muir Hamilton** · 2022-10-06 13:31 UTC

(though a server-side solution would be more efficient and could consult richer data for heuristics, and maybe would mix better with an explicit language tagging scheme)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-12 19:36 UTC

@Aaron Muir Hamilton thanks for all the context! I'm a little swamped with release management work this week, and haven't had a chance to study your explanation in detail, but perhaps someone else will be able to. If not, please be encouraged to remind me of this thread in a couple weeks.

## "more topics" loading

*2022-10-21 to 2022-11-02 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/.22more.20topics.22.20loading/with/1453500)*

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-10-21 05:16 UTC

Sometimes the "more topics" view takes a while to load. When this happens, the search box doesn't load until everything is loaded.

Would it be possible for the search box to load first? If you start using it before all the topics are loaded, would it only filter the topics that have loaded already?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-21 22:52 UTC

From reading the code, we do the network call in parallel with after it's attempted to render the view. So I think whatever is slow here is likely a frontend-side performance issue (worth investigating via a profiler).

(I think we have logic that hides that input while rebuilding the region, so we may be able to remove that logic, but probably better would be to figure out why this can be slow)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-21 22:57 UTC

OK having briefly profiled this, I think the problem is basically that we're not using a paginated system for the post-"more topics" display; so if you're looking at a stream like this one with 1500 topics, we're inserting 1000 rows into the DOM, and then the browser takes a few hundred milliseconds painting all of those rows in the DOM.

I would not be surprised if this turns out to be a regression in some sense -- it's very possible that CSS changes have increased the cost from 0.1ms per row to 0.3ms per row.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-21 22:58 UTC

But likely the thing we should do is use something like our our `list_widget` library for this component, so that we only have the ~100 most recent topics rendered in the DOM before you scroll down, without forcing users to experience an explicit pagination UI; that would make entering the view ~15x faster.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-21 23:02 UTC

I think there is another bug here -- somehow we're doing an additional paint after showing the content before showing the search box; I can't readily figure out why.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-21 23:09 UTC

I think probably the search box flickering is somehow related to this sequence removing and then re-adding it in the wrong; not entirely sure as I'm out of time for debugging. It's possible just swapping the order of those last two steps would fix that detail, and possible it won't because `.append` is what is adding the search box to the DOM.
```
        const replace_content = (html) => {                                                              
            this.remove();                                                                               
            this.$parent_elem.append(html);                                                              
            this.update_topic_search_input();                                                            
        };                                                                                               
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-10-22 03:07 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> But likely the thing we should do is use something like our our `list_widget` library for this component, so that we only have the ~100 most recent topics rendered in the DOM before you scroll down, without forcing users to experience an explicit pagination UI; that would make entering the view ~15x …

FYI, although Zulip’s initial implementation probably predates the wide spreading of this idea, it’s now a standard concept known as “virtual scrolling”, which is a useful keyword to know about when evaluating modern libraries and frameworks we might want to adopt.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-31 23:43 UTC

Does anyone have time to looking at fixing this lag over the next week? It is pretty noticable, and also @Alya Abbott pointed out to me today, it's pretty annoying in that the filter box appearing later means it can cause what you were able to click on to shift downwards a row.

## watchdog setInterval interaction

*2022-11-10 to 2022-11-10 · 2 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/watchdog.20setInterval.20interaction/with/1462485)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-10 20:54 UTC

So I realized we probably have a second setInterval bug similar to the one discussed in #**production help>overriding RATE_LIMITING_RULES**; it's not uncommon to see "Restarting get_events due to unsuspend" happen 50 times in a row, which presumably has the same root cause of chrome calling `setInterval` a large number of times all at once. 

Thinking about this more, I think one possibility is that the sequence is that you unsuspend the device, but to save power, the browser doesn't process the Zulip window's timer events until the user actually clicks into that window, and they can accumulate during that time?

@Sahil Batra FYI.

[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/a1/-exi4WXoC2EHHxXYDCohRSlb/image.png)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-10 20:54 UTC

The thing which I don't understand is how this code ends up calling the check more than once in a row; it would seem that `new_time` would get updated after the first instance, and the rest of a bunch of queued requests would be ignored...

``` js
export function check_for_unsuspend(): void {                               
    const new_time = Date.now();                                            
    if (new_time - watchdog_time > 20000) {                                 
        // 20 seconds.                                                      
        // Defensively reset watchdog_time here in case there's an          
        // exception in one of the event handlers                           
        watchdog_time = new_time;                                           
        // Our app's JS wasn't running, which probably means the machine was
        // asleep.                                                          
        for (const callback of unsuspend_callbacks) {                       
            callback();                                                     
        }                                                                   
    }                                                                       
    watchdog_time = new_time;                                               
}                                                                           
                                                                            
export function on_unsuspend(f: () => void): void {                         
    unsuspend_callbacks.push(f);                                            
}                                                                           
                                                                            
setInterval(check_for_unsuspend, 5000);                                     
```

    const pos = $textarea.caret();
    let before_str = $textarea.val().slice(0, pos);

    // If before_str ends with a newline, trim all trailing newlines from it
    if (before_str.endsWith("\n")) {
        before_str = before_str.trimEnd();
    }

    // If after_str starts with a newline, trim all leading newlines from it
    if (after_str.startsWith("\n")) {

$ git grep '<h6' static/templates/ templates/zerver/
$ git grep '<h5' static/templates/ templates/zerver/
static/templates/settings/organization_profile_admin.hbs:                <h5 class="realm-logo-title">{{t 'Day logo' }}</h5>
static/templates/settings/organization_profile_admin.hbs:                <h5 class="realm-logo-title">{{t 'Night logo' }}</h5>

Generally our goal is to eliminate all CSS reset so that one can design individual components without needing to think about overriding CSS that's applied to all `input` elements -- this makes it a lot easier to do design work, since you just need to specify the properties you want, not also undo CSS that isn't associated with a CSS class.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-11-30 18:45 UTC

I am extremely suspicious of any attempt to factor out “common” CSS rules across more than one component. That always makes it difficult to verify that a change you want to make to those rules has the intended effect across all the various components it affects.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-11-30 18:49 UTC

As programmers we’ve all been taught that code duplication is evil, but the truth is that while a good abstraction is better than duplication, a *bad* abstraction usually ends up being *much worse*. And in CSS, there are no good abstractions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-30 18:49 UTC

Yeah, and that sort of action-at-a-distance, in turn, makes it hard to refactor anything. (A big part of the reason removing Bootstrap is a pain is because we need to track down every element that happens to inherit that CSS and verify it).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-30 18:50 UTC

One thing that we can probably do is define some components that explicitly extend the CSS of another component. But I think it's not worth stressing much about a bit of code duplication. 

The type of CSS that we're going to end up duplicating here is stuff like this (for radio inputs): 

```
            width: auto;
            cursor: pointer;
            margin: 4px 0 0;

            &:focus {
                outline: 1px dotted hsl(0, 0%, 20%);
                outline: 5px auto -webkit-focus-ring-color;
                outline-offset: -2px;
            }
```

I think it's possible much of that class of CSS could just be deleted; I'd kinda be surprised if `cursor: pointer` (switching to `cursor: not-allowed` if disabled) isn't in the default browser user agent stylesheet for this radio inputs.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-30 18:52 UTC

But I think if we're trying to be expedient, it's better to have that sort of CSS explicitly on a component, so that if we redesign the element, we can just replace that with new CSS we've tested in isolation; doing so means we can clean up our CSS naturally as part of redesign work.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-12-01 07:52 UTC

Nah. The consequences of forgetting a local `border-radius` rule is that you’ll immediately notice that the thing you’re currently working on looks wrong, so you’ll edit it and fix it. Meanwhile, the consequences of relying on global CSS action at a distance are subtle and devastating to large-scale maintainability. That’s the main reason we’ve been having so much trouble getting the redesign project off the ground. Just don’t.

    await page.waitForSelector(

## success and failure notice in settings UI

*2022-11-25 to 2022-11-29 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/success.20and.20failure.20notice.20in.20settings.20UI/with/1469694)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-11-25 17:06 UTC

The current success and failure notices shown in settings UI get weird in some cases when the message is long or on small screen sizes.

#23653 is one example, where the success message gets long due to long email.

For failure cases, we show message in modal in cases where modal is used to complete the action, but there are still some cases when the message is shown besides the heading. Though, we hide UI elements appropriately to not allow actions that are not allowed, but still race conditions can return error to the client. Sharing an example screenshot below where the error message is long and the `Add custom profile field` button also moves down.
[Normal window width](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/2f/DxGoeJB0RH7oGIS_AFtaLfMd/Screenshot-from-2022-11-25-22-09-50.png)
[Small window width](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/7c/fq2PJFo42idZHkxpdixGvOCx/Screenshot-from-2022-11-25-22-10-28.png)

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-11-25 17:23 UTC

I don't think clipping the messages would be good solution especially in case of error messages, as it may confuse the users due to incomplete information. Another possible solution could be to show the message in a separate line (and not in the same line as heading) and allow message to have multiple lines. Would to love hear to other ideas or feedback.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-28 21:35 UTC

I think probably having the full error messages be on a separate line after the heading might be the simplest option? I'm not sure how best to do it; one version would be "Save failed" stays in the heading line but if there's an additional message, that appears on its own line rather than after a `:`. I'm not sure though; @Alya Abbott may have thoughts on other changes to our patterns that might impact what makes sense here.

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-11-29 00:21 UTC

As discussed a bit on the linked PR, I think the advantage of having the message be on the same line as the heading is that it avoids unnecessary up-down motion. But this tradeoff doesn't seem worth it when the result is recurring alignment bugs.

**Alya Abbott** · 2022-11-29 00:22 UTC

Having a small whitelist of short notices that can go on the same line as the heading, and putting everything else on its own line below, could be a reasonable compromise.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-29 19:41 UTC

As a general rule, we try to avoid having common error messages at all; for example, avoiding letting you select more things than you're allowed to select (so that only in the event of a race or similar would you see a longer error message like this one).

**css: Use grid layout for messages.**

- Using grid layout moves us away from fixed widths and position for items where possible, which will make it easier to make messagebox changes without breaking formatting.
- Visual changes expected in this commit:
    - When the action buttons overlap the message content, it will no longer visually overlap but completely cut off the content — which is good, but means the messages can’t be as wide on narrow width views. There’s a slight improvement to this in an upcoming commit.
    - `/me` is temporarily broken (maybe we want to merge the /me fix with this commit?)

**message: Hide first action button on narrow widths.**

- Fixes #19759
- Before grid, there was overlap of action buttons and text (photo 1). With grid, there was just very little space for messages (photo 2). With this commit, the message gets a bit more space (photo 3).
- This helps us add more width to the content column of message on narrow widths. Note that it will still always be less than before grid, since we are explicitly preventing overlap.

## add globe icon in Web-public streams

*2022-12-04 to 2022-12-13 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/add.20globe.20icon.20in.20Web-public.20streams/with/1474016)*

**Sameep Aher** · 2022-12-04 19:02 UTC

Issue: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/23496
PR: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/23529

The second part of the issue states that ```Web-public streams should be shown with a globe icon, rather than a #```.

As suggested by @Tim Abbott  , we can directly use ```static/templates/stream_privacy.hbs``` for the icon bit. So I tried directly using ```{{>stream_privacy}}``` in ```static/templates/invite_subscription.hbs``` for rendering the icons.

Following this procedure leads to - 

[Screenshot_12.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/79/6ESq-JRf3fiVefozjkP8uCzR/Screenshot_12.png)

Reason for checkbox surrounding the hashtag icon - ```static/styles/components.css``` has a property ```border: 1px solid hsla(0, 0%, 0%, 0.6)``` under the ```span``` tag which is used to render the hashtag icon (```<span class="hashtag"></span>``` ) in ```static/templates/stream_privacy.hbs```.

One fix I can make is instead of using the ```span``` tag (with a class ```hashtag```) in ```static/templates/stream_privacy.hbs``` we can directly use ```#``` (without the ```span```) which leads to - 

[Screenshot_13.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/c3/o8SdyE56DhZE0xPww07XCVDQ/Screenshot_13.png)

Notice there’s a space after ```#```.

Some relevant parts of code for the above mentioned solution are - 

1) ```static/templates/stream_privacy.hbs``` - 

```
{{#if invite_only}}
<i class="fa fa-lock" aria-hidden="true"></i>
{{else if is_web_public}}
<i class="zulip-icon zulip-icon-globe" aria-hidden="true"></i>
{{else}}
#
{{/if}}
```

2) ```static/templates/invite_subscription.hbs``` - 

```
{{>stream_privacy}} {{name}}
```

**Please let me know if this works or not.**

**Sameep Aher** · 2022-12-04 19:10 UTC

Another fix I considered was conditionally rendering icons (```invite_only``` and ```is_web_public```) from ```static/templates/stream_privacy.hbs``` and using ```#``` in ```static/templates/invite_subscription.hbs``` itself (to avoid the space between # and name of the stream). 

The code in ```static/templates/invite_subscription.hbs``` looks like - 

```

*2022-12-14 to 2022-12-15 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/typeahead.2Ftextcomplete.3A.20event.20handling/with/1479731)*

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-14 06:58 UTC

As I outlined in #**frontend>typeahead**, I'm testing [Textcomplete](https://github.com/yuku/textcomplete). It was trivial to add our custom handler for Escape: `textarea_editor.on('esc', listener);`.

While trying to implement our `>` based stream+topic typeahead, I encountered some issues where it looks like the data model falls apart.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-14 07:00 UTC

It was easy to get the library to throw an event for `>` by extending a class:

```js
class ZTextareaEditor extends TextareaEditor {
    getCode(e) {
        if (e.keyCode === 190 && e.shiftKey) {
            this.emitNextEvent();
        }
        return super.getCode(e);
      }
      emitNextEvent() {
        const event = createCustomEvent("next", { cancelable: true })
        this.emit("next", event)
        return event
      }
}
```

However, once we get to processing that event, our tools get limited.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-14 07:01 UTC

```js
class ZTextcomplete extends Textcomplete {
    startListening() {
        super.startListening()
        console.log(this);
        const handleNext = this.handleNext.bind(this);
        this.editor.on("next", handleNext)
    }
    handleNext(e) {
        const beforeCursor = this.editor.getBeforeCursor();
        const re = /\B#([\-+\w]*)$/;
        if (re.test(beforeCursor)) {
            // Yep, we're in a stream typeahead; pretend we pressed enter and selected the stream.
            this.handleEnter(e);
            // now, do some text parsing on this.editor and trigger a
            // change event, calling the next typeahead in line
        }
    }
}
```

There's no straightforward way to tell the renderer to render the final selection full in one mode (Enter) and partially in the other (>). Which means, we'll have to resort to string parsing again. I'm sure this library can get us 90% of the way to our current setup, but our requirements are somewhat unique at this point IMO.

Maybe using this library's architecture as a base, and rolling our own solution in Typescript is the best bet?

## undo friendly typeahead

*2022-12-14 to 2022-12-19 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/undo.20friendly.20typeahead/with/1479895)*

**Nehal Sharma** · 2022-12-14 18:26 UTC

This is to discuss possible solutions in reference to #14311 (Autocomplete breaks undo)

Following up with @Tim Abbott's suggestion in an issue comment, I replaced the 1 problematic line `this.$element.val(this.updater(val, e)).trigger("change");` with the following piece of code:
```js
const new_content = this.updater(val, e);
replace(this.$element[0], this.$element.val(), () => new_content, "after-replacement");
```
where `replace` is a method from the undo friendly `text-field-edit` module.

This results in the following behaviour (note that the typeahead completion is followed by hitting `ctrl+Z` repeatedly):
[Untitled.mp4](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/2b/6x5JAch_vn3wqLbW-ZPMAEdz/Untitled.mp4) 

The reason that the entire text is highlighted when undoing the typeahead is that the `updater()` function in typeahead returns the entire updated new value for the textarea, and so the entire value for the textarea is reset instead of changing only the autocompleted text (which would, for example just change `#a` to `#**announce**` and highlight just that). If this highlighting issue is not too big a deal, then this solution should work well enough.

However, if we would like only the autocompleted part to be highlighted while undoing, that would mean having to change the API of typeahead to have the updater function, which is passed in as a parameter, return the both text to be replaced / autocompleted and the replacement (autocompleted), instead of the entire value of the textarea after replacement. That is, the change wouldn't be local to the typeahead module, and all the updater functions that are passed to it would have to changed.

Slightly unrelated to the question, but I wonder the current code triggers the "change" event after resetting the textarea's value. I don't see any noticeable changes on removing that, so would be nice if someone could shed light on that!

FYI @Rohitt Vashishtha @Tim Abbott

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-14 18:41 UTC

It shouldn't be too hard to quickly diff the before and after strings just before updating, right? We don't do any complex operations on the text, so the beginning and possibly the end of the string would remain static.

**Nehal Sharma** · 2022-12-14 20:40 UTC

Diffing them did strike me, but I can't seem to find a simple way to do that... Any suggestions @Rohitt Vashishtha ?

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-14 20:45 UTC

There must be a more elegant way for this, but to be clear, the most complex case of our typeahead changes is a removal of some text going from `#**stream** ` to `#**stream>`.

So, if you just write a loop that goes

```
let common_upto = 0;
for (i=0,i<min(before.length, after.length;i++) {
if (before[i] === after[i]) common_upto = i;
}
```
Even this would cover 90% of the cases where people's cursors are at the end of the string and the typeahead changes something near the end.

Edit: formatting is hard on mobile.

**Nehal Sharma** · 2022-12-14 20:55 UTC

Oh right, thanks, this is a great starting point

**Nehal Sharma** · 2022-12-14 22:18 UTC

This is what I was able to come up with:
```javascript
function get_string_diff(string1, string2) {
    // This function gets the diff between 2 strings. For example, the
    // diff between "#ann" and "#**announce**" is "ann" and "**announce**"
    const length_diff = string2.length - string1.length;

    let forward_same_till = -1;
    for(let i = 0; i < Math.min(string1.length, string2.length); i++) {
      if (string1.charAt(i) === string2.charAt(i)) {
        forward_same_till = i
      } else {
        break;
      }
    }

    let backward_same_till = string1.length;
    for(let i = string1.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
      if (string1.charAt(i) === string2.charAt(i + length_diff)) {
        backward_same_till = i
      } else {
        break;
      }
    }
    const diff1 = string1.substring(forward_same_till+1, backward_same_till);
    const diff2 = string2.substring(forward_same_till+1, backward_same_till+length_diff)
    return [diff1, diff2];
  }
```
And this can be used like:
```javascript
const [to_replace, replacement] = get_string_diff(this.$element.val(), this.updater(val, e))
if (to_replace.length) {
  // replace text as needed then place cursor right after it
  replace(this.$element[0], to_replace, () => replacement, "after-replacement");
} else {
  // simply insert text at the cursor if there is nothing to be replaced
  insert(this.$element[0], replacement)
}
```
This works well, except in the common case of there being multiple substrings same as `to_replace`. And `text-field-edit`'s `replace` method doesn't seem to provide a way to replace at a specific index (afaik). :sad: 

I'll try to figure this out tomorrow but until then any ideas would be really helpful!

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-12-14 22:41 UTC

Call [`setSelectionRange()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLInputElement/setSelectionRange) and then use `insert`.

I'm starting some work on forking [textcomplete](https://github.com/yuku/textcomplete) to fit Zulip better, calling it Zcomplete unless a better inspiration strikes.. Looking at the activity level of that project, I'm not inclined to create PRs to upstream because we might want to change the internals quite significantly.

Also, I'm linking the relevant discussion threads on CZO here for later reference:

- #**frontend>typeahead**
- #**frontend>typeahead/textcomplete: always-visible and focus issue** 
- #**frontend>typeahead/textcomplete: event handling** 
- #**frontend>typeahead/textcomplete: DOM changes**

I'm deciding between two approaches:

1. Keep `zcomplete` as a separate repo from `zulip/zulip`.
2. Import this code into `zulip/zulip`.

I suppose both approaches have their pros and cons. I'm tempted to develop zcomplete inside zulip/zulip because of our existing linters etc, as well as possibility to make modifications faster.

If we want to later release this library back to the community, we can still do that if we just ensure zcomplete doesn't use any Zulip specific functions or terminologies.

Thoughts?

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-16 18:01 UTC

A somewhat comprehensive list of features I'm targeting, in addition to what Textcomplete currently offers:

1. Support textareas, inputs and contenteditables.
2. Support custom header and footer htmls.
3. Follow cursor position without jumping around on input.
4. Allow custom completion triggers (like our `>` for topic completion.
5. Allow showing the typeahead on focus, without typing an characters.
6. Use something like Textcomplete's Strategies to keep code pieces of different types of typeaheads closer.
7. Use Typescript.
8. Add unit tests. (Textcomplete currently doesn't have them at all).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-07 23:25 UTC

Well the question in my mind was whether the rendering of RTL messages is correct.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-07 23:26 UTC

I would treat `rtl.js` as a block box; @Shayan Toqraee wrote it and may be able to help if we need to change something.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-07 23:28 UTC

I suppose it's possible we should try to adjust the logic to better handle the case where you've just got RTL in a name at the start of a mention block.... but fundamentally the whole thing is a heuristic, and I'm not entirely sure there's a good answer.

I guess @Shayan Toqraee FYI in case you have ideas.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-01-09 09:54 UTC

There’s no way that a low-level Unicode algorithm with character-specific data that hasn’t been maintained in six years is still correct. We should be looking at browser APIs and modern libraries to replace it. [bidi-js](https://www.npmjs.com/package/bidi-js) is one candidate, although it would be better if we can figure out how to make HTML and CSS do the right thing for us without explicit checks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-09 19:00 UTC

I think we kinda need to make a determination for where we think a given message is RTL, if we want to handle situations like mentioning someone with an RTL name in a LTR sentence.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-09 19:00 UTC

But switching to that library for the Unicode part sounds good as a step forward.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-01-09 20:14 UTC

Why do we need to make that determination, instead of letting the browser decide automatically? We probably want [`unicode-bidi: isolate`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/unicode-bidi) for mentions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-09 20:39 UTC

I think it's in order to make a bunch of `rendered_markdown` style changes like this:
```
    /* Swap the left and right margins of bullets for Right-To-Left languages */
    &.rtl ul {                                                                  
        margin-right: 20px;                                                     
        margin-left: 0;                                                         
    }                                                                           
```

I haven't thought about this in years, but there's a few dozen rules of that form intended to make message-interior formatting not look broken (by basically just reflecting margins and the like), and have a consistent idea for "is this message RTL or LTR", so you don't have weird alternation between paragraphs because one of them happened to only contain digits or a URL or something.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-09 20:41 UTC

(I'm pretty sure the only thing we do for RTL is toggling that `rtl` class, in case that information is helpful.)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-01-09 20:43 UTC

That makes sense as a historical motivation, but now we have `margin-inline-start` and `margin-inline-end` for that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-10 23:50 UTC

Yeah, looks like that's been around since 2020, or earlier under a `-webkit` type name, so should be usable.

The markdown syntax has to be parsed up to the point that the first "**real**" directional character is found (which is used to determine the message direction). And it should be done efficiently. **Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-10 23:43 UTC

@Evy this is a good question. I don't think you posted a link to the specific files involved, which would be helpful in answering.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-10 23:43 UTC

In general, it is a goal for us to have 100% node test coverage on JS data layer modules. There is no such goal for UI modules, in part because it is hard to do non-shallow testing on them, and the time writing shallow tests on UI code might be better spent doing manual testing of it or other architectural work to make the thing work well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-10 23:44 UTC

(And you never really get to skip manual testing for UI code, because there's CSS/visual issues to consider)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-10 23:47 UTC

So one possibility is to just add this file to the list of files excluded from wanting 100% coverage.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-10 23:48 UTC

(The tooling could better communicate this somehow, but I do think the default of asking for 100% coverage on new files makes sense, since often new files are data modules and we do often want to enforce that they get tests).

@Evy yeah I think it's fine to do exclusions for those files.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-20 23:44 UTC

In general, I care a lot about node tests that verify logic -- things like the `filter.js` test suite. 

Most testing of jQuery stuff doesn't actually verify much of value -- the reason to write tests with jQuery stubs is if we have a function with logic that we do want to test that has some jQuery side effects, and this is the best way to test that logic (It's not always easy to refactor to separate the logic from rendering code).

## new-style CSS class

*2023-01-28 to 2023-06-09 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/new-style.20CSS.20class/with/1498423)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-28 01:09 UTC

So I'd like to talk about cleaning up the mess that is the `new-style` CSS class. The background is that some components that were changed in a 2017 era redesign were wrapped with this class to avoid some CSS changes that were made at the time from applying incorrectly. I was never really happy with the concept, but it is what it is. In any case, there's a few things that it is used for:

* Apparently, the  `.tab-switcher` component, in `app_components.css`, are needlessly defined inside an outer `.new-style` block. We should remove that logic -- if we want a tab switcher, we should just get our standard tab switcher without requiring the developer to add a weird `new-style` class in something containing it. This is probably a trivial change to make the `.tab-switcher` CSS top-level.
* Apparently we have a CSS reset block of this form: `.new-style input[type="text"] {`. @Sahil Batra you should aim to remove this while removing the Bootstrap CSS reset for those inputs.
* The styling for our standard Zulip checkboxes is apparently at its outer layer `.new-style label.checkbox`. I think we can probably just drop the outer `new-style` there while doing Bootstrap removal here, since the `checkbox` CSS class is a Bootstrap thing; the simplest plan might be just to move to a world where `.checkbox` be the CSS class name for our standard checkboxes, but have the CSS for it be entirely in one place in `.components.css`, and not be inside a `new-style` block.
* There's a `.button` class that needs a similar investigation to the above.
* A few other things that we can manage once the above are done.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-06-06 13:55 UTC

So as of this morning, I did some grepping for `new-style` in the frontend files, and I found that we have:

* 34 instances in `templates/`
* 34 instances in `web/templates/`
* 16 instances in `web/styles/`
* 0 instances in `web/src/`(thankfully)

Some of those instances are quite old, and presumably unrelated to the current, ongoing redesign. For example, `templates/zerver/reset.html` uses a `new-style` class introduced in a commit from May of 2017.

As just that one commit reveals, of course, `new-style` has a very limited shelf life, and anticipates and invites abominations like a future `new-new-style` class.

I wanted to open up this topic to discuss how we might do two things:

1) Clean the codebase of all existing references to `new-style` while there are still relatively few of them
2) Come up with an alternate plan for introducing/isolating new styles/structures while proceeding with the redesign

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-06-06 16:28 UTC

The count in CSS files is deceptive because of CSS nesting. After nesting expansion, there are 113 affected rules.

**Notification Bot** · 2023-06-08 16:57 UTC

2 messages were moved here from #**frontend>about that .new-style class...** by @Karl Stolley.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-06-09 23:08 UTC

I don't think we need to come up with a special plan for managing this sort of thing -- we should be able to just rip it out in favor of semantically named things like `.settings-checkbox` and `.settings-button` -- `new-style` was intended to be a temporary hack circa 2018 that we were going to remove a few months later, but the project it was part of got interrupted. 

We gave something a name of that form once 5 years ago, I wasn't happy with it at the time, but because we were in a rush (and a much smaller team/community) I allowed it to be merged with the promise it'd go away, and then the work to make it go away didn't happen.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-06-09 23:10 UTC

The naming pattern I like to do if we end up having two versions of something, and where we for some technical or readability reason want the new thing to get the name the old thing currently has, is to rename the existing one we're trying to get rid of something like `legacy_foo` and then add the new thing called `foo`, and that way you never end up in a state where there's a thing misleadingly called `new_foo`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-06-09 23:13 UTC

But most of the time the right model is to just have components or pseudocomponents that have a clear name and CSS scope, and then when you want to change the styles, just change the CSS for that component, and not try to have new/old versions of something, which is basically a thing you only do in a CSS reset world where you've got styles on `<button>` as part of the old design that you need to override.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-06-09 23:13 UTC

(The main actual problem `new-style` was created to address was overriding Bootstrap CSS reset styles.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:27 UTC

@Evy yeah, that's a good question. I think there's basically the following situations I can articule where we want to do this:
* When you click something in a popover whose function is to add content to the compose box. For example, if you click the "Quote and reply" button in a message popover, we want that to leave the compose box focused. Ideally, those individual click handlers would manage doing the focus for us.
* Probably also when you click something that copies something -- like the "Copy mention syntax" item in user popovers. Probably it would also be reasonable for those individual click handlers to be responsible for adjusting focus if required, though it's possible some of them don't do that because of this code existing.
* The thing which motivated this hacky block of code, which is that if you click a link with `target=_blank` somewhere in the app, that opens the link in a new window, the browser's default behavior will move the window's focus to the element you clicked, rather than the compose box, which ends up being very annoying -- if you click back into your Zulip tab and then hit Enter, for example, that Enter will reopen the link you just clicked. Probably "a link inside a `rendered_markdown` CSS class" is an effective definition for this category -- that'll cover any user content links appearing in the app.
* If you click a link somewhere in the app that navigates, that may also adjust focus away from the compose box, but that may be what users expect in cases where doing so does not outright close the compose box; in any case, that logic can theoretically live in the `narrow.js` code path.
* Possibly some other things that I haven't thought about.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:29 UTC

So my theory would be that we should make the hacky refocusing logic only apply to `.rendered_markdown a`, and then test basically spend an hour testing all the buttons in the app's main screen and in the ~8 main screen popovers and see if any of them behave differently following that change, make a list, and decide if we need to fix any click handlers that might be in those first couple categories to do something with compose box focus.

## clean_user_content_links perf

*2023-02-01 to 2023-05-02 · 31 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/clean_user_content_links.20perf/with/1500278)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-01 00:47 UTC

So I had a bad experience just now where using the `U` keyboard shortcut in a topic with 3 total messages took a visibly long time to update. Profiling where the time is going, it appears that a very large chunk is `clean_user_content_links`:

[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/15/RAtinO-e-3IfimaZB6XtsNIQ/image.png)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-01 00:49 UTC

I think what's happening is:
* "mark as unread" is triggering a full rerender of the "All messages" view, which isn't even visible
* `clean_user_content_links` seems to be quite expensive on a rerender, even though it should in theory be possible for it to be a pure function of the message's content and thus be a noop during this class of rerender.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-01 00:52 UTC

It looks like a large portion of the time is just `parseFromString`, i.e. work that will be hard to avoid, but maybe `clean_user_content_links` could just have a local memory cache of the `string => output` it has done in the current session?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-01 00:55 UTC

We should open an issue to avoid the expensive full rerender for now reason, but I think a simple cache here might be a significant and easy improvement, if we can tune to not leak memory (which I imagine any basic caching library would let us configure an expiry policy). @Anders Kaseorg does that sound like a reasonable design?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-02-01 01:17 UTC

Caches come with their own problems, and should be the last plan, not the first. Why are we rerendering everything?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-02-01 01:22 UTC

(This is the kind of issue we wouldn’t even have to think about if we were on a reactive framework.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 00:53 UTC

I'm pretty sure we're rerendering everything because we were lazy when adding the feature and someone added an explicit global rerender -- as I said, we should fix that as a separate issue coming from this investigation: #24263. But that will just fix this symptom of the fact that 40% of the time we spend rendering a message feed is in `clean_user_content_links`.

A cache would improve performance for rendering any messages that we've rendered before in the current session -- a reactive framework isn't going to take care of that sort of thing for us -- a cache is the standard solution to that class of problem.

And `clean_user_content_links` is a pretty clean interface for caching -- it takes a string and returns a string.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-21 22:52 UTC

I moved some messages about #24263 implementation details (avoiding a rerender in this case) to #**frontend>#24263 help** to avoid them distracting from the discussion of the caching question. I continue to think that a cache for this function, which is expensive and turns a string into another string (for most inputs, I'm pretty sure it's essentially a whitespace mutating identity function) would improve performance of rendering messages that we've previously rendered (whether in the current view or other views) without obvious downsides.

So I think we should look at adding an in-memory cache for this function again. I did some profiling in #**design** on chat.zulip.org, using `s/S` to switch between a view showing the full stream, after noticing that switching to show the full stream was surprisingly slow.

*2023-02-01 to 2023-02-02 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/New.20compose.20banners.20for.20muted.20topics/with/1500610)*

**Sahil Singh** · 2023-02-01 15:26 UTC

I have been investigating issue [#24246](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/24246) and I believe that the implementation of banners for muted topics or streams can be achieved by modifying the ```get_local_notify_mix_reason()``` function within the ```notifications.js``` file.
```
if ($row.length > 0) {
        // If our message is in the current message list, we do
        // not have a mix, so we are happy.
        if (message.type === "stream" && user_topics.is_topic_muted(message.stream_id, message.topic)) {
            return $t({defaultMessage: "Your message was sent to a topic you have muted. You can unmute the topic to receive notifications about new messages."});
        }
    
        if (message.type === "stream" && stream_data.is_muted(message.stream_id)) {
            return $t({defaultMessage: "Your message was sent to a stream you have muted. You can unmute the topic to receive notifications about new messages."});
        }

        return undefined;
    }
```

I suspect that about half of these references are things where we mean "Is recent topics the current center pane, because we're going to do some recent topics thing" and the other half are where we mean "is a message feed visible, because we need to know if we need to rerender it".

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 20:44 UTC

We need to convert the latter category into a function that asks that question precisely, both for readability and because that new function should be extended to handle the inbox view case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 20:47 UTC

So I propose we add something like `narrow_state.is_message_feed_visible` that works very similarly to `recent_topics_util.is_visible` in terms of accessing a JavaScript variable (so we don't need to think about DOM querying costs when accessing it) and is maintained in `narrow.activate` and other functions that mutate the center pane.

I guess another idea would be to make a simple `main_panel_state.js` that holds a bundle all functions related to "What type of view is present in the center pane".

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 20:48 UTC

export function update_bot_settings_tip() {
    const permission_type = bot_creation_policy_values;
    const personal_settings_tip_element = $("#personal-bot-settings-tip");
    const org_settings_tip_element = $("#admin-bot-settings-tip");
    let for_org_settings = false;

    if (page_params.realm_bot_creation_policy === permission_type.admins_only.code) {
        tip_text = $t({

        });
    } else if (page_params.realm_bot_creation_policy === permission_type.restricted.code) {
        tip_text = $t({defaultMessage: "Only organization administrators can add generic bots."});
    } else {
        tip_text = $t({defaultMessage: "Anyone in this organization can bots."});
        for_org_settings = true;
    }

    org_settings_tip_element.text(tip_text);
    personal_settings_tip_element.text(tip_text);

    if (page_params.is_admin) {
        org_settings_tip_element.show();
    } else if (for_org_settings) {
        org_settings_tip_element.hide();
    } else {
        org_settings_tip_element.show();
        personal_settings_tip_element.show();
    }
}

## Tippy appentTo `parent` vs `body` as default

*2023-03-02 to 2023-03-02 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Tippy.20appentTo.20.60parent.60.20vs.20.60body.60.20as.20default/with/1516831)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-03-02 13:47 UTC

The main benefit of having the tooltip appended to `parent` as a default is that the tooltip cleanly removes itself from DOM when the parent element is hidden or destroyed. This is not the case for tooltips attached to `body` for which we rely on the browser to send a signal to tippy to hide the tooltip, in which we have seen problems in the past like the ones for the right sidebar user list.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-03-02 13:48 UTC

This is reply to Tim's comment [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/24459#issuecomment-1451025069):
> One thing I noted in the new comments is I'm not sure whether the appendTo of "parent" is the right default -- we've changed that to body manually for like a dozen specific tooltips at this point to work around problems caused by it, and I'm not sure under what circumstances we would prefer the parent default -- maybe you can start a #frontend thread on this.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-03-02 13:49 UTC

So, as a default `parent` makes sense to avoid tooltips going wild as much as possible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-03-02 20:07 UTC

Ok, that is a good motivation; though maybe there's a better way to fix that orphaning problem. In the meantime, I guess we should update the comment to explain that problem statement and maybe how to check do that when using the body placement instead?

## CSS selector refactoring

*2023-03-14 to 2023-03-23 · 23 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/CSS.20selector.20refactoring/with/1524458)*

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-03-14 18:39 UTC

I’d be interested to contribute a refactoring of the codebase’s CSS, which I think would be an asset to the ongoing redesign efforts. 

I’d start by addressing inconsistencies around selector style and nesting. That work would pave the way for later progress into the thornier issue of the order and grouping of properties, and their consolidation.

I’m very early in my thinking (and new to the project!), but I’m envisioning something like this:

1. **Work towards a uniform class- and ID-selector style**: There is a mix of hyphens (-, aka kebab-case) and underscores (_, aka snake_case) in multi-name classes and IDs in the codebase. Both styles can be found side-by-side even in the same component file. [The config for stylelint](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/stylelint.config.js) sidesteps this issue, but the “yet” in the comment there—`Disable standard rules we don't comply with yet`—suggests the Zulip project intends to move toward stylelint’s standard kebab-case.
2. **Work towards uniform use of postcss-nested**: Within a single CSS file, some selectors are nested, while others are written out longhand as descendent selectors (e.g., the selector `.private-message .message_reactions .message_reaction` in [`reactions.css`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/web/styles/reactions.css#L117)). That represents another consistency issue, but it also impacts the ease of hunting down and reasoning about the styles a selector will apply.

Both of those should be reflected in expanded guidance in [the HTML/CSS portion of the code style guide](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing/code-style.html#html-css).

I’m planning to open a draft PR illustrating how this work could proceed, but I wanted to ask the community: Are there any gotchas I ought to be aware of, including parallel work on refactoring the CSS?

Thanks, everyone.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 19:50 UTC

Those surface-level details actually have very little to do with the core maintainability problems in our CSS. The main problem is that our CSS is not modular. We have two main sources of anti-modularity:

1. Basically all of our styles are entangled with the global defaults inherited from our forked copy of Bootstrap v2. There is an ongoing effort to remove Bootstrap that has made significant progress but still has a ways to go.
2. Long and nested selectors mean that lots of our CSS is overly context-sensitive. This inhibits our ability to refactor things, because many seemingly reasonable DOM changes have unpredictable non-local effects. It also prevents us from testing components in isolation. I think that overuse of nesting has actually contributed to this problem (#**frontend>CSS nesting**).

A style guide may be able to help with these problems, but it needs to be designed with real modularity in mind and not just surface-level tidiness.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 19:56 UTC

A better solution would be to use CSS modules or a component-scoped style system to *enforce* a discipline that limits the non-local effects of styling. (I flippantly remarked in the office—but still wholeheartedly believe—that *nobody wants their stylesheets to cascade!*)

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-03-14 20:56 UTC

Thank you for your response and detailed thoughts here, Anders!

100% agreed that the work I’m proposing will not by itself solve the modularity issues you mentioned. That’s a separate problem.

I do think that cleaning up existing CSS offers two benefits to the project in approaching the modularity problem, though:

1. It should make it easier to salvage and replicate existing styles to a new modular system, whatever that might be
2. It should make it easier to compare the benefits and drawbacks of any new modular system—just by seeing what’s there, and comparing it against a new modular form

It might help me understand things better if I understood the plan for implementing the redesign: would that take place as part of introducing a new modular system? Or would the modular system be put in place first? Last?

Also, has the core team talked at all about [CSS `@layer` rules](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer)? I could imagine that as a part of a longer-term solution—and one that might also make it less of a pain point to clear out the remaining vestiges of the Bootstrap CSS.

I like your flippant but cogent observation that nobody wants their stylesheets to cascade :) But the cascade is obviously going to happen, and it’s a fundamental part of how CSS behaves. I prefer to try to work with the cascade, rather than tool it out of existence.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 21:29 UTC

`@layer` is too new to have good browser support yet. And although it would give us a bit more control over ordering and specificity of those global rules, we really want to remove them completely.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-03-14 21:34 UTC

Oh, it's definitely new--but I like to think about where CSS is going (the [PostCSS polyfill seems promising, too](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@csstools/postcss-cascade-layers)).

Is there a particular solution you're leaning towards or advocating for?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 21:38 UTC

I’m still open to suggestions, but the kinds of solutions I’m interested in are [CSS modules](https://github.com/css-modules/css-modules) (which we could maybe start migrating to now) and component-based libraries like [solid-styled-components](https://github.com/solidjs/solid-styled-components) or [solid-styled-jsx](https://github.com/solidjs/solid-styled-jsx) or [Vue scoped CSS](https://vue-loader.vuejs.org/guide/scoped-css.html) (which we should consider as part of a larger JS framework migration that I hope we’ll be able to start in the medium term).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 21:40 UTC

We could probably get by without such tooling if we were extremely disciplined about adhering to a system like [BEM](https://getbem.com/), but I’m not optimistic about our ability to do that consistently in a project with so many new contributors joining all the time.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 21:42 UTC

In such a big project, the difference between “we mostly follow these conventions” and “our tooling enforces these rules” makes all the difference in the confidence with which one can proceed with large refactors.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-03-14 21:54 UTC

Got it. I'm generally not a fan of watching CSS get slurped up into JavaScript, but I have not worked closely with systems like the ones you list.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 21:55 UTC

Well it’s not about the surface syntax—it’s about being able to look at a CSS change and *know* what components might be affected by it.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-03-14 22:03 UTC

With you on that. Some of the shadow DOM trickery possible with Web Components intrigues me in that regard, too.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 22:04 UTC

Yeah, I’ve played a bit with Web Components too, but I think they would add too much runtime overhead at the scale at which we would need to use them.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-03-14 22:11 UTC

There’s some chance that scoping [becomes part of the CSS standard](https://css.oddbird.net/scope/) some day, but the future is still unclear.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-03-21 23:38 UTC

I think it would probably be useful to standardize on kebab style for CSS classes, wither a linter enforcing it, mainly just to remove another source of entropy in the codebase. ## Unmute Topic UI #24244 & #24243

*2023-03-17 to 2023-04-07 · 35 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Unmute.20Topic.20UI.20.2324244.20.26.20.2324243/with/1527316)*

**Hardik Dharmani** · 2023-03-17 20:54 UTC

Hi everyone :wave: ,
I want to work on issues [#24244](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/24244) and [#24243](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/24243). Which are currently in @Prakhar Pratyush 's [plan](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/3-backend/topic/Unmute.20Topics/near/1519871). I had a chat with him on PM. He is okay with me working on these issues. He also provided me the links for previous work done on this project "[Add support for unmuting certain topics within a muted stream(#2517)](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/2517)".I went through the work done on this issue and here are my findings on the issue which I also discussed with him:

To achieve unmuting a topic in a muted stream [(#2517)](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/2517), we have shifted to a new model called userTopic instead of the previous model, MutedTopic. The UserTopic model has the following fields: ```stream_id, topic, last_updated, and visibilityPolicy```.

The visibilityPolicy has four options: muted, unmuted, inherit/normal, and followed (which is not currently implemented in this project).

Muted: A muted topic is not counted in the total unread messages and is not shown in the stream, all messages, recent conversations, etc. (the same in both muted and unmuted streams). The topic is only visible by opening that particular topic.
Inherited/Normal: This is the default state when the topic is not in UserTopic. It is the same as an unmuted topic in the current version, meaning it is counted in unread count and visible in stream messages. It is visible in all messages/recent topics if in an unmuted stream and not visible if in a muted stream.
Unmuted: This is a new special case that is equal to a current unmuted topic in an unmuted stream. It will be visible everywhere, even if in a muted stream. In a muted stream, it shows the total unread count of all topics (excluding muted topics within the stream, i.e., total of unread messages in normal visibility topics) if no topic in a stream is specially unmuted, but if some topics are specially unmuted in a muted stream, it shows only the total count of unmuted topics within that muted stream.

Since the issue is not currently labeled as "help wanted," I would like to request permission from maintainers to work on it. I look forward to contributing to this project and appreciate any guidance or feedback you can provide. Thank you in advance for your consideration.

Zulip was started a decade ago when the frontend development ecosystem was very different.
