## CSS optimization

*2023-10-19 to 2023-10-19 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/CSS.20optimization/with/1665704)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-10-19 19:04 UTC

This was initiated by @Karl Stolley 's comment [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/27197#discussion_r1364319975):
> We should get out of the habit of having inner-most selectors as element selectors. The reason being is that browsers evaluate selectors from right to left, meaning that every time a selector ends in an element, the browser has to work that much harder whenever and wherever on a page it encounters the element.

Followed by Tim's comment:
> We should probably start a #frontend discussion on this -- might be worth purging and then adding a stylelint rule to ban.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-10-19 19:04 UTC

So, I couldn't find a stylelint rule for it.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-10-19 19:16 UTC

Using something like `max-nesting-depth` could be better direction according to a few discussion I read about it online.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-19 19:18 UTC

A more fundamental problem with selectors like that is that descendant selectors are almost always too broad. If we style `#gear-menu-dropdown .org-info li a`, then any component we might want to use recursively inside `.org-info` that happens to contain a `li` that happens to contain an `a` will be unexpectedly styled.

We should stop nesting CSS at all. If you want to style a unique element, give it a unique class.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-10-19 19:20 UTC

Is it even possible to do a migration like that with our code?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-19 19:20 UTC

What do you mean? Is it possible to add classes to HTML?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-10-19 19:22 UTC

What do you think is the best plan to do such a migration then?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-19 19:24 UTC

The idea of planning such a migration sort of implicitly assumes that there’s some kind of obstacle that needs to be overcome first, which there isn’t. We can just do it.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-19 19:25 UTC

And even if we’re not going to do it all at once now, we can at least stop making the problem worse.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-10-19 19:32 UTC

I can do this migration for inbox as a start sometime later. It would help to set some guidelines for what the end result should look like.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-19 19:54 UTC

I think the trick is to do that without inviting a lot of code duplication. I take a sunnier view than most on inheritance and the cascade. Yes, they both take work to get right, and it's easy to walk into really bad traps without evening trying (witness all of the lamentable uses of `!important` across the codebase). But done incorrectly, and class-itis becomes little better than dropping `style=""` properties on individual elements.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-19 19:58 UTC

We have hundreds of contributors that aren’t experienced enough to avoid those traps, so completely avoiding features with the potential for traps is a good tradeoff for us even if it’s not for smaller projects.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-19 20:33 UTC

I appreciate that perspective, Anders. I also think it's part of our mission to help educate developers, including on points like these. Avoiding those traps takes experience, yes, but that experience has to be pretty intentionally both passed on and learned.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-19 21:01 UTC

It’s also a matter of scale, not just education. If you have to reason about every component in the entire app to decide whether some CSS might interact with it, that’s reasonable for small projects and not reasonable for us.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-19 21:03 UTC

In that sense, the potential for traps *is itself a trap*.

## Stream Membership Input Bug. #19544

*2023-10-22 to 2023-10-24 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Stream.20Membership.20Input.20Bug.2E.20.2319544/with/1666947)*

**Rohan Gudimetla** · 2023-10-22 18:42 UTC

According to the [Issue](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/19544) mentioned, while entering the input into the Stream Membership field of Subscribers tab, when we select the entire field, and press backspace then the input field won't be removed.

So, I was playing with this issue, and realised these:
- The main issue here is that whenever the ```anchorOffset``` is 0, i.e., whenever you select some text from starting of input field till some (any) point and press backspace, then it won't remove the selected portion.
- The [issue](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/19544) mentioned occurs because ```ctrl+a``` selects entire input field from  ```anchorOffset ===0``` till the end ==> Hence when you press backspace, it won't delete the text.
- However, when you select the entire text from end of the field till beginning (till ```anchorOffset ===0```), then on pressing backspace you can remove the entire text input.

On observing the Code I found out the reason for this issue is this [snippet](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/a7890f046bef8ae308f9909f0de08f2fa997251f/static/js/input_pill.js#L268-L278) condition, which satisfies in ONE CASE only:
- When  the selection is made from ```anchorOffset ===0``` till some point and backspace is pressed ==> it prevents default approach of removing text, and executes some other functionality, which is supposed to remove the selected text field **BUT IS MANAGING TO WORK ONLY WHEN THERE IS A POSSIBLE TYPEAHEAD FOR WHAT IS BEING ENTERED** (I couldn't figure out the reason for this irregularity).

**Rohan Gudimetla** · 2023-10-22 18:44 UTC

**I managed to fix this issue (as far as I have tested) by removing the mentioned condition in the** [snippet](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/a7890f046bef8ae308f9909f0de08f2fa997251f/static/js/input_pill.js#L268-L278) , since when ```anchorOffset != 0```, we had no problem plus we didn't prevent default behaviour of backspace/delete of selected field there (not preventing default here shouldn't hurt any here too then).

So, I wanted some Views on the significance of this [conditionality](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/a7890f046bef8ae308f9909f0de08f2fa997251f/static/js/input_pill.js#L268-L278), and the use of the ```removeLastPill()``` since without the section the issue appears to be fixed

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-24 20:00 UTC

That logic seems straightforward to me: If you're in the process of inputting a pill, `backspace` deletes a character of that input, but if you're not, it deletes a pill -- this seems like what one would expect from pill UI.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-24 20:01 UTC

I think it likely is just missing logic checking the selection range -- the logic just doesn't consider the possibility something might be selected.

**Rohan Gudimetla** · 2023-10-24 20:07 UTC

@Tim Abbott  thanks for responding.
I have fixed this issue. Here is the [PR](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/27341)

## alphas in color definitions

*2023-10-26 to 2023-10-29 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/alphas.20in.20color.20definitions/with/1670065)*

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 17:44 UTC

I've [brought this up in passing before](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/101-design/topic/video.20preview.20.2320449/near/1620623), but I think we do need to think a little more carefully about when it's appropriate or necessary to specify colors with alpha channels, especially on background colors.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 17:48 UTC

I just put up a WIP PR, #27394, that includes alpha-free approximations of the background hover and focus-visible colors in the redesigned navbar. Since the message is pretty lengthy, and includes some method stuff that I know will interest and probably alarm @Anders Kaseorg, I'm going to repost it in digestible bits here:

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 17:48 UTC

[The border around the unread dot](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/27390#issuecomment-1781444484) is a case where the use of alpha channels in HSL color values shows its limits.

The use of an alpha channel is necessary for the background elements for the top navbar elements, because they sit over the top of the navbar's bottom border (actually an inset shadow).

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 17:48 UTC

However, it's impossible to use the alpha-channel based color on elements like the unread dot, where the border actually sits on top of the element itself--meaning that the effect would be a larger dot with an imperceptibly darker ring around it.

So what I have done here is to capture the value of the alpha- based background, but as an opaque color suited for use on elements that sit above the true alpha-based background.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 17:49 UTC

To do this is a tricky proposition, but I used this method:

1. CSS uses the sRGB color space, and that is supported uniformly across modern browsers.
2. macOS provides a Digital Color Meter capable of reading color values on a per-color-space basis. I switched it to sRGB mode, to match the sRGB color space of CSS, and sampled the alpha colors as displayed in Firefox (that shouldn't matter, but I list it in case we discover it *does* matter).
3. I entered the sRGB values in an sRGB-aware RGB to HSL converter at ColorMine: http://colormine.org/convert/rgb-to-hsl
4. I established new `-no-alpha` color variables adjacent the alpha based ones already in the stylesheet, and rounded the resulting HSL values from ColorMine to two decimal places, where needed.
5. After placing the new color variables, I again used the sRGB color meter, which is sensitive down to the individual pixel, to ensure that there was NO shift in those values whatsoever in moving from the alpha-based background color to the border around the unread dot.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-26 18:12 UTC

Indeed, that is alarming. Quantizing one 8-bit colorspace to another can lead to significant rounding errors that won’t be detected by your procedure.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 18:17 UTC

Probably. And I think it would be better to just use non-alpha colors at their source, from @Vlad Korobov. The experiment here probably benefits somewhat from these being shades of gray (e.g., the same value across all three RGB channels). 

But given the inherent mixing in colors with alpha channels, I don't know of a better way to proceed.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-26 18:20 UTC

You can make CSS do the calculation for you: [`color-mix(in srgb, #34c9eb 20%, white)`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/color_value/color-mix).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-26 18:22 UTC

(For constant arguments, postcss-preset-env [compiles this to a flat color](https://preset-env.cssdb.org/playground/#), so we don’t need to worry about browser support.)

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 18:24 UTC

That's handy. Thanks! That still leaves me uncertain as to how to reliably convert the non-alpha parts of HSL to an sRGB value, though.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-26 18:26 UTC

You don’t need to, you can specify it with any notation CSS supports: `color-mix(in srgb, hsl(191 82% 56%) 20%, white)`.

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 18:27 UTC

Oh, that's awesome. I didn't get the sense from the MDN docs that you could specify color in a different space than what you're mixing in.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-26 18:27 UTC

(But also, HSL is a pretty [dumb colorspace](https://wildbit.com/blog/accessible-palette-stop-using-hsl-for-color-systems) and there’s not a good reason for us to be using it.)

**Karl Stolley** · 2023-10-26 19:54 UTC

Updated the PR to use Anders's suggested technique: #27394. Obviously correcting that little halo isn't a priority, but it seemed worth it to have a working example of this technique to use in other situations that might come up.

**Vlad Korobov** · 2023-10-29 18:55 UTC

waaait, are you guys saying that its ok to use css color-mix functions already? Or is just a way to extract non transparent value for a situation?

@Karl Stolley sorry but I don't want to default to "don't use transparency". Number of cases when transparency isn't a good approach isn't that big and worth of solving on a case by case basis. I have such case in the left sidebar...bg on ... button shouldn't be transparent because of pin icon under it. It was a good case when I tuned a color of bg to be a bit more vibrant compare to other colors of similar buttons, because ... is an important button:
[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/83/KDQTb6OKMMThuc6doCOqpb2X/image.png)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-29 19:39 UTC

We can use `color-mix` *with constant arguments* (no `var()`) because PostCSS will compile it away.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-29 19:45 UTC

[Full postcss-preset-env feature list](https://github.com/csstools/postcss-plugins/blob/main/plugin-packs/postcss-preset-env/FEATURES.md).


## input_pill typescript

*2023-10-26 to 2024-04-17 · 37 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/input_pill.20typescript/with/1670357)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-26 22:34 UTC

This function in `input_pill` is annoying in that it can return `undefined`. I think the situations where it does so are all programming errors with the wrong options being passed; so we should be able to fix this by just enforcing the types passed in, right?

```
export function create<T>(opts: InputPillCreateOptions<T>): InputPillContainer<T> | undefined {         
    if (!opts.$container) {                                                                             
        blueslip.error("Pill needs container.");                                                        
        return undefined;                                                                               
    }                                                                                                   
                                                                                                        
    if (!opts.create_item_from_text) {                                                                  
        blueslip.error("Pill needs create_item_from_text");                                             
        return undefined;                                                                               
    }                                                                                                   
                                                                                                        
    if (!opts.get_text_from_item) {                                                                     
        blueslip.error("Pill needs get_text_from_item");                                                
        return undefined;                                                                               
    }                                                                                                   
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-26 22:34 UTC

(There's a bunch of downstream things that inherit this undefined type, notably in #24580 which I happen to be looking at)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-26 22:38 UTC

Yeah this is the classic overdefensive check that multiplies the fallout of every unexpected `undefined` by creating more `undefined`s that are now the caller’s responsibility.

export function query_matches_person(query, person) {

export function query_matches_name(query, user_group_or_stream) {

}                                                                                                       
```

Once we don't have further PRs touching it in flight (https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/26396 is the main one I have in mind), we should rename `pm_list.js`, the module for the left sidebar direct messages component. Thoughts on what to call it?

I think `left_sidebar_direct_messages.js` might be a reasonable name for it, to be parallel to `left_sidebar_navigation_area.js`? We have `stream_list.js` as a parallel module name today, but I think that module name is also painfully non-specific.

Could be `direct_messages_navigation` and `stream_navigation` or something?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 19:07 UTC

Which is why was proposing just having `left_sidebar` in the name -- it's super explicit. Also note that `pm_list`, the one that would have a pretty long/verbose name, isn't referenced in many places, and all but a handful are single-line function calls, so it seems like a pretty minimal cost to have a long name.
```
$ git grep pm_list web/src/ | grep -v web/src/pm_list.js | wc -l
36
$ git grep stream_list web/src/ | grep -v web/src/stream_list.js | wc -l
70
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-27 19:52 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-27 19:53 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 19:54 UTC

Directories don't really help with the core problem, which is that when one sees `pm_list.handle_narrow_activated(filter);` in `narrow.js`, one wants the combination of module and function name to clearly hint what that function does without having to go look anything up.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 19:57 UTC

And while I don't love the function name part in that particular case either, I don't really see the module name `stream_navigation` as hinting that main panel left sidebar component vs like "Some popup that navigates between streams" or "a helper module that isn't related to UI at all but you call into from click handlers that navigate to a different stream".

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 19:58 UTC

So I would like us to have a module name here that describes the component a bit more explicitly. And humans use the term "left sidebar" to talk about the left sidebar constantly when doing development, so to me that feels very clear/explicit to someone working on the project.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 20:05 UTC

This thread was motivated in part by https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/26717#pullrequestreview-1700838808, where the module naming did not clearly hint what that module was for, leading to a module import cycle in that PR that seems to have wasted nontrivial time. I'm not entirely sure that `direct_messages_navigation` would necessarily avoid that problem; maybe @Evy can comment on that.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-27 20:06 UTC

We could have docstrings that describe what our modules are for.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 20:08 UTC

I really don't think docstrings are a substitute for naming things well. Especially when you're looking at some other code that calls into something, it really really helps one read it quickly if the individual calls into other modules speak for themselves as to what they do.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 20:09 UTC

I imagine one can get VSCode to show you docstrings on hover, but a lot of development/review/etc. happens when looking at code on GitHub or chat.zulip.org, where that isn't going to be available.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-27 20:14 UTC

Readability mainly requires unique, consistent names; they don’t need to be verbose or comprehensive.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 20:16 UTC

Yeah, I think that cluster would be happier with user defaults panel having `settings_user_defaults` as its main name -- we don't have anything else called "user defaults".

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-10-27 20:17 UTC

That’s the kind of logic we should use more. Take it even further—why not just `user_defaults`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 20:17 UTC

But consistency is the priority in that name choice -- and `realm_user_settings_defaults` is what we called it in the API, so we're a bit stuck with that prefix.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 20:19 UTC

I'm pretty happy with having the `settings_` prefix on all modules for the settings UI. If the feature did anything in the web app, we might have a separate `user_defaults` module for its functionality -- see e.g. `linkifiers.js` and `settings_linkifiers.js`. The former is the main data store and logic module for making linkifiers for what they do, the latter defines a settings panel for administrators managing linkifiers.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 20:19 UTC

But that feature only does something on the server during user creation, so it doesn't have a module for web app logic at all.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-27 20:25 UTC

I find it incredibly helpful as a code organization policy that the 9K lines of code across 26 files that is our settings subsystem all have `settings_` at the start of their names. This sort of file naming convention being preferable to having a bunch of files with shorter names in a `settings/` directory may change as we work on using SolidJS in the codebase, just because it might become the case that essentially nothing else calls into `settings_` modules at all... but I'm not sure.

I really like being able to do `git grep settings_linkifiers[.]` letting me find all the code that interacts with a module, and having a `settings/linkifiers.js` and a `linkifiers.js` really breaks the ability to do that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-30 18:18 UTC

I would kinda prefer we not have any file names with `pm` in them; we have 8 between `web/src` and `web/templates/`.

I don't really want to spend a lot of attention on talking about each individual case, but I think a substantial portion of places where we have a variable with `pm` in it, I'd be happier to have it be `direct_message` in it instead. I think `more_pms.hbs` is a great example; the only line of code that references it is this:

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-30 18:20 UTC

Which as you can see, the person writing the TS code to actually reference it felt the need to rename it for clarity when importing it, because I guess they felt `render_more_pms` was a bad function name? **Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-30 18:22 UTC

I do think `dm_` is one of the few abbreviations that almost anyone will correctly interpret, and in that sense it's not terrible, but it is also one of the very few abbreviations that are common in the web codebase, and often is used in a randomly mixed fashion with spelling the thing out. For example:
```
$ git grep private_message web/src/pm_list.js | wc
     42     140    3237
$ git grep pm web/src/pm_list.js | wc
     21      96    1715
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-30 18:23 UTC

So my overall preference would be to turn every `pm` into `direct_message` while renaming things; having two ways to refer to the same thing chosen basically randomly each time never really feels nice, and that's what we have right now.

While implementing, we have a race condition to tackle. 

current approach is:
on success of `add_reaction` operation, we select the `.change_visibility_policy` element in the message header and create a tippy instance on it. Then `instance.show()`

Since the `user_topic` event results in the updating the `id` of `<div class="recipient_row" id="message_group_140">` and the icon; so there is a race between the `instance.show()` and the DOM update due to `user_topic` event.

any suggestions to tackle it?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-02 20:35 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-02 20:36 UTC

## buddy list update on narrow

*2023-11-16 to 2023-11-17 · 23 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/buddy.20list.20update.20on.20narrow/with/1682998)*

**Evy** · 2023-11-16 01:57 UTC

There are some issues with the buddy list not updating every time the narrow changes. Right now this the buddy list updates on hashchange.

So my initial two questions

(1) Is hashchange an okay place for this? I put it there partially to avoid circular imports, and if I wasn't considering that I'd probably put it in `narrow.activate` and `narrow.deactivate`

(2) Why isn't hashchange called sometimes? For example when clicking on a recipient bar.

**Evy** · 2023-11-16 01:58 UTC

I think (2) is related to the change happening from clicking on a link, so the hash changed by url click? Not totally sure.

**Evy** · 2023-11-16 01:59 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:20 UTC

No, `hashchange` is not the correct place for this. https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/hashchange-system.html, linked at the top of that file, may have helpful context (I've not double-checked). But the main entrypoint in `hashchange`, `hashchange.hashchanged`, is only called when the cause for your change in view is a change in the URL.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:20 UTC

The back button will definitely do this, and many of our click handlers that don't need to pass pararameters will do this, but any other click handlers that work via calling `narrow.activate` or various wrappers will not use that code path.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:22 UTC

The `opts.change_hash` parameter to `narrow.activate` is worth noting to understand this.

**Evy** · 2023-11-16 02:23 UTC

Thanks for sharing, that makes sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:23 UTC

Any changes to other parts of the app than the center pane that are triggered by changing the view should occur in `handle_post_view_change` for narrowing, or `views_util.js` for Recent/Inbox.

Do you have recommendations for how to call `activity_ui.build_user_sidebar();` from `handle_post_view_change` without causing circular imports?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:24 UTC

You can see that those places already have hooked to update all the left sidebar logic; the right sidebar doesn't in `main` have anything that depends on the state of the center pane, but you should add whatever you need next to functions like `pm_list.handle_message_view_deactivated();` that update the left sidebar.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:26 UTC

For circular imports, the lazy answer is to make a `views_util.initialize` method and pass `activity_ui.build_user_sidebar`  into the module as a parameter from `ui_init`.

See, for example, `topic_list.initialize`. 

The reason I see the lazy answer is that it doesn't involve actually thinking about the module structures at all.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:27 UTC

What is the actual path from which `activity_ui` imports `views_util` such that there'd be a cycle?

**Evy** · 2023-11-16 02:30 UTC

`handle_post_view_change` is in `narrow.js`, `activity_ui` imports from `narrow.js`, so it's a direct path between them.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:32 UTC

OK the right fix is to pass effectively `narrow.by("dm", email, {trigger: "sidebar"});` into `activity_ui.initialize` from `ui_init` as `on_user_click` in the same way that `on_topic_click` works for `topic_list.js`

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-16 02:33 UTC

That fits the pattern we're using already in like 4 places of passing a `narrow` function to initialize a component with a click handler to narrow to something.

## jQuery .data

*2023-11-21 to 2023-11-21 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/jQuery.20.2Edata/with/1686087)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-21 01:42 UTC

Should we migrate of jQuery `.data("foo")` accesses and lint-ban in in favor of `.attr("data-foo")`? Some reasons to want to do this:
* It is more greppable, since you can `git grep data-foo` and find all the uses.
* It is easier to translate to code that doesn't use jQuery.
* jQuery `.data("foo", "bar")` is somewhat evil in that after you do that, `.data("foo") != .attr("data-foo")`, because it writes changes just to its own thing, not the DOM `data-foo` attribute (which it does read), which means that using it sometimes and `.attr("data-foo")` other times can lead to weird bugs that are very hard to track down.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-11-21 01:57 UTC

Sound good to me.

**Evy** · 2023-11-21 02:11 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-21 02:12 UTC

Well if you use `.attr` consistently, that's the thing that works reliably.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-21 02:12 UTC

## remove_diacritics performance

*2023-11-27 to 2024-03-05 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/remove_diacritics.20performance/with/1689797)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-27 21:03 UTC

So while looking at #27882, I did some profiling on chat.zulip.org of `@` mention typeahead, which is basically fast enough so as to not be disruptive on my very fast computer, had some moments where it had "Long tasks". And looking at where the time is going; 20-50% of the time is in this function, which we call from `query_matches_string`:
```
export function remove_diacritics(s: string): string {                                                                  
    return s.normalize("NFKD").replace(unicode_marks, "");                                                              
}                                                                                                                       
```

It seems like that might be worth working on?

Since this is a pure function, we could quite easily cache the answers to that function and presumably make this a lot faster, in that unicode normalization is presumably a lot more expensive than doing a lookup... but there might be more clever things we could do too.

**Greg Price** · 2024-02-22 18:39 UTC

Caching those seems like a good solution. That's the approach we're taking [in the Flutter app](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/c7f9383d87e9ee5ffa0f94083b7dc25893d0d5a6/lib/model/autocomplete.dart#L325-L333).

The following code snippet is from `read_receipts.js` .

```
                          success(data)

The above function maps the `user_ids` and returns an array(`users`) of object (which is not of type `User`) .The problem with this is `people.compare_by_name`function  takes parameters of type `User` as defined in `people.ts` file. ```
                      const raw_users = data.user_ids.map((id) => {
                            const raw_user = people.get_user_by_id_assert_valid(id);
                            return raw_user;
                        });

                        raw_users.sort(people.compare_by_name);

                                    user_id: raw_user.user_id,
                                    full_name: raw_user.full_name,
                                    avatar_url: people.small_avatar_url_for_person(raw_user),


                            }
                        })

```
Now the `raw_user` is of type `User`,  and can be passed to `people.compare_by_name`. We can then map `users` array from the sorted array(of `raw_users`) that contains object with the three properties needed to create  a modal out of it.

## Splitting page_params

*2024-01-04 to 2024-02-14 · 26 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Splitting.20page_params/with/1713115)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-04 05:23 UTC

We currently initialize the `page_params` object by merging the state data from `do_events_register` into other data from `build_page_params_for_home_page_load`. For normal users, this merging happens on the server within `build_page_params_for_home_page_load`, but for spectators, it happens on the client late after module load via a secondary `POST /json/register` request in `ui_init.js`. That’s a huge type safety hole for TypeScript, since reading that data at module load time for spectators silently results in `undefined` rather than its declared type. So in #28392 I propose splitting out that data into a separate `state_data` object.

Tim wants to go further and split some of this data into `realm_settings` and `server_settings` objects. It’s unclear to me exactly where to draw that distinction, and I also don’t see a clear case for doing it. *Everything* the client gets from a realm applies within the context of that realm, and a client should never need to know or care whether some property applies to the entire server. This seems like more of an artistic endeavor than a type safety cleanup.

But Tim, if you want to make a concrete proposal, here’s a [spreadsheet listing everything in `page_params`](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D17U4sGGraY2Frji47qbtRanjYBHpa03gpSe_xktmf0/edit#gid=0) and where it comes from.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-04 05:28 UTC

I have a plan for fixing type safety for the non-state data in `page_params` that’s conditionally present depending on which page is loaded (home, marketing, stats, team, upgrade), but there’s no reason to sequence that before #28392, so we can focus on the state data for now.

**Steve Howell** · 2024-01-04 17:55 UTC

FWIW I firmly agree with the principle that "a client should never need to know or care whether some property applies to the entire server."  A sort of similar principal applies to streams and subscriptions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-04 17:59 UTC

So the background here is that we have an API design plan that we would probably want to spec out and complete as a follow-up to this that would make there be a top-level `realm` object and a top-level `server` object in the API response to `/json/register` from the server, rather than a ton of little `realm_` and `server_` fields; this would match the approach we took with the change we made in #**api design>user settings response in /register**.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-04 18:00 UTC

The reason we need separate buckets for `realm` and `server` is that we have some fields with identical names where the values differ, e.g. for the `jitsi_server_url`, there's a value configured for the server that serves as the default value for your realm if you haven't manually configured it, which I think is represented as something like `realm_jitsi_server_url=None`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-04 18:01 UTC

So my motivation here was to, while we're refactoring the web app codebase for `page_params`, end in a state where we'd basically not need to make further changes to the web app to support such an API reorganization of `/json/register`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-04 18:07 UTC

Doing this backward-compatibly is going to add a lot of complexity.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-04 18:39 UTC

For the API change, I think it would be roughly the same complexity we had with `user_settings_object`? What I'm imagining is that if the client doesn't have declare the client capability, we basically have a giant map that's used to move the fields from the 9.x location that to the 8.x name for that field.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-04 19:23 UTC

Currently there are five pairs of keys with both `realm_` and `server_` versions: `avatar_changes_disabled`, `inline_image_preview`, `inline_url_embed_preview`, `jitsi_server_url`, `name_changes_disabled`.

There’s security value in having `server_inline_image_preview` and `server_inline_url_embed_preview` since the server admin might want to disallow user-controlled outgoing network requests (these two could be combined for that use case), but I don’t see the value in having the other three—is it just backwards compatibility from before they were realm settings?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-04 20:59 UTC

I think the name/avatar change ones could be removed with an appropriate "upgrade notes" item... though there's some argument for the current model making sense in that you usually want those things if you are syncing those fields from LDAP or similar, and you configure that in `/etc/zulip/`.

`jisti_server_url` cannot; see #**api design>realm_jitsi_server_url** for some context, but basically the use case for the server-level one would be if we wanted to run our own Zulip Cloud Jitsi server that's the default for cloud customers while still allowing individual realms to configure their own.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-04 21:02 UTC

LDAP settings are per-server even though they shouldn’t be, but whether LDAP is enabled is per-realm.

**Greg Price** · 2024-01-26 00:44 UTC

It sounds like there's a positive, but small, number of items where we naturally have two values that relate to each other as "realm" vs. "server".

In particular it seems like that number is a lot smaller than the total number of `realm_*` keys. To me that suggests that the realm/server contrast shouldn't be the overarching basis for how we organize this data.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-02-07 23:01 UTC

Moving `queue_id` to `server_events.js` creates an import cycle `echo.js` ↔ `server_events.js`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-08 19:37 UTC

Hmm. I guess `queue_id` is immutable state, so an option is to just dump it into `state_data` for now and think about moving it later.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-08 19:38 UTC

But reading the code using it:
```
    // Always re-set queue_id if we've gotten a new one                                                 
    // since the time when the message object was initially created                                     
    message.queue_id = page_params.queue_id;                                                            
    message.resend = true;                                                                              
```

I suspect that code is just bogus -- AFAIk the Zulip web app never gets a new queue ID.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-08 19:40 UTC

It was introduced in 53739622fdb7c9a96fa6687e05f0913af1114d03, and very much looks like just defensive programming for a thing we might have implemented, but never in fact did.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-08 19:41 UTC

So I think the best answer is to just delete that line (and its comment) and proceed.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-02-14 03:07 UTC

`max_message_id` needs a home. (Or we should figure out how to kill it, since its only use is for constructing evil floating-point local IDs when `all_messages_data` is empty.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-14 03:28 UTC

I think it might have other applications in the future so probably better to give it a home. Could just sit with the realm I guess, it's a realm level property?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-02-14 03:37 UTC

It doesn’t seem like a realm property. I’m imagining realm properties as ones that don’t vary from user to user, and this one does. It’s [computed in `fetch_initial_state_data`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/144c2c2f110605e2efee25b49c970c97d5271ee9/zerver/lib/events.py#L200) by calling [`max_message_id_for_user`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/144c2c2f110605e2efee25b49c970c97d5271ee9/zerver/lib/users.py#L1059-L1071), but also [overridden in `build_page_params_for_home_page_load`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/144c2c2f110605e2efee25b49c970c97d5271ee9/zerver/lib/home.py#L241-L252) in the `narrow_stream` case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-14 23:17 UTC

Yeah IDK maybe that's a good thing to leave into the generic state module, if we still have one, and think about it later.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-02-14 23:25 UTC

I wasn’t planning on having one. My goal here was to fix type safety bugs, not to do a bunch of rearrangement; I don’t want to split things further than necessary, especially if it’s not going to be along a clear bright line.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-14 23:36 UTC

Yeah, I was trying to suggest we just do what is laziest for that one so that we can address the type safety issue without an extra rabbit hole.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-14 23:37 UTC

But I guess if it's only used in `local_message.ts`, it could live there pending further work on it?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-02-14 23:49 UTC

#28930 is the current progress on this extra splitting.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-14 23:58 UTC

Cool, did a skim and the strategy for what you have so far looks solid.

## Status emoji picker logic is inconsistent #28464

*2024-01-09 to 2024-01-09 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Status.20emoji.20picker.20logic.20is.20inconsistent.20.2328464/with/1716175)*

**Sayam Samal** · 2024-01-09 16:27 UTC

@Tim Abbott could you take a look at PR #28493, and check if this is the right approach? I found that the major cause for `toggle_reaction` being called via the status emoji picker  was due to the logic in `process_enter_while_filtering`:

```js
            if (is_composition($first_emoji)) {
                $first_emoji.trigger("click");
            } else {
                toggle_reaction($first_emoji.attr("data-emoji-name"), e);
            }
```

While pressing enter while on the emoji filter input, in the case of the status emoji picker the `else` part of the conditional was being executed, which was the bug. We can simply in all the cases use the `$first_emoji.trigger("click");`, and the rest would be handled by the appropriate click handler.

**Sayam Samal** · 2024-01-09 16:31 UTC

I have also simplified all the click handlers into one and added a single function `handle_emoji_clicked` to handle what needs to be done with the selected emoji based on the type of the emoji.

## pygments_data typescript

*2024-01-11 to 2024-01-13 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/pygments_data.20typescript/with/1718206)*

**Evy** · 2024-01-11 19:50 UTC

I have a line of code that indexes `pygments_data` like this: `pygments_data.langs[lang_a];`

And typescript is giving this error:

```
expression of type 'string' can't be used to index type '{ abap: { priority: number; pretty_name: string; }; amdgpu: { priority: number; pretty_name: string; }; apl: { priority: number; pretty_name: string; }; abnf: { priority: number; pretty_name: string; }; ... 881 more ...; spoiler: { ...; }; }'.
```

What do I need to do to make `pygments_data.langs` the correct type here?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-11 21:11 UTC

So it's currently loaded via `import generated_pygments_data from "../generated/pygments_data.json";`.

Probably the right fix involves making a module `web/src/pygments_data.ts` that does that import and re-exports it with a declared type for use by other modules.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-11 21:48 UTC

Open feature request for what we actually want: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/52994.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-11 22:02 UTC

You can do something like

```ts
Object.hasOwn(generated_pygments_data.langs, lang_a)
    // eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/consistent-type-assertions
    ? generated_pygments_data.langs[lang_a as keyof typeof generated_pygments_data.langs]
    : undefined
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-11 22:06 UTC

Or

```ts
const langs: Record<string, {priority: number; pretty_name: string} | undefined> =
    generated_pygments_data.langs;
langs[lang_a]
```

**Evy** · 2024-01-13 20:06 UTC

Great, thanks!

## Information density: typographic foundations

*2024-01-16 to 2024-03-25 · 91 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Information.20density.3A.20typographic.20foundations/with/1720258)*

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-16 17:16 UTC

I just filed #28586 as the first of two large issues outlining and tracking progress on the user-selectable information density project as requested in #12611.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-16 17:17 UTC

This first issue concerns only the technical typographic foundations (CSS patterns, element sizing and position) necessary to advance the project; more design-specific questions (e.g., exactly how much space should there be between two rendered markdown elements?) will get their own discussion in #**design** as the project progresses.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-16 17:19 UTC

I'll follow up in the coming days with a second issue that will plan and track progress on a UI mechanism for presenting users with information-density options to choose from.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-16 18:18 UTC

One question in my mind is whether it makes sense to have font size and line height be semi-independent axes in user-selectable density, and not just a single font size slider (with the line-height being a fixed function of that).

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-16 18:19 UTC

I certainly don't want to put a lot of effort into that sort of flexibility if it slows down work on the main font size control, but I do have a vague sense that user preferences vary both on font size and how much space they want between things (especially in lists like the sidebars, where more space between items usually looks nicer but packs less densely).

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-16 18:28 UTC

Yes. I think that we should think carefully about the relationships between spacing (line-height, margin, padding) and font-size. I doubt the best solution is going to be 1:1 (which is effectively what browser zoom is going to do anyway).

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-16 18:30 UTC

What I suspect we'll get to is a few (3? 5?) different density settings that are nicely tuned to look their best, and presented behind preset class names, but that all have a tolerance for further customization through additional controls and modifier classes (e.g., for someone who generally likes one of the preset options, but wants a bit less space between things, or a larger typeface).

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-16 18:32 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I certainly don't want to put a lot of effort into that sort of flexibility if it slows down work on the main font size control

No, I think that that sort of flexibility is absolutely warranted. Having an adjustable `font-size` is just one part of what'll take to have customizable information density that feels good and has an appeal at different configurations. But a lot of what makes for good reading comfort isn't the text itself or even its size, but how much space there is around a given bit of text, and how rhythmic and predictable that space is.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-16 18:33 UTC

I think our intent should be to make 16px the default, at least for new users, eventually; but we might want to keep 14px as the default for an intermediate period during which the 16px size is more buggy. And could consider leaving it the default for existing users, especially if we advertise the new setting once it's ready for production use.

> While we should continue to support the current 14px size and perhaps default to it—especially because it will be familiar and, to some users, comfortable—it might be better to proceed establishing some consistent sizing relationships based on a 16px base font-size.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-16 18:33 UTC

A denser information presentation is going to have a faster rhythm (tighter line-heights, less space between elements), whereas a looser presentation will have a slower rhythm (more generous line-heights, more space overall)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-16 18:36 UTC

Overall the write-up looks pretty good to me. It's probably worth @Vlad Korobov and others giving it a read as well.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-16 18:45 UTC

Sure thing. I'm eager for feedback; I've deliberately tried to stay away from design things like "There should be X amount of space between paragraphs," though I will be putting my typesetting skills to work to set up some foundational things that we can pick and poke at and discuss further over in #**design**.

**Alya Abbott** · 2024-01-18 00:58 UTC

Thank you for the detailed writeup! (I don't have any comments, but I found it very informative.)

**Vlad Korobov** · 2024-01-20 00:33 UTC

I'm open to work on different density settings once we implemented at least one according to the design. Since only after this work it would be clear what are the variables we should change.

My typography suggestions overall was "lets make font a bit bigger by default" and "lets make standard text and elements look a bit nicer". Zulip still doesn't have that, at this point I don't think that my input would influence anything in this big no end project :)

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-20 03:21 UTC

With you, as always, 100% @Vlad Korobov

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 14:36 UTC

So [studying the Figma file](https://www.figma.com/file/jbNOiBWvbtLuHaiTj4CW0G/Zulip-Web-App?type=design&node-id=3154-252558&mode=design&t=LMRVmjyM9rb9SZfI-0) this morning, it looks like your examples have a 15px/19px setting for most message elements (15px font-size, 19px line-height), which isn't far off from the 16px/20px setting I think we should target to start.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-22 18:58 UTC

I'm not entirely sure which of those values will be best without playing with them. But if the strategy is to make it flexible, then those both seem like options we'd offer.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 19:07 UTC

Agreed. I think it's most important to start that we get some consistent size and space relationships in place. Fine-tuning can come later, and of course @Vlad Korobov's input will be invaluable at that point

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 19:08 UTC

I'll be engineering this all for maximum flexibility and ease of trying out different things with as few fiddly adjustments as possible

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 19:09 UTC

I do think we have agreement that the de facto browser standard of 16px for font-size is the place to start, but as I tried to express in #28586, the spatial relationships are the real nut to crack in terms of a comfortable reading experience--regardless of the font size in play.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-22 19:45 UTC

I don't think the browser standard is itself important to what we use as the default -- different fonts look differently big at a given font size. The decision for what we make the default should be based on what feels most comfortable / looks the best overall.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 19:46 UTC

Got it. We're talking about two different things :) I'm looking for values to start from for teasing out the size relationships, which may be different from what feels best as a default that ships for users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-22 20:02 UTC

Yeah for that sort of engineering analysis, I would start with at least 16px just because a bigger delta will make more things stand out.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-22 20:02 UTC

When @Anders Kaseorg and I were doing early audits for what breaks, I think we just tried changing font-size to like 24px.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-22 20:02 UTC

And then looking at everything that looked very different from just zooming in.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:16 UTC

Sure. I'm taking a different approach that's more focused on line-heights and inter-element spacing. We've got a mix of absolute and relative values that makes just whacking at the font-size a less precise way to work.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 20:18 UTC

The relative line height contributes more to the feeling of Zulip being cramped than the font size does. It’s currently 17px ÷ 14px = 1.214, and I worry that the ratios you’re proposing aren’t different enough: 19px ÷ 15px = 1.267, 20px ÷ 16px = 1.250.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 20:22 UTC

Not that we should blindly copy anyone, but for comparison, Discord uses 1.375 and Slack uses 1.467.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:26 UTC

Sure. And again, what I'm proposing isn't even a *proposal*. It's just a starting point for developing size relationships.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:27 UTC

The relative/em values are a good check on where things stand, but the other piece is that we've got 3px, 5px, and 6px margins between different Markdown elements (there are others, but those are the most frequent ones), and a value like 20px lends itself to half- and quarter-line values that can build a better, rhythmic sense for reading comfort.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:28 UTC

Eyeballs like to have predictable lines of space and spatial values, so that you're not straining to go from the end of one line, or the end of one block, to the start of the next. That gets exacerbated at smaller font sizes, especially when the leading is tight--but it's worst still when the leading is unpredictable and varies between a blockquote and a paragraph, or a paragraph and a list.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 20:30 UTC

Divisibility of the line-height into halves and quarters sounds like pseudoscience to me. The actual line-height ÷ font-size ratio is much more visually important. (You know that an `em` is based on the font-size, not the line-height, right?)

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:33 UTC

No--I'm not saying that eyeballs like quarter- and half-line values. That would be pseudoscience. But some kind of predictable rhythm is good typesetting, because when confronted with repeated patterns that are predictable, your eye has less work to do going from one line to the next.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:34 UTC

And yes. I'm aware of what `em` units are, and how they are calculated and determined at any given point based on the `font-size` in question.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:35 UTC

What I am saying is that it's not helpful to rush to a relative unit. If I have a 22px line-height and a 17px font-size, I can better reason about adjusting those two in relation to each other while working in pixels. Conversion to relative units comes later, but just knowing 22/17 = ~1.294 is a good marker for how dense things are.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 20:41 UTC

Declaring line-height unitlessly is important because we have many different font sizes, even in message content (e.g. headings). While we could try to force ourselves to declare a unique line-height for every unique font-size, it doesn’t sound fun, and getting every contributor to remember that sounds even less fun.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:44 UTC

Ah, but that's the catch. If I have `line-height: 1.214` then yes, every different font size **will** have a different line-height as it appears on the page (which is what we have now, especially in regard to headings).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 20:45 UTC

As they should.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:46 UTC

They should, but the line-height shouldn't be just relative to a particular element's font size.

To use some rough illustrative numbers: If I know my base line-height is, say, 20px, then I might opt for a 30px line-height for smaller headings (line and a half) or a 40px line-height for larger headings. Ordinary copy sits on its 20px baseline, and gives everything a consistent, predictable look.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:50 UTC

Here's a blog post that talks a bit about what I'm aiming at here: https://iamsteve.me/blog/a-guide-to-vertical-rhythm

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 20:50 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 20:50 UTC

That very post specifically recommends picking a unitless line-height.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:53 UTC

It does, and I disagree with that aspect *early on* in getting to a baseline grid. Relative units should be converted as such later. The problem with `line-height: 1.4` is that it's relative to the font-size. So it has no meaning, other than to say "For this element, the line height is 1.4 times the size of the typeface." Fine. That means that the invisible lines that text sits on--whether a heading, a paragraph, a list, or even a code block--have no visual relationship to one another whenever the font size changes (and like you say, our font sizes are different within the message area).

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 20:58 UTC

A baseline grid is like a metronome. It's sole job is to provide a steady, constant beat. Font size and additional spacing (e.g., between a paragraph and a list) should work predictably within that beat, just like quarter notes can follow a 4/4 beat, or extend into half-notes, or subdivided into eighth notes.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 20:59 UTC

That’s where things start going off into pseudoscience for me. The unitless line-height ratio has a lot of meaning: it directly measures (the reciprocal of) what fraction of the line is taken up by the text. That’s a much more visually important concept than the ratios of anything across lines of different sizes.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 21:03 UTC

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 21:09 UTC

Whether a given ratio is 1/3 or whatever of the baseline is immaterial at this stage--it's that we have a basis to get to that ratio to begin with. "This is a 60-floor building, but each floor is 1.214 times the height of the doors. But each door is different, depending upon reasons."

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 21:14 UTC

We’re not building a 60-floor building. Some lines of text *are* different, depending upon reasons. And larger lines of text do naturally require a correspondingly larger line-height. A unitless line-height gives us that.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 21:22 UTC

A line height that is always relative to font-size is going to create jarring differences from element to element. That's the root cause of the ramshackle look of text in the message area right now. It does not look good, and it is not comfortable to read.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 21:23 UTC

Your premise doesn’t make sense. Almost everything in the message area has the same font-size; there are no such element-to-element differences.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 21:23 UTC

What will give order a predictability to the text are two things 1) a line height large enough to accommodate the text being set, and 2) neighboring line-heights that bear a relationship to each other. **Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-22 21:25 UTC

Where there *are* font-size differences, there *should* be line-height differences. Where there *are not* font-size differences, there *are not* line-height differences.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 21:27 UTC

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-01-22 21:35 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-25 19:52 UTC

This third feature is I think meant to represent spacing between paragraphs (or between a paragraph and a bulleted list), which is an independent property from line-height. I'm not sure that we actually will have a reason to make this customizable. Right now, we have code like this in `rendered_markdown.css`:

```
    /* The default top/bottom margins for paragraphs are small, to make sure                            
       they look nice next to blockquotes, lists, etc. */                                               
    & p {                                                                                               
        margin: 3px 0;                                                                                  
    }                                                                                                   
                                                                                                        
    /* The spacing between two paragraphs is significantly larger.  We                                  
       arrange things so that this spacing matches the spacing between                                  
       paragraphs in two consecutive 1-line messages. */                                                
    & p + p {                                                                                           
        margin-top: 10px;                                                                               
    }                                                                                                   
```

So I think the claim is such a setting would facilitate some logic that given the font size, line-height and this other spacing setting and computes what those values are. I am not entirely sure we need that to be a setting, but it is an independent variable. We do probably need it to be a setting in development, just because the values we use in the redesign with larger fonts may be different from the values we use in `main`, and it'll be nice to be able to do PRs that make the new thing work but avoid having to think about whether we're changing the existing/default UI in a problematic way during development.

I propose using the `dense_mode` setting that we introduced a long time ago for storing that information; the default of `true` is the legacy design, and `false` would be what we're transitioning to.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-25 19:52 UTC

So effectively we'd just have "Compact" (legacy) and "Default" (future) as the initial possible values of that, which seems probably good enough for developing a new "Default".

## typescript: marked

*2024-01-20 to 2024-01-22 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/typescript.3A.20marked/with/1723136)*

**Evy** · 2024-01-20 19:11 UTC

I'm working on creating a typescript stub for `web/third/marked/lib/marked`, in parallel with migrating the `markdown` module, and have made a decent amount of progress.

One thing I haven't figured out is how to import the stub and code properly in `markdown.ts`. How does the import work to get both the `web/third/marked/lib/marked` file and the new stub? Maybe I should be putting the stub in a different place?

PR is here for reference: #28652

**Lalit** · 2024-01-21 04:14 UTC

Hi Evy :wave: ,
I looked at your PR it is looking good, I have raised a PR on your fork: [Refactor marked.js Stubs](https://github.com/evykassirer/zulip/pull/7) correcting the placement of your declaration file and fixed some type definitions as well.

So basically `web/third/marked/lib/marked` module is part of our source code so treat it like it is a module written inside `src` directory and not an external module installed in `node_modules`.
And while writing a declaration file for a source module you have to make sure that it is in the same directory as your `.js` file and the name of the declaration file is also same as the corresponding javascript file.

**Lalit** · 2024-01-21 04:20 UTC

And the syntax `declare module "module"` will also not work here since again `third/marked/lib/marked` is not an external module. You just need to directly export your types from the declaration file.
You can see how I did this for `css_variables` module [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/web/src/css_variables.d.ts).

## Input pill code optimization

*2024-01-25 to 2024-01-26 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Input.20pill.20code.20optimization/with/1725827)*

**Dhruv Chouhan (ecxtacy)** · 2024-01-25 12:44 UTC

Working with input pills, I observed the `removePill()` function in `input_pills` module.
```ts
// this searches given the DOM node for a pill, removes the node
// from the DOM, removes it from the array and returns it.
// this would generally be used for DOM-provoked actions, such as a user
// clicking on a pill to remove it.
removePill(element: HTMLElement) {
    let idx: number | undefined;
        for (let x = 0; x < store.pills.length; x += 1) {
            if (store.pills[x].$element[0] === element) {
                idx = x;
            }
        }
    // ...............
    // ..............
}
```

We could just add the `break` statement once we find out the pill we have to remove.

```ts
        for (let x = 0; x < store.pills.length; x += 1) {
            if (store.pills[x].$element[0] === element) {
                idx = x;
                break;
            }
        }
```

Although its a small change but I think might provide some optimization. 
I want to know if its reasonable to do so.

**Notification Bot** · 2024-01-25 12:46 UTC

This topic was moved here from #**general>Input pill code optimization** by @Lauryn Menard.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-25 18:36 UTC

That is probably clearer code. I kinda suspect that code could be written better another way, but I don't want to spend time thinking about that right now. Feel free to add a commit to whatever you're working on with that improvement.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-25 19:16 UTC

A clearer solution is

```js
const idx = store.pills.findIndex((pill) => pill.$element[0] === element);
```

(returns `-1` if not found rather than `undefined`).

**Dhruv Chouhan (ecxtacy)** · 2024-01-26 02:06 UTC

Yeah ! Thanks :big_smile:

export function set_message_booleans(raw_message: RawMessage & Partial<FlagStatus>): void {

Cross-posting the more frontend-y part of this set of questions in design -- when using `Intl.NumberFormat`, what's the way to properly internationalize it and have the correct locale passed in?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-02-09 20:00 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-09 20:24 UTC

We might also need a polyfill for older browsers; worth checking (I remember that being an issue for `Intl.ListFormat`)

**Evy** · 2024-02-09 20:37 UTC

Ah yes here:

```js
// Formats an array of strings as a Internationalized list using the specified language.
export function format_array_as_list(
    array: string[],
    style: Intl.ListFormatStyle,
    type: Intl.ListFormatType,
): string {
    // If Intl.ListFormat is not supported
    if (Intl.ListFormat === undefined) {
        return array.join(", ");
    }

    // Use Intl.ListFormat to format the array as a Internationalized list.
    const list_formatter = new Intl.ListFormat(user_settings.default_language, {style, type});

    // Return the formatted string.
    return list_formatter.format(array);
}
```

So would we want to fall back to the previous logic for the rounding if `Intl.NumberFormat` isn't supported?

That's an old issue, and this is not the way we should be doing things. **Kislay Udbhav Verma** · 2024-02-29 04:39 UTC

In the review, @Tim Abbott pointed out that the algorithm I am using to split the messages is not quite clear. Let me elaborate on it.

* Previously there was a function `send_message` in `compose.js` which would generate a request object from the compose state content and then attempt to send it.
* I thought the simplest way to send split messages would be to create an intermediary function, which, depending on whether the option is enabled or not, would split the message and call `send_message` with each part - keeping in mind that the next call should only be after the current message is successfully sent.
* I renamed `send_message` to `send_individual_message` and then defined `send_message` as:
```
export function send_message() {
    if (!will_split_into_multiple_messages()) {
        send_individual_message();
        return;
    }
    let current_part_index=-1;
    let split_parts = message_content_split_parts();
    // start the message sending chain
    send_next_message(true);

    /**
     * @param {boolean} success whether previous message was successfully sent
     */
    function send_next_message(success) {
        if (!success) {
            const remaining_message_content = split_parts.slice(current_part_index)
                .join(SPLIT_DELIMITER);
            const $text_area = $("textarea#compose-textarea");
            $text_area.val(remaining_message_content).trigger("focus");
            compose_ui.autosize_textarea($text_area);
            update_split_messages_info_banner();
            return;
        }
        current_part_index++;
        if (!split_parts[current_part_index]) {
            // end the message sending chain
            update_split_messages_info_banner();
            return;
        }
        const req = create_message_object(split_parts[current_part_index]);
        // when the message is going to be split, there won't be any local echo 
        // and all unsent messages will remain in the compose box in case of any error
        send_individual_message(req, send_next_message, false);
    }
}
```

The callback inside is responsible for the actual logic flow: if the previous message was successful, it calls `send_individual_message` with the next part of the message, which it has access to by capturing the array `split_parts` from its parent scope.
In case of an error, the callback will restore the remaining content into the compose box.
The variable `current_part_index` keeps track of what portions of the message are already sent.

I've added some parameters to the `send_individual_message` (previously `send_message`) function:

```
function send_individual_message(
    request = create_message_object(),
    next_message_send_callback = () => {},
    try_local_echo = true,
) {
```
* request: same as earlier
* next_message_send_callback: It is invoked after an attempt is made to send the current part of the message.
* try_local_echo: Because as discussed earlier, we don't wish the split parts of a message be locally echoed.


I've examined some error cases with this, like turning the server off amidst sending the message parts.
It behaved as it should: Restored the unsent part of the message.

**Kislay Udbhav Verma** · 2024-03-02 09:07 UTC

Hmm, I have done away with callbacks entirely and implemented these suggestions.
I reverted to the original definition of `send_message`, and added a few things-
```
export function send_message(
    message_content = compose_state.message_content(),
    split_messages = is_split_messages_enabled(),
) {
    const [content_to_send, rest_of_the_content] = split_message(
        message_content,
        split_messages,
    );
    if(!content_to_send){
        return;
    }
    const request = create_message_object(content_to_send);
    ...
```

The splitting logic is handled by the function `split_message`, which returns two strings: the first one being the part of the message which will be sent in the current recursive call, and the second one being the remaining part. If the option to split is disabled, the function just returns the entire message_content as `content_to_send`, and the logic takes its normal course (sending only one message).

The `split_message` is recursively called on the success callback of current message part. To handle errors, I have defined a function `set_compose_state` which restores the unsent message part and also handles the visibility of `split_messages_info_banner`.

```
function set_compose_state(content) {
    const $text_area = $("textarea#compose-textarea");
    $text_area.val(content).trigger("focus");
    compose_ui.autosize_textarea($text_area);
    update_split_messages_info_banner();
}
```

When splitting the message parts, there are a few cases to be taken care of, due to which the function seems a bit bloated.
```
/**
 * 
 * @param {string} message_content the content to be split
 * @param {boolean} split_messages whether the option is enabled
 * @returns a pair of strings: the first being the individual split message, the second being the
 * remaining part of the message, which will be undefined when there are no further parts 
 * to send
 */
function split_message(message_content, split_messages) {
    if(!split_messages){
        return [message_content];
    }
    if(!message_content){
        return [""];
    }
    const index= message_content.indexOf(SPLIT_DELIMITER);
    if(index == -1) {
        return [message_content]
    }
    const parts = [message_content.slice(0,index),message_content.slice(index+SPLIT_DELIMITER.length)]
    if(!parts[0]){
        // there are too many "\n\n\n" sequences, so some parts are empty strings
        return split_message(parts[1],true);
    }
    return parts;
}
```

I'd say it is a significant improvement over the previous implementation, as the code now seems more cohesive, and there's no passing around of callbacks, and fewer default arguments. I'll see if  I can further simplify it.

**Kislay Udbhav Verma** · 2025-05-14 07:53 UTC

In a [review comment](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/28974#issuecomment-2816242602), it was noted that:

>This feature doesn't seem to interact correctly with the message length limit. That should be checking the length of each message, not the entire contents of the compose box.

This means that if the message length is 1000, and we've used delimiters to split the message into 4 parts, then the max. total text length in the compose box can be 4000.

This didn't seem to me to be one of the goals of the feature. Reading around #**design>splitting long compositions@1638632** I gather that the primary purpose is to be able to access smaller parts of the message which are easier to digest, react to, etc - meaning that as long as the message is in the compose box, it is still seen as *one* single message.

 As such, the message length limit should not be imposed for each individual message fragment.

I'd like to hear others' opinions on this though.

**Alya Abbott** · 2025-05-14 15:48 UTC

What are the goals of the message length limit? I dunno about the technical side, but from the user perspective, I think it's because super long messages make the reading experience more awkward.

**Alya Abbott** · 2025-05-14 15:49 UTC

If that's the motivation, then what matters is how long the sent messages are (as @Tim Abbott suggested), not how long the compose box content was.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-05-15 23:13 UTC

There are two goals of the 10K character limit:
- Preventing extremely long messages -- the UI may not handle those perfectly. 
- Managing DoS risk -- the total amount of Markdown you can make the server process and the size of the largest document are both relevant for DoS, and limiting maximum request size helps here. Ultimately this part would probably be better server by a rate limit that's more structured around the total number of characters you can ask the server to process or some similar fancier metric. But it is helpful for now.

**Kislay Udbhav Verma** · 2025-05-16 07:12 UTC

In that case, it doesn't make sense to set such a high limit on individual split message fragments since this feature tries to **split** a message that could have grown to be near the length limit into smaller chunks. If a fragment can grow as long as an unsplit message, then it might as well be a separate message.

It would only be relevant in an extreme case, say, if the user wishes to enter text 40k characters long and send it as chunks, in which case, we complain that each individual chunk should not exceed 10k characters (the overall message length limit).
Typing out so much text isn't practical, and we're already working on #33107 to put long pasted text in a file.

I therefore think we should only care about the text length of all fragments summed together. This better reflects the idea of sending one single very long message into smaller pieces.

This is based on my understanding of the issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-05-16 18:22 UTC

It's fairly practical to write more than 10k characters of text if you include pasting a few blocks of reference material. And we'll want to do #33107 thoughtfully where it's still possible to paste things when using this feature. (Possibly #33107 just is turned off when using this feature, so you can write your drafts elsewhere and then paste them into Zulip? Not sure).

**Alya Abbott** · 2025-05-28 18:29 UTC

> * Preventing extremely long messages -- the UI may not handle those perfectly.

This lines up with having the limit apply to each individual message that gets sent, right?

## Code improvement in `DropdownWidget`.

*2024-02-23 to 2024-02-24 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/Code.20improvement.20in.20.60DropdownWidget.60.2E/with/1743720)*

**Dhruv Chouhan (ecxtacy)** · 2024-02-23 10:08 UTC

While working with `DropdownWidget`, in its `setup()` function we have
```js
        const delegate_container = this.$events_container.get(0);
        if (!delegate_container) {
            blueslip.error(
                "Cannot initialize dropdown. `$events_container` empty.",
                this.$events_container,
            );
        }
```
This basically just checks if the `$events_container` we provided in the constructor is empty or not. I think its better to write something like.
```js
if(this.$events_container.length === 0) {
    blueslip.error(
                "Cannot initialize dropdown. `$events_container` empty.",
                this.$events_container,
            );
}
```

Okay. I am not sure this has any impact on the performance or readability though.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-23 17:45 UTC

Yeah I am not sure it's better at all, since then one needs to still compute `delegate_container` just afterwards in order to use it.

**Dhruv Chouhan (ecxtacy)** · 2024-02-24 04:01 UTC

Yeah, thanks for the analysis. :big_smile:

}

*2024-02-29 to 2024-03-08 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/6-frontend/topic/id.20attributes.20for.20incoming.20webhook.20events/with/1748439)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2024-02-29 15:18 UTC

In #28294, I've been working with @Sujal Shah🦚 to implement adding the `only_events` parameter in the modal for generating a URL for an incoming webhook bot; see GitHub issue [#27628](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/27628).

We noticed that some events are formatted with spaces, for example here are some of the events for the [GitLab integration](https://zulip.com/integrations/doc/gitlab):
`Push Hook`, `Tag Push Hook`, `Test Hook`, `Issue Hook open`, `Issue Hook close`, `Issue Hook reopen`, `Issue Hook update`, `Confidential Issue Hook open`, `Confidential Issue Hook close`

Originally, #28294 used the event string as the `id` for the event checkbox input that was created, but since [the id attribute](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Global_attributes/id) should not contain any white-space, that was removed.

Currently, the PR just adds the events options as checkboxes without any `id` attribute set. This means that the checkbox must be directly clicked on to be checked/unchecked. Normally, in our modals, one can click on the label to check/uncheck a checkbox.

I wanted to check in here to see if folks had thoughts on not setting the `id` attribute or if we should create an `id` based on the event string for the integration that removes any whitespace.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-29 20:29 UTC

It seems to me like translating those event names to use dashes would be fine.
